21.x: Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, subject to the constitutional and judicial limitations. Article 31A concerns estate acquisition and agrarian reform, Article 31B concerns Ninth Schedule laws, and Article 350B creates the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
21.tq: Check each Article against its precise subject and identify the only correctly matched pair.
xs: **Art. 31C — laws implementing Art. 39(b), (c)** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Art. 31C** saves such laws from **Arts. 14, 19**; it was inserted by the **25th Amendment, 1971**.
Option 1 is wrong: estates and agrarian reform belong to **Art. 31A**. Option 2 is wrong: the **Ninth Schedule** goes with **Art. 31B**.
xa: **Art. 31A** saves laws on acquisition of estates, agrarian reform from **Arts. 14, 19** — inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951**.
The **Ninth Schedule** was created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**.
⚠ Kesavananda struck down the part of **Art. 31C** that barred courts from questioning a law declared to give effect to DPSP.

21.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court?
o: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
Article 31C primacy, prospective overruling and colourable legislation
Unlimited amending power, territorial nexus and harmonious construction
21.x: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines. Article 31C primacy, Article 13(4) and unlimited amending power were created through constitutional amendments, while prospective overruling originated in Golaknath.
21.tq: Eliminate sets containing a Parliament-created amendment rule or a separately identified doctrine.
xs: **Eclipse, severability and pith and substance** are all Supreme Court-made doctrines — option **(1)**.
**Art. 31C primacy** came from Parliament's **25th Amendment (1971)**; **unlimited amending power** from the **42nd Amendment**.
So options 2, 3 and 4 each mix in a **Parliament**-made rule.
xa: Other judge-made doctrines: **colourable legislation**, **harmonious construction**, **territorial nexus**.
**Prospective overruling**: Supreme Court — **Golaknath (1967)**.
**Basic structure**: Supreme Court — **Kesavananda (1973)**.

21.s: In Kesavananda Bharati, which part of Article 31C was struck down as violating the basic structure?
o: The provision giving effect to any Directive Principle an absolute priority over the Constitution
The provision creating the Ninth Schedule
The provision enabling Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights
The provision barring courts from questioning whether a law gives effect to the Directive Principles
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati struck down the part of Article 31C that barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to a Directive Principle. Judicial review was held to be part of the basic structure.
21.tq: Identify the precise judicial-review restriction rather than confusing it with the general objective of Article 31C.
xs: Kesavananda struck down the part **barring courts from questioning** whether a law gives effect to the **Directive Principles** — option **(4)**.
Reason: **judicial review is basic**.
The **Ninth Schedule** came from the **1st Amendment** with **Art. 31B**, not Art. 31C; the power to amend FRs was **upheld** (24th Amendment).
xa: **Art. 31C** was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)** for **Art. 39(b), (c)** laws.
The **42nd** widened it; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck the widened form down.
Art. 31C = DPSP primacy — a **Parliament**-made rule, not a judge-made doctrine.

21.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court of India in which case?
21.x: Prospective overruling is a judge-made doctrine that the Supreme Court first applied in Golaknath (1967). Kesavananda (1973) propounded the basic structure; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art. 368(4),(5); Shankari Prasad (1951) upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs.
21.tq: Golaknath = prospective overruling + FRs transcendental.
xs: **Prospective overruling** was first applied by the Supreme Court in **Golaknath (1967)** — option **(2)**.
It is a **judge-made** doctrine, like eclipse, severability and pith and substance.
**Kesavananda (1973)** propounded the **basic structure**; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)**; **Shankari Prasad (1951)** held Art. 368 includes power to amend FRs.
xa: Golaknath: FRs **"transcendental and immutable"**; an amendment **is** "law" under **Art. 13**.
Bench: **11 judges, 6:5**; it challenged the **17th Amendment**.
Parliament's reply: the **24th Amendment (1971)**, amending **Arts. 13 and 368**.

21.s: The basic structure doctrine primarily rests on which constitutional principle?
o: Supremacy of Parliament over the Constitution
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
Supremacy of conventions over written provisions
Supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts
21.x: The doctrine rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of courts to review constitutional amendments against its basic features.
21.tq: Test the underlying constitutional principle rather than the name of the doctrine.
xs: The doctrine rests on the **supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts** — option **(4)**.
The judicial review principle **accepts the theory of supremacy of Courts** = supremacy of the **Constitution and the courts** over Parliament (APPSC-G2 2017 key).
As a limit, basic structure means supremacy of the **Constitution**, not of **Parliament** — so option 1 is the reverse.
xa: Indian Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**.
**Judicial review** is itself basic, so it **cannot be removed even by amendment**.
The doctrine keeps **Art. 368** limited.

21.s:
Assertion (A): The basic structure doctrine has been criticised as judicial rewriting of the Constitution.
Reason (R): The doctrine has no explicit textual definition and its content is developed by unelected judges case by case.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
21.x: Both statements are true. The absence of a textual definition and the open-ended judicial development of the doctrine form the basis of this criticism.
21.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the criticism stated in the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
A is true: critics call the doctrine a "**rewriting of the Constitution**" by **unelected judges**.
R is true and explains A: it has **no textual basis** and its **list is open-ended**, so its content is uncertain.
xa: Critics also call it "**judicial supremacy**"; it is described as **vague and unlisted**.
Defence: it is among the **biggest contributions of the Indian judiciary** to constitutionalism.
Supporters call it the Constitution's **shield against majorities**.

21.s: The restriction imposed by the 42nd Amendment on High Courts’ power to review central laws was removed by the:
21.x: The 42nd Amendment attempted to bar High Courts from reviewing central laws, and the 43rd Amendment Act, 1977 removed that restriction.
21.tq: Use the amendment sequence to identify the restoring constitutional change.
xs: The **43rd Amendment Act, 1977** removed the bar — option **(2)**.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** had barred High Courts from declaring central laws invalid; after the 43rd, **High Courts can** do so.
xa: **Constitutional amendments can** also be challenged on **basic structure** grounds.
⚠ Trap: both "cannot" statements are false (**UPSC 2019**).
The **42nd Amendment**'s Art. 368(4), (5) and widened Art. 31C were struck down in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

21.s: Which of the following statements regarding the debate on the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, is correct?
o: The Supreme Court struck down the Bill for violating judicial independence.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated before the JPC that the Bill did not violate the basic structure, while U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised doubts.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated that simultaneous polls necessarily violate the basic structure.
Former CJIs U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna rejected all basic-structure concerns about simultaneous polls.
21.x: B.R. Gavai told the Joint Parliamentary Committee that the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, did not violate the basic structure, whereas former Chief Justices U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised basic-structure doubts.
21.tq: Match each public position with the correct constitutional office-holder.
xs: Ex-CJI **B.R. Gavai** told the **JPC** the **129th Amendment Bill, 2024** does **not** violate basic structure, while **U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna** raised doubts — option **(2)**.
The Bill concerns **simultaneous polls**; it has not been struck down by the Supreme Court.
Options 3 and 4 reverse the views of Gavai and of Lalit and Khanna.
xa: Basic structure = what **cannot be amended** under **Art. 368**.
**Free and fair elections** and **federalism** are among the listed basic features.
Critics call the doctrine **vague and unlisted**, even "**judicial supremacy**".

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Judicial Review is an inherent power of constitutional courts.
II. Judicial Review examines legislative enactments and executive actions for constitutional validity.
III. Basic structural features may be destroyed through Article 368.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x: I and II are correct: judicial review is an inherent power of constitutional courts to test laws and executive action. III is false because the basic structure cannot be destroyed even under Article 368.
21.tq: Find the statement that contradicts the Basic Structure Doctrine.
n: Judicial Review is an inherent power of constitutional courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Judicial Review examines legislative enactments against constitutional validity. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Judicial Review examines executive actions against constitutional validity. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Core structural features of the Constitution cannot be abrogated or destroyed even through Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — so option **(1) I and II only** is correct.
I and II: **Judicial Review** is an **inherent power** of constitutional courts to examine **legislative enactments** and **executive actions**.
III is wrong: per **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, core features **cannot be abrogated or destroyed**, even through **Article 368**.
xa: ⚠ Basic Structure is **not** defined in **Part XX** — it is **judge-made**.
The idea came from **Germany** (Basic Law); jurist **Dietrich Conrad** argued for **implied limits**.
First applied in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: cut-off date **24 April 1973**.

21.s: Which one of the following most accurately describes the basic structure doctrine?
o: The Supreme Court alone may amend the Constitution when required
Only the Preamble can be amended subject to judicial approval
Parliament may amend every constitutional provision without limitation
Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage or destroy its core features
21.x: The doctrine permits amendment of any part of the Constitution under Article 368, but prohibits alteration, damage or destruction of features that give the Constitution its identity.
21.tq: Choose the precise statement distinguishing the amending power from its constitutional limitation.
xs: Under the basic structure doctrine, **Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage or destroy its core features** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 368** lets Parliament amend any part, including **Fundamental Rights** and the **Preamble**, so "every provision without limitation" (option 3) ignores the limit.
The power to amend lies with **Parliament**, not the Supreme Court; and the doctrine is not about "the Preamble alone".
xa: Basic structure = what **cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Art. 368** (APPSC-G1 2018 key).
The idea was borrowed from **Germany** (Basic Law) and propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)**.
⚠ PYQ 2024 key: "**core features cannot be amended or altered by Parliament**".

21.s: Which of the following best describes the present position on the Preamble?
o: It is part of the Constitution and amendable, subject to the basic structure
It is not a part of the Constitution
It is part of the Constitution but cannot be amended at all
It alone constitutes the basic structure
21.x: The Preamble is part of the Constitution and amendable subject to the basic structure doctrine, which is not confined to the Preamble.
xa: **PYQ G1 2018**: the Preamble's objectives embody the basic structure, so they "**cannot be amended**" under Art. 368.
The word **'secular'** entered the Preamble by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**, yet secularism was basic even before.
Basic structure is **judge-made**, first propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.

21.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about secularism and the basic structure?
o: Secularism was recognised as a basic feature even before the word was put in the Preamble
The word 'secular' was inserted into the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
Secularism became a basic feature only because of its textual insertion in 1976
S.R. Bommai held secularism to be part of the basic structure
21.x: Secularism was treated as a basic feature even before the 42nd Amendment added the word 'secular' to the Preamble.
xa: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** reaffirmed **secularism**, with **federalism**.
Bommai was a **nine-judge bench** (APPSC-G2 2008 key).

21.s: The Supreme Court of India has propounded the ‘Doctrine of Basic Structure’ of the Constitution in which of the following cases?
21.x: The doctrine of the basic structure of the Constitution owes its evolution to the majority judgment of the Supreme Court in the landmark case, Keshvananda Bharati Vs. State of Kerala (1973), which was approved in Minerva Mills Vs. Union of India (1980) case.

21.s: Which one of the following cases outlined the basic structure doctrine of the Indian Constitution?
Which one of the following cases propounded the concept of ‘Basic structure’ of the Indian Constitution?
The Supreme Court of India enunciated the doctrine of ‘Basic Structure of the Constitution’ in
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Free and fair elections — Minerva Mills
High Court powers under Articles 226 and 227 — S.R. Bommai
21.x: B is correct: Indra Sawhney (1992) is listed for the principle of equality. Free and fair elections go with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (and Kuldip Nayar), not Minerva Mills; HC powers under Arts. 226-227 with L. Chandra Kumar (1997), not S.R. Bommai; independent judiciary with All India Judges Association and the NJAC case, not Waman Rao.
21.tq: Use the case-specific association and watch for swapped case names.
xs: **Principle of equality — Indra Sawhney** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**Free and fair elections** go with **Raj Narain (1975)** and **Kuldip Nayar (2006)**, not Minerva Mills.
**HC powers under Arts. 226, 227** go with **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**, not S.R. Bommai; **independent judiciary** with **All India Judges Association** and **NJAC**, not Waman Rao.
xa: **Indra Sawhney (1992)** is also cited for **rule of law**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: **secularism** and **federalism**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: Ninth Schedule cut-off **24 April 1973**.

21.s: The source of the ‘Basic Structure Theory of the Constitution’ in India is
21.x: The Parliament could not use its amending powers under Article 368 to ‘damage,’ destroy,’ ‘abrogate,’ change’ or alter the ‘basic structure’ or framework of the Constitution. The view expressed in the Keshavananda Bharati Case was subsequently approved in the Minerva Mills' Case, 1980.

21.s: The basic structure theory of the Constitution of India implies that –
o: Certain features of the Constitution are so essential to
Fundamental rights cannot be abridged or taken away
The Constitution cannot be amended except in
The Preamble of the Constitution cannot be amended
21.x: The basic structure theory of the Constitution of India implies that certain features of the Constitution are so essential to it that they cannot be abrogated. The Supreme Court made it clear in its judgment in the case of Keshavananda Bharati Vs State of Kerala, 1973, that there are certain basic features of the Constitution which cannot be amended in any case.

21.s: Coelho case is related to which Schedule of the Constitution of India?
21.x: The Coelho case is a landmark case which upheld the authority of the Judiciary to review laws - including those under the 9th schedule - against violation of the Basic structure of the constitution. It is also known as the 9th schedule case.

22.s: Which one of the following propositions was laid down in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India?
o: Procedure established by law need not satisfy standards of fairness.
The right to life includes a life with dignity and the procedure under Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable.
The right to travel abroad is exclusively a statutory right.
22.x: Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 protects more than mere existence, includes dignity and travel abroad, and requires a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable. This interpretation also binds the legislature.
22.tq: Distinguish the expanded constitutional meaning from the narrow pre-Maneka interpretation of Article 21.
xs: Maneka Gandhi held the right to life includes a life **with dignity** and Art. 21 procedure must be **just, fair and reasonable** — option **(3)**.
Art. 21 is **not mere existence** (option 1 wrong), and it covers the **right to travel abroad** (option 4 wrong).
The fairness standard **now binds the legislature too** — so option 2 is wrong.
xa: The case arose from **passport impounding** in **1978**.
Decided by a **7-judge** bench.
⚠ **ADM Jabalpur (1976)**: FRs incl. Art. 21 **unenforceable in Emergency** — the "darkest day", effectively overruled.

22.s: Which statement correctly describes ADM Jabalpur (1976)?
o: It struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act.
It held that Fundamental Rights, including Article 21, were unenforceable during Emergency.
It held that Article 21 remained fully enforceable during Emergency.
It established privacy as a fundamental right.
22.x: ADM Jabalpur held that Fundamental Rights, including Article 21, could not be enforced during the Emergency. The reasoning was later effectively overruled and rejected in Puttaswamy.
22.tq: Discriminate between a discredited earlier ruling and the later judgment that rejected it.
xs: **ADM Jabalpur (1976)** held **FRs incl. Art. 21 unenforceable in Emergency** — option **(2)**.
It is called the "**darkest day**" and has been **effectively overruled**; **Puttaswamy** rejected its reasoning.
**Sec. 66A** fell in **Shreya Singhal (2015)**; privacy came in **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
xa: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: Art. 21 procedure must be **fair, just and reasonable**.
**Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)**: **bail is the rule** even under the **UAPA**.
Puttaswamy: **nine judges**, CJI **J.S. Khehar**.

22.s: Which one of the following cases is associated with the compulsory registration of marriages?
o: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
22.x: In Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006), the Supreme Court directed compulsory registration of marriages.
22.tq: Match the social reform direction with the correct judgment.
xs: **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)** directed **compulsory registration of marriages** — option **(1)**.
**Vishaka** = workplace harassment; **Shayara Bano** = triple talaq; **Prem Shankar Shukla** = handcuffing.
xa: **Arts. 32, 141, 142** let judgments like **Vishaka, Seema** fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts.
**D.K. Basu (1997)**: arrest memo, informing kin, medical checks.
**Lalita Kumari (2013)**: **FIR mandatory** for cognizable offences.

22.s: The Supreme Court judgment concerning handcuffing only in exceptional cases is associated with:
o: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
22.x: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980) held that handcuffing should be confined to exceptional cases.
22.tq: Recall the specific liberty-related holding attached to the case.
xs: **Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980)** — **handcuffing only in exceptional cases** — option **(2)**.
**Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)** is about **bail** being the rule under the **UAPA**.
xa: **D.K. Basu (1997)**: arrest memo, informing kin, medical checks.
**Lalita Kumari (2013)**: FIR mandatory (**Sec. 173 BNSS**).
**Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**: compulsory registration of marriages.

22.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: A.K. Gopalan gave a narrow interpretation of Article 21.
Berubari Union held that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
S.R. Bommai laid guidelines against arbitrary misuse of Article 356.
Champakam Dorairajan held that Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs in case of conflict.
22.x: Option B is incorrect: Berubari Union (1960) held that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution. Kesavananda Bharati later held that it is.
22.tq: Discriminate Berubari (not part) from Kesavananda (part).
n: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras gave Article 21 a narrow interpretation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Berubari Union Case held that the Preamble is not an integral part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India laid down guidelines against arbitrary misuse of Article 356. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Champakam Dorairajan held that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles of State Policy in case of conflict. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Berubari Union** held the **Preamble** an integral part — option **(2)**.
**Berubari Union (1960)** held the Preamble **not** an integral part; overturned by **Kesavananda Bharati** and **S.R. Bommai**.
**A.K. Gopalan** gave a **narrow** reading of **Article 21**; **S.R. Bommai** set guidelines on **Article 356**; **Champakam** held FRs **prevail over** DPSP.
xa: **Berubari** is linked to **Article 3** and the Preamble.
**Champakam (1951)** led to the **First Amendment, 1951** and **Article 15(4)**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** was a **Nine-judge** bench.

22.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: P. Sambamurthy – 52nd Amendment and the Tenth Schedule
Champakam Dorairajan – Fundamental Rights prevailing over DPSPs
A.K. Gopalan – Preventive detention and procedure established by law
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain – Judicial scrutiny of high constitutional elections
22.x: P. Sambamurthy concerned judicial review and special provisions for Andhra Pradesh; the Tenth Schedule case is Kihoto Hollohan.
n: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras focused on “procedure established by law”. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras concerned preventive detention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Champakam Dorairajan held that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles of State Policy in case of conflict. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
The struck-down parts of the 39th Amendment barred judicial review of election disputes involving the Prime Minister and the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
P. Sambamurthy v. State of A.P. concerned judicial review. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
P. Sambamurthy v. State of A.P. concerned special provisions for Andhra Pradesh. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xa: **P. Sambamurthy (1987)** struck down portions of the **32nd Amendment**.
**Raj Narain (1975)** held **free and fair elections** part of the Basic Structure.
**A.K. Gopalan** was decided in **1950**.

22.s: Which case established the ‘golden triangle’ involving Articles 14, 19 and 21?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
22.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) held that Articles 14, 19 and 21 work together, the 'golden triangle', so any law affecting liberty must satisfy all three.
22.tq: Recall the case behind the golden triangle.
n: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India established the golden triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Articles 14, 19, and 21 are mutually inclusive under the golden triangle doctrine. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xs: The **golden triangle** comes from **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India** — option **(1)**.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)** linked **Articles 14, 19 and 21** as mutually inclusive.
Procedure must be **just, fair and reasonable**; it **widened** Article 21 incl. the **right to travel abroad**.
**A.K. Gopalan** read Art. 21 **narrowly**; **S.R. Bommai** dealt with **Article 356**.
xa: Maneka was about **passport impounding** and a life **with human dignity**.
Maneka was a **7 judges** bench.
**ADM Jabalpur (1976)**: FRs incl. Art. 21 unenforceable in Emergency — the "darkest day".

22.s: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain is linked to which Constitutional Amendment?
22.x: Raj Narain concerned the 39th Amendment; Sambamurthy the 32nd, Kihoto Hollohan the 52nd and Champakam led to the 1st.
n: Champakam Dorairajan directly led to the First Constitutional Amendment, 1951. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
The 32nd Amendment was associated with special provisions for Andhra Pradesh. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
The 52nd Amendment was associated with the Anti-Defection Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
The 39th Amendment was associated with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xa: The **39th** was later nullified by the **44th**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992–93)**: the **Speaker's** ruling is subject to **judicial review**.

22.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about cases on the Preamble?
o: Kesavananda Bharati held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution
The Berubari Union case held that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution
S.R. Bommai held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution
Golaknath was about the amending power
22.x: Berubari held the opposite, that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution.
n: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala recognized the Preamble as part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Berubari Union Case held that the Preamble is not an integral part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India reaffirmed the Preamble as an integral part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xa: **Berubari** is linked to **Article 3**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** also held **secularism** and **federalism** basic features.
**Bommai** was a **Nine-judge** bench.

22.s: In which year was the Berubari Union case decided?
22.x: Berubari was 1960, after A.K. Gopalan (1950) and Shankari Prasad (1951) and before Sajjan Singh (1965).
n: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India was decided in 1951. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan was decided in 1965. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras was decided in 1950. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Berubari Union Case was decided in 1960. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras preceded Shankari Prasad v. Union of India chronologically. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India preceded Champakam Dorairajan chronologically. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Champakam Dorairajan preceded Berubari Union Case chronologically. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Berubari Union Case preceded Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan chronologically. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xa: After Sajjan Singh: **Golaknath** → **Kesavananda Bharati** → **Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain**.
Then **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** → **Minerva Mills (1980)** → **Kihoto Hollohan** → **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
**Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** sits between **Shankari Prasad** and **Berubari**.

22.s: The 39th Constitutional Amendment was nullified by which Amendment?
22.x: The 44th Amendment (1978) undid the 39th Amendment's changes. The 42nd (1976) was the Emergency-era amendment, and the 52nd added the anti-defection law.
22.tq: Recall that the 44th Amendment undid the Emergency amendments.
n: The 39th Amendment was nullified by the 44th Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xs: The **39th Amendment** was nullified by the **44th Amendment** — option **(4)**.

22.s: 'Right to Privacy' is protected under which Article of the Constitution of India?

Initially assigned to a Five-Judge Bench, the matter was later referred to a Nine-Judge Bench. In a landmark decision on August 24, 2017, the Bench unanimously recognised the fundamental right to privacy for every individual, as Indian Polity: Constitutional Framework PMF IAS IP – 11 guaranteed by the Constitution, specifically within Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty) and Part III as a whole. The right to privacy is also enshrined in Article 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which India is a party.

22.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Statement-I: The Supreme Court of India has held in some judgements that the reservation policies made under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India would be limited by Article 335 for maintenance of efficiency of administration.
2. Statement-II: Article 335 of the Constitution of India defines the term 'efficiency of administration'. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is the correct
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is not the correct
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
22.x: Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect: The Supreme Court of India has consistently referred to the notions of "efficiency" and "merit" while adjudicating the validity of various reservation policies. The Court has held in several judgments — Indra Sawhney v Union of India 1993; M Nagaraj v Union of India 2006 — that the reservation policies made under Article 16 (4) of the Constitution would be limited by Article 335, which provides for "maintenance of efficiency of administration," while considering the claims of the Scheduled Castes (SCs) and the Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the making of appointments to public services and posts. This was done while the Constitution does not define the term "efficiency of administration. "This gap in interpretation was filled by a twojudge bench in the B K Pavitra (II) v Union of India (2019), as it held that "efficiency of adminis­tration in the affairs of the union or of a state must be defined in an inclusive sense, where diverse segments of society find representation as a true aspiration of governance by and for the people." Indian Polity: Organs of the State PMF IAS IP – 83 PMF Concept Hack: Statement II is clearly wrong because the Constitution often mentions concepts without clearly defining them. Article 335 refers to "efficiency of administration" but does not define it. Hence, Statement II is incorrect, making option (c) the correct answer.

23.tq: Select the interpretation that preserves both apparently conflicting provisions.
xs: **Harmonious construction**: read conflicting provisions so **both operate** — option **(2)**.
Its field: **FR vs DPSP**; provision vs provision — so it does not make one side automatically win.
xa: Case: **Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958)** — temple entry (**Art. 25(2)(b)**) reconciled with **Art. 26(b)**.
**Minerva Mills**: **FR-DPSP harmony** — "FRs are means, DPSPs the ends".
**Incidental and ancillary**: power over an entry covers matters incidental to it.

23.s: The doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers implies that:
o: An incidental matter must always be placed in the Residuary List
Parliament has no power over matters not expressly listed
A legislative entry covers matters incidental to the subject expressly assigned to it
A State legislature can legislate on every subject connected with public order
23.x: A legislative power over a subject includes powers over matters incidental and ancillary to that subject. Legislative entries are given a wide meaning for this purpose.
23.tq: Apply the main-entry rule to an ancillary matter.
xs: **Incidental and ancillary**: power over an entry **covers matters incidental to it** — option **(3)**.
Entries get the **widest meaning**.
xa: Cases: **R.D. Joshi v Ajit Mills**; **Calcutta Gas**.
Residuary power is with Parliament (**Art. 248**).
**Pith and substance**: incidental trespass is fine.

23.s: Constitutional morality is best understood as:
o: Following the opinion of the numerical majority in every case
Giving priority to customary morality over constitutional text
Fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality
Applying only the personal morality of judges
23.x: Constitutional morality requires fidelity to constitutional values, even where those values conflict with prevailing or popular morality. The phrase is associated with Ambedkar, drawing on Grote.
23.tq: Distinguish constitutional values from popular or customary morality.
xs: **Constitutional morality** = **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality** — option **(3)**.
It is not the majority's opinion or customary morality.
xa: The phrase is **Ambedkar's, after Grote**.
Applied in **Navtej Johar (2018)**, **Sabarimala (2018)**, **NCT Delhi (2018)**.
Criticism: attacked as **subjective** → route to **judicial overreach**.

23.s: The phrase “constitutional morality” is associated with B.R. Ambedkar’s reference to:
23.x: Ambedkar used the phrase constitutional morality after Grote.
23.tq: Recall the thinker linked to the phrase through Ambedkar.
xs: Ambedkar used "**constitutional morality**" **after Grote** — option **(4)**.
**Montesquieu** is linked with **separation of powers**, not this phrase.
xa: Meaning: **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality**.
Cases: **Navtej Johar**, **Sabarimala**, **NCT Delhi** (all **2018**).
⚠ Criticised as **subjective**.

23.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)?
o: It is associated with the doctrine of pith and substance
The Act only incidentally touched imports
The Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure
The Prohibition Act was struck down because it touched imports
23.x: The Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure even though it incidentally touched imports.
xa: ⚠ **1951** = **Balsara** (pith and substance); **1957** = **R.M.D.C.** and **A.S. Krishna**.
Pith and substance is borrowed from **Canada**.
It is the APPSC answer for reconciling **Central & Provincial laws** (PYQ G2 2017).

23.s:
Assertion (A): State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957) is associated with the doctrine of territorial nexus.
Reason (R): The case concerned the State's taxation of prize competitions conducted from outside the State.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
23.x: Taxing prize competitions run from outside the State needed a nexus with the State, which is why the case is associated with territorial nexus.
xa: ⚠ **1957** = **R.M.D.C.** (territorial nexus) and **A.S. Krishna** (true character).
Territorial nexus: State law valid outside the State if there is a **sufficient nexus**.
Field: **extra-territorial operation**.

23.s: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) is associated with harmonious construction in the context of reconciling:
23.x: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) reconciled temple-entry provisions under Article 25(2)(b) with the rights of religious denominations under Article 26(b).
23.tq: Start from the sure case-article pairing.
xs: **Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958)** reconciled **Articles 25(2)(b) and 26(b)** — option **(1)**.
Temple entry under **Art. 25(2)(b)** was read with **Art. 26(b)** by **harmonious construction**.
xa: Harmonious construction: read conflicting provisions so **both operate**.
**Minerva Mills** applied it to **FR-DPSP harmony**.
Order of lists: **Union > Concurrent > State**.

23.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The true character of a law is determined by examining the whole Act, its object and its effect.
2. A.S. Krishna (1957) is associated with this approach.
3. The doctrine examines only the title given to the legislation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
23.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the true character is not determined merely by the title; the whole Act, its object and its effect are considered.
23.tq: Reject the narrow title-only formulation and retain the whole-Act test.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **true character** is read from the **whole Act, its object and its effect**.
Statement 2: this is **A.S. Krishna (1957)**. Statement 3 is wrong: the doctrine looks at the whole Act, not the title alone.
xa: This is part of **pith and substance**, borrowed from **Canada**.
**F.N. Balsara (1951)** is the classic pith and substance case.
⚠ **A.S. Krishna** and **R.M.D.C.** are both **1957**.

23.s: Which of the following doctrines is correctly matched with its foreign origin?
23.x: The doctrine of pith and substance was borrowed from Canada. Prospective overruling is associated with the United States, pleasure with England, and public trust with Roman law.
23.tq: Start with the sure foreign-origin pairing and eliminate the swapped origins.
xs: **Pith and substance — Canada** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Prospective overruling** = **USA**; **pleasure** = **England**; **public trust** = **Roman law**.
xa: **Separation of powers** = **Montesquieu (France)**.
**Basic structure** = **Germany**.
"**Procedure established by law**" = **Japan**.

23.s: The basic structure doctrine is commonly traced to the constitutional jurisprudence of which country?
23.x: The basic structure doctrine is identified with Germany as its foreign origin in the given constitutional comparison.
23.tq: Distinguish the origin of basic structure from the origin of separation of powers.
xs: **Basic structure** = **Germany** — option **(2)**.
**Japan** = "procedure established by law"; **Canada** = pith and substance; **France** = separation of powers.
xa: **Separation of powers** is part of the basic structure (**Kesavananda**).
**Public trust** = **Roman law**.
**Pleasure** = **England**; **prospective overruling** = **USA**.

23.s:
Consider the following pairs of a doctrine or expression and its foreign origin:
1. 'Procedure established by law' — Japan
2. Separation of powers — Montesquieu (France)
3. Prospective overruling — England
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
23.x: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct: 'procedure established by law' comes from Japan and separation of powers from Montesquieu (France). Pair 3 is wrong: prospective overruling comes from the USA; the pleasure doctrine is the one from England.
23.tq: Japan = procedure established by law; USA = prospective overruling; England = pleasure.
xs: Pairs **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
"**Procedure established by law**" = **Japan**; **separation of powers** = **Montesquieu (France)**.
Pair 3 is wrong: **prospective overruling** = **USA**; it is **pleasure** that comes from **England**.
xa: **Pith and substance** = **Canada**.
**Basic structure** = **Germany**; **public trust** = **Roman law**.
Prospective overruling was first applied in **Golaknath (1967)**.

23.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied in India in:
23.x: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court in Golaknath (1967).
23.tq: Use the chronology of leading constitutional cases to identify the anchor case.
xs: **Prospective overruling** was first applied in **Golaknath (1967)** — option **(3)**.
**Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)** concerns **separation of powers**; **Kesavananda** the basic structure.
xa: Origin: **USA**.
**Stare decisis**: **Art. 141** — SC's law binds all courts.
**Pleasure**: **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards.

23.s: The doctrine of pleasure in relation to civil services is primarily contained in:
o: Article 310, subject to safeguards under Article 311
23.x: Article 310 embodies the pleasure doctrine, while Article 311 provides safeguards for civil servants against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
23.tq: Pair the principal Article with its constitutional safeguard.
xs: The **pleasure** doctrine is in **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards — option **(1)**.
Art. 311 protects **civil servants**.
xa: Origin of the pleasure doctrine: **England**.
**Stare decisis** = **Art. 141**.
**Prospective overruling** = **Golaknath (1967)**, origin **USA**.

23.s: Which statement correctly describes the doctrine of separation of powers as understood in Indian constitutional law?
o: It is completely rigid and excludes all overlap among organs
It is functional rather than rigid
It applies only to the executive and judiciary
It is not connected with the basic structure doctrine
23.x: Indian separation of powers is functional rather than rigid. Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) illustrates this approach, while separation of powers is also regarded as part of the basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati.
23.tq: Reject the absolute “rigid” formulation and identify the Indian adaptation.
xs: Indian **separation of powers** is **functional, not rigid** — option **(2)**.
Case: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**.
It is also part of the **basic structure** (**Kesavananda**) — so option 4 is wrong.
xa: Origin: **Montesquieu (France)**.
**Pleasure**: **Art. 310**; **stare decisis**: **Art. 141**.
**Basic structure** origin: **Germany**.

23.s: Article 141 embodies the principle of stare decisis by providing that:
o: The law declared by every High Court binds all courts in India
Only advisory opinions of the Supreme Court are binding
Parliament must approve every Supreme Court judgment
The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India
23.x: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within India, reflecting the principle of stare decisis.
23.tq: Link the doctrine to the exact constitutional effect of Article 141.
xs: **Art. 141**: the **law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts** — option **(4)**.
This is **stare decisis**; it is the SC's law, not a High Court's.
xa: **Prospective overruling**: first in **Golaknath (1967)**, origin **USA**.
**Pleasure**: **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards.
**Separation of powers**: functional, not rigid (**Ram Jawaya Kapur, 1955**).

23.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 254(2)?
o: A State law on a Concurrent List matter may prevail in that State if it receives the President's assent
President's assent makes the State law permanently immune from Parliamentary legislation
It concerns matters in the Concurrent List
Parliament may subsequently override such a State law
23.x: Parliament may later override a State law even after it has received the President's assent.
xa: General rule (**Art. 254**): Parliament's law **prevails** over a repugnant State law.
Order: **Union > Concurrent > State**.
Residuary power: **Art. 248**.

23.s: Which doctrine is used to reconcile apparent conflicts between Central and Provincial (State) laws by examining a law's true nature?
23.x: The doctrine of pith and substance is used to reconcile Central and Provincial, or Union and State, legislative powers by examining the true nature of the law.
23.tq: Recall the doctrine associated with Union-State legislative reconciliation.
xs: **Pith and substance** reconciles **Central & Provincial laws** — option **(4)** (PYQ G2 2017).
It judges a law by its **true nature**; incidental trespass is fine.
**Territorial nexus** is about extra-territorial operation; **colourable legislation** about competence.
xa: Origin: **Canada**.
Case: **State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara (1951)** — Prohibition Act upheld as **public health** despite touching imports.
**A.S. Krishna (1957)**: true character read from the **whole Act, its object and its effect**.
23.fixed: oddly worded 'identified in an APPSC question'

23.s: Which one of the following is a criticism of constitutional morality?
o: It is considered subjective and a possible route to judicial overreach
It makes all Directive Principles directly enforceable
It gives unlimited legislative power to State governments
It prevents courts from referring to constitutional values
23.x: Critics argue that constitutional morality may be subjective and may provide a route to judicial overreach.
23.tq: Identify the recognised criticism rather than a consequence not stated.
xs: "Constitutional morality" is attacked as **subjective** → a route to **judicial overreach** — option **(1)**.
It does not make DPSPs enforceable or prevent reference to constitutional values.
xa: Meaning: **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality**.
Applied in **Navtej Johar**, **Sabarimala**, **NCT Delhi**.
No **2025-26** ruling applies these doctrines by name.

24.s: A constitutional government by definition is a
24.x: A constitutional government refers to a system where the powers and functions of the government are defined and restricted by a constitution. This form of government operates within a legal framework that ensures all government actions are bound by established laws, thereby protecting individuals' rights and liberties. The Constitution ensures that the government cannot act arbitrarily or exceed its authority, as all actions must align with constitutional provisions. The principle of a constitutional government emphasises the rule of law, meaning that all citizens, including government officials, are subject to the law. This promotes accountability, transparency, and fairness in governance. Additionally, the separation of powers between the executive, legislative, and judicial branches prevents any one branch from becoming too powerful, fostering a system of checks and balances. Overall, a constitutional government seeks to limit the scope of government power to protect the freedoms and rights of its citizens, maintaining a just and orderly society.

24.s: Which one of the following factors constitutes the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy?
24.x: In a liberal democracy, the separation of powers among the legislature, executive, and judiciary acts as a key safeguard for individual liberty. This principle allocates legislative, executive, and judicial responsibilities to distinct branches, enabling them to check one another and prevent arbitrary government action. By keeping these branches from overstepping their boundaries, the separation of powers maintains a system of checks and balances.

24.s: Constitutional government means
o: a representative government of a nation with federal
a government whose Head enjoys nominal powers
a government whose Head enjoys real powers
a government limited by the terms of the Constitution
24.x: Constitutional government or Constitutionalism, means that a government's authority is determined by a body of laws or constitution. Although constitutionalism is sometimes regarded as a synonym for limited government, that is only one interpretation and by no means the most prominent one. Thus, option (d) is the correct answer.

24.s: According to Montesquieu, the most effective means of protecting liberty is:
24.x: Montesquieu held that division of powers was the most effective way to protect liberty.
xa: His work: **"The Spirit of Laws" (1748)**; he drew on the **British constitution**.
UPSC 2021 key: best safeguard of liberty = **separation of powers**.
Separation of powers is a **presidential (USA)** principle; India and the UK follow **fusion**.

24.s: Which one of the following statements is correct in relation to constitutionalism and majoritarianism?
o: Constitutionalism requires the judiciary to exercise all legislative powers.
Majoritarianism may override constitutionalism whenever a legislative majority is secured.
A majoritarian position cannot override constitutionalism.
Constitutionalism has no application to decisions supported by an elected majority.
24.x: A legislative or political majority cannot override constitutionalism. Constitutional limitations remain binding even when a decision is supported by a majority.
24.tq: Reject the extreme claim that electoral majority automatically removes constitutional limitations.
xs: **Majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism** — option **(3)** (SC).
Constitutionalism = powers within **constitutional limits**, **rule of law**, **judicial review**, **FRs** — limits that bind even a majority.
xa: **Constitutional government** = **limited government** (UPSC 2020, 2021).
Every legislative override of a judgment is tested against the **basic structure**.
Criticism: **judicial overreach vs activism** debate.

24.s:
Assertion (A): Constitutional Government is synonymous with Limited Government.
Reason (R): Constitutional provisions define, restrain and check governmental power to prevent executive tyranny.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
24.x: Both are true: constitutional government means limited government, because the constitution defines and checks power to prevent tyranny. R explains A.
24.tq: Ask whether checks on power explain 'limited government'.
n: Constitutional Government is synonymous with Limited Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Constitutional Government defines power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Constitutional Government restrains power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Constitutional Government checks power through constitutional provisions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Constitutional provisions prevent executive tyranny under Constitutional Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Constitutional Government = Limited Government**, limited by the terms of the Constitution.
Its provisions **define, restrain and check** power to prevent **executive tyranny** — which is why it is limited.
xa: UPSC **2020, 2021** keys: constitutional government = **limited government**.
**Constitutionalism**: rule of law + **checks and balances** + **judicial review** + protection of FRs.
Best safeguard of liberty = **separation of powers** (UPSC **2021**); **Montesquieu**, "**The Spirit of Laws**" (**1748**).

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Public Interest Litigation promotes access to justice for disadvantaged persons.
II. Public Interest Litigation is an indispensable prerequisite for the existence of the Rule of Law.
III. The Rule of Law existed before the evolution of Public Interest Litigation.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: I and III are correct: PIL widens access to justice for the disadvantaged, and the rule of law existed before PIL through Articles 14, 32 and 226. II is false because PIL is not a precondition for the rule of law.
24.tq: Discriminate what strengthens the rule of law from what is required for it.
n: Public Interest Litigation promotes access to justice for disadvantaged persons. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Public Interest Litigation strengthens access to justice for disadvantaged persons. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Public Interest Litigation is not an indispensable prerequisite for the existence of the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law existed before the evolution of Public Interest Litigation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law existed through Articles 14, 32, and 226 before the evolution of Public Interest Litigation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: Statements **I and III** are correct — so option **(3) I and III only** is correct.
I: **PIL** promotes **access to justice** for disadvantaged persons.
III: the **Rule of Law** existed before PIL through **Articles 14, 32 and 226**.
II is wrong: PIL is **not indispensable** for the Rule of Law.
xa: India has **no rigid separation** of powers; there are **checks and balances**.
**Art. 50**: State shall **separate the judiciary from the executive**.
**Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: no rigid separation of powers in India.

24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about parliamentary and presidential systems?
o: In India the President is the real executive and the Council of Ministers the nominal executive
The principal checks in the US system are checks and balances among the three organs
The parliamentary system rests on fusion of powers
In the USA the President is independent of Congress
24.x: In India the President is the nominal head and the Council of Ministers the real executive.
xa: Parliamentary checks: **questions**, **confidence/no-confidence votes**.
The USA has a **single real executive**.
⚠ Ambedkar preferred **responsibility over stability**.

24.s: Article 50 of the Constitution directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in
o: the public services of the State
24.x: Article 50, a Directive Principle, directs separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
24.tq: Read the exact constitutional scope of Article 50 instead of expanding it to all institutions.
xs: **Art. 50 (DPSP)**: State shall **separate the judiciary from the executive** in the **public services of the State** — option **(1)**.
It is a Directive Principle, not about Governors, elections or Parliament.
xa: **Judiciary insulated**: Arts. **50, 121, 211, 235** (control of subordinate courts).
**AP angle**: Madras Presidency separated the **Collector's judicial powers** in **1816**.
India has **no rigid separation**; it is **implicit**, not absolute.

24.s: Separation of powers in India is:
o: Implicit, not absolute, with overlapping functions creating checks and balances
Absolute, as in a pure presidential system
24.x: India has no rigid separation; it is implicit, and overlapping functions create checks and balances.
xa: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: the Constitution does **not** recognise a rigid separation of powers.
**Legislature-executive fusion** under the parliamentary system; **judiciary insulated**.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers among the **basic features**.

24.s: Which of the following was NOT a consideration behind the framers' choice of the parliamentary system?
o: Familiarity with parliamentary institutions under the Acts of 1919 and 1935
The need to accommodate India's diversity
The desire to avoid American-style executive–legislature conflict
Ambedkar's preference for stability over responsibility
24.x: Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability, which is why the parliamentary system was chosen.
xa: Parliamentary system = **fusion** of legislature and executive; ministers must be legislators.
Council of Ministers stays only while it has **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.

24.s: Collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha is provided under
24.x: Article 75(3) provides for the collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha.
24.tq: Match the constitutional provision with the Union-level responsibility rule.
xs: **Article 75(3)** makes the Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 164(2)** is the State parallel (Assembly); **Art. 85** = summon/prorogue; **Art. 61** = President's impeachment.
xa: Council stays only with **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.
**No-confidence motion** — Lok Sabha only.

24.s: A no-confidence motion for removal of the government can be moved only in:
24.x: A no-confidence motion lies only in the Lok Sabha; Question Hour and Zero Hour give day-to-day watch over administration.
xa: **Adjournment** motions also draw attention to lapses.
Financial control: **Budget**, **cut motions**, **PAC** and **Estimates Committees**.
BPSC 2001 key: **executive subordinate to the legislature**.

24.s: The Governor summons and prorogues the State Legislature under Article:
24.x: The Governor acts under Article 174 (the President under Article 85); Article 175 is the Governor's address and messages. The gap between sessions cannot exceed six months.
xa: Ordinances: **Art. 123** (Union), **Art. 213** (State).

24.s: An ordinance, including one used to alter the legal basis of a judgment, can be issued when:
o: The legislature is not in session
A National Emergency is in force
24.x: An ordinance is issued when the legislature is not in session; it is subject to judicial review and must be laid before the House.
xa: Criticism: the **ordinance** route is said to erode **separation of powers**.
Union ordinance **Art. 123**; State **Art. 213**.
Other route: **review / curative petition** (**Art. 137**).

24.s: The Governor's ordinance-making power is contained in Article:
24.x: Article 213 covers State ordinances; Article 123 Union ordinances, Article 175 the Governor's addresses and Article 86 the President's addresses.
xa: President's messages also = **Art. 87**; Governor's = **Art. 176**.
Assent: **Art. 111** (President), **Art. 200** (Governor); reservation for President **Art. 201**.
Summon/prorogue: **85 - 174**.

24.s: Which one of the following correctly states the constitutional provisions relating to assent and reservation of Bills?
24.x: Article 111 concerns presidential assent, Article 200 concerns the Governor's assent, and Article 201 concerns Bills reserved for the President.
24.tq: Separate the Union and State assent provisions from ordinance and reference Articles.
xs: **President — Art. 111; Governor — Art. 200; reservation for President — Art. 201** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 123 / 213** are the ordinance pair; **Art. 143** is the Presidential reference to the SC.
xa: **Art. 143** advice is **not binding** on the President.
Ordinances are subject to **judicial review** and must be **laid before the House**.

24.s: A law declared ultra vires by the courts in exercise of judicial review is:
24.x: Judicial review covers laws and executive action, rests on Articles 13, 32 and 226, and an ultra vires law is void.
xa: **Art. 142** "complete justice" fills gaps — risk of overreach.
**Arts. 122, 212**: courts cannot question legislative proceedings on irregular procedure.
**Minerva Mills** struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review.

24.s: Which Article bars discussion in Parliament on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge, except on a motion for removal?
24.x: Article 121 bars it in Parliament and Article 211 in State Legislatures; Articles 122 and 212 stop courts inquiring into legislative proceedings for irregular procedure.
xa: ⚠ **121 / 211** = legislature cannot discuss judges; **122 / 212** = courts cannot question legislative procedure.
**Art. 235**: control of subordinate courts.
**Art. 50**: separation of judiciary from executive.

24.s: Article 142 enables the Supreme Court to do which of the following?
o: Prevent all legislative proceedings from judicial scrutiny
Issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session
Remove a High Court judge without parliamentary procedure
Do complete justice and fill legal gaps in appropriate cases
24.x: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice and may allow it to fill legal gaps. Its use can raise concerns about judicial overreach, and its scope is not precisely defined.
24.tq: Apply the constitutional power to a legal-gap situation rather than confusing it with ordinance or removal powers.
xs: **Art. 142** lets the SC do **"complete justice"** and **fill gaps** — option **(4)**.
Example: **Vishaka** guidelines before the **POSH Act, 2013**.
Ordinances are issued by the executive (**Art. 123/213**), not the Court.
xa: Risk: **overreach**; scope **undefined**.
Frequent **Art. 142** use is said to erode **separation of powers**.
Judicial review rests on Arts. **13, 32, 226**.

24.s: Which one of the following correctly reflects the ruling in Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)?
o: The executive can exercise power only after receiving prior approval from the judiciary.
The Indian Constitution does not recognise a rigid separation of powers, and executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.
The Indian Constitution establishes a rigid separation of powers among the three organs of government.
The legislature may decide disputes arising from judicial proceedings.
24.x: In Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution does not provide for a rigid separation of powers. It also recognised that executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.
24.tq: Test the precise holding of a constitutional case rather than accepting the extreme phrase ‘rigid separation’.
xs: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: **no rigid separation of powers**; **executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws** — option **(2)**.
So option 3 (rigid separation) is the reverse of the holding.
Deciding disputes is a **judicial function** (Raj Narain) — so option 4 is wrong.
xa: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**: separation of powers among the **basic features**.
In India separation is **implicit**, not absolute.
Overlapping functions create **checks and balances**.

24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about separation of powers in India?
o: Kesavananda Bharati recognised separation of powers as a basic feature
Raj Narain held that the legislature could finally decide an election dispute
Raj Narain was connected with the challenge to the 39th Amendment
Deciding an election dispute is a judicial function
24.x: Raj Narain held the legislature cannot decide an election dispute because it is a judicial function.
xa: **Minerva Mills**: the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review struck down.
**I.R. Coelho**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 Apr 1973** reviewable.
**Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: no rigid separation of powers.

24.s: Which Amendment placed Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation law in the Ninth Schedule?
24.x: The 76th Amendment did so; after I.R. Coelho, such post-24 April 1973 entries can be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.
xa: Override routes are all tested against the **basic structure**.
**Minerva Mills** struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review.
**24th Amendment** overrode **Golaknath**.

24.s: The 42nd Amendment's bar on judicial review was struck down in:
o: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
24.x: Minerva Mills struck down the bar; Raj Narain struck down the 39th Amendment's validation of the PM's election, and Golaknath predates the 42nd Amendment.
xa: Raj Narain: the legislature **cannot decide an election dispute** — a judicial function.
**I.R. Coelho**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 Apr 1973** reviewable.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers a **basic feature**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court can review its own judgment under Article 137.
2. Under Article 143 the President may seek the advice of the Supreme Court, and that advice is binding on the President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 1 is correct: review of its own judgments is under Art. 137. Statement 2 is wrong: the President can seek advice under Art. 143, but that advice is not binding on the President. Hence only 1; options B and C wrongly accept 2, and D wrongly rejects 1.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: review of its own judgment is under **Art. 137**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Art. 143** advice is **not binding** on the President.
xa: The executive may also seek a **curative petition**.
Parliament may change the law or Constitution, subject to the **basic structure**.
A **simple resolution** cannot overrule a judgment.

24.s: The 77th Constitutional Amendment (promotion quota) followed which judgment?
24.x: The 77th followed Indra Sawhney; the 24th followed Golaknath, the 26th Madhav Rao and the 1st Champakam Dorairajan.
xa: **Limit**: every override is tested against the **basic structure**.
Exam angle: Parliament **cannot** overrule a judgment by a **simple resolution**.
**76th Amdt** placed the TN **69%** quota in the Ninth Schedule.

24.s: Parliament can override a judicial judgment by:
o: Changing the law or constitutional basis underlying it
A resolution of a joint sitting
24.x: Parliament can override a judgment only by changing its legal or constitutional basis, subject to the basic structure; a simple resolution cannot do it.
xa: Examples: **24th** (Golaknath), **26th** (privy purses), **77th** (Indra Sawhney).
A validating law cannot **decide the dispute itself**.
**Raj Narain** struck down the **39th Amendment**'s validation of the PM's election.

24.s: The One Nation One Election Bill, as described in the context of electoral synchronisation, proposes amendments to which of the following Articles?
24.x: The One Nation One Election Bill is associated with amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327. Critics argue that fixed tenure may weaken collective responsibility under Articles 75 and 164.
24.tq: Use article-number discrimination and avoid substituting the related collective-responsibility provisions.
xs: The **One Nation One Election Bill** amends **Arts. 83, 172, 327** — option **(1)**.
Critics: **fixed tenure** weakens **collective responsibility** under **Arts. 75, 164** — these are not the amended Articles.
xa: Collective responsibility: **Art. 75(3)** (Union), **Art. 164(2)** (States).
SC: **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.
Council of Ministers stays only with **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.

25.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Elected members of the Lok Sabha – Vote in both the Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections
Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha – Vote in the Vice-Presidential but not the Presidential election
Members of State Legislative Councils – Vote in the Presidential election
Elected members of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies – Added to the Presidential Electoral College by the 70th Amendment
25.x: Members of State Legislative Councils vote in neither the Presidential nor the Vice-Presidential election.
n: The Electoral College for the Presidential election consists of elected members of both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The Electoral College for the Presidential election consists of elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The Electoral College for the Presidential election consists of elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The inclusion of elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry was made by the 70th Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: VP electoral college = **only MPs**, elected and **nominated**.
A CM sitting in the **Legislative Council cannot vote**.
⚠ Election: elected MLAs vote, nominated MPs do not; impeachment: **nominated MPs take part**, elected MLAs do not.

25.s: The system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote used in the election of the President was borrowed from the Constitution of
25.x: The Presidential election method of proportional representation by single transferable vote was borrowed from Ireland.
25.tq: Use the source-country association for a distinctive constitutional device.
xs: The **single transferable vote** system for the President's election was borrowed from **Ireland** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It works by **proportional representation** with a **secret ballot** (**Art. 55(3)**).
xa: ⚠ **Impeachment** of the President is borrowed from the **USA**; the election method from **Ireland**.
Disputes over the election are decided **only by the Supreme Court** (**Art. 71**).

25.s: In the Presidential election, the value of an MLA's vote = (population of the State / number of elected MLAs) × ____.
25.x: An MLA's vote value is State population divided by elected MLAs, multiplied by 1/1000, so it varies with the State's population.
xa: Population base: **1971 Census**, frozen till the first Census after **2026**.

25.s: The population base for calculating the value of votes in the Presidential election is the Census of:
25.x: The 1971 Census is the base, frozen under the 84th Amendment till the first Census after 2026.
xa: **MLA vote** = (State population / elected MLAs) x **1/1000**.
**MP vote** = total value of all MLAs' votes / total elected MPs.

25.s: Disputes connected with the election of the President under Article 71 are decided by:
o: The Supreme Court or the High Courts
25.x: Only the Supreme Court decides them; acts done before an election is declared void remain valid, and a vacancy in the electoral college is no ground for challenge.
xa: An election **declared void** is a cause of vacancy; the new election must be held **within 6 months** (**Art. 62**).
The new President gets a **full 5-year term**.

25.s:
Consider the following statements about the presidential election:
1. It is an indirect election.
2. Nominated members of Parliament vote in it.
3. Disputes about it are decided by the Supreme Court.
Which of the above statements are correct?
25.x: The election is indirect and its disputes are decided by the Supreme Court. Nominated MPs do not vote in it.
n: The President is elected indirectly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
Nominated members of Parliament do not participate in the Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The Presidential election uses proportional representation by means of the Single Transferable Vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The Presidential election is conducted by secret ballot. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The Supreme Court decides disputes regarding the Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President is not directly elected. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
Nominated members do not vote in the Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: Vote values use the **1971 Census**, frozen.

25.s: In the Presidential election, the value of an MP's vote is calculated to ensure:
o: Equality between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha
Parity between the Union and the States
25.x: MP vote values ensure parity between the Union and the States, while MLA vote values ensure uniformity among States.
n: The value of an MLA’s vote is calculated to ensure uniformity among the states. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The value of an MP’s vote is calculated to ensure parity between the Union and the states. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: MLA vote = (State population / elected MLAs) x **1/1000**.
MP vote = total value of all MLAs' votes / total elected MPs.

25.s: The electoral college for the election of the Vice-President consists of:
o: All MPs and the State Legislative Assemblies
All members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated
25.x: All MPs, elected and nominated, vote by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and secret ballot; State Assemblies do not take part.
n: The Electoral College for the Vice-Presidential election consists of members of both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Elected Members of Parliament participate in the Vice-Presidential Electoral College. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Nominated Members of Parliament participate in the Vice-Presidential Electoral College. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
State Legislative Assemblies do not participate in the Vice-Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is elected by proportional representation by means of the Single Transferable Vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-Presidential election is conducted by secret ballot. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Only Members of Parliament participate in the Vice-Presidential Electoral College. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Nominated Members of Parliament vote in the Vice-Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
State Legislative Assembly members do not vote in the Vice-Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is elected indirectly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-Presidential election differs from the Presidential election because State Legislative Assemblies do not participate in it. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is elected and is not appointed by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: The **11th Amdt, 1961** ended the joint-meeting method for VP election.
The President's college includes **elected** MLAs, incl. **Delhi and Puducherry**.
VP qualification is linked to the **Rajya Sabha**.

25.s:
Consider the following statements about the Presidential election:
I. Nominated MPs and nominated MLAs cannot vote.
II. Members of Legislative Councils cannot vote.
III. The nomination requires 50 proposers and 50 seconders.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
25.x: All three are correct: nominated members and MLCs cannot vote for the President, and a candidate needs 50 proposers and 50 seconders.
25.tq: Recall who is left out of the Presidential electoral college.
n: Nominated Members of Parliament cannot vote in the Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Nominated Members of State Legislative Assemblies cannot vote in the Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Members of State Legislative Councils cannot vote in the Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
A Presidential nomination requires 50 proposers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
A Presidential nomination requires 50 seconders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
State Legislative Councils are excluded from the Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xs: **All three** statements are correct — option **(2) I, II and III**.
I: **nominated** MPs and **nominated** MLAs cannot vote.
II: members of **State Legislative Councils** are **excluded**.
III: nomination needs **50 proposers** and **50 seconders**.
xa: Voters: **elected** MPs of **both Houses**, elected MLAs of States, and **Delhi and Puducherry** (**70th Amendment, 1992**).
APPSC-G2 **2023** key: elected MPs, elected MLAs, **Delhi/Puducherry**.
A CM in the **Legislative Council cannot vote**.

25.s: The emoluments of the President of India are:
o: Fixed by the Union Cabinet and listed in the First Schedule
Fixed by the Finance Commission and listed in the Fourth Schedule
Fixed by Parliament by law and listed in the Second Schedule
Fixed by the Supreme Court and listed in the Third Schedule
25.x: Parliament fixes the President's emoluments by law; they are listed in the Second Schedule and cannot be reduced during the term.
xa: **Art. 59:** official residence **rent-free**; the President cannot be a member of any legislature.
Conditions of office (no office of profit, emoluments) are in **Art. 59**.

25.s: The President of India addresses his resignation to the:
25.x: The President resigns in writing to the Vice-President, who informs the Speaker; the CJI administers the oath under Article 60.
xa: The President swears to "**preserve, protect and defend the Constitution** and the law".
Emoluments are **charged** on the **Consolidated Fund of India** and cannot be diminished during the term.
⚠ The **Vice-President** resigns to the **President**.

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 65 — Vice-President to act as President
Article 72 — Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
25.x: Article 65 provides for the Vice-President acting as President in specified circumstances. Article 72 concerns pardon, Article 74 concerns aid and advice by the Council of Ministers, and Article 76 concerns the Attorney General.
25.tq: Use neighbouring constitutional provisions as distractors and identify the exact article-subject pairing.
xs: **Article 65 — Vice-President to act as President** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Art. 72** = **pardon**; **Art. 74** = Council of Ministers to **aid and advise**.
**Art. 78** = PM's duty to **inform the President**; the **Attorney General** is **Art. 76**.
xa: While acting, the VP **stops functioning as Rajya Sabha Chairman**.
**Art. 71** = election disputes.

25.s: The Eleventh Constitutional Amendment of 1961 is associated with which of the following changes?
o: Removal of nominated members from the Vice-Presidential electoral college
Providing for election of the Vice-President by State Legislatures
Ending the joint-meeting method for the election of the Vice-President
Introduction of direct election to the office of Vice-President
25.x: The Eleventh Amendment ended the earlier joint-meeting method and provided for election of the Vice-President by the members of both Houses of Parliament.
25.tq: Test the amendment by identifying the precise institutional procedure it altered, not the broader office concerned.
xs: The **11th Amendment, 1961** **ended the joint-meeting method** of electing the Vice-President — so option **(3)** is correct.
The VP's electoral college is **all MPs, elected and nominated**, with **no MLAs** — so nominated members were not removed and States play no part.
xa: ⚠ The President's electoral college **excludes nominated MPs** but includes **elected MLAs**.
A **VP vacancy** (**Art. 68**) has **no** 6-month deadline.

25.s: Under Article 58, the minimum age for election as President of India is:
25.x: A candidate must be an Indian citizen, have completed 35 years, be qualified for the Lok Sabha and hold no office of profit.
n: A Presidential candidate must be a citizen of India under Article 58. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
A Presidential candidate must have completed 35 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
A Presidential candidate must be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
