A Presidential candidate must not hold any office of profit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: **Term**: **five years** (**Article 56**); re-election any number of times (**Article 57**).
⚠ The **Vice-President**'s qualification is linked to the **Rajya Sabha**.
**Art. 59**: not a member of any legislature; rent-free residence.

25.s: The term of office of the President of India is prescribed as five years under which Article of the Constitution?
25.x: Article 56 fixes the President's term at five years. Article 57 is re-election, 61 impeachment and 65 the Vice-President acting as President.
25.tq: Link the term of office to Article 56.
n: The term of the President is five years under Article 56. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xs: The President's five-year term is under **Article 56** — option **(1)**.
**Article 56** fixes the term at **five years**; the outgoing President continues until the successor enters office.
**Article 57** = **re-election**; **Article 61** = **impeachment**; **Article 65** = VP **acts as President**.
xa: **Article 58** = **qualifications**; **Article 60** = **oath**.
**Article 62** = time of election to fill a vacancy.
**Article 71** = election disputes.

25.s: A candidate for Vice-President must be qualified for election as a member of the:
25.x: A Vice-President must be qualified for the Rajya Sabha, besides being an Indian citizen aged 35 holding no office of profit.
n: A Vice-President must be a citizen of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
A Vice-President must have completed 35 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
A Vice-President must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
A Vice-President must not hold any office of profit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The qualification for election as Vice-President is linked to eligibility for the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: The **President**'s qualification is linked to the **Lok Sabha**.
The VP resigns to the **President**.
The VP is **not** part of Parliament; the President is.

25.s: Impeachment can be imposed on the President of India on which of the following grounds?
o: Carrying on a vocation of profit

25.s: How many terms may a person serve as President of India?
25.x: The President holds office for five years and may be re-elected; the Constitution prescribes no limit on terms.
xa: Only **Rajendra Prasad** served two full terms (elected **1952**, **1957**).
⚠ Contrast: **US 22nd Amendment** = two terms; **South Korea** = single 5-year term.

25.s: The emoluments of the President of India:
o: May be diminished by Parliament during the term
Are decided afresh by each Finance Commission
Cannot be diminished during the term
Can be cut by the Council of Ministers
25.x: The President's emoluments cannot be diminished during the term; the President also gets a rent-free residence and cannot be a member of any legislature.
xa: Emoluments are listed in the **Second Schedule**.
**Art. 58**: no **office of profit** under the Union, a State or any local/other authority.

25.s: The impeachment resolution against the President must be signed by at least ____ of the members of the House, after 14 days' notice.
25.x: One-fourth of the members must sign after 14 days' notice; the charge may start in either House, and no President has been impeached so far.
xa: Passed by **two-thirds of the total membership** of the initiating House; the other House investigates.
⚠ **Nominated MPs take part**; **elected MLAs do not**.

25.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the impeachment of the President under Article 61?
o: The other House investigates the charge
The initiating House may pass the charge by a simple majority
The President has the right to appear and be represented during the investigation
The other House must pass the charge by two-thirds of its total membership
25.x: Both Houses must pass the charge by a two-thirds majority of their total membership; a simple majority is not enough.
xa: Charges need a resolution signed by **one-fourth** of members after **14 days'** notice.
Ground: **"violation of the Constitution"** only (**Art. 61**).

25.s: Who among the following does NOT take part in the impeachment of the President?
o: Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha
Elected members of the Lok Sabha
25.x: Elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament take part; elected MLAs of the States, Delhi and Puducherry do not.
xa: ⚠ Election: **elected MLAs vote, nominated MPs do not**; impeachment: the reverse.
The VP's electoral college is also **all MPs, elected and nominated**, with no MLAs.

25.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about filling a vacancy in the office of the President?
o: On expiry of the term, the election must be completed before the term expires
A person elected to fill a vacancy holds office only for the predecessor's unexpired term
A vacancy by death, resignation or removal must be filled within six months
The rule on vacancy by expiry of term is in Article 62(1)
25.x: A President elected to fill a vacancy gets a full five-year term, not the unexpired part.
xa: The outgoing President **continues until the successor enters office** (**Art. 56**).
⚠ A **VP vacancy** (**Art. 68**) has **no** 6-month deadline.

25.s: While the Vice-President acts as President under Article 65, the Rajya Sabha is presided over by the:
o: Senior-most member of the Rajya Sabha
25.x: The Vice-President stops functioning as Chairman while acting as President, and the Deputy Chairman presides.
xa: **Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned (July 2025)** → **C.P. Radhakrishnan** elected — a mid-term VP vacancy.
**B.D. Jatti** acted after **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed** died in office.

25.s: Under Article 240, the President may make regulations for Puducherry:
o: Only with the consent of the Lieutenant Governor
When its Legislative Assembly is suspended or dissolved
25.x: Article 240 covers UTs such as Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep and DNH-DD, and Puducherry when its Assembly is suspended or dissolved.
xa: The President administers **UTs** through **administrators**.
Ordinances are under **Art. 123**.

25.s: The Comptroller and Auditor General is appointed under Article:
25.x: Article 148 concerns the CAG; Article 76 the Attorney General, 155 Governors and 324 the Election Commission.
xa: CAG, Governors and AG are appointed **on the advice of the PM / Council of Ministers** (**Art. 74**).

25.s: In the formal sense under Article 74, the CJI, judges, the Attorney General and Governors are appointed by the President on the recommendation of the:
25.x: Under Article 74 the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the PM, so these appointments are formally on the PM's recommendation.
xa: In practice judges are chosen by the **collegium** (**CJI + 4** senior-most, **Third Judges Case 1998**).

25.s: A joint sitting of Parliament is summoned by the ____ and presided over by the ____.
o: President; Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
President; Speaker of the Lok Sabha
25.x: Summoning a joint sitting is a legislative function of the President, and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over it.
xa: A **joint sitting** is presided over by the **Speaker**.
He also **nominates 12 to the RS** and issues **ordinances** (**Art. 123**).

25.s: How many members does the President nominate to the Rajya Sabha?
25.x: The President nominates twelve members to the Rajya Sabha; under Article 79 the President is part of Parliament.
xa: The President can **summon/prorogue** both Houses, **dissolve Lok Sabha** and summon a **joint sitting**.
Prior recommendation is needed for **Art. 3** and **money bills**.
Ordinances are issued under **Art. 123**.

25.s: The President's prior recommendation is required for the introduction of:
o: An Ordinary Bill in the Rajya Sabha
25.x: Prior recommendation is needed for a Money Bill and a Bill under Article 3, not for every Private Member's Bill.
xa: **Demands for grants** also need his recommendation.
⚠ For a **Money Bill** he can only **assent or withhold** — no suspensive veto.

25.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the pardoning powers of the President and Governor?
o: The President may pardon a death sentence
The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence but may suspend, remit or commute it
The President may exercise pardoning power in court-martial cases
The Governor may grant pardon in a court-martial case
25.x: The Governor has no power to pardon a court-martial sentence; only the President has.
xa: President: offences against **Union laws**; Governor (**Art. 161**): **State laws**.
**Kehar Singh (1989):** no right of oral hearing; **Epuru Sudhakar (2006)**: limited judicial review.

25.s: Under Article 72, the President's power of pardon does NOT necessarily cover which of the following?
o: Sentences imposed under State laws, in every case
Offences against laws within the Union's executive power
All cases involving a death sentence
25.x: Article 72 covers court-martial sentences, Union-law offences and all death sentences, but not sentences under State laws in every case.
xa: Forms: **pardon, commutation, remission, respite, reprieve**.
**Amnesty** lies outside **Art. 72**.

25.s: The suspensive veto of the President is NOT available in respect of:
25.x: A suspensive veto returns an Ordinary Bill once for reconsideration, with assent mandatory if passed again; it does not apply to Money Bills.
xa: ⚠ "Suspensive veto on Money Bills" is a **trap** (**APPSC-G1 2024**).
The President's veto is under **Article 111**.

25.s: Who is the only Chief Justice of India to have acted as President?
25.x: M. Hidayatullah acted as President in 1969; V.V. Giri won on second-preference votes, and S. Radhakrishnan was the first President from South India.
xa: **N. Sanjiva Reddy**: only President elected **unopposed**; from **AP**; first CM of AP (**1956**).
**Rajendra Prasad**: only President **elected twice** (**1952, 1957**).
⚠ Died in office: **Zakir Husain** and **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed**; acted: **M. Hidayatullah** and **B.D. Jatti**.

25.s: Who was the only President of India elected unopposed?
25.x: N. Sanjiva Reddy (President 1977–82), from Andhra Pradesh, was elected unopposed; he was earlier Lok Sabha Speaker and AP's first Chief Minister.
xa: He came from **Anantapur / Nandyala**.
⚠ Elected President in **1977** (some notes say **1978**).
He was the **6th** President.

25.s: The electoral college for the election of the President is provided in Article:
25.x: Article 54 covers the electoral college; Article 52 creates the office, 60 is the oath and 71 election disputes.
xa: **Art. 55** = manner of election (value of votes, **STV**).
**Art. 61** = impeachment; **Art. 62** = time of election to fill a vacancy.

25.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Article 60 deals with the President's eligibility for re-election
Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President
Article 56 deals with the President's term and resignation to the Vice-President
Article 58 lays down the qualifications for election as President
25.x: Article 60 concerns the President's oath or affirmation; eligibility for re-election is in Article 57.
xa: **Art. 59** = conditions of office (no office of profit, emoluments).
**Art. 65** = VP to act as President.

25.s: The impeachment of the President for violation of the Constitution is dealt with in Article:
25.x: Article 61 governs impeachment; either House can prefer the charge and each must pass it by a special majority.
n: The President can be removed by impeachment for violation of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The impeachment procedure is provided under Article 61. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
A charge for impeachment of the President can be preferred by either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
Impeachment of the President requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: Resolution signed by **one-fourth** of members after **14 days'** notice.
Passed by **two-thirds of the total membership** of each House.
**No President has ever been impeached**.

25.s: Which of the following is exercised by the President on ministerial advice and is NOT a situational discretionary power?
o: Appointing a PM in a hung Parliament
Dismissing a government that has lost its majority
25.x: Appointing Ambassadors is done on ministerial advice; the other three are listed as situational discretion.
n: The President may appoint a Prime Minister in case of a hung Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President may dismiss a government that has lost its majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President may dissolve the Lok Sabha as a limited discretionary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: The **pocket veto** is another limited discretion.
The **44th Amendment** let the President **return advice** **once** for reconsideration.
⚠ **42nd** = advice binding; **44th** = one reconsideration, then binding.

25.s: Minimum number of electors needed to be proposer of the presidential candidate is -
25.x: According to Article 55 of the Constitution, as far as practicable, there shall be uniformity in the scale of representation of different States in the election of the President. Every elected Member of Legislative Assembly of a State shall have as many votes as there are multiples of one thousand in the quotient obtained by dividing the population of the State by the total number of the elected members of the assembly. So, in the above statements only statement 2 is correct, therefore option (b) is correct.

25.s: The President of India is elected by-
o: Only the members of Rajya Sabha
Only the members of Lok Sabha
Only by the Members of State Legislative Assemblies
By the Elected Members of Rajya Sabha Lok Sabha

25.s: Which of the following is not an essential qualification for the candidature of President?
o: Qualified for election as a member of the House of People
25.x: Article 58(1) of the Indian Constitution enumerates qualifications for election as President – No person shall be eligible for election as President unless he – (a) is a citizen of India (b) has completed the age of 35 years and (c) is qualified for election as a member of the House of the People.

25.s: Which one of the following statements about the use of the term “impeachment” in the constitutional context is correct?
o: It is used for the removal of the President, judges of the Supreme Court and the Vice-President alike.
It is used for every constitutional office-holder removed by Parliament.
It is used only for the President; judges and the Vice-President are removed through procedures described as removal.
It is used only for the Vice-President and Governors.
25.x: In the constitutional terminology stated here, impeachment is used only for the President. Judges and the Vice-President are described as being removed.
25.tq: Discriminate between closely associated constitutional terms rather than treating impeachment as a generic word for removal.
xs: "Impeachment" is used **only for the President**; **judges** and the **Vice-President** are **"removed"** — so option **(3)** is correct.
So it is not used for judges, the VP or Governors.
xa: Ground: **"violation of the Constitution"** (**Art. 61**).
Passed by **two-thirds of the total membership** of each House.

25.s: Jagdeep Dhankhar’s resignation as Vice-President in July 2025 and the subsequent election of C. P. Radhakrishnan are relevant primarily to which constitutional provisions?
25.x: Articles 65 and 68 deal respectively with the Vice-President acting as President and the filling of a vacancy in the office of Vice-President. The July 2025 resignation therefore invoked these provisions.
25.tq: Use the office-function pairing: identify the Articles dealing with acting arrangements and a Vice-Presidential vacancy.
xs: The resignation tested the arrangements of **Articles 65 and 68** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned (July 2025)** → **C.P. Radhakrishnan** elected — the **third** mid-term VP vacancy.
**Art. 61** = impeachment, **Art. 72** = pardon, **Art. 74** = aid and advice, **Arts. 52-53** = the President and executive power.
xa: **Art. 65:** VP acts as President; meanwhile the **Deputy Chairman** presides over the Rajya Sabha.
⚠ Unlike a Presidential vacancy, **Art. 68** has **no** 6-month deadline.

25.s: Which of the following correctly states the comparison concerning presidential term limits?
o: The United States permits only one presidential term, whereas South Korea permits two five-year terms.
The United States limits a President to two terms, whereas South Korea provides for a single five-year term.
Both the United States and South Korea prescribe two presidential terms.
Both the United States and South Korea prescribe a single five-year presidential term.
25.x: The Twenty-Second Amendment of the United States limits a President to two terms. South Korea follows a single five-year presidential term.
25.tq: Handle comparison questions by checking both parts of the pair rather than recognising only one correct country.
xs: The **US** limits a President to **two terms** and **South Korea** has a **single 5-year term** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The US limit comes from its **22nd Amendment**.
xa: India has **no term limit** (**Art. 57**: re-election allowed).
India borrowed **impeachment** from the **USA**.

25.s:
Assertion (A): The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
Reason (R): Article 64 assigns this role to the Vice-President.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
25.x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 64 is the provision that makes the Vice-President ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
25.tq: Check whether R is the source of the role in A.
n: Article 64 makes the Vice-President the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Article 64** makes the VP the **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**.
So R states the provision that creates the role in A.
xa: While acting as President (**Article 65**), the VP **stops functioning as Rajya Sabha Chairman**; the **Deputy Chairman** presides.
**Article 63**: there shall be a **Vice-President**.
The VP is removed by a **Rajya Sabha resolution** agreed to by the Lok Sabha.

25.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 63 provides that there shall be a Vice-President.
2. Article 65 provides for the Vice-President to act as President.
3. Article 66 deals with the election of the Vice-President.
Which of the above statements are correct?
25.x: All three are correct: Article 63 creates the office, 65 covers acting as President and 66 the election; Article 67 deals with term and removal.
n: Article 63 provides that there shall be a Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 65 provides for the Vice-President to act as President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 66 concerns the election of the Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 67 concerns the term and removal of the Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Article 64**: VP is **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**.
VP vacancy (**Art 68**) has **no** 6-month deadline.
VP electoral college = **all MPs, elected and nominated**, no MLAs.

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 240 — Regulations for certain Union Territories
Article 143 — Consultation with the Supreme Court
Article 360 — Appointment of the Comptroller and Auditor General
25.x: Article 360 concerns financial emergency. The Comptroller and Auditor General is appointed by the President under Article 148, whereas Articles 123, 143 and 240 correspond to the powers stated in the other pairs.
25.tq: Find the wrong article-power pair by matching each article with its constitutional subject.
xs: **Article 360 — Appointment of the CAG** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 360** is an **Emergency** article; the **CAG** is appointed under **Art. 148**.
Correct pairs: **Art. 240** = UT regulations; **Art. 123** = ordinances; **Art. 143** = consulting the SC.
xa: Emergency articles: **352, 356, 360**.
**Governors** under **Art. 155**; **Attorney General** under **Art. 76**.

25.s: The advice tendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 is:
o: Binding only during a financial emergency
Binding after approval by the Rajya Sabha
25.x: Under Article 143, the President may consult the Supreme Court, but the advice given by the Court is not binding.
25.tq: Discriminate between consultation and compulsory compliance by focusing on the legal effect of the advice.
xs: Advice given under **Art. 143** is **not binding** on the President — so option **(3)** is correct.
The President **consults the SC**; the advice is advisory only.
xa: Other judicial power: **pardons** under **Art. 72**.
⚠ Contrast **Art. 74**: Council of Ministers' advice **is binding** (**42nd Amendment**).

25.s: Financial Emergency is provided under Article:
25.x: Financial Emergency is Article 360; Article 352 is National Emergency, 356 failure of constitutional machinery in a State and 143 advisory jurisdiction.
xa: Emergency powers of the President: **Arts. 352, 356, 360**.
**Art. 143** advice is **not binding**.

25.s: Which one of the following is a financial power of the President of India?
o: Fixing the repo rate for the Reserve Bank of India
Advancing money from the Contingency Fund of India
25.x: The President can authorise advances from the Contingency Fund of India. The Budget is laid before Parliament in the President's name, and recommendations are required for Money Bills and demands for grants.
25.tq: Identify the function that belongs to the President's constitutional financial role without assigning executive or monetary-policy powers to that office.
xs: Advances from the **Contingency Fund** of India are a **financial power** of the President — so option **(3)** is correct.
Other financial powers: the **budget** is laid in his name; **money bills** and **demands for grants** need his recommendation.
No tax can be imposed without Parliament; repo rate and audits are not his powers.
xa: The **CAG** is appointed by the President (**Art. 148**).
The **Finance Commission** is also appointed by the President.

25.s: Articles 52 to 78 of the Constitution of India constitute
o: Part V, Chapter I dealing with the Union Executive
Part VI, Chapter I dealing with the State Executive
Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights
Part V, Chapter II dealing with Parliament
25.x: Articles 52 to 78 fall under Part V, Chapter I, which deals with the Union Executive.
25.tq: Distinguish the Part and Chapter classification from the adjacent chapter on Parliament.
xs: **Arts. 52-78** form **Part V, Chapter I** — **The Executive** (Union) — so option **(1)** is correct.
It opens with **Art. 52** (there shall be a President) and ends with **Art. 78** (PM's duty to inform the President).
xa: **Art. 74** = Council of Ministers to aid and advise; **Art. 76** = Attorney General.
**Art. 53**: executive power of the Union vested in the President.

25.s: President Droupadi Murmu promulgated the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026. What change did the Ordinance provide?
o: Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 37 to 40, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, including the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 31 to 33, excluding the CJI
25.x: The 2026 Ordinance increased the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, with the Chief Justice of India excluded from this count.
25.tq: Separate the numerical change from the counting exception relating to the Chief Justice of India.
xs: The Ordinance raised SC judges from **33 to 37, excluding the CJI** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Promulgated by **Droupadi Murmu**; gazette dated **16 May 2026**.
xa: It was **criticised as ordinance misuse**.
Ordinances are issued under **Art. 123**.

25.s:
Assertion (A): The President normally appoints the leader of the majority party as Prime Minister.
Reason (R): The President can seek information from the Prime Minister under Article 78.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
25.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: appointing the majority leader as PM is a convention; Article 78's right to seek information is a separate relationship.
25.tq: A later right does not explain an appointment convention.
n: The President normally appoints the leader of the majority party as Prime Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President can seek information from the Prime Minister under Article 78. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A: the President appoints the **Prime Minister** — normally the **leader of the majority party**.
R: under **Article 78** the President can seek **information** from the PM — a separate power.
xa: The President also appoints **Governors**, **CAG**, **Attorney General**, judges of the **Supreme Court** and **High Courts**.
President = **nominal/de jure** executive; PM = **real/de facto** executive.
In a **hung Parliament** the President uses limited discretion to appoint a PM.

25.s:
Consider the following statements about the President's powers:
1. The President declares war on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
2. The President appoints Ambassadors.
3. The President appoints High Commissioners.
Which of the above statements are correct?
25.x: All three are correct: the President declares war and concludes peace on the Council of Ministers' advice and appoints Ambassadors and High Commissioners.
n: The President declares war on the advice of the Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President concludes peace on the advice of the Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President appoints Ambassadors. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President appoints High Commissioners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: The President is the **Supreme Commander** of the armed forces.
Treaties are negotiated in the President's name.
Emergencies: **352** (National), **356** (State), **360** (Financial).

25.s: The pardoning power of the President under Article 72 and of the Governor under Article 161 respectively relates primarily to offences against:
25.x: The President deals with offences against Union laws, while the Governor deals with offences against State laws.
25.tq: Use the Union–State jurisdiction contrast to avoid reversing the two constitutional provisions.
xs: The President's power covers offences against **Union laws** and the Governor's against **State laws** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 72** (President) → **Union** law; **Art. 161** (Governor) → **State** law; option (2) reverses them.
xa: The Governor **cannot pardon a death sentence** but can **suspend, remit or commute** it.
The Governor has **no power** over **court-martial** sentences.
**Madras HC** Full Bench (**Apr 2026**): Governor bound by Cabinet advice on **remission**.

25.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the forms of the pardoning power?
o: Pardon – Removal of both sentence and conviction
Reprieve – Permanent cancellation of the sentence
Commutation – Substitution of a heavier punishment with a lighter one
Remission – Reduction in duration without changing the sentence's character
25.x: A reprieve is only a temporary postponement of execution; removal of sentence and conviction is a pardon.
n: Pardon completely removes the sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pardon completely removes the conviction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Commutation substitutes a heavier form of punishment with a lighter form. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Remission reduces the period or duration of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Remission does not change the fundamental character of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a temporary stay of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a postponement of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xa: **Respite**: a **lesser sentence** due to **pregnancy**, **mental** or **physical disability**.
⚠ **Commutation** = lighter **form**; **remission** = shorter **period**.
**Article 72** covers **court-martial**, **Union law** offences and **death sentence**.

25.s: Which of the following statements regarding executive pardoning powers is incorrect?
o: Reprieve completely removes both the sentence and the conviction.
Commutation substitutes a heavier punishment with a lighter one.
Respite grants a lesser sentence because of special personal circumstances.
Remission reduces the duration of a sentence without changing its fundamental character.
25.x: Option A is incorrect: a reprieve only postpones execution. Removing both sentence and conviction is a pardon. Commutation, respite and remission are described correctly.
25.tq: Discriminate a reprieve from a pardon.
n: Pardon completely absorbs the sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pardon completely removes the sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pardon completely absorbs the conviction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pardon completely removes the conviction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pardon places the offender in the same position as if the offence had never been committed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Commutation substitutes a heavier form of punishment with a lighter form. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Remission reduces the period or duration of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Remission does not change the fundamental character of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Respite awards a lesser sentence in place of the original penalty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Respite is granted due to special personal circumstances. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pregnancy is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Mental disability is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Physical disability is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a temporary stay of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a postponement of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve especially applies to the death penalty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve allows time to seek a Presidential pardon. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Reprieve** removes both **sentence and conviction** — option **(1)**.
**Reprieve** is only a **temporary stay / postponement** of execution, giving time to seek a **Presidential pardon**.
Removing both **sentence** and **conviction** is a **Pardon**; commutation, respite, remission are described correctly.
xa: **Remission** example: **two years** rigorous imprisonment → **one year**.
**Commutation** example: **death sentence → rigorous life imprisonment**.
**Amnesty** lies outside **Art 72**.

25.s: Which pardoning power awards a lesser sentence because of special personal circumstances such as pregnancy or physical disability?
25.x: A respite gives a lesser sentence because of special circumstances such as pregnancy or disability. Remission shortens a sentence without changing its nature.
25.tq: Discriminate a respite from remission.
n: Commutation substitutes a heavier form of punishment with a lighter form. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Remission reduces the period or duration of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Respite awards a lesser sentence in place of the original penalty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Respite is granted due to special personal circumstances. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pregnancy is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Mental disability is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Physical disability is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a temporary stay of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a postponement of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve especially applies to the death penalty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: The power is **Respite** — option **(4)**.
**Respite** awards a **lesser sentence** due to **special personal circumstances** — **pregnancy**, **mental** or **physical disability**.
**Commutation** changes the **form**; **Remission** cuts the **period**; **Reprieve** **postpones** execution.
xa: **Pardon** makes it as if the offence had **never been committed**.
**Article 72** vs **Article 161**: President covers **Union laws**; Governor **State laws**.
Judicial review of pardons is **limited** — **mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant** grounds.

25.s: Which form of executive pardon may substitute a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment?
25.x: Commutation replaces a punishment with a lighter one, such as a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment. Remission only shortens the term.
25.tq: Discriminate commutation from remission.
n: Commutation may substitute a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: The pardon is **Commutation** — option **(1)**.
**Commutation** substitutes a **lighter** form of punishment — e.g. **death sentence → rigorous life imprisonment**.
**Pardon** wipes out sentence and conviction; **Respite** is due to personal circumstances; **Remission** only shortens the **period**.
xa: ⚠ **Commutation** = lighter **form**; **remission** = shorter **period**, same character.
The Governor cannot pardon a **death sentence** but can **commute** it.
**Maru Ram (1980)**: exercised on **Council of Ministers' advice**.

25.s: With reference to the pocket veto of the President of India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It can be exercised only for a period of six months.
It permits the President to return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
It keeps an Ordinary Bill pending without any constitutional time limit for decision.
It is a veto that can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Parliament.
25.x: Pocket veto means keeping a Bill pending without taking a decision. The Constitution prescribes no time limit for the President to act in this manner, and it applies to Ordinary Bills.
25.tq: Separate pocket veto from suspensive veto by focusing on the absence of a constitutional time limit.
xs: The **pocket veto** keeps an **Ordinary Bill pending** with **no time limit in the Constitution** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It has no six-month limit, is not a return of a Money Bill, and cannot be overridden by a higher majority.
xa: An overridable veto (e.g. by **2/3**) is the **qualified veto** — **US practice**, not available in India.
**Money Bill:** only **assent or withhold**.

25.s: In respect of which of the following must the President give assent, so that the absolute veto cannot apply?
o: A Government Bill when the Cabinet resigned before assent
25.x: A Constitutional Amendment Bill must receive assent; absolute veto may apply to a private member's Bill or a Government Bill after the Cabinet resigns.
xa: **Pocket veto**: Bill kept pending — **no time limit** in the Constitution.
**Suspensive veto**: return **once**; then must assent.

25.s: The 15% size limit on the Council of Ministers is contained in Article:
25.x: Article 75(1A) sets the size limit; Article 74 is aid and advice, 75(3) collective responsibility and 76 the Attorney-General.
n: Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 75(3) provides for collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 75(1A) concerns the size limit of the Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 76 concerns the Attorney-General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Article 77** = **conduct of business** of the Government of India.
**Article 78** = PM's duty to inform the President.

25.s: Which one of the following best describes the constitutional position of the President and the Prime Minister?
o: The President is the real executive and the Prime Minister is the nominal executive.
The President is the nominal or de jure executive, while the Prime Minister is the real or de facto executive.
The Prime Minister is the constitutional head and the President is only a ceremonial officer without executive status.
Both are independent real executives with equal authority in all matters.
25.x: The President is the nominal or de jure executive, while the Prime Minister, heading the Council of Ministers, functions as the real or de facto executive.
25.tq: Use the nominal-versus-real executive distinction and reject the reversal of roles.
xs: The President is the **nominal / de jure** executive and the PM the **real / de facto** executive — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Council of Ministers headed by the PM** aids and advises the President (**Art. 74**).
xa: All executive action is taken **in his name**.
⚠ **42nd** = advice binding; **44th** = one reconsideration, then binding.

25.s: After returning the advice of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration, the President must:
o: Refer it to the Supreme Court
25.x: The 42nd Amendment made advice binding; the 44th allows one return, after which the President must act according to the advice.
xa: President = **nominal** executive; PM = **real** executive.

25.s: Under Article 74(2), which of the following is correct regarding the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers?
o: The advice tendered to the President cannot be inquired into by any court.
The advice becomes public automatically after being tendered.
Any court may inquire into the advice if the President requests it.
Only the Supreme Court may inquire into the advice.
25.x: Article 74(2) provides that the question, if any, and what advice was tendered by Ministers to the President cannot be inquired into by any court.
25.tq: Identify the constitutional bar on judicial inquiry and reject options that create exceptions not provided here.
xs: Under **Art. 74(2)** the advice **cannot be inquired into by any court** — so option **(1)** is correct.
No court, not even the Supreme Court, may inquire into it.
xa: **Art. 74(1):** Council of Ministers aids and advises; advice binding since the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.
**Maru Ram (1980):** even the pardoning power is exercised on the **Council of Ministers' advice**.

25.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about cases on the pardoning power?
o: Maru Ram (1980) held that the power is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers
Kehar Singh (1989) held that the President may examine the evidence afresh
Epuru Sudhakar (2006) allowed limited judicial review on mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds
Kehar Singh held that a convict has a right to an oral hearing before the President
25.x: Kehar Singh held that the President may examine evidence afresh but the convict has no right to an oral hearing.
xa: **Epuru Sudhakar** arose from **AP**.
**Madras HC** Full Bench (**Apr 2026**): Governor bound by Cabinet advice on **remission**.
⚠ The Governor (**Art. 161**) cannot pardon a **death sentence** and has no power over **court-martial**.

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Zakir Husain — First President from South India
Rajendra Prasad — Only President elected twice
S. Radhakrishnan — First President to die in office
M. Hidayatullah — Only President elected unopposed
25.x: Rajendra Prasad was the only President elected twice, in 1952 and 1957. Radhakrishnan was the first President from South India, Zakir Husain was the first to die in office, and Hidayatullah acted as President.
25.tq: Use the wrong-person-with-deed trap by matching each President with the correct distinction.
xs: **Rajendra Prasad — only President elected twice** (**1952, 1957**) is correct — option **(2)**.
**Zakir Husain** was the first to **die in office**; **S. Radhakrishnan** the first from **South India**.
**M. Hidayatullah** was the only **CJI** to act as President; the only one elected **unopposed** was **N. Sanjiva Reddy**.
xa: ⚠ Died in office: **Zakir Husain** and **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed**; acted: **M. Hidayatullah** and **B.D. Jatti**.
**S. Radhakrishnan** was earlier the **first VP**.

25.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Vice-President – Administers the oath to the President
25.x: The President's oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India, not the Vice-President. The other three pairs are correct.
n: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
Pratibha Patil was the first woman President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
Droupadi Murmu was the first tribal President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The Chief Justice of India administers the oath to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: **Rajendra Prasad** is the **longest-serving** — **two** terms.
**Droupadi Murmu** is the **15th** President (from **25 July 2022**).
**K.R. Narayanan** was the **First Dalit** President.

25.s: A Chief Minister who is a member of the Legislative Council of a State, rather than its Legislative Assembly, is entitled to
o: not vote in the election of the President
vote only if nominated by the Governor
vote in the election of the President by virtue of being the Chief Minister
vote only in the election of the Vice-President
25.x: Only elected members of State Legislative Assemblies form part of the Presidential electoral college. Membership of a Legislative Council does not confer this right, even on a Chief Minister.
25.tq: Apply the precise constitutional distinction between the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council.
xs: A CM who sits in the **Legislative Council** does **not vote in the election of the President** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Only **elected members of State Legislative Assemblies** (and elected MPs) form the electoral college; **all members of Legislative Councils**, elected or nominated, are excluded.
Being **Chief Minister** gives no vote, and the Governor nominates no one into the electoral college.
xa: This exact point was an **APPSC-GS 2025** key.
**Elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry** vote, added by the **70th Amendment, 1992**.
⚠ The **VP's electoral college** is **all MPs, elected and nominated**, and has **no MLAs**.

25.s: The procedure of impeachment of the President and the method of electing the President in the Indian Constitution were borrowed respectively from
25.x: Impeachment of the President is modelled on the USA, while election by proportional representation through the single transferable vote is taken from Ireland. 'Ireland and USA' reverses them; the UK has no elected President to impeach; Canada is the source of a strong Centre and residuary powers, not impeachment.
25.tq: Impeachment = USA; PR-STV election = Ireland.
xs: **Impeachment** was borrowed from the **USA** and the **election method** from **Ireland** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses them.
xa: Election: **proportional representation by STV**, **secret ballot** (**Art. 55(3)**).
Impeachment ground: **"violation of the Constitution"** (**Art. 61**).

25.s: Which of the following statements regarding vacancy in the office of the President is incorrect?
o: In case of death, resignation, removal or otherwise, the Vice-President acts as President.

25.x: Article 71 of the Indian Constitution provides matters relating to, or connected with, the election of a President or Vice-President. As per Article 71(1), all doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice-President shall be inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court, whose decision shall be final. Article 71(2) says, If the election of a person as President or Vice-President is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done by him in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office of President or Vice-President, as the case may be, on or before the date of the decision of the Supreme Court shall not be invalidated by reason of that declaration. As per Article 71 (4), the election of a person as President or Vice President shall not be called in question on the ground of the existence of any vacancy for whatever reason among the members of the Electoral College electing him. Thus, postponement is not an option. As regards the Indian President, the Constitution does not prescribe any time-limit within which he has to take the decision with respect to a bill presented to him for his assent. Hence all three statements are incorrect.

25.s: Which Article of the Indian constitution provides the Provisions related to the impeachment of the President?
25.x: Article 61 of the Indian Constitution provides the procedure for impeachment of the President. As per this provision, the President can be removed from office by a process of impeachment (a quasi-judicial procedure in the Parliament) for ‘violation of the Constitution’. However, the Constitution does not define the meaning of the phrase “violation of the Constitution’. The impeachment charges can be initiated by either House of Parliament after giving a 14 days’ Prior-notice to the President. These charges should be signed by one-fourth of the members of the House (that framed the charges). After the impeachment resolution is passed by a majority of two-thirds of the total membership of that House, it is sent to the other House, which should investigate the charges. If the other House also sustains the charges and passes the impeachment resolution by a majority of two-thirds of the total membership, then the President stands removed from his office from the date on which the resolution is so passed. However, no President has so far been impeached.

26.s:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :

II. An Ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right.
III. An Ordinance can come into effect from a back date.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: The scope of an ordinance is the same as the scope of the ordinary legislative powers of Parliament. An ordinance can amend any Central Act, but it cannot amend the Constitution. Therefore, Statement I is correct. An ordinance “is subject to the same constitutional limitations as an Act of Parliament; therefore, it cannot take away or abridge any Fundamental Right in a manner that violates the basic structure of the Indian Constitution.” Therefore, Statement II is incorrect. In Indian law, a “retrospective law” is one that is enacted later but is made effective from an earlier date. Like any other Act, an ordinance can also be made effective retrospectively; therefore, Statement III is correct. Therefore, only Statements I and III are correct.

⚠ The **President** resigns to the **Vice-President** — the reverse pair is a common trap.
xa: The VP's **oath** is administered by the **President** (**Art 69**).
**Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned on health grounds under **Art 67(a)** in **July 2025**.
Term: **5 years**, re-eligible **any number of times**.

27.s: Which Article makes the Vice-President the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
27.x: Article 64 makes the Vice-President ex-officio Chairman; 63 creates the office, 66 covers election and 67 the term.
n: Article 63 provides for a Vice-President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha under Article 64. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The term of office of the Vice-President is five years under Article 67. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: **Article 69:** VP's **oath**, administered by the **President**.
**Article 71:** election disputes decided by the **Supreme Court** — final.
**Article 65:** VP **acts as President** during a vacancy, for at most **six months**.
⚠ **Article 68:** vacancy election "as soon as possible", **no deadline** — unlike the President's **6 months** (Art 62).

27.s: The office of the Vice-President of India is modelled on that of the:
o: Deputy Prime Minister of the UK
27.x: The Indian Vice-President's office is modelled on the American Vice-President.
n: The Vice-President holds the second-highest constitutional office after the President in the Order of Precedence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The office of the Vice-President is modelled on the American Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is eligible for re-election any number of times. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: **Dr. S. Radhakrishnan** was also the **longest-serving** VP — **two** terms (**1952-62**).
**Mohammad Hamid Ansari:** only VP to serve **two full terms** (**2007-17**).
⚠ **S. Radhakrishnan** = first VP; **C.P. Radhakrishnan** = present VP (**2025**).

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President:
1. He is eligible for re-election any number of times.
2. He has a casting vote in case of a tie in the Rajya Sabha.
3. He does not preside when a resolution for his removal is under consideration.
Which of the above statements are correct?
27.x: All three are correct: the Vice-President can be re-elected any number of times, has a casting vote in a tie, and does not preside while his own removal is considered.
n: The Vice-President is eligible for re-election any number of times. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President presides over the sittings of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President has a casting vote in case of a tie in the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President does not preside when a resolution for the Vice-President’s removal is under consideration. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: Removal: **Rajya Sabha resolution** by a **majority of all the then members**, agreed to by the **Lok Sabha**.
**Fourteen-day** notice; **no formal impeachment** like the President's.
The VP is **not a member** of either House — **not a part of Parliament**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Parliament consists of the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
2. The Vice-President, as ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, is a constituent part of Parliament.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
27.x: Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha but is not a constituent part of Parliament.
n: The Parliament consists of the President, the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The Vice-President is not a constituent member of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xa: The VP is elected by **members of both Houses** — **elected and nominated** MPs.
**State Legislatures** have **no role** in the VP's election.
Method: **proportional representation** by **Single Transferable Vote**, **secret ballot**.

27.s:
Assertion (A): The President of India is removed by impeachment by Parliament.
Reason (R): The impeachment procedure requires 14 days’ notice and a two-thirds majority of the total membership.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
27.x: Both are true: the President is removed by impeachment under Article 61, which needs 14 days' notice and two-thirds of the total membership of each House. R only describes the procedure; it does not explain why removal is by impeachment.
27.tq: Ask whether R gives a reason or merely a procedure.
n: The President of India is removed by impeachment by Parliament under Article 61. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The impeachment of the President of India requires 14 days’ notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The impeachment of the President of India requires two-thirds of the total membership. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is not the explanation** of A — option **(2)**.
A: the **President** is removed by **impeachment** by **Parliament** — **Article 61**.
R: impeachment needs **14 days'** notice and **two-thirds** of the **total membership** — it describes the procedure, not why.
xa: The **VP** has **no formal impeachment** — removal by a **Rajya Sabha resolution** agreed to by the **Lok Sabha**.
The **Governor** is removed by the President **at pleasure**, **without impeachment**.
President's impeachment may begin in **either House**.

27.s: Who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
27.x: The Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
n: The President appoints the Prime Minister under Article 75(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The President appoints other Union Ministers on the advice of the Prime Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The President is the Head of State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The Prime Minister is the Head of Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
xa: Executive power is constitutionally vested in the **President** — **Article 53**.
The VP holds the **second-highest** office in the Order of Precedence.

27.s: Who administers the oath of office to the Vice-President of India?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The senior-most judge of the Supreme Court
27.x: Under Article 69 the President administers the Vice-President's oath; the CJI administers the President's oath.
xa: The VP is **re-eligible any number of times**.
Removal resolution: **only in the RS**, by **effective majority**; LS agrees by **simple majority**; **no grounds** stated.
Resignation is addressed to the **President** (**Art 67(a)**), effective immediately.

27.s: Which of the following is NOT a duty of the Prime Minister under Article 78?
o: Furnishing information relating to administration when called for by the President
Submitting for the consideration of the Council any matter decided by an individual Minister when the President requires it
Communicating to the President decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to administration and legislative proposals
Administering the oath of office and secrecy to all Union Ministers
27.x: Options A, B and C are duties of the Prime Minister under Article 78 (communicating Council decisions, furnishing information, and placing a minister's individual decision before the Council when the President requires). Administering the oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers is done by the President, not the PM.
27.tq: Find the one function belonging to the President rather than the Prime Minister.
xs: **Administering the oath** to Union Ministers is NOT a PM duty under Art 78 — the **President** administers it — so option **(4)** is correct.

**Art 78** duties: **communicate all decisions** of the CoM and legislative proposals; **furnish information** called for; submit a minister's sole decision to the **CoM** if the President requires — options (1)-(3).
xa: **Art 77(1):** all executive action is **expressed in the President's name**.
**Art 74(2):** ministerial advice is **not inquired into** by any court.
The PM's own oath is also administered by the **President**.

27.s: Who was the first Deputy Prime Minister of India?
27.x: Sardar Patel was the first Deputy PM; the office is not mentioned in the Constitution and its holder takes oath as an ordinary Minister.
xa: Table of Precedence: **President 1, VP 2, PM 3**.
The **PMO** is also not mentioned in the Constitution — an **extra-constitutional staff agency**.
**Leader of the House (LS)** is likewise **not a constitutional office**.

27.s: Who administers the Oath of Office and the Oath of Secrecy to a Union Minister?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
27.x: The President administers the oath of office and the oath of secrecy to Union Ministers, in the forms given in the Third Schedule.
27.tq: Recall who swears in Union Ministers.
n: The President administers the Oath of Office to Union Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The President administers the Oath of Secrecy to Union Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The Oath of Office and Oath of Secrecy are provided under the Third Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
xs: The **President** administers the Oath of Office and Secrecy to Union Ministers — option **(1)**.
The oath forms for Ministers are in the **Third Schedule**; the oath is under **Article 75(4)**.
The **Vice-President** takes his oath before the President but administers none to Ministers.
xa: The **President's** own oath (**Article 60**) is given by the **Chief Justice of India**.
The **Governor's** oath (**Article 159**) is given by the **Chief Justice** of the **High Court**.
⚠ Oaths of the **President**, **VP** and **Governor** are codified in their **Articles**, **not** in the **Third Schedule**.

27.s: To whom does the Governor of a State address his resignation?
o: The Chief Justice of the High Court
27.x: The Governor resigns to the President; the High Court's Chief Justice administers his oath.
n: The oath of the Governor of a State is administered by the Chief Justice of the High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The oath of the Governor of a State may be administered by the senior-most High Court Judge if the Chief Justice is unavailable. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor of a State addresses resignation to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor takes oath from the Chief Justice of the State High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor resigns to the President of India under Article 156(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xa: The Governor is removed by the **President** **at pleasure** — **Article 156** — **without impeachment**.
The **VP** resigns to the **President**; his oath (**Article 69**) is given by the **President**.

27.s: Which of the following pairs (office – Article on its oath) is correctly matched?
27.x: The Vice-President's oath is in Article 69. The President's is in Article 60, the Governor's in Article 159 and Union Ministers' in Article 75(4).
n: The governing oath article for the President of India is Article 60. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The governing oath article for the Vice-President of India is Article 69. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The governing oath article for the Prime Minister and Union Ministers is Article 75(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The governing oath article for the Governor of a State is Article 159. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xa: ⚠ Forms for **60**, **69** and **159** are written in the Articles themselves — **not** in the **Third Schedule**.
President's oath is given by the **Chief Justice of India**; the VP's by the **President**.

27.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The forms of oath for the President, Vice-President and Governor are codified directly in their respective Articles.
The Governor’s oath is governed by the Third Schedule.
The Vice-President’s oath is governed by Article 69.
The President’s oath is governed by Article 60.
27.x: Option B is incorrect: the Governor's oath is written into Article 159 itself, like the President's (60) and Vice-President's (69). The Third Schedule holds the other oaths.
27.tq: Recall the three oaths written into their own Articles.
n: The governing oath article for the President of India is Article 60. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The governing oath article for the Vice-President of India is Article 69. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The oath form for the President is codified directly in Article 60. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The oath form for the Vice-President is codified directly in Article 69. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The oath form for the Governor is codified directly in Article 159. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The oath forms for the President, Vice-President and Governor are not contained in the Third Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Governor's oath is governed by the Third Schedule** — option **(2)**.
The Governor's oath form is **codified directly** in **Article 159**.
Likewise the **President's** oath is in **Article 60** and the **VP's** in **Article 69**.
xa: Union Ministers' oath forms (oath of **office** and **secrecy**) are in the **Third Schedule**.
The Governor's oath is administered by the **Chief Justice** of the **High Court**.
CM and State Ministers swear under **164(3)** before the **Governor**.

27.s: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha addresses his resignation to the:
o: Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha
27.x: Under Article 94 the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker.
n: The Vice-President communicates the President’s resignation to the Lok Sabha Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Vice-President of India addresses resignation to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor of a State addresses resignation to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Chief Minister and State Ministers address resignation to the Governor of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor resigns to the President of India under Article 156(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xa: The VP **communicates** the President's resignation to the **Lok Sabha Speaker**.
Union Ministers **route** resignations **through** the **Prime Minister**; State Ministers **through** the **Chief Minister**.

27.s:
Assertion (A): A State Minister’s removal route is through the Chief Minister’s advice.
Reason (R): The Chief Minister and State Ministers take the oath of office and secrecy under Article 164(3).
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
27.x: Both are true: the Governor dismisses State Ministers on the Chief Minister's advice, and they take their oaths under Article 164(3). The oath does not explain removal, so R does not explain A.
27.tq: Ask whether an oath provision explains a removal route.
n: The governing oath article for the Chief Minister and State Ministers is Article 164(3). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
Article 164(3) covers the oath of office and oath of secrecy for the Chief Minister and State Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor dismisses State Ministers on the advice of the Chief Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is not the explanation** of A — option **(2)**.
A: State Ministers are **dismissed** by the **Governor** on the **advice** of the **Chief Minister**.
R: CM and State Ministers take oath of **office** and **secrecy** under **Article 164(3)** — the oath does not explain removal.
xa: They also go upon **loss** of the **Assembly majority**.
State Ministers **route** their resignations **through** the **Chief Minister** to the **Governor**.
Union counterpart: **Article 75(4)** oath; dismissal by the **President** on the **PM's advice**.

27.s: Prime Minister of India is generally-
27.x: The Prime Minister of India is generally a member of the Lok Sabha, but this is not compulsory or restricted. He can be a member of the Rajya Sabha. Indira Gandhi was the first PM from the Rajya Sabha at the time of appointment but later became a member of the Lok Sabha.

27.s: Who among the following was the member of Lok Sabha during his Prime Ministership?
27.x: Deve Gowda, I.K. Gujral, and Dr. Manmohan Singh were not members of the Lok Sabha during their Prime Ministership, while Chandra Shekhar was the Prime Minister of India from 1990 to 1991 and also a Member of Parliament from Balia Lok Sabha Constituency.

27.s: Who is the head of the National Defence Committee?
27.x: The National Defence Committee is headed by the Prime Minister.

27.s: The Prime Minister is –
o: Nominated by the Party in Majority of Lok Sabha
27.x: Article 75(1) says that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. Article 75(2) says that the Ministers shall hold the office during the pleasure of the President.

27.s: Who presides over the meetings of the National Development Council of India?
o: Deputy Chairman of Planning Commission of India

27.s: The Vice-President of India is ex officio President of which of the following bodies?
27.x: The Vice-President is also the ex-officio President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA).
27.tq: Use the exact institutional title to distinguish ICWA from other national bodies.
xs: The VP is ex officio **President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
His other ex-officio role is **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** (**Art. 64**).
xa: VP qualifications: **citizen**, **35 years**, eligible for election to the **Rajya Sabha**.
Electoral college: **members of both Houses**, elected **and nominated**, by **PR-STV**.
⚠ The VP holds **no other office of profit**, but ex-officio posts like these are part of the office.

27.s: A vacancy in the office of the Vice-President of India is to be filled
o: Within six months of the vacancy in every case
As soon as possible, without a constitutionally prescribed six-month deadline
Within one year, after approval by the Supreme Court
Only at the next general election to the Lok Sabha
27.x: Article 68 requires an election to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President as soon as possible. Unlike the vacancy in the office of President, no six-month deadline is prescribed for this election.
27.tq: Compare the vacancy rules for President and Vice-President, especially the presence or absence of a fixed deadline.
xs: A VP vacancy is filled **"as soon as possible"**, with **no deadline** (**Art 68**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **six-month** limit applies to a **President's** vacancy (**Art 62**), not the VP's.
xa: **Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned in **July 2025** — the **third mid-term vacancy** after **V.V. Giri (1969)** and **Krishan Kant (2002)**.
**C.P. Radhakrishnan** was elected after that vacancy (**September 2025**).
The VP continues in office till the successor takes charge (**Art 67(c)**).

27.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the tenure of the Prime Minister?
o: The Prime Minister can be removed only by the Supreme Court.
The Prime Minister holds office for life unless removed by impeachment.
The Prime Minister continues in office while commanding the confidence of the Lok Sabha, subject to the President's pleasure in the constitutional sense.
The Prime Minister has a fixed tenure of five years irrespective of legislative support.
27.x: The Prime Minister has no fixed tenure and ordinarily continues while enjoying the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The Constitution formally states that Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure.
27.tq: Reject the fixed-term trap and connect tenure with legislative confidence.
xs: The PM has **no fixed tenure**: he holds office during the **President's pleasure**, in practice while he commands a **Lok Sabha** majority — so option **(3)** is correct.
There is **no five-year fixed term**, no **impeachment**, and no removal by the **Supreme Court** for the PM.
xa: **Art. 75(2):** ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President**, who removes a minister only **on the PM's advice**.
**No term limit for the PM:** **Ambedkar** preferred daily parliamentary accountability to fixed terms.
PM = **de facto** head of government; President = **de jure** head of State.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the Prime Minister of India:
1. He is appointed by the President under Article 75(1).
2. He must be a member of the Lok Sabha at the time of appointment.
3. His oath of office is administered by the President.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: the President appoints the PM under Article 75(1), by convention the leader of the Lok Sabha majority. Statement 2 is wrong: the PM may belong to either House, and a non-member can be PM for six months. Statement 3 is correct: the President administers the oath. Hence '1 and 3 only'; options with 2 are wrong.
27.tq: PM: either House, or none for 6 months.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **President** appoints the PM under **Art 75(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the PM **may belong to either House**, and a non-member can be PM for **six months**.
Statement 3 is correct: the PM's **oath** is administered by the **President** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: By convention the PM is the leader of the **Lok Sabha majority**.
**P.V. Narasimha Rao** became PM in **1991** without being an MP and later won **Nandyal**.
⚠ The **UK PM** must belong to the **House of Commons**; the Indian PM may come from either House.

27.s: Which one of the following correctly states the ruling in S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)?
o: A non-member cannot be repeatedly reappointed as Minister without getting elected.
Only a member of the Lok Sabha can be appointed as a Minister.
A non-member may be reappointed as Minister indefinitely without election.
A non-member cannot be appointed as Prime Minister under any circumstances.
27.x: The Supreme Court held that the constitutional provision for a non-member Minister cannot be used for repeated reappointments without the person securing election to the legislature.
27.tq: Discriminate the judicial limitation from the general six-month rule.
xs: In **S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)**, a non-member **cannot be re-appointed** repeatedly as minister **without getting elected** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art 75(5)** lets **any person** be a minister for **six months**, so options (2), (3) and (4) are wrong — a non-member can even be **PM** for six months.
xa: The six-month rule is **six consecutive months** and **applies to the PM** too.
UPSC notes spell the case name **"S.R. Chauhan"**.
The PM **may belong to either House** of Parliament.

27.s: A non-member appointed as a Union Minister must become a member of either House of Parliament within:
27.x: The six-month rule applies to every non-member Minister, including the Prime Minister.
xa: **S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001):** no repeated **re-appointment** without election.
**P.V. Narasimha Rao (1991)** became PM without being an MP and later entered the LS from **Nandyal**.
Ministers are appointed by the President on the **PM's advice**.

27.s: During a National Emergency, the President of India
o: acquires unrestricted discretion to disregard the advice of the Council of Ministers
continues to be bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers
becomes the real executive in place of the Prime Minister
may dismiss the entire Council without following constitutional advice
27.x: A National Emergency does not confer discretionary power on the President to disregard the binding advice of the Council of Ministers. The parliamentary executive relationship continues.
27.tq: Guard against the emergency-powers trap by checking whether the constitutional advice requirement has been altered.
xs: During a **National Emergency** the President **continues to be bound** by the CoM's advice — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ The President does **not** acquire **discretionary powers** in an emergency — a PYQ trap; options (1), (3), (4) assume such powers.
xa: **Art 74(1):** advice is binding **after one reconsideration**.
**Art 74(2):** advice is **not inquired into** by any court.
PM = **de facto** head of government; President = **de jure** head of State.

27.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the position of the Prime Minister in the United Kingdom from that in India?
o: The UK Prime Minister must belong to the House of Lords, whereas the Indian Prime Minister must belong to the Lok Sabha.
The UK Prime Minister must belong to the House of Commons, whereas the Indian Prime Minister may belong to either House of Parliament.
Both the UK and Indian Prime Ministers must be members of the lower House.
Neither the UK nor the Indian Prime Minister may be a member of the upper House.
27.x: The UK Prime Minister must belong to the House of Commons, while the Indian Prime Minister may be a member of either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.
27.tq: Use the House-membership distinction to separate the British and Indian parliamentary arrangements.
xs: The **UK PM** must belong to the **House of Commons**, while the **Indian PM** may belong to **either House** — so option **(2)** is correct.
India has had Rajya Sabha PMs: **Indira Gandhi** (first, **1966**), **Deve Gowda**, **I.K. Gujral**, **Manmohan Singh** — so options (1), (3), (4) fail.
xa: A **non-member** can be PM for **six months** (**Art 75(5)**).
By convention the PM is the leader of the **Lok Sabha majority**.
The PM is appointed by the **President** under **Art 75(1)**.

27.s: What is the maximum period for which the Vice-President may act as President when the office of President falls vacant or the President is unable to discharge functions?
27.x: The Vice-President can act as President for at most six months, within which a new President must be elected.
27.tq: Recall the six-month limit.
n: The maximum period for which the Vice-President acts as President is six months. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
An election for a new President must be held within six months when the Vice-President acts as President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President acts as President under Article 65 when the office of the President falls vacant. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President acts as President when the President is unable to discharge the President’s functions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xs: The VP can act as President for a maximum of **six months** — option **(1)**.
A new President must be **elected within six months** of the vacancy (**Article 65** context; Art 62).
He acts on **death, resignation, removal**, or when the President is **unable to discharge functions** (absence, illness).
xa: While acting as President he **ceases to be RS Chairman** → the **Deputy Chairman** presides.
He draws the **President's salary, allowances and privileges**, not the Chairman's.
As Chairman of the RS his salary is **not charged** on the **Consolidated Fund of India**.

27.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Prime Minister is the real Executive Head of the Union.
The Prime Minister can be a member of either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.
The Prime Minister is responsible to the Rajya Sabha.
The Prime Minister is appointed by the President.
27.x: C is incorrect: the Prime Minister and his Council are responsible only to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), even if he is a Rajya Sabha member. He is the real executive head, appointed by the President.
27.tq: Collective responsibility runs to the Lok Sabha alone.
n: The Prime Minister is the real executive head of the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 20-22]
The Prime Minister can be a member of either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 20-22]
The Prime Minister can be a member of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 20-22]
The Prime Minister is not responsible to the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 20-22]
The Prime Minister is responsible only to the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 20-22]
The Prime Minister is appointed by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 20-22]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **PM is responsible to the Rajya Sabha** — option **(3)**.

27.x: The Constitution (Ninety-First Amendment) Act, 2003, restricted the size of Council of Ministers to 15% of legislative members with the objective of strengthening the Anti Defection laws. 28.x: state of decline. The parliamentary government is also known as cabinet government, responsible government, or the Westminster model of government, and is prevalent in Britain, Japan, Canada, and India, among others. A fundamental principle of this system is Collective Responsibility, under which ministers are collectively accountable to Parliament, specifically the Lok Sabha (House of the People), under Article 75. It ensures that the executive is collectively responsible to the legislature and, through it, to the people. The principle also implies that the Lok Sabha can remove the ministry (i.e., council of ministers headed by the prime minister) from office by passing a vote of no confidence.
