30.s: Present Chairman of Rajya Sabha is -
30.x: The Council of States, the Upper House of the Indian Parliament, was constituted in the year 1952. However, the origin of the idea for a Second Chamber can be traced to the “Montague- Chelmsford Reform of 1919”. The Constitution First Amendment Act was enacted in 1951. At that time, the Rajya Sabha did not exist. Article 80 of the Constitution deals with the composition of the Council of States. Clause 1 of this Article provides that the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250, out of which 12 members are nominated by the President and 238 are representatives of the States and of the Union territories. The present strength, however, is 245 members, of whom 233 are representatives of the States and Union territories and 12 are nominated by the President. Currently, there are 8 members ( 3 from NCT Delhi, 1 from Puducherry and 4 from Jammu and Kashmir) elected to the Rajya Sabha. The first Vice-President, Dr. S. Radhakrishnan, is not the only Chairman of the Rajya Sabha who has been in the office for two consecutive terms from 13 May, 1952 to 12 May 1962; Mohammad Hamid Ansari has also been Vice-President/ Chairman of Rajya Sabha for two consecutive terms (2007-2017). The Joint Sitting (Article 108) of the Indian Parliament has been called for only 3 bills: the Dowry Prohibition Bill, 1962, the Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill, 1978 and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill, 2002.

**Parliament + State Legislature:** resign the State seat within **14 days**, else the **Parliament** seat goes.
⚠ **10 days** = both Houses; **14 days** = Parliament + state; **60 days** = absence.

30.s: The allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha to the States remains frozen on the basis of the 1971 Census until
o: the completion of the 2031 Census only
30.x: The 84th Amendment Act, 2001 froze the allocation of Lok Sabha seats based on the 1971 Census until the first Census after 2026.
30.tq: Read the endpoint of a constitutional freeze precisely.
xs: The **84th Amendment (2001)** froze LS seat allocation on the **1971 census** till the first census **after 2026** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **87th Amendment** readjusted constituencies on the **2001** census, without changing the allocation.
xa: Debate: raising LS strength by **50% (to ~815)** once the freeze lifts.
The **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** sought an LS max of **850**; it was defeated (**298 for, 230 against**).
Tamil Nadu resolved to freeze the LS at **543**.

30.s: The readjustment of Lok Sabha constituencies on the basis of the 2001 Census was done by the Delimitation Commission headed by:
30.x: The 87th Amendment enabled readjustment on the 2001 Census; the work was done by the Delimitation Commission under Justice Kuldip Singh.
xa: ⚠ **Kuldip Singh** = Delimitation Commission; **Kuldip Nayar** = RS domicile case.
Largest LS constituency by electors: **Malkajgiri** (Telangana).
Largest by area: **Ladakh**.

30.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Largest Lok Sabha constituency by number of electors — Malkajgiri
Largest Lok Sabha constituency by area — Ladakh
Smallest Lok Sabha constituency by area — Mumbai South
Smallest Lok Sabha constituency by number of electors — Lakshadweep
30.x: C is wrong: the smallest Lok Sabha constituency by area is Chandni Chowk (Delhi), not Mumbai South. Malkajgiri is the largest and Lakshadweep the smallest by number of electors, and Ladakh is the largest by area.
30.tq: Separate area-based comparisons from elector-based comparisons.
xs: **Smallest by area – Mumbai South** is wrong; it is **Chandni Chowk** (Delhi) — so option **(3)** is correct.
The rest are right: **Malkajgiri** largest by electors, **Ladakh** largest by area, **Lakshadweep** smallest by electors.
xa: **Malkajgiri** is in **Telangana**.
Delimitation Commission under Justice **Kuldip Singh** (**2001** census).
Delhi has **7** LS seats.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A candidate for Parliament must be a registered elector in a parliamentary constituency.
2. A Rajya Sabha candidate must be domiciled in the State from which he is elected.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
30.x: A parliamentary candidate must be a registered elector in a parliamentary constituency; the domicile requirement for Rajya Sabha candidates was removed in 2003.
xa: Minimum age: **25** (LS) and **30** (RS).
Must **not hold an office of profit**.
**No minimum educational qualification**.

30.s: Which is the second-largest Lok Sabha constituency by geographical area?
30.x: Ladakh is the largest, Barmer the second-largest and Kachchh the third; Chandni Chowk is the smallest.
n: Ladakh is the largest Lok Sabha constituency by geographical area. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The area of the Ladakh Lok Sabha constituency is 173,266 square kilometres. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Barmer is the second-largest Lok Sabha constituency by geographical area. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The area of the Barmer Lok Sabha constituency is 55,074 square kilometres. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Kachchh is the third-largest Lok Sabha constituency by geographical area. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The area of the Kachchh Lok Sabha constituency is 41,414 square kilometres. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Chandni Chowk in Delhi is the smallest Lok Sabha constituency by geographical area. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xa: Fourth- and fifth-largest: **Arunachal East** and **Arunachal West**.
Largest by electors: **Malkajgiri** (Telangana); smallest: **Lakshadweep**.
⚠ **Kuldip Singh** = Delimitation Commission; **Kuldip Nayar** = RS domicile case.

30.s: Women Members elected to Loksabha in the 2009 general elections are:
30.x: A record 59 women members were elected to the 15th Lok Sabha in the 2009 general elections.

30.s: Which Lok Sabha was extended during the National Emergency of 1975–1977?
30.x: The Fifth Lok Sabha, constituted for the period 1971–1977, was extended during the 1975–1977 Emergency.
30.tq: Discriminate between closely numbered Lok Sabhas and their distinct events.
xs: The **5th Lok Sabha** (**1971-77**) was extended during the **1975-77** Emergency — so option **(4) Fifth Lok Sabha** is correct.
The **4th** (**1970**) and **6th** (**1979**) were dissolved early, not extended.
xa: Extension is **by law**, **1 year at a time**, not beyond **6 months** after the emergency.
**6th LS (1977)** had the **lowest share** of women MPs.
**18 Lok Sabhas** constituted so far.

30.s: Which one of the following statements regarding women’s representation in Parliament is correct?
o: Women constitute less than 5 per cent in both Houses of Parliament.
Women constitute about 15 per cent in the Lok Sabha and about 14 per cent in the Rajya Sabha.
Women constitute more than one-third in both Houses of Parliament.
Women constitute about 14 per cent in the Lok Sabha and about 15 per cent in the Rajya Sabha.
30.x: Women’s representation is approximately 15 per cent in the Lok Sabha and 14 per cent in the Rajya Sabha. These figures are separate from the future constitutional reservation of one-third seats.
30.tq: Compare the two Houses carefully instead of transferring the percentage from one House to the other.
xs: Women are **about 15% in the LS** and **about 14% in the RS** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the two; neither House is below 5% or above one-third.
xa: The **Union CoM** has **11 women**.
The **106th Amendment, 2023** reserves **33%** of LS and Assembly seats for women.

30.s: In which Lok Sabha did women members cross 10 per cent of the total membership for the first time?
30.x: Women members crossed 10 per cent of the total strength of the House for the first time in the 15th Lok Sabha, elected in 2009.
30.tq: Link the threshold event with the correct Lok Sabha number and election period.
xs: Women crossed **10%** for the first time in the **15th Lok Sabha** (**2009**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
xa: This was an **APPSC-G2 2023** key.
⚠ FIRST above 10% = **15th**; highest = **17th** (**78**); lowest share = **6th** (**1977**).

30.s: In which year was the first Women's Reservation Bill introduced?
30.x: The first Bill came in 1996 and was passed by the Rajya Sabha in 2010; the 106th Amendment was enacted in 2023.
xa: It reserves **33%** (one-third) of seats in the Lok Sabha and state Assemblies (**Art. 334A**).
The reservation lasts **15 years**, extendable.
It is called the **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam**.

30.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: 15th Lok Sabha — 2009 — Women crossed 10 per cent for the first time
30.x: The 106th Constitutional Amendment providing one-third reservation for women was enacted in 2023, not 2010. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
30.tq: Check the year attached to the constitutional amendment against the years of the Lok Sabha milestones.
xs: **106th Amendment — 2010** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**; the 106th Amendment is of **2023**.
**2010** is when a Women's Reservation Bill **passed the Rajya Sabha**.
xa: The first Bill was introduced in **1996**.
The **106th Amendment** inserted **Art. 334A**.

30.s:
Consider the following about the veto powers of the President:
1. Absolute veto
2. Suspensive veto
3. Pocket veto
Which of the above does the President possess?
30.x: The President has an absolute veto, a suspensive veto (returning a Bill once) and a pocket veto (keeping it pending).
n: The President has an absolute veto. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President has a suspensive veto. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President has a pocket veto. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President may exercise a pocket veto as a limited discretionary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: **Article 123:** **Ordinances** when Parliament is **not in session**.
**Article 87:** special address at the **first session of each year** and after each **general election**.
**No bill becomes law without his assent** — why he is part of Parliament.

30.s: Reservation of Lok Sabha seats for SCs and STs was initially provided for:
30.x: Seats are reserved for SCs and STs in proportion to their population; the reservation was first given for ten years.
n: Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes in the Lok Sabha in proportion to their population. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
Seats are reserved for Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha in proportion to their population. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
Reservation of Lok Sabha seats was initially provided for 10 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
xa: The **104th** Amendment extended it until **2030**.
The same Amendment ended **Anglo-Indian** nomination from **25 Jan 2020**.
**87th Amendment:** constituencies readjusted on the **2001** census.

30.s: The lowest representation of women, only 19 MPs, was recorded in which Lok Sabha?
30.x: The 6th Lok Sabha (1977) had the fewest women members, only 19 MPs.
n: The 6th Lok Sabha had the lowest representation of women among the stated electoral milestones. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #76 · pp 207-210]
The 6th Lok Sabha was elected in 1977. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #76 · pp 207-210]
The 6th Lok Sabha had 19 women Members of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #76 · pp 207-210]
xa: **15th** LS (**2009**): **59** women — first time above **10%**.

30.s: Parliament in India normally holds which three sessions in a year?
30.x: There is no fixed constitutional calendar, but Parliament normally has Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions.
xa: **Art. 85** sets **no minimum number of sitting days**.
Monsoon Session **2026** ran from **20 July** and was adjourned sine die on **13 Aug**.

30.s:
Arrange in the correct procedural sequence after the business of a session concludes:
1. Prorogation by the President
2. Adjournment sine die by the Speaker or Chairman
3. Reassembly in a new session
4. Recess
30.x: The Speaker or Chairman first adjourns the House sine die, the President then prorogues it, a recess follows and the House reassembles in a new session.
xa: **Recess** = period between **prorogation and reassembly in a new session**.
**Adjournment** only suspends a sitting for a specified time.

30.s: A Member of Parliament enjoys freedom from arrest in civil cases during the session and:
30.x: The privilege covers civil arrest during the session and forty days before and after it; it does not cover criminal cases or preventive detention.
xa: Members are also exempt from **jury service**.
Privileges are **co-terminous with membership**.

30.s: Which Article deals with Appropriation Bills?
30.x: Article 114 covers Appropriation Bills; 100 is voting and quorum, 105 privileges and 113 the procedure for estimates.
n: Article 100 concerns voting and quorum in Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 105 concerns the powers and privileges of the Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 113 concerns the procedure for estimates. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 114 concerns Appropriation Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: Quorum under **Article 100** is **one-tenth** of the total membership.
**Article 112:** **Annual Financial Statement (Budget)**.
**Article 123:** President's power to promulgate **Ordinances**.

30.s: Under Article 123, the President can promulgate an Ordinance when:
o: A National Emergency is in operation
The Rajya Sabha rejects a Bill
30.x: The President issues Ordinances under Article 123 only when Parliament (either House) is not in session.
n: The President promulgates Ordinances when Parliament is not in session under Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President’s Ordinance-making power is co-extensive with the legislative power of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: **Prorogation** ends a **session**, not the House; **dissolution** applies **only to the Lok Sabha**.
The President **summons** each House under **Article 85**.
Maximum gap between two sessions: **six months**.

30.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: A sitting is a daily meeting of the House during a session.
Prorogation terminates the House itself but not its session.
Dissolution ends the life of the House and applies only to the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment terminates a sitting for a specified period.
30.x: Prorogation ends the session, not the House; only dissolution ends the House, and only the Lok Sabha can be dissolved.
n: A sitting is a daily meeting of a House during a session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Adjournment terminates a daily sitting for a specified time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation terminates a session of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation does not terminate the House itself. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution ends the life of the House entirely. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution applies only to the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The specified period of an adjournment may be hours, days, or weeks. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation terminates a session and may be effected by the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution terminates a House and may be effected by the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xa: **Adjournment sine die** ends a sitting **without fixing a date** for reassembly.
Adjournment is by the **Presiding Officer**; prorogation by the **President**.
The **Rajya Sabha** is permanent and cannot be dissolved.

30.s: Termination of a session of a House, without ending the life of the House, is called:
30.x: Prorogation ends the session; adjournment ends a sitting for a set time, adjournment sine die ends it without a date, and dissolution ends the House.
n: Adjournment terminates a daily sitting for a specified time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Adjournment sine die terminates a sitting without assigning a day for reassembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation terminates a session of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution ends the life of the House entirely. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The specified period of an adjournment may be hours, days, or weeks. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation terminates a session and may be effected by the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution terminates a House and may be effected by the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xa: Prorogation usually follows **adjournment sine die**.
**Recess:** period between **prorogation** and a new session.
Adjournment may be for **hours, days or weeks**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Recess is the period between the prorogation of a session and the start of a new session.
2. During recess, the President may issue ordinances under Article 123.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
30.x: A recess is the gap between prorogation and the next session, and during it the President can issue ordinances under Article 123.
n: A recess is the period between the prorogation of a session and the commencement of a new session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The President may issue ordinances under Article 123 when Parliament is in recess. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xa: Maximum gap between sessions: **six months** (**Article 85**).
**Session:** from the **first sitting** to **prorogation or dissolution**.
**Sitting:** a **daily** meeting — **morning** and **post-lunch** sittings.

30.s: The quorum for conducting official business in a House of Parliament is what fraction of its total membership?
30.x: Under Article 100, the quorum is one-tenth of the House's total membership.
30.tq: Recall the quorum fraction.
n: Quorum is the minimum number of members required to conduct official business. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The quorum under Article 100 is one-tenth of the total membership of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: The quorum is **one-tenth** of the total membership — option **(1)**.
**Article 100** deals with **voting and quorum**; the same fraction applies to the **Rajya Sabha**.
xa: **Art. 98:** separate secretarial staff for each House.
**Art. 118:** rules of procedure; **Art. 120:** language — **Hindi or English**.
Lok Sabha Secretariat is under the **Speaker**; Rajya Sabha Secretariat under the **Chairman**.

30.s: The provision that the Speaker or Chairman may refuse to accept a member's resignation if satisfied that it is not voluntary or genuine was introduced by the
30.x: The 33rd Amendment Act, 1974 amended Article 101(3)(b) so that a resignation takes effect only on acceptance, and the presiding officer may reject it if it is not voluntary or genuine. The 24th Amendment concerned Parliament's amending power, the 42nd was the 'mini-Constitution' of the Emergency, and the 52nd added the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection).
30.tq: 33rd Amendment (1974) = resignation must be voluntary and genuine; 52nd (1985) = anti-defection.
xs: The **33rd Amendment Act, 1974** streamlined acceptance of resignation — it **may be rejected if not voluntary or genuine** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Resignation is **subject to acceptance** under **Art 101(3)(b)**, unlike judges or the President.
xa: **61st Amendment (1987)**: voting age **18 years**.
**84th Amendment (2001)**: froze LS seat allocation on the **1971 census**.

30.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Demands for grants — Rajya Sabha may vote on them
Money Bill — Rajya Sabha to return it within fourteen days
Joint sitting — Presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
30.x: The Rajya Sabha may discuss the Budget but cannot vote on demands for grants. A Money Bill is returned within fourteen days, a joint sitting is presided over by the Lok Sabha Speaker, and a no-confidence motion is moved in the Lok Sabha.
30.tq: Find the option that reverses the financial or accountability superiority of the Lok Sabha.
xs: **Demands for grants — RS may vote on them** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**.
The RS may **discuss the budget** but **cannot vote on demands for grants**.
Correct pairs: Money Bill returned in **14 days**; **joint sitting** presided by the **Speaker**; **no-confidence motion** in the LS.
xa: The **Speaker** decides what is a **Money Bill**.
At a **joint sitting**, LS numbers prevail.

30.s: A Financial Bill of category I:
o: Can be introduced in either House of Parliament
Can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha
Can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and both Houses have equal powers in its passage
Can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days
30.x: A Financial Bill of category I can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, but unlike a Money Bill both Houses have equal powers in its passage.
xa: A Money Bill must be returned by the RS within **14 days**.
The President may return **Financial Bills (I) and (II)** for reconsideration.

30.s: If the two Houses of Parliament disagree on a constitutional amendment bill, which one of the following is the consequence?
o: The bill fails because no joint sitting is permitted for such a bill.
The Lok Sabha may pass the bill by a simple majority in a second sitting.
The Supreme Court decides which version of the bill shall prevail.
The President convenes a joint sitting under Article 108.
30.x: There is no provision for a joint sitting in respect of a constitutional amendment bill. Failure to secure the required approval in either House causes the bill to fall.
30.tq: Ask whether the ordinary deadlock mechanism applies; Article 108 does not apply here.
xs: For a **constitutional amendment bill** there is **no joint sitting**, so the bill fails — option **(1)**.
It needs a **special majority in each House**.
xa: ⚠ A **joint sitting** is presided by the **Speaker**; LS numbers prevail.
Amendments are made under **Art. 368**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 93 deals with the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
2. Article 108 deals with a joint sitting.
3. Article 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement.
Which of the above statements are correct?
30.x: All three are correct: Article 93 – Speaker and Deputy Speaker; Article 108 – joint sitting; Article 112 – Annual Financial Statement.
n: Article 93 concerns the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 108 concerns a joint sitting of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 112 concerns the Annual Financial Statement, or Budget. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Article 113:** procedure for **estimates**; **Article 114:** **Appropriation Bills**.
**Article 116:** **Votes on Account** and **Votes of Credit**.
**Article 117:** special provisions for **Financial Bills**.

30.s: The powers of the Rajya Sabha are restricted in the case of:
30.x: The Rajya Sabha has equal powers on Constitutional Amendment Bills and can introduce Ordinary and Amendment Bills; it is restricted only for Money Bills.
n: The Rajya Sabha has equal powers with the Lok Sabha in Constitutional Amendment Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The Rajya Sabha can introduce Ordinary Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The Rajya Sabha can introduce Constitutional Amendment Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
xa: **Article 249:** authorises Parliament to legislate on a **State List** subject — **two-thirds** present and voting.
**Article 312:** initiates new **All-India Services**.
**Art. 67(b):** removal of the **Vice-President** can be moved **only in the Rajya Sabha**.

30.s: Which Article deals with the procedure for impeachment of the President?
30.x: Impeachment is under Article 61; Article 109 covers the Rajya Sabha's 14 days on Money Bills and 90(c) the Deputy Chairman's removal.
n: Fourteen days is the prior-notice period for the impeachment of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Article 61 governs the prior notice for the President's impeachment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Fourteen days is the period for consideration of a Money Bill by the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Article 109 governs the Rajya Sabha's consideration of a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Fourteen days is the period for resolving simultaneous membership of Parliament and a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
The Representation of the People Act, 1951 governs simultaneous membership resignation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Fourteen days is the notice period for removing the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Article 90(c) governs the removal notice for the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
xa: All four carry a **fourteen-day** limit.
Simultaneous membership is also governed by the **Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950**.

30.s: How many Rajya Sabha seats does Andhra Pradesh have?
30.x: Andhra Pradesh has 11 Rajya Sabha seats; Telangana has 7, Uttarakhand 3 and Tripura 1.
xa: APPSC **2023** asked AP's RS seats → **11**.
AP: **25** Lok Sabha seats, Assembly **175**.
Telangana: **17** LS, **119** Assembly.

30.s: During a National Emergency, the term of the Lok Sabha can be extended by law for:
30.x: The term can be extended one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the Emergency ends.
xa: The **5th Lok Sabha** (**1971-77**) was extended during the **1975-77** Emergency.
Only the LS can resolve to **discontinue a National Emergency**.

30.s: An existing law made by Parliament can be changed only by:
30.x: Only Parliament can change an existing law it has made (APPSC-GS 2024); it legislates on the Union and Concurrent Lists and reviews delegated legislation.
xa: **Art. 249**: RS resolution lets Parliament legislate on a **State List** subject.
**Art. 253**: laws to implement **international treaties** on any subject.

30.s: Which of the following is a judicial function of Parliament?
30.x: Impeachment of the President, removal of the Vice-President, recommending removal of judges and punishing breach of privilege are Parliament's judicial functions.
xa: **Constituent** function: amends the Constitution under **Art. 368**, but cannot alter the **basic structure**.
**Electoral** function: elects the VP and presiding officers.

30.s: Parliamentary privileges in India, which remain uncodified, continue under:
30.x: Parliamentary privileges have not been comprehensively codified; they continue under Article 105(3), historically based on those of the British House of Commons.
xa: Codification is urged to protect **press freedom** and **citizens' rights**.
**Art. 122** bars courts from inquiring into proceedings; it codifies nothing.

30.s: On which of the following matters do the two Houses of Parliament NOT have equal powers?
o: Passing a resolution to discontinue a National Emergency
Approval of an Ordinance promulgated by the President
Removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court
30.x: Only the Lok Sabha can pass a resolution to discontinue a National Emergency; the Houses are equal on the other three.
xa: **No-confidence motion** — only in the LS.
Also equal: **constitutional amendment bills** — special majority in each House, no joint sitting.

30.s: If the Rajya Sabha approves a National Emergency while the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the new Lok Sabha must approve it within ____ of its first sitting.
30.x: The Rajya Sabha may approve the proclamation for the time being; the newly constituted Lok Sabha must approve it within thirty days of its first sitting.
xa: This covers Emergencies under **Arts. 352, 356, 360**.
RS special powers: **Art. 249**, **Art. 312**, **Art. 67(b)**.

30.s: A Bill under Article 3 to form a new State can be introduced in Parliament only on the recommendation of the:
30.x: Such a Bill needs the President's recommendation; the State Legislature's views are sought but are not binding on Parliament.
xa: **Andhra State (1953)** and the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** were both made under **Art. 3**.
**Art. 253**: law to implement **international treaties** on any subject.

30.s: Under which Article can the Rajya Sabha authorise the creation of new All-India Services?
30.x: Article 312 covers new All-India Services; 249 deals with State List legislation in the national interest and 67(b) with initiating the Vice-President's removal.
xa: ⚠ **APPSC-G1 2017** trap: RS does **not** "authorise State Assemblies" to legislate.
Returning a **money bill with recommendations** is also an RS power.

30.s: A Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 must be supported by:
o: a simple majority of members present and voting
two-thirds of members present and voting
a majority of the total membership
30.x: It needs two-thirds of members present and voting, is valid for one year and can be renewed one year at a time.
xa: **Art. 250**: State List law during a **National Emergency**.
**Art. 356-357**: during President's Rule, Parliament legislates for the state.

30.s: The Law Commission's 170th Report, submitted in 1999, proposed which of the following alternatives in the context of parliamentary representation?
o: A 50 per cent reduction in Rajya Sabha seats
A 25 per cent increase in seats through a party-list system
Direct election of the President by the people
Abolition of reserved seats in the Lok Sabha
30.x: The Law Commission's 170th Report of 1999 proposed increasing representation by 25 per cent through a party-list system.
30.tq: Link the institutional proposal with the report number and year.
xs: The Law Commission's **170th Report (1999)** proposed **25%** more seats via a **party list** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was an alternative in the LS expansion debate; it did not seek RS cuts, direct presidential elections or abolition of reserved seats.

30.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: The Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, enacted in 1959, which has been amended five times (1993, 1999, 2000, 2006, 2013) to include offices that have been exempted (such as Minister of union or state, Leader of opposition in the Parliament) from the purview of 'office of profit' disqualification in spite of salary and other perks. Statement 3 is incorrect: The Constitution do not clearly define what constitutes an office of profit, but the definition has evolved over the years with interpretations made in various court judgments. An office of profit has been interpreted as a position that brings to the office-holder some financial gain, advantage, or benefit. The amount of such profit is immaterial. The office of profit law simply seeks to enforce a basic feature of the Constitution, the principle of separation of powers between the legislature and the executive. For example: In 2004, Jaya Bachchan, Rajya Sabha MP from the Samajwadi Party, was appointed chairperson of the UP Film Development Council (UPFDC). The apex court held that it was an Office of Profit and disqualified her from membership in the Upper House. PMF Concept Hack: In Indian Polity, if a statement says a term is well-defined in the Constitution, it is usually suspicious. It stayed empty through the **17th** and **18th** Lok Sabhas.
He is **not subordinate** to the Speaker.

31.s: The date of election of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is fixed by the:
31.x: The President fixes the Speaker's election date and the Speaker fixes the Deputy Speaker's.
n: The date of election of the Deputy Speaker is fixed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under Rule 8(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The President fixes the date of election of the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker addresses resignation to the Speaker under Article 94(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Speaker addresses resignation to the Deputy Speaker under Article 94(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xa: The **Secretary-General** communicates the Deputy Speaker's election date.
⚠ Neither resigns to the **President**.
RS **Deputy Chairman** resigns to the **Chairman**.

31.s:
While a resolution for his removal is under consideration, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha:
1. cannot preside over the House.
2. may vote in the first instance but not in the event of a tie.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
31.x: Under Article 96 the Speaker cannot preside during consideration of his removal resolution, but may speak, take part and vote in the first instance, though not cast a vote in case of a tie.
xa: ⚠ The **RS Chairman**, in the same situation, **cannot vote** at all but may speak.

31.s: In normal sittings of the Lok Sabha, the Speaker:
o: does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote in a tie
votes in the first instance and also has a casting vote
votes in the first instance like any member
31.x: Under Article 100 the Speaker does not vote in the first instance but gives a casting vote when votes are tied.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
During normal parliamentary sittings, the Speaker does not vote in the first instance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
During normal parliamentary sittings, the Speaker exercises a casting vote under Article 100 upon an equality of votes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xa: During his **own removal resolution** (**Article 96**) he cannot preside, but **can vote** in the first instance — **no casting vote**.
⚠ Removal pending: Speaker **can vote**; the RS **Chairman cannot vote**.

31.s: When not in the Chair, the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha:
o: can only give a casting vote
can debate, move motions and vote in the first instance
31.x: Out of the Chair the Deputy Speaker is an ordinary member who can debate, move motions and vote in the first instance, unlike the Speaker.
n: The Deputy Speaker sits as an ordinary member of the House during normal proceedings when not in the Chair. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker can participate in debates during normal proceedings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker can move motions during normal proceedings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker can vote in the first instance during normal proceedings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xa: In his **own removal** resolution (**Article 96**) he **cannot preside** and has **no casting vote**.
The **Speaker** does **not** vote in the first instance in normal sittings.
The Deputy Speaker presides when the Speaker is **absent** or the office is **vacant**.

31.s: While a resolution for his own removal is under consideration, the Deputy Speaker can:
31.x: The Deputy Speaker cannot preside then but may speak, take part and vote in the first instance; no casting vote is allowed.
n: The Deputy Speaker cannot preside over the sitting during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution, even if present in the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker has the right to speak during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker has the right to participate during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker has the right to vote in the first instance during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker cannot exercise a casting vote when votes are equally divided during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker can speak and vote in the first instance during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s removal under Article 96. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xa: The **Speaker** is under the same rule during his own removal.
⚠ The RS **Chairman** during his removal **cannot vote**, but may speak.
Removal needs an **effective majority** after **fourteen days'** notice.

31.s: Who certifies the money bill?
31.x: If any question arises about whether a Bill is a money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is final. His decision in this regard cannot be questioned in any court of law or in either the House of Parliament or even the President. When a money bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha for recommendation & presented to the president for assent, the speaker endorses on the bill his certificate that it is a money bill.

31.s: Which Article provides for the election of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
31.x: Article 93 provides that the House of the People shall choose two members to be Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
31.tq: Match the constitutional article with the office it creates.
xs: **Article 93**: the LS elects the **Speaker and Deputy Speaker** from its members — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 89** is about the RS **Chairman and Deputy Chairman**; **Art. 100** = quorum / casting vote; **Art. 85** = sessions.
xa: **Art. 94**: Speaker resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; removal by a **majority of all the then members** after **14 days'** notice.
The **Deputy Speaker** is elected **after the Speaker**.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the powers of the Speaker?
o: The Speaker recognises the Leader of the Opposition, subject to the party-strength requirement.
The Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule are beyond judicial review.
The Speaker appoints chairmen of parliamentary committees.
Rulings of the Speaker are protected by Article 122.
31.x: The Speaker decides Tenth Schedule cases, but those decisions remain subject to judicial review.
xa: LoP recognition needs at least **one-tenth** of the House's strength.
The LoP became statutory under the **1977 Act**.

31.s: The party seeking recognition of the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha is required, according to the Speaker’s direction, to have at least:
31.x: Recognition of the Leader of the Opposition requires the party to have at least one-tenth of the strength of the House, according to the Speaker’s direction. The office has statutory status since the 1977 Act.
31.tq: Distinguish the one-tenth threshold from other parliamentary fractions.
xs: The party needs at least **one-tenth of the House's strength** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This comes from the **Speaker's direction**; the LoP is **statutory since the 1977 Act**.
xa: Quorum is also **one-tenth** of total members (**Art 100(3)**).
The Speaker also decides **Tenth Schedule** cases.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
o: The Deputy Speaker is elected after the election of the Speaker.
The Deputy Speaker resigns by writing to the Speaker.
The Deputy Speaker is subordinate to the Speaker in exercising the office's functions.
The Deputy Speaker presides over a joint sitting when the Speaker is absent.
31.x: The Deputy Speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker while exercising the functions of the office.
xa: By convention he is from the **Opposition**.
He becomes **chairman of any committee** he is appointed to.

31.s: Under which Article may the President send messages to either House of Parliament regarding a pending Bill?
31.x: Article 86 lets the President address either or both Houses, require members' attendance and send messages on pending Bills.
xa: **Art 87**: **special address** at the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**.
The address is debated on a **Motion of Thanks**.

31.s: A ruling given by the Deputy Speaker while in the Chair:
o: can be appealed to the Speaker
must be ratified by the Speaker
cannot be appealed to the Speaker
can be appealed to the President
31.x: While presiding, the Deputy Speaker has the Speaker's powers, and his rulings cannot be appealed to the Speaker.
n: The Deputy Speaker exercises the same powers as the Speaker when presiding over a sitting of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
There is no appeal to the Speaker against a ruling given by the Deputy Speaker while the Deputy Speaker is in the Chair. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker presides over joint sittings of Parliament when the Speaker is absent under Article 118(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker automatically becomes the chairman of any Parliamentary Committee to which the Deputy Speaker is appointed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xa: After him, the **Deputy Chairman** of the Rajya Sabha presides at a joint sitting.
The Speaker's **Panel of Chairpersons** has up to **10** members.
RS equivalent: **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons** nominated by the **Chairman**.

31.s: If both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker are absent from a joint sitting of Parliament, it is presided over by the:
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
senior-most member of the Lok Sabha
31.x: The Speaker presides over a joint sitting (Art. 118(4)), then the Deputy Speaker, then the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 118. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker is the sole and final authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill under Article 110(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker presides over joint sittings of both Houses of Parliament under Article 118(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
In the absence of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker presides over a joint sitting before the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xa: Joint sitting is provided in **Art 108**.
The Speaker's certificate is **final** when the Bill goes to the **Rajya Sabha** and the **President**.

31.s: The constitutional provisions governing the Speaker of the Lok Sabha are contained in which one of the following groups of Articles?
31.x: The Speaker is covered by Articles 93–96 (election, vacation, removal), 100 (casting vote), 110 (Money Bill certificate) and 118 (joint sitting rules).
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is governed under Part V of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 93. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 94. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 95. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 96. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 118. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The Speaker is governed by **Articles 93–96, 100, 110 and 118** — option **(3)**.
**Article 93:** election; **94:** resignation and removal; **96:** own removal resolution.
**100:** casting vote; **110:** Money Bill certification; **118:** joint sitting.
xa: **Art 97:** salary charged on the **Consolidated Fund**.
**Art 122:** the Speaker's rulings are **protected**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992):** Tenth Schedule decisions subject to **judicial review**.

31.s: Who appoints the Pro-Tem Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
31.x: The President appoints the Pro-Tem Speaker; adjourning sine die, Tenth Schedule decisions and fixing the Deputy Speaker's election date are the Speaker's.
n: The Speaker exercises adjournment sine die. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker decides questions of member disqualification arising out of defection under the Tenth Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker fixes the date for the election of the Deputy Speaker under Rule 8(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President under Article 95(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xa: The Speaker recognises the **Leader of the Opposition** — party needs **one-tenth** of the House.
He **appoints committee chairmen**.
He adjourns or suspends a sitting when there is **no quorum** (**one-tenth**).

31.s: Which of the following pairs of removal motions against Lok Sabha Speakers is correctly matched?
31.x: Removal motions against G. V. Mavalankar in 1954, Hukum Singh in 1966 and Balram Jakhar in 1987 failed. The motion concerning Om Birla was listed for debate in 2026, not 1987.
31.tq: Pair each office-holder with the correct year and reject swapped dates.
xs: **G.V. Mavalankar — 1954** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Hukum Singh** faced his motion in **1966**, **Balram Jakhar** in **1987** — all failed.
**Om Birla**'s motion was signed by **118** MPs and listed for debate on **9 Mar 2026**.
xa: ⚠ **1954 – 1966 – 1987** = Mavalankar – Hukum Singh – Jakhar.
The LS rejected the Om Birla resolution by **voice vote**.

31.s: In January 2026, the Supreme Court upheld the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman's power under Article 91 to decide a judge-removal motion (Chairman's office vacant) in the:
31.x: In the Justice Varma case (January 2026), the Supreme Court upheld the Deputy Chairman's power under Article 91 to decide a judge-removal motion while the Chairman's office was vacant.
xa: **Harivansh**'s term as Deputy Chairman ended **9 Apr 2026**.
Under **Art 91** the Deputy Chairman also presides when the VP acts as President.

31.s: As of 2026, who is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
31.x: C.P. Radhakrishnan, as Vice-President, is the ex officio Chairman; Harivansh was Deputy Chairman (term ended 9 April 2026) and S. Radhakrishnan was the first Chairman (1952-62).
xa: The Chairman has a **casting vote only**.
RS has a **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons** nominated by the Chairman.

31.s: Until Parliament makes a law regulating recruitment and conditions of service of the secretarial staff of the Houses, rules may be made by the President after consultation with the:
o: Chief Justice of India and Attorney-General of India
Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha and Secretary-General of the Rajya Sabha
Prime Minister and Union Home Minister
Speaker of the Lok Sabha and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
31.x: In the absence of a law by Parliament, the President may make rules after consulting the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
31.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish the constitutional consultees from parliamentary officials and ministers.
xs: Until Parliament legislates, the **President** makes rules **after consulting the Speaker/Chairman** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not the CJI, the Secretaries-General or the PM.
xa: **Art 98** provides each House a **separate secretarial staff**.
Each Secretariat is headed by a **Secretary-General**.

31.s: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions directly under the control and guidance of the:
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
31.x: The Lok Sabha Secretariat works directly under the Speaker's control and guidance, not under the executive, which keeps the House independent.
31.tq: Recall who controls each House's secretariat.
n: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions directly under the control and guidance of the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The **Lok Sabha Secretariat** works under the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha** — option **(2)**.
It functions under the Speaker's **control and guidance**, **independent of the executive**.
The **Rajya Sabha Secretariat** is under the **Chairman**.
xa: **Art 98:** each House has a **separate secretarial staff**; posts **common to both Houses** may be created.
Head: the **Secretary-General**, appointed by the presiding officer.
Until Parliament legislates, recruitment rules are made by the **President** after consulting Speaker/Chairman.

31.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: First Speaker of the Lok Sabha – Meira Kumar
31.x: G.V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker (1952–56); Meira Kumar was the first woman Speaker and Sumitra Mahajan the second.
n: G. V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
G. V. Mavalankar served as Speaker from 1952 to 1956. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
Meira Kumar was the first woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
Sumitra Mahajan was the second woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xa: A removal motion against **Mavalankar** (**1954**) failed.
First AP Assembly (**1956**) Speaker: **Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao**.
⚠ **S. Radhakrishnan** = first RS Chairman; **C.P. Radhakrishnan** = present Chairman.

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is incorrect?
o: The Speaker's endorsement is final when the Bill is presented to the President
The Speaker's endorsement is final when the Bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha
The Rajya Sabha may overrule the Speaker's certification by a simple majority
The Speaker is the sole authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill
31.x: Option C is incorrect. Under Article 110(4), the Speaker alone certifies a Money Bill, and the certificate is final when the Bill goes to the Rajya Sabha and to the President. The Rajya Sabha cannot overrule it.
31.tq: Remember that the Speaker's Money Bill certificate is final.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker is the sole and final authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill under Article 110(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker’s Money Bill endorsement is final when the Bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker’s Money Bill endorsement is final when the Bill is presented to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Rajya Sabha may overrule** the Speaker's certification — option **(3)**.
Under **Article 110(4)** the Speaker is the **sole and final** authority to certify a **Money Bill**.
The endorsement is **final** when the Bill goes to the **Rajya Sabha** and to the **President**.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes cite **Art 110(3)** for the Speaker's final say.
The Speaker also presides over a **joint sitting** (**Art 118(4)**).
His **anti-defection** decisions, unlike this, are subject to **judicial review**.

31.s: The period between prorogation of Parliament and the commencement of its next session is known as:
31.x: The period from prorogation to the next session is called a recess. It is different from adjournment, which interrupts a sitting within a session.
31.tq: Discriminate between a break within a session and the interval between two sessions.
xs: The period from **prorogation to the next session** is a **recess** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Adjournment sine die** ends a sitting; **dissolution** ends the life of the LS.
xa: **Session** = first sitting → prorogation/dissolution.
**Prorogation** is ordered by the **President** (**Governor** in States).

31.s: A quorum in either House of Parliament is ordinarily:
o: One-half of the total membership, including the presiding officer
One-tenth of the total membership, including the presiding officer
One-fourth of the elected membership, excluding nominated members
One-twentieth of the total membership, excluding the presiding officer
31.x: Under Article 100(3), the quorum is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, including the presiding officer.
31.tq: Check both the fraction and whether the presiding officer is included.
xs: Quorum is **one-tenth of total members, including the presiding officer** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The provision is **Art 100(3)**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes list it as **Art 100(1)**, but **100(1)** actually carries the **casting vote**.
State Assemblies averaged only **24 sittings** in **2025** (**Odisha 43**, **Nagaland 7**).

31.s: Which of the following does NOT lapse on the prorogation of Parliament?
31.x: Bills do not lapse on prorogation, although pending notices generally lapse except notices to introduce bills.
xa: On **dissolution**, many bills **lapse**.
In States, prorogation is by the **Governor**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Speaker on dissolution of the Lok Sabha:
1. The Speaker vacates office immediately on dissolution.
2. The Speaker continues until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Lok Sabha.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
31.x: The Speaker does not vacate office on dissolution; he continues until just before the new Lok Sabha first meets.
n: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker does not vacate office immediately. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The regular Speaker continues in office through dissolution until the next House meets. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xa: The **Deputy Speaker** **vacates office immediately** on dissolution.
The Speaker **vacates office** on ceasing to be a member (**Art 94**).

31.s:
Assertion (A): Prorogation ends the very life of the Lok Sabha.
Reason (R): Adjournment suspends the work in a sitting for a specified time.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
31.x: Prorogation only ends a session; it is dissolution that ends the Lok Sabha itself. R correctly describes adjournment.
n: Adjournment suspends the work of a sitting for a specified time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Adjournment sine die terminates the sitting of the House indefinitely. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Adjournment sine die does not name a day for reassembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Prorogation terminates a session of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Dissolution ends the very life of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The specified period for an adjournment may be hours, days, or weeks. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xa: Under adjournment sine die, pending bills **continue** to the next session.
On prorogation pending **bills are unaffected**; **notices lapse**.
On dissolution pending **bills, motions and resolutions lapse** (subject to **Article 107**).

31.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Adjournment – Presiding Officer, suspending a sitting for a specified time
Adjournment sine die – Presiding Officer, without naming a day of reassembly
31.x: The President prorogues under Article 85(2)(a); Article 85(2)(b) is dissolution.
n: The Presiding Officer, namely the Speaker or Chairman, exercises adjournment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Presiding Officer, namely the Speaker or Chairman, exercises adjournment sine die. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The President of India exercises prorogation under Article 85(2)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The President of India exercises dissolution under Article 85(2)(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xa: ⚠ Adjournment / sine die = presiding officer; prorogation / dissolution = President.
The President prorogues on the advice of the **Council of Ministers** (**Governor** in States).
Only the **Lok Sabha** can be dissolved — the **Rajya Sabha** is permanent.

31.s: The President's power to dissolve the Lok Sabha is provided in:
31.x: Article 85(2)(b) covers dissolution and 85(2)(a) prorogation; Article 123 is about ordinances.
n: Article 85 governs the summoning of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The President of India exercises prorogation under Article 85(2)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The President of India exercises dissolution under Article 85(2)(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The maximum interval between two Parliamentary sessions is six months under Article 85. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The maximum validity of an Ordinance after reassembly is six weeks under Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Six months cannot intervene between the last sitting of one session and the date appointed for the first sitting of the next session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Constitution mandates only the maximum six-month gap between parliamentary sessions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xa: **Article 86:** President may address either House and send **messages**.
**Article 87:** **special address** at the first session after each **general election** and of each year.
The President's address is debated on a **Motion of Thanks**.

31.s: The lapse of pending bills on dissolution of the Lok Sabha is subject to the rules in:
31.x: Dissolution ends the Lok Sabha and its pending business lapses, subject to Article 107; the Rajya Sabha is permanent.
n: Dissolution ends the very life of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Dissolution causes pending bills to lapse, subject to Article 107 rules. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Dissolution causes pending motions to lapse, subject to Article 107 rules. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Dissolution causes pending resolutions to lapse, subject to Article 107 rules. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xa: **Prorogation** ends only the **session**; pending bills are unaffected.
The **Speaker** continues after dissolution till the new House's **first meeting**.

31.s:
With reference to Article 98 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
1. Each House of Parliament has separate secretarial staff.
2. Posts common to both Houses may be created.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
31.x: Article 98 gives each House its own secretarial staff while permitting the creation of posts common to both Houses.
xa: Head: **Secretary-General**, appointed by the **presiding officer**, rank = **Cabinet Secretary**.
The Secretariat is **independent of the executive**.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Secretary-General of a House of Parliament?
o: Each House has a Secretary-General as head of its secretarial staff.
The Secretary-General is appointed by the Union Government.
The parliamentary secretariat is independent of the executive.
The Secretary-General holds rank equal to the Cabinet Secretary.
31.x: The Secretary-General is appointed by the presiding officer of the House concerned, keeping the secretariat independent of the executive.
xa: **Posts common to both Houses** may be created (**Art 98**).
Recruitment: Parliament may regulate **by law**.

31.s: The six-month maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament is counted from:
o: the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next
the first sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next
the date of prorogation to the date of the next summons
the date of summons to the date of prorogation
31.x: The rule runs from the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next; the Budget, Monsoon and Winter names are only conventions.
xa: Hence at least **two sessions a year**.
States follow the same six-month rule under **Art 174**.

31.s: The President's special address at the first session after each general election and the first session of each year is made under:
31.x: Article 87 provides for this special address; it is not required after every prorogation.
xa: It **outlines government policy**, debated on a **Motion of Thanks**.
**Art 86** covers addresses **at any time** and **messages**.

31.s: The address of the President outlining the policies of the Government is debated in Parliament through a:
31.x: The President’s address outlining Government policy is debated through a Motion of Thanks in Parliament.
31.tq: Match the constitutional address with the parliamentary motion that follows it.
xs: The President's address is debated through a **Motion of Thanks** — so option **(1)** is correct.

31.x: The provisions regarding vacation, resignation and removal from the offices of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are given in Article 94 of the Indian Constitution. In the second proviso to the same Article, it is clearly stated that when the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate his office on such dissolution, and shall continue in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly constituted Lok Sabha. Therefore, Statement I is correct. The Constitution nowhere mentions that a member of the Lok Sabha, upon being elected as Speaker, must compulsorily resign from his political party immediately. Therefore, Statement III is correct.

31.x: According to Article 100(1) of the Constitution, All questions at any sitting of either House or joint sitting of the Houses shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting, excluding the speaker or person acting as chairman or speaker. The Speaker or chairman, or person acting as such, shall not vote in first instance. But shall exercise a casting vote in the case of equality of votes (i.e. a tie) and hence decide the matter. In this case, the Speaker's vote will count. According to an additional provision under Article 96(1), if the Speaker's position is challenged by a motion in the Lok Sabha, they will continue to remain in their position until the motion is disposed of. According to Article 96(2), in such cases, if there is a motion of no confidence against the Speaker, they will not be allowed to vote during the debate on the motion, as their presence will not influence the vote. However, during other matters, the Speaker is entitled to cast their vote in case of a tie. This right is known as the casting vote. The Speaker may also delegate this casting vote to other members of the House.

Consider the following statements:
1. A Select Committee on a Bill consists of members of one House only.
2. A Joint Committee on a Bill consists of members of both Houses.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
32.x: A Select Committee has members of one House; a Joint Committee has members of both Houses and is formed on a motion adopted in the House.
xa: A Joint Committee is formed on a **motion adopted in the House**.
Ad hoc committees **end when the task is done**; standing committees are permanent.
Inquiry committees (e.g., **MPLADS**, **Railway Convention Committee**) are the other ad hoc type.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the removal of the Speaker under Article 94(c)?
o: A notice of fourteen days is required.

32.x: Removal needs a majority of all the then members of the House (an effective majority); a simple majority is not enough.
xa: A resolution against Speaker **Om Birla** was **dismissed by voice vote** (**Mar 2026**).
The Speaker has **discretion to admit or reject** a no-confidence motion.
⚠ A no-confidence motion (vs the government) also needs **50 members**, under **Rule 198**.

32.s: Which of the following statements regarding Zero Hour is incorrect?
o: It has a maximum duration of one hour in the Lok Sabha.
It is used for raising urgent matters of public importance.
It is an informal parliamentary convention.
It is taken before Question Hour in the Lok Sabha.
32.x: Option D is incorrect: Zero Hour comes right after Question Hour (noon to 1 PM in the Lok Sabha), not before it. It is an informal convention lasting at most one hour.
32.tq: Recall the order: Question Hour first, then Zero Hour.
n: Zero Hour immediately follows Question Hour in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
Zero Hour runs from 12:00 Noon to 1:00 PM in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
Zero Hour is used for raising urgent matters of public importance without prior notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
Zero Hour is an informal convention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
The maximum duration of Zero Hour in the Lok Sabha is one hour. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
xs: The incorrect statement is that Zero Hour is **taken before Question Hour in the Lok Sabha** — option **(4)**.
In the LS it **immediately follows** Question Hour — **12:00 Noon to 1:00 PM**.
It is an **informal convention** for raising **urgent matters** of public importance, generally up to **one hour**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes say its duration is **not fixed**.
Ministers are **not bound to reply**.
Members only **intimate** the Presiding Officer the same day; no prior notice as for a question.

32.s: Which of the following is not one of the three primary categories of Parliamentary Questions?
32.x: The three kinds of parliamentary question are starred, unstarred and short notice. There is no 'adjournment question'; adjournment is a motion.
32.tq: Discriminate kinds of question from kinds of motion.
n: The three primary categories of parliamentary questions are Starred Questions, Unstarred Questions, and Short Notice Questions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 85-87]
xs: **Adjournment Question** is not a category — option **(1)**.
The three primary categories are **Starred**, **Unstarred** and **Short Notice** questions.
**Adjournment** is a **motion**, not a type of question.
xa: All three are taken up during **Question Hour**.
Questions **to a private member** (on his bill/resolution) are on **yellow** paper.
Starred: at most **20** listed for oral answer daily.

32.s: Which of the following statements about the Calling Attention Motion is incorrect?
o: It carries an element of condemnation or censure.
It draws a Minister’s attention to an urgent public matter.
It may be admitted in either House.
It requires the permission of the Presiding Officer.
32.x: Option A is incorrect: a calling attention motion has no element of censure, unlike an adjournment motion. It draws a Minister's attention to an urgent matter, needs the presiding officer's permission and is allowed in either House.
32.tq: Discriminate the calling attention motion from the adjournment motion.
n: A Calling Attention Motion draws a Minister's attention to an urgent public matter. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Calling Attention Motion is admissible in either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Calling Attention Motion requires the permission of the Presiding Officer. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Calling Attention Motion has no condemnation or censure element. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the Calling Attention Motion **carries an element of condemnation or censure** — option **(1)**.
It has **no** element of condemnation — unlike the **Adjournment Motion**.
It draws a **Minister's attention** to an **urgent public matter**, in **either House**, with the **Presiding Officer's** permission.
xa: It is an **Indian** innovation, since **1954**.
It does **not** disrupt the daily agenda.
Calling attention notices **restricted** the scope of the **Adjournment Motion**.

32.s: A privilege motion is referred to the:

n: A No-Confidence Motion is admissible only in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]

A Calling Attention Motion is admissible in either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
An Adjournment Motion is admissible only in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Privilege Motion is admissible in either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
xa: The Adjournment Motion also needs **50 members**' support.
Calling attention may be admitted in **either House**.
No-confidence: **Rule 198**; no **reasons** required.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: A Calling Attention Motion does not disrupt the scheduled daily agenda.

An Adjournment Motion interrupts normal parliamentary business. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 82-85]
An Adjournment Motion suspends normal parliamentary business. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 82-85]
A Calling Attention Motion has no element of condemnation or censure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 82-85]
An Adjournment Motion involves censure or condemnation of the Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 82-85]
xa: Calling Attention: **either House**; Adjournment Motion: **Lok Sabha only**.

32.x: The Business Advisory Committee sets the timetable; the Rules Committee proposes rule changes and the Assurances Committee tracks Ministers' promises.

The Committee on Petitions examines representations submitted to the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #35 · pp 87-91]

The Rules Committee recommends additions to the Rules of Procedure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #35 · pp 87-91]

xa: Petitions Committee is the "**Ombudsman**" of Parliament.
**Committee on Subordinate Legislation:** checks **delegated** rule-making stays within **statutory limits**.

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

n: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation has 15 members in each House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #35 · pp 87-91]
Ministers cannot be members of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #35 · pp 87-91]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation** of A — option **(2)**.
A: the **Committee on Subordinate Legislation** has **15** members in **each House**.
R: **Ministers cannot** be members — barring Ministers does not explain the committee's size.
xa: It checks that **delegated** rule-making — **regulations, bye-laws and sub-rules** — stays within **statutory limits**.

32.s: What is the constitutional quorum for a House of Parliament?
32.x: Under Article 100, the quorum of either House is one-tenth of its total membership.

n: The constitutional quorum of a House is one-tenth of its total membership. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]

xs: The quorum is **one-tenth** of the **total membership** — option **(1)**.

One-half, one-third and one-twentieth are distractors.

32.s: What is true about Censure Motion?
o: It is not different from No-confidence motion
It is different from the No-confidence motion
It is not mandatory to mention the reasons in this
Permission of the House is not essential to present it

For a Censure Motion, separate “leave of the House” is not required. Factually, both (b) and (d) are correct. That is why the Bihar Public Service Commission removed (deleted) this question from evaluation.

32.s: A privilege motion, moved when a member feels that a minister or member has committed a breach of privilege, is raised in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha respectively under
32.x: A privilege motion is governed by Rule 222 of the Lok Sabha rules and Rule 187 of the Rajya Sabha rules. Rule 184 (LS) is a discussion followed by a vote, Rule 193 (LS) is a short-duration discussion without a vote, Rule 180A-E (RS) covers Special Mentions, and Rule 198 (LS) is the no-confidence motion.
32.tq: Privilege: LS 222 / RS 187. No-confidence: LS 198.
xs: A privilege motion is under **Rule 222** (LS) and **Rule 187** (RS) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Rule 184** = discussion with vote; **Rule 193** = short-duration discussion; **Rule 180A-E** = Special Mentions (RS); **Rule 198** = no-confidence motion.
xa: A privilege motion concerns a **breach of privilege** by a minister or member and is available in **both Houses**.
A privilege notice was given in the Rajya Sabha against the **Union Education Minister** (**May 2026**).
Committee of Privileges: **15** members (LS, by the Speaker); **10** (RS, by the Chairman).

32.s: The first no-confidence motion against the Union Council of Ministers was moved against Jawaharlal Nehru in 1963 by:
32.x: The first no-confidence motion against Jawaharlal Nehru was moved in 1963 by J.B. Kripalani.
32.tq: Link the event, year and mover rather than relying on the event alone.
xs: The first no-confidence motion, against **Nehru** in **1963**, was moved by **J.B. Kripalani** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Gouthu Latchanna** moved the motion against the **Prakasam** ministry in **Andhra State** (Nov **1954**).
xa: The Andhra motion was carried **69 for, 68 against**; the ministry fell after **13 months**.
President's Rule followed: **16 Nov 1954 - 27 Mar 1955**.
No-confidence is moved under **Rule 198** with **50 members'** support.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: A Censure Motion may be directed against a Minister, a group of Ministers or the whole Council.
A No-confidence Motion is directed against the entire Council of Ministers.
Passing a Censure Motion compels the Council of Ministers to resign.
Passing a No-confidence Motion requires the Council of Ministers to resign.
32.x: A passed Censure Motion does not compel resignation; a passed No-confidence Motion does.
xa: Censure **must state reasons**; no-confidence needs **no reasons**.
Censure seeks **disapproval of a policy**.
No-confidence: **only in Lok Sabha**, **50 members**, **Rule 198**.

32.s: A resolution moved under a constitutional or statutory provision is called a:
32.x: Such a resolution is a statutory resolution; a Government resolution is one moved by a minister, e.g. to approve a treaty.
xa: Private member's resolutions: **alternate Fridays**, afternoon.

32.s: Which of the following statements regarding confidence and no-confidence motions is incorrect?
o: A Confidence Motion demonstrates the Government's majority.
A No-Confidence Motion is moved by the Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
A No-Confidence Motion is moved by the Council of Ministers to demonstrate its majority.
A Confidence Motion is moved on the floor by the Council of Ministers or the Government.
32.x: C is incorrect: a confidence motion is moved by the government to prove its majority; a no-confidence motion is moved by the Opposition (Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha).
32.tq: Remember who moves each motion.
n: A Confidence Motion is moved on the floor by the Council of Ministers or the Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
A Confidence Motion demonstrates the majority of the Council of Ministers or Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
A No-Confidence Motion is moved by the Opposition in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
xs: The incorrect statement is that a **No-Confidence Motion is moved by the Council of Ministers** to demonstrate its majority — option **(3)**.
A **No-Confidence Motion** (**Rule 198**) is moved by the **Opposition** in the **Lok Sabha**.
A **Confidence Motion** is moved by the **Government** (Council of Ministers) to **demonstrate its majority**.
xa: If a confidence motion is defeated, the **Government falls**.
The no-confidence motion needs **50** members' support; **no reasons** need be stated.
First no-confidence motion: **J.B. Kripalani**, **1963**, against **Nehru**.

32.s: A motion raised against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts is a:
32.x: A privilege motion targets a Minister who withheld or distorted facts; a censure motion disapproves of specific policies.

A Confidence Motion proves majority floor support. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Censure Motion expresses strong disapproval of specific policies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Censure Motion expresses criticism of specific policies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Privilege Motion is raised against a Minister for withholding facts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Privilege Motion is raised against a Minister for distorting facts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
xa: Censure motion: **reasons must be stated**; does **not** force resignation.
Privilege motion goes to the **Committee of Privileges** — **Rule 222 (LS)**, **Rule 187 (RS)**.

The motion is referred to the Committee of Privileges

xa: A passed **No-Confidence Motion** also forces the **whole Council** to resign.

32.s: Which of the following statements about a Privilege Motion is incorrect?
o: It automatically forces the Government to resign.
It may be raised against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts.

n: A Privilege Motion is raised against a Minister for withholding facts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Privilege Motion is raised against a Minister for distorting facts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Privilege Motion is admissible in either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]

xs: The incorrect statement is that a privilege motion **automatically forces the Government to resign** — option **(1)**.

n: A No-Confidence Motion requires the support of 50 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]

32.s:

n: The maximum gap between Parliamentary sessions is six months. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]

32.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Simple closure — Only important clauses are debated
Closure by compartments — All pending clauses are voted on when time ends
Kangaroo closure — Only important clauses are debated and the others are taken as passed

32.x: C is correct: under kangaroo closure only the important clauses are debated and the rest are taken as passed. 32.tq: Discriminate among similar closure terms by matching each device with its exact operation.
xs: **Kangaroo closure — only important clauses debated, others taken as passed** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Simple closure** = matter sufficiently discussed, put to vote; **closure by compartments** = clauses grouped into parts, debated and voted part by part.
Voting all pending clauses when time ends is the **guillotine**, not simple closure.
xa: ⚠ Kangaroo = only important clauses debated; guillotine = **undiscussed** clauses voted when allotted time ends.
**Point of order**: raised when proceedings depart from rules; no debate.
Whips: **one-line** informative, **two-line** attendance, **three-line** strict voting.
