Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
39.x: Both are true: Justice M. Fathima Beevi became the first woman Supreme Court Judge in 1989 and was also the first Muslim woman in the higher judiciary.
n: Justice M. Fathima Beevi was the first woman Judge of the Supreme Court in 1989. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-6]
Justice M. Fathima Beevi was the first Muslim woman in the higher judiciary. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-6]
xa: **Sarojini Naidu**: **first woman Governor** — **Uttar Pradesh** (**1947**).
**Sucheta Kripalani**: **first woman CM** — **Uttar Pradesh** (**1963**).
**E. M. S. Namboodiripad**: **first non-Congress CM** — **Kerala**, **1957**.
First President of the **BJP**: **Atal Bihari Vajpayee**, **1980**.

39.s: Which of the following statements regarding the qualifications of the Governor is incorrect?
o: The person must have completed 35 years of age.
The person must be a citizen of India.
The person should not hold any office of profit.
The person may continue as a member of Parliament after becoming Governor.
39.x: Option D is incorrect: a Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature, and must give up any such seat on appointment. They must be a citizen, at least 35, and hold no office of profit.
39.tq: Recall the Governor's qualifications under Articles 157 and 158.
n: The Governor must be a citizen of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must have completed 35 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must not be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
A person appointed as Governor must vacate a parliamentary or State Legislature seat held by that person. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must not hold any office of profit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the person may continue as a member of Parliament after becoming Governor** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
**Art. 158**: the Governor must **not** be an MP or MLA and must **vacate** any such seat.
**Art. 157**: he must be a **citizen of India** and have completed **35** years; he must hold **no office of profit** — so (1), (2), (3) are correct.
xa: The Governor is **appointed by the President** by **warrant** under his hand and seal (**Article 155**).
Emoluments are fixed by **Parliament** by law and **cannot be reduced** during the term.
Conventions: an **outsider** to the state; the state **CM is consulted**.

39.s:
Consider the following statements about the Governor:
1. The Governor's emoluments are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
2. If one person is Governor of two or more States, the salary is shared in a proportion determined by the President.
3. The Governor's oath is administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
Which of the above statements are correct?
39.x: All three are correct; the oath by the High Court Chief Justice is under Article 159.
n: The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court administers the Governor’s oath under Article 159. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The emoluments and allowances of the Governor are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State under Article 202. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
When the same person is Governor of two or more States, the President determines the proportion in which the salary is shared. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The same person can be appointed as Governor of two or more States under the Seventh Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xa: The **7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956** allowed **one person to be Governor of 2 or more states**.
Immunity (**Article 361**): **no criminal proceedings** during the term; civil proceedings only after **2 months' notice**.
The Governor **resigns to the President**.

39.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 154 – Executive power of the State vested in the Governor
39.x: Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor. Article 153 provides a Governor for each State, 159 the oath, and 213 ordinances.
n: Article 153 provides for a Governor for each State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court administers the Governor’s oath under Article 159. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor promulgates Ordinances when the Legislature is not in session under Article 213. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xa: **Article 155**: appointment by the **President**; **Article 156**: office during the **pleasure of the President**.
**Article 157**: **citizen**, at least **35 years**; **Article 158**: no seat in a legislature, no office of profit.
The Governor is an **integral part** of the State Legislature — **Article 168**.

39.s: Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional position of the Chief Minister in a State?
o: The Chief Minister is the real executive head, while the Governor is the nominal or constitutional head
The Chief Minister is the nominal head, while the Governor is the real executive head
The Chief Minister and Governor are jointly the real executive heads
The Governor is the head of the Council of Ministers, while the Chief Minister is its nominal head
39.x: The Chief Minister is the real executive head of the State and heads the Council of Ministers. The Governor is the nominal or constitutional head, like the President at the Centre.
39.tq: Discriminate the nominal head from the real executive.
n: The Chief Minister is the real executive head of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Governor is the nominal and constitutional head of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Chief Minister is the head of the State Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
xs: **The Chief Minister is the real executive head, while the Governor is the nominal or constitutional head** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **CM** and **Council of Ministers** are the **real executive**; the CM **heads** the Council.
The Governor is the **nominal / constitutional head**, so options (2), (3), (4) misplace the roles.
xa: The CM is the **leader** of the majority in the **Legislative Assembly** and **chief spokesperson** of the State Government.
**Article 154**: executive power of the State is vested in the **Governor** — exercised on ministerial advice.
**Art. 167**: the CM is the **chief link** between Governor and Council.

39.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the State Council of Ministers?
o: State Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Chief Minister
A non-member may be a Minister but must become an MLA or MLC within six months
The Governor appoints the Chief Minister, normally the Assembly majority leader
Article 164 deals with the State Council of Ministers
39.x: State Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor, not the Chief Minister.
xa: Union parallel: ministers hold office at the **President's** pleasure, not the PM's.
**91st Amendment (2003)**: ministers ≤ **15%** of the Assembly; **minimum 12** (**Art. 164(1A)**).
A **Minister for Tribal Welfare** is mandatory in **Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha**; Bihar dropped by the **94th Amendment, 2006**.

39.s: The Governor's special address at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year is under Article:
39.x: The special address under Article 176 is mandatory on both occasions and is delivered on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
xa: ⚠ **175** = optional address; **176** = mandatory special address.
In **Jan 2026**, Governors walked out of or skipped the **Art. 176** address in Opposition-ruled states.
Under **Nabam Rebia**, the address must reflect **Cabinet policy**.

39.s: When a Governor is appointed administrator of an adjoining Union Territory under Article 239(2), he acts:
o: On the aid and advice of his own State Council of Ministers
Independently of his own State Council of Ministers
Only on the advice of the State Legislature
Only with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court
39.x: Under Article 239(2), the Governor administering an adjoining UT acts independently of his State's Council of Ministers; it is an express discretion. He is not bound by State ministers, the legislature or the High Court in this role.
39.tq: Art. 239(2) = express discretion, independent of State ministry.
xs: Under **Art. 239(2)**, as administrator of an adjoining UT, the Governor acts **independently of his own state Council of Ministers** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is an **express discretion** (UPSC).
xa: Other express discretion: **Art. 200** reservation, **Art. 356** report, **Art. 167** information.
The Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.
**Art. 163(2):** his decision on what is discretionary is **final**.

39.s: A State Bill imposing restrictions on inter-State trade requires the previous sanction of the President before introduction under:
39.x: Article 304(b) requires previous Presidential sanction before a Bill restricting inter-State trade is introduced. Article 288 concerns taxes on water/electricity in inter-State river projects, Article 254(2) Concurrent List repugnancy, and Article 31C property-related protection.
39.tq: Inter-State trade restriction = Art. 304(b), prior sanction (PYQ 2018).
xs: **Article 304(b)** requires **previous sanction of the President** before introducing a bill restricting inter-state trade — option **(3)** is correct (PYQ **2018**).
**Art. 288** = taxes on water/electricity in inter-state river projects; **Art. 254(2)** = Concurrent-List repugnancy; **Art. 31C** = property acquisition.
xa: ⚠ **304(b)** = prior sanction, **not** reservation after passage.
Other protective reservations: money bills during a **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**.
Such controls show the **Centre's control over state legislation**.

39.s: During President's Rule, the State Legislative Assembly may be:
39.x: During President's Rule the Assembly may be suspended or dissolved, while Parliament legislates for the State.
xa: **Bommai:** Assembly **not dissolved before Parliament approves**; ministry can be **restored**.
Example: the **Water Amendment Act** extended to **Manipur** (**Dec 2025**).

39.s: Parliamentary legislation for a State under President's Rule is enabled by which Article?
39.x: Article 357 provides for the exercise of legislative powers under a proclamation issued under Article 356.
39.tq: Match the emergency provision with the related legislative-power provision.
xs: **Article 357** lets **Parliament legislate** for a state under President's Rule — option **(3)** is correct.
**Art. 164** concerns the CM and ministers; **Art. 153** a Governor for each state.
xa: Central laws reach the state only through an **Art 357(1)(a)** resolution.
Example: **Water Amendment Act**, extended to **Manipur** (**Dec 2025**).
The Assembly is **suspended or dissolved** during President's Rule.

39.s: The Governor nominates what proportion of the members of the Legislative Council?
39.x: Under Article 171, the Governor nominates one-sixth of the members of a State Legislative Council from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in specified fields.
39.tq: Test the constitutional fraction directly against nearby Legislative Council proportions.
xs: The Governor **nominates one-sixth** (**1/6th**) of the Legislative Council — option **(2)** is correct.
This is under **Art. 171**.
xa: **Art. 174:** summons, prorogues and **dissolves** the Assembly.
⚠ **175** = optional address; **176** = mandatory special address.
He places reports of the **CAG**, **SPSC** and **State Finance Commission** before the legislature.

39.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Appointment of the State PSC Chairman and members – Article 316
All executive action of the State Government – Article 165
Appointment of the Chief Minister and Ministers – Article 164
39.x: Executive action in the Governor's name is under Article 166; Article 165 concerns the Advocate-General.
xa: ⚠ **SPSC**: Governor appoints (**316**), only the **President** removes.
**243K / 243I:** State Election Commissioner and State Finance Commission.
**Art. 213:** ordinance; **Art. 161:** pardon.

39.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Governor's power to recommend President's Rule — Article 360
39.x: The Governor's report recommending President's Rule is associated with Article 356, not Article 360. Articles 243K, 243I and 213 are correctly matched.
39.tq: Find the wrong Article by checking the constitutional provision attached to each function.
xs: **NOT correctly matched**: recommending President's Rule is **Art. 356**, not **Article 360** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 360** is the **Financial Emergency**.
**243I** (State Finance Commission), **213** (ordinance) and **243K** (State Election Commissioner) are correct.
xa: President's Rule: **6 months** at a time, maximum **3 years**.
Recommending President's Rule (**Art. 356**) is a **constitutional discretion**.
Money bills may be reserved during a **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**.

39.s: In January 2026, Governors in Opposition-ruled States drew controversy by walking out of or skipping the mandatory address under:
39.x: The controversy concerned the mandatory Governor's address under Article 176; under Nabam Rebia, the address must reflect Cabinet policy.
xa: **Art. 176:** special address at the first session after each general election + first session of each year.
⚠ **175** = optional; **176** = mandatory.
**Shamsher Singh (1974):** public criticism of Cabinet policy is an "**unconstitutional faux pas**".

39.s: In May 2026, after Mamata Banerjee refused to resign despite losing the election, which provision was cited as allowing the Governor to dismiss a Chief Minister who has lost majority?
39.x: Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure under Article 164, which allows dismissal of a CM who has lost majority. Article 356 is President's Rule, Article 163(3) bars inquiry into ministerial advice, and Article 361 grants the Governor immunity.
39.tq: CM who lost majority → Art. 164 pleasure.
xs: The **Art. 164 "pleasure" clause** lets the Governor dismiss a CM who has lost majority — option **(1)** is correct.
**Mamata Banerjee** refused to resign after losing (**5 May 2026**).
**Art. 356** is President's Rule, **Art. 163(3)** bars inquiry into advice, **Art. 361** gives immunity.
xa: Dismissing a ministry that has lost majority is **situational discretion**.
**Art. 164(1):** ministers hold office during the **Governor's pleasure**.
Once a new CM is sworn in, the old one **ceases**.

39.s:
Assertion (A): The President is bound by the advice of the Union Council of Ministers after returning it once for reconsideration.
Reason (R): The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 permits the President to return advice once but requires acceptance of the advice thereafter.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
39.x: Both are true: the 44th Amendment, 1978 lets the President return ministerial advice once for reconsideration, but the advice binds after that. This rule is exactly why the President is bound, so R explains A.
39.tq: Recall the 42nd and 44th Amendment changes to Article 74.
n: The President can return the advice of the Union Council of Ministers once under the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The President is bound by the Union Council of Ministers’ advice after reconsideration. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The Union Council of Ministers aids and advises the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **44th Amendment Act, 1978** lets the **President** return the Council's **advice once** for reconsideration.
After reconsideration he is **bound** by the advice — which is exactly why A holds.
xa: The 44th Amendment also inserted the word "**Cabinet**" into **Article 352**.
**Article 74**: the Council of Ministers **aids and advises** the President; the State counterpart is **Article 163**.
The **Governor** is bound by ministerial advice except in **discretionary** areas.

39.s: Which Article provides for the State Council of Ministers aiding and advising the Governor?
39.x: Article 163 provides for a State Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor, like Article 74 for the President. Article 164 deals with appointment of Ministers.
39.tq: Discriminate the Union and State parallels: 74 with 163, 75 with 164.
n: The constitutional basis of the State Council of Ministers is Article 163. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The State Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The Council of Ministers is an executive body aiding and advising the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xs: **Article 163** provides for the State Council of Ministers to **aid and advise** the **Governor** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 74** is the Union counterpart (aid and advice to the **President**).
**Article 164** deals with **appointment** of the CM and ministers; **Article 171** relates to the **Legislative Council** (Governor nominates **one-sixth**).
xa: **Art. 163(2)**: the Governor's own decision on whether a matter is discretionary is **final**.
**Art. 163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into in any court**.
Collective responsibility: Union — **Article 75(3)** to the **Lok Sabha**; State — **Article 164(2)** to the **Legislative Assembly**.

39.s:
Assertion (A): The Governor can reserve a Bill for the President even when the Council of Ministers advises otherwise.
Reason (R): The Governor is not bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers in all matters.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
39.x: Both are true: the Governor can reserve a bill for the President against ministerial advice because the Governor is not bound by that advice in every matter. R explains A.
39.tq: Ask whether limited discretion explains acting against advice.
n: The Governor can reserve a Bill for the President even when the Council of Ministers advises otherwise. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor is not bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers in all matters. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Governor may **reserve a Bill** for the President **even against the Council's advice** — a **discretionary power**.
This is possible because he is **not bound** by the Council of Ministers' advice in **all** matters.
xa: Reserving a bill (**Art. 200**), recommending President's Rule (**Art. 356**) and seeking information (**Art. 167**) = **constitutional discretion**.
Appointing a CM in a **hung Assembly** = **situational discretion**.
The only **mandatory** reservation: a bill that **derogates from the powers of the High Court**.
Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.

39.s:
Assertion (A): The State Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
Reason (R): If a No-Confidence Motion is passed, the entire Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, must resign.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
39.x: Both are true: under Article 164(2), the ministry is collectively answerable to the Assembly, which is why a passed no-confidence motion forces the whole ministry, Chief Minister included, to resign. R explains A.
39.tq: Ask whether resigning together explains collective responsibility.
n: The Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State under Article 164(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
If a No-Confidence Motion is passed, the entire Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, must resign. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
Article 164 deals with the appointment, tenure, responsibility and other provisions relating to Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
Article 164 concerns other provisions relating to Ministers, including appointment, responsibility and size limit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Council, including the CM, is **collectively responsible** to the **Legislative Assembly** — **Article 164(2)**.
So a passed **No-Confidence Motion** forces the **entire** Council, including the CM, to **resign**.
xa: Responsibility is **not** to the **Legislative Council**.
Union counterpart: collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha** — **Article 75(3)**.
On **loss of majority**, the CM must resign or be **dismissed**.

39.s: Compared with the President, the constitutional discretion of the Governor is:
39.x: The Governor's discretion is wider than the President's; the Constitution confers no comparable general discretion on the President.
xa: Constitutional discretion: reserving a bill (**Art. 200**), **Art. 356** report, seeking information (**Art. 167**), adjoining UT (**Art. 239**).
Situational discretion: appointing a CM in a **hung Assembly**, dismissing a ministry that lost majority.

39.s: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that a proclamation under Article 356 is
o: reviewable only after approval by the State Legislature
subject to judicial review, and the Union must disclose relevant material
beyond judicial review in all circumstances
reviewable only by the Governor of the concerned State
39.x: The nine-judge Bench in S.R. Bommai held that an Article 356 proclamation is subject to judicial review and that the Centre must show relevant material supporting it.
39.tq: Test the constitutional safeguard against an extreme claim of complete immunity from judicial review.
xs: **S.R. Bommai (1994)**: an **Art. 356** proclamation is **subject to judicial review** and the Centre **must show relevant material** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is not beyond review, and review is by **courts**, not the Governor.
xa: Majority tested by a **floor test**, not in **Raj Bhavan**.
Assembly **not dissolved before Parliament approves**; ministry can be **restored**.
**Secularism** is a basic feature; a government violating it can be dismissed.

39.s: The Governor of a State is the Chancellor of
o: the State universities, as provided by the applicable university laws
all Central universities located in that State
39.x: The Governor is also the Chancellor of State universities under the applicable State university laws. This role does not extend to all Central or private universities.
39.tq: Distinguish the Governor's State-level university role from Union-level higher-education institutions.
xs: The Governor is **Chancellor** of the **State universities** and appoints their **VCs** as Chancellor — option **(1)** is correct.
The role does not extend to **all Central** or **private** universities, or to the UGC.
xa: He does **not appoint HC judges** — the **President** does.
He appoints the **Advocate-General** (**Art. 165**) and **SPSC** members (**Art. 316**).
All executive action is taken in the Governor's name (**Art. 166**).

39.s: Which one of the following can the Governor of a State NOT do?
o: Appoint the Chairman of the State Public Service Commission
Remove a member of the State Public Service Commission
39.x: Although the Governor appoints SPSC members, only the President can remove them. The Governor does appoint the Advocate-General (Art. 165), the SPSC Chairman (Art. 316) and the State Election Commissioner (Art. 243K).
39.tq: Governor appoints SPSC, but only the President removes.
xs: The Governor **cannot remove a member of the State Public Service Commission** — only the **President** can — option **(3)**.
He does appoint the **Advocate-General** (**Art. 165**), the **SPSC** Chairman (**Art. 316**) and the **State Election Commissioner** (**Art. 243K**).
xa: ⚠ **SPSC**: Governor appoints (**316**), only the **President** removes.
He also does **not appoint HC judges**.
He **fixes the Advocate-General's pay**.

39.s: Which one of the following is associated with the Tamil Nadu Kurian Joseph Committee of 2026?
o: A proposal to replace Governors with elected Chief Ministers
A proposal for a new Schedule codifying the Governor’s discretion
A proposal to transfer all State finances to local bodies
39.x: The Kurian Joseph Committee was reported to have proposed a new Schedule to codify the Governor’s discretion.
39.tq: Match the committee with its specific institutional proposal.
xs: The **Kurian Joseph Committee (TN, 2026)** proposes a **new Schedule** to **codify the Governor's discretion** — option **(2)** is correct.
It also revisits Rameshwar Prasad's **"cooling-off" period** before a politician becomes Governor.
xa: **Art. 163(2):** the Governor's decision on what is discretionary is **final**.
**Discretion is subject to judicial review** (Rameshwar Prasad, Nabam Rebia).
Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.

39.s: The Governor's ordinance-making power is provided under Article:
39.x: The Governor's ordinances are under Article 213 (State and Concurrent subjects); the President's under Article 123.
n: The ordinance-making power of the President is governed by Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The ordinance-making power of a State Governor is governed by Article 213. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The President can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Union List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The President can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can promulgate ordinances on matters in the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xa: Both can be issued only when the legislature (or either House) is **not in session**.
Both **lapse six weeks** after the legislature **reassembles**, unless approved earlier.
The Governor needs **prior Presidential instructions** in **three** cases: Bills needing **prior sanction**, **reservation** or **Presidential assent**.

39.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: A President’s ordinance must be approved by Parliament.
A Governor’s ordinance must be approved by the President.
Approval of a Governor’s ordinance is not given by the Union Council of Ministers.
A Governor’s ordinance must be approved by the State Legislature.
39.x: B is incorrect: a Governor's ordinance must be approved by the State Legislature, not by the President (though some need prior Presidential instructions). A President's ordinance needs Parliament's approval.
39.tq: Each ordinance goes back to its own legislature.
n: A Presidential ordinance must be approved by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
A Governor's ordinance must be approved by the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
A Governor's ordinance requires approval by the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
A Governor's ordinance does not require approval by the Union Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
A Governor's ordinance does not require approval by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xs: The incorrect statement is that a **Governor's ordinance must be approved by the President** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
A Governor's ordinance is approved by the **State Legislature** — **not** the President or the Union Council of Ministers.
A President's ordinance is approved by **Parliament** — so options (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: The Governor's ordinance power is under **Article 213**; the President's under **Article 123**.
The Governor needs the **President's instructions** beforehand in **three** cases — but that is not approval.
Both ordinances can be **withdrawn at any time**.

39.s: The Governor's pardoning power, limited to offences against State laws, is under Article:
39.x: The Governor pardons under Article 161 (State laws only); the President under Article 72 (all cases).
n: The President makes Ordinances under Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The President has pardoning power under Article 72 in all cases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xa: Governor's pardoning covers **pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions**, and he may **suspend** or **commute** sentences.
**Perarivalan (2022)**: the Governor is **bound by Cabinet advice** on pardon/remission under **Art. 161**.
President's discretion is **very limited**; the Governor's is **comparatively more**.

39.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Governor of Jammu and Kashmir was earlier called Sadr-e-Riyasat.
2. The designation Sadr-e-Riyasat was changed to Governor in 1965.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
39.x: Both are true: the head of State of Jammu and Kashmir was called Sadr-e-Riyasat until 1965, when the title became Governor.
n: The Governor of Jammu and Kashmir was earlier called Sadr-e-Riyasat. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The designation Sadr-e-Riyasat in Jammu and Kashmir was changed to Governor in 1965. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xa: Former J&K had **6 months** of **Governor's Rule** under **Sec 92 of the J&K Constitution**, then Art 356.
After **2019**, J&K was under President's Rule under the Reorganisation Act until **Oct 2024**.
**Padmaja Naidu** was the first woman Governor of **West Bengal**.

39.s: Which of the following is a constitutional or express discretionary power of the Governor?
o: Dissolving the Assembly after a ministry loses its majority
Dismissing a ministry that has lost its majority
Reserving a Bill for the consideration of the President
Appointing a Chief Minister in a hung Assembly
39.x: Reserving a Bill for the President under Article 200 is an express constitutional discretion. The other options describe situational discretion.
39.tq: Distinguish express constitutional discretion from discretion arising out of political circumstances.
xs: **Reserving a Bill for the President** (**Art. 200**) is a **constitutional (express) discretion** — option **(3)** is correct.
Dissolving the Assembly or dismissing a ministry after loss of majority, and appointing a CM in a **hung Assembly**, are **situational** discretion.
xa: Other express discretion: **Art. 356** report, **Art. 167** information, **Art. 239** adjoining UT.
⚠ **Hung Assembly** = situational; **Art. 200** reservation = constitutional.
Reservation is **an example of central control over states** (**APPSC 2025** key).

39.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Seeking information from the Chief Minister – Article 239
Reserving a Bill for the President – Article 200
Administration of an adjoining Union Territory – Article 239
39.x: The Governor seeks information from the Chief Minister under Article 167; Article 239 concerns administration of Union Territories.
xa: Also express: **Sixth Schedule** royalty share and special responsibilities under **Art. 371-371J**.
⚠ **Hung Assembly** is **situational**, not constitutional, discretion.

39.s: Which of the following statements regarding judicial review of the Governor's discretion is NOT correct?
o: The Governor's discretion is completely immune from judicial review under Article 163(2).
Rameshwar Prasad rejected dissolution based on subjective fear of horse-trading.
Reports under Article 356 are reviewable by courts.
The floor test principle was affirmed in S.R. Bommai.
39.x: Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision final on whether a matter is discretionary, but it does not create complete immunity from judicial review. The other statements correctly reflect the cited judgments.
39.tq: Distinguish limited constitutional finality from complete judicial immunity.
xs: The NOT correct statement is (1): **Art. 163(2)** makes the decision final, but the Governor's discretion is **not completely immune** — option **(1)**.
**Discretion is subject to judicial review**: **Rameshwar Prasad (2006)** rejected dissolution on a subjective fear of **horse-trading** and held **Art. 356 reports reviewable**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: majority to be tested **on the floor**.
xa: Rameshwar Prasad struck down the **Bihar Assembly dissolution**.
**Nabam Rebia (2016):** **no general discretion** for the Governor.
Bommai also held **Art. 356** subject to **judicial review**.

39.s: Which one of the following is the correct constitutional method for determining whether a State ministry enjoys majority support?
o: Assessment by the Governor in Raj Bhavan
A report of the State Election Commission
A floor test in the Legislative Assembly
39.x: S.R. Bommai established that majority must ordinarily be tested on the floor of the House, not in Raj Bhavan.
39.tq: Ask who should perform the majority test instead of accepting the Governor's personal assessment.
xs: Majority is tested by a **floor test in the Legislative Assembly** — option **(3)** is correct.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: **on the floor**, **not in Raj Bhavan**.
xa: **Sarkaria** recommended a mandatory **floor test**.
In a hung Assembly, an **early floor test** follows the invitation.
**Tamil Nadu (May 2026):** **C. Joseph Vijay** invited with an early floor test.

39.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about a State Bill reserved for the President under Article 201?
o: A returned Bill must be reconsidered by the State Legislature within six months
Article 201 prescribes no fixed time limit for the President's decision
The President is not bound to assent even after the Bill is passed again
The President may direct the Governor to return even a Money Bill for reconsideration
39.x: Only a non-Money Bill can be returned to the State Legislature for reconsideration.
xa: **No time limit** is prescribed for the President (**Apr 2025**: assent withheld to TN's **anti-NEET Bill**).
Nov 2025 Reference: the President **need not seek SC advice** on each reserved bill.
Under **Art. 200**, a re-passed bill must get the **Governor's** assent.

39.s: Under Article 200 of the Constitution, which one of the following is NOT an option available to the Governor in respect of a Bill passed by the State Legislature?
o: To withhold assent to the Bill
To reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President
To return a Money Bill for reconsideration
39.x: The Governor may return a Bill for reconsideration only if it is not a Money Bill. The other three are options available under Article 200.
39.tq: Identify the exception by applying the special constitutional rule for Money Bills.
xs: The Governor **cannot return a Money Bill** for reconsideration — option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 200** gives four options: **assent**, **withhold**, **return** once (not a Money Bill), or **reserve** for the President.
xa: A **re-passed** bill must get the Governor's **assent**.
Mandatory reservation: a bill **derogating from the powers of the High Court**.
Nov 2025 Reference: Governor **not bound by advice** in choosing among Art. 200 options.

39.s: When a Bill returned by the Governor is passed again by the State Legislature, which one of the following is constitutionally correct?
o: The Governor must assent to the Bill and cannot withhold assent again.
The Bill automatically becomes law without any further action.
The Bill must necessarily be reserved for the President.
The Governor may withhold assent again at his discretion.
39.x: If the Legislature re-passes a Bill that was returned for reconsideration, the Governor must assent to it and cannot withhold assent again.
39.tq: Test the effect of re-passage rather than the Governor's initial alternatives.
xs: If a returned bill is re-passed, the Governor **must assent** and **cannot withhold assent again** — option **(1)** is correct (**APPCA 2026**).
**Punjab (2023)** also held **a re-passed bill must get assent**.
xa: A bill may be **reserved only once**; a re-enacted bill cannot be reserved again unless **materially altered**.
**TN v. Governor (8 April 2025):** **1 month** for assent after re-passage.
⚠ The Nov 2025 **Art. 143** opinion rejected **deemed assent** and court-imposed timelines.

39.s: A Bill once reserved for the consideration of the President may be reserved again after re-enactment only when it has been:
o: Approved by the State Cabinet unanimously
39.x: A Bill may be reserved only once. A re-enacted Bill cannot ordinarily be reserved again unless it has been materially altered.
39.tq: Use the qualifying condition to distinguish a general rule from its exception.
xs: A bill may be reserved **only once**; a re-enacted bill can be reserved again only if **materially altered** — option **(1)** is correct.
**TN (April 2025)** held that referring **10 re-enacted bills** to the President was **unconstitutional**.
xa: A **re-passed** bill must get the Governor's **assent**.
The SC used **Art 142** to grant **"deemed assent"** to those **10 bills**.
⚠ The **Nov 2025** Reference held **deemed assent** unconstitutional.

39.s: Reservation by the Governor for the President is mandatory for a Bill that:
o: Derogates from the powers of the High Court
39.x: A Bill derogating from the High Court's powers must be reserved; not every Bill affecting State finances needs mandatory reservation.
xa: Money bills during a **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)** may be reserved.
**Art. 304(b):** **previous sanction** of the President for bills restricting inter-state trade (PYQ **2018**).

39.s: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with which of the following?
39.x: Under Article 233, the Governor appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court.
39.tq: Recall Article 233.
n: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: The Governor appoints **District Judges** in consultation with **the High Court** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **State PSC** chair and members are themselves appointed by the Governor (**316**); the **State Election Commissioner** is also his appointee.
The **Chief Minister** advises on appointing **ministers**, not district judges.
xa: The Governor does **not** appoint **HC judges** — the **President** does.
He **cannot remove** SPSC members — only the **President** can.
He appoints the **Advocate-General** (**165**) and acts as **Chancellor** of state universities.

39.s: Under Article 163(1) of the Constitution, the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister aids and advises the Governor
o: Except in matters where the Governor is required to act in his discretion
Only when the Legislative Assembly is in session
39.x: Article 163(1) provides for aid and advice by the Council of Ministers except where the Governor is required to exercise discretion.

xs: Under **Art. 163(1)**, the Council of Ministers headed by the CM advises the Governor **except where he must act in his discretion** — option **(1)** is correct.

xa: **Art. 163(2):** the Governor's decision on what is discretionary is **final**.
**Art. 163(3):** ministers' advice **cannot be inquired into in any court**.
The Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.

39.s: Which provision bars courts from inquiring into the advice tendered by Ministers to the Governor?
39.x: Article 163(3) bars courts from inquiring into ministers' advice; Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision on discretion final.
xa: Even so, **discretion is subject to judicial review** (Rameshwar Prasad, Nabam Rebia).
**Nabam Rebia (2016):** **no general discretion** for the Governor.
**Art. 167:** the CM must **communicate** Cabinet decisions to the Governor.

39.s: The Governor's special responsibility for law and order in Arunachal Pradesh is provided under Article:
39.x: Article 371H gives the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh law and order responsibility; Article 371A does so for Nagaland.
xa: Other express discretion: **Art. 200**, **Art. 356**, **Art. 167**, **Art. 239**.
**AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (Sec. 8):** special responsibility for **law and order** and government buildings, mainly in **Hyderabad**.
That Sec. 8 role lapsed on **2 June 2024**.

39.s: The Supreme Court's decision in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor (2023) held that the Governor:
o: Could reserve every State Bill for the President without giving reasons
Could keep Bills pending indefinitely if no time limit was expressly stated
Must act as soon as possible and cannot keep Bills pending indefinitely
Could reject a Bill permanently after returning it once
39.x: The 2023 Punjab case held that the Governor must act as soon as possible and cannot keep Bills pending indefinitely. It also affirmed the consequence of re-passage of a returned Bill.
39.tq: Test the operative judicial direction using the precise phrase “as soon as possible”.
xs: **Punjab (2023)**: the Governor **must act "as soon as possible"** and **cannot keep bills pending indefinitely** — option **(3)** is correct.
It also held that **a re-passed bill must get assent**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: **TN v. Governor (8 April 2025)** went further and read **time limits** into **Art. 200**.
The **Nov 2025** Reference: no court-imposed timelines, but prolonged inaction invites **limited mandamus**.
**Longest delays:** **Kerala** and TN.

39.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion?
o: The President need not seek the Supreme Court's advice on each reserved Bill
Judicial review is limited to issues such as mala fides and procedure
Courts may impose a fixed deadline for every Bill pending before a Governor
39.x: The opinion rejected court-imposed timelines, permitting only limited intervention in cases of prolonged unexplained inaction.
xa: Prolonged, unexplained inaction → **limited mandamus**.

39.s: In the context of the 16th Presidential Reference, the Governor was described as the:
o: Permanent representative of the Union Cabinet in the State
Final constitutional sovereign of the State
Judicial guardian of the State Legislature
Guide, philosopher and friend of the government

xs: The **Nov 2025** Reference called the Governor the "**guide, philosopher and friend**" of the government — option **(4)** is correct.
The same opinion held the Governor **not bound by advice** in choosing among the **Art. 200** options.
xa: It was the **16th Presidential Reference** under **Art. 143**, a **5-judge** bench.

39.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Presidential Reference opinion of November 2025 from the ruling in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu dated 8 April 2025?
o: The ruling concerned Article 248, whereas the Reference concerned Article 254.

The Reference accepted deemed assent, whereas the ruling rejected it.
Both decisions prescribed identical rigid deadlines.
39.x: The 8 April 2025 ruling prescribed timelines and recognised deemed assent, while the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejected rigid deadlines and deemed assent.

xs: The **Nov 2025 Reference** rejected rigid deadlines and **deemed assent**, while the **8 April 2025** ruling prescribed **timelines** including deemed assent — option **(2)** is correct.
The ruling set **1 month** (withheld on advice), **3 months** (against advice), **1 month** after re-passage.
xa: ⚠ **Art 142** = deemed assent granted (Apr 2025); **Art 143** Reference = deemed assent rejected (Nov 2025).
⚠ Some notes (**APPCA 2026**) date the TN case to **2023** and treat deemed assent as good law.
The Reference allowed only a **limited mandamus** for prolonged inaction.

39.s: In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, decided on 8 April 2025, which timeline was associated with the Governor's action on Bills?
o: Two months, three months and two months on re-passage
Three months, six months and three months on re-passage
One month, three months and one month on re-passage
One month, six months and one month on re-passage
39.x: The ruling referred to timelines of one month, three months and one month on re-passage, along with the concept of deemed assent.
39.tq: Retain the three-part timeline as a numerical sequence rather than relying on general impressions.
xs: **TN v. Governor (8 April 2025)**: **one month** if withheld on advice, **three months** against advice, **one month** after re-passage — option **(3)** is correct.
The Court **read time limits into Art. 200**.
xa: It granted **"deemed assent"** to **10 bills** using **Art 142**.
**NCRWC 2002** had suggested assent within about **4 months**.

39.s: In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu (April 2025), the Supreme Court held that the referral of ten re-enacted Bills to the President was:
o: Valid because the Governor has absolute discretion under Article 200
Invalid only because the Bills were Money Bills
Unconstitutional, and the Court declared the Bills assented to by invoking Article 142
Valid because a re-enacted Bill must always be reserved for the President
39.x: The Supreme Court held that the referral of the ten re-enacted Bills was unconstitutional and used Article 142 to declare them assented to.

xs: Referring **10 re-enacted bills** was **unconstitutional**, and the Court **declared them assented** using **Art 142** — option **(3)** is correct.
A bill may be **reserved only once**; a re-enacted bill cannot be reserved again unless **materially altered**.
xa: A re-passed bill must get the Governor's **assent**; he **cannot withhold** again.
⚠ The **Nov 2025** **Art 143** Reference held **deemed assent** unconstitutional.
The judgment was dated **8 April 2025**.

39.s: Under Section 8 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, the Governor was given special responsibility mainly in relation to which area?
o: Law and order and allocation of government buildings in Hyderabad
Conduct of elections to all local bodies in both States
Appointment of judges to the Telangana High Court
39.x: Section 8 assigned special responsibility to the Governor for law and order and allocation of government buildings, mainly in Hyderabad as the common capital.
39.tq: Identify the specific statutory responsibilities instead of broad constitutional powers.
xs: **Sec. 8** of the **AP Reorganisation Act 2014** gave the Governor special responsibility for **law and order and allocation of government buildings**, mainly in **Hyderabad** — option **(2)** is correct.
Hyderabad was the **common capital**.
xa: It lapsed when the **10-year** common-capital period ended on **2 June 2024**.

39.s: The special responsibility assigned to the Governor under Section 8 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 ceased with the expiry of the common-capital period on:
39.x: The ten-year common-capital period ended on 2 June 2024, after which the special responsibility under Section 8 lapsed.

xs: The **10-year** common-capital period ended on **2 June 2024**, and **Sec. 8** lapsed — option **(1)** is correct.
**17 August 2026** is the Monsoon Session date, not a lapse date.
xa: Sec. 8 covered **law and order** and **government buildings** in **Hyderabad**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu** became CM again from **June 2024**.
**S. Abdul Nazeer** is Governor from **Feb 2023**.

39.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Governor's action on State Bills is incorrect?
o: The Governor must return an ordinary Bill within a fixed time limit.
The Governor may return an ordinary Bill for reconsideration.
The Governor may give assent to a State Bill.
The Governor may withhold assent to a State Bill.
39.x: Option A is incorrect: the Governor may return an ordinary bill, but the Constitution sets no time limit for acting on it. The Governor can also assent or withhold assent.
39.tq: Recall that no time limit is fixed for the Governor.
n: The Governor can give assent to a Bill under Articles 200 and 201. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Governor can withhold assent to a Bill under Articles 200 and 201. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Governor can return an ordinary Bill under Articles 200 and 201. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
There is no fixed time limit for the Governor to act on a returned ordinary Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the Governor must return an ordinary Bill within a fixed time limit** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
**Articles 200 and 201**: the Governor can **give assent**, **withhold** assent, **return** an ordinary Bill, or **reserve** it — with **no fixed time limit**.
A Bill may be returned **once** for reconsideration, but **not a Money Bill**.
xa: A **re-passed** bill: the Governor **must assent**.
**Nov 2025 Presidential Reference (Art. 143)**: courts **cannot fix timelines** and **deemed assent** is rejected.
⚠ **Art 142** = deemed assent granted (**Apr 2025**); **Art 143** Reference = deemed assent rejected (**Nov 2025**).

39.s: The Supreme Court's decision in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) established that
o: the Governor's office is completely independent of the President's pleasure
a Governor cannot be removed arbitrarily or merely because the Centre's Government has changed
a Governor can be removed only after impeachment by Parliament
a Governor can be removed whenever the Union Government changes
39.x: The pleasure doctrine is not unfettered: removal cannot be arbitrary or based merely on a change in the Government at the Centre. Such removal is open to limited judicial review.
39.tq: Use the case-law principle to reject both absolute executive power and the invented impeachment procedure.
xs: **B.P. Singhal (2010)**: a Governor **cannot be removed arbitrarily** or **merely because the Centre's government changes** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **pleasure doctrine is not unfettered**, so (1) and (4) are wrong; there is **no impeachment** route, so (3) is wrong.
xa: Reasons for removal **need not be given**, but removal must not be **arbitrary**.
Being **out of tune with the Centre** is not a ground; **limited judicial review** applies.
The Constitution states **no grounds for removal** of a Governor.

39.s: According to the November 2025 opinion in the 16th Presidential Reference, the Governor, while choosing among the options under Article 200, is:
o: Required to refer every Bill to the Supreme Court
Bound in every case by the advice of the State Council of Ministers
Not bound by such advice in choosing among the Article 200 options
Required to follow the advice of the President alone
39.x: The Presidential Reference opinion stated that the Governor is not bound by the advice of the State Council of Ministers while choosing among the options available under Article 200.
39.tq: Test the distinction between constitutional discretion under Article 200 and ordinary aid-and-advice situations.
xs: The Governor is **not bound by advice** in choosing among the **Art. 200** options — option **(3)** is correct.
No reference to the **Supreme Court** is required; the President **need not seek SC advice** on each reserved bill either.
xa: Art. 200 options: **assent**, **withhold**, **return** once (not a Money Bill), **reserve**.
Courts **cannot fix timelines** or declare **deemed assent**.
Contrast: **Perarivalan (2022)** held the Governor bound by Cabinet advice on **pardon** under **Art. 161**.

39.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that summoning, proroguing and dissolving the Assembly under Article 174 are not discretionary powers of the Governor?
39.x: Nabam Rebia held these powers and the address under Articles 175–176 are exercised on aid and advice, rejecting a general discretion.
xa: Under Nabam Rebia, the **Art. 176** address must reflect **Cabinet policy**.
In **Jan 2026**, Governors walked out of or skipped the **Art. 176** address in Opposition-ruled states.
⚠ **175** = optional address; **176** = mandatory special address.

39.s: The judgment that reaffirmed that the Governor is bound by Cabinet advice regarding pardon or remission under Article 161 is:
39.x: The Perarivalan judgment of 2022 held that the Governor is bound by Cabinet advice on pardon or remission under Article 161; this position was reaffirmed subsequently.
39.tq: Use the subject of the power—pardon or remission—to identify the relevant case.
xs: **Perarivalan (2022)** held the Governor bound by **Cabinet advice** on **pardon/remission** under **Art. 161** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was **reaffirmed in 2026**.
**Rameshwar Prasad** concerns Assembly dissolution; **Bommai** the floor test; **Nabam Rebia** summoning the House.
xa: **Art. 161:** **pardon**, reprieve, remission for offences under **state law**.

39.s:

B. Shamsher Singh

xs: Order: **Shamsher Singh (1974)** → **S.R. Bommai (1994)** → **Nabam Rebia (2016)** → **Perarivalan (2022)** — **B, D, C, A**, option **(1)**.

39.s: Which case rejected the dissolution of an Assembly based on unproven fears of horse-trading?

39.s: After the Ayodhya events of December 1992, BJP governments of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and ____ were dismissed.

39.s: Rameshwar Prasad referred to the Sarkaria Commission in connection with which issue?
o: Misuse of reports under Article 356 and a cooling-off period before politicians become Governors
The procedure for electing the Governor
The Governor's power to appoint judges of the High Court
The distribution of royalty under the Sixth Schedule

39.s: Which of the following pairs of Bills reserved for the President and the relevant Article is wrongly matched?

This makes it clear that in some spheres the Governor acts in his/her discretion. Therefore, Statement I is correct. The Constitution nowhere provides that the President can, on his/her own (suo motu), reserve any State Bill for the President’s consideration without it being reserved and sent by the Governor. Therefore, Statement II is incorrect.

III. Members of a State Legislature are not liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said within the House.

39.x: Article 361 of the Constitution of India grants special protection from legal accountability to the President and the Governor. Under Article 361(1), the Governor is not answerable to any court for acts done in the exercise of the powers and duties of his office. The same Article 361 under clause (2) clearly states that, during the Governor’s term of office (same in the case of the President), no criminal proceedings of any kind can be instituted, nor can such proceedings be continued. In this manner, he enjoys complete criminal immunity during his tenure. The provision regarding privileges and immunity for members of the State Legislature is contained in Article 194(2) of the Constitution. According to it, no member of a State Legislature shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in the Legislature or any committee thereof. This immunity is absolute, provided the proceedings relate to something said or a vote given within the House or any of its committees. Thus, all three statements are in accordance with the constitutional provisions; therefore, the correct answer is option (d).

40.s: Under the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025, a PM, CM or Minister in custody for 30 consecutive days for an offence punishable with five years or more is removed on the:

40.s: The Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh has 175 seats. On the stated maximum-size rule for a State Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, the maximum number of ministers would be:
40.x: The stated maximum is 15 percent of the Assembly strength. Fifteen percent of 175 is 26.25, giving a maximum of 26 ministers when expressed as the applicable whole-number limit.

xs: For AP's **175**-seat Assembly, the maximum Council of Ministers is **26** — option **(2)**.
The cap is a share of **Assembly strength**, which works out to **26** for **175** seats; options (1), (3) and (4) do not match it.
xa: The **Governor appoints** the CM, and ministers on the CM's advice; the CM **recommends portfolios**.
The CM **can drop ministers**.
United AP's first cabinet (**1956**) had **13** ministers.

40.s: How many times has Ms. Mayawati, the BSP leader, become the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, including her latest oath-taking as Chief Minister on May 3, 2002?
40.x: Mayawati first became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh in 1995, followed by subsequent short terms in 1997 and 2002 as head of BSP-led coalition governments. Counting her May 2002 oath-taking, this marked her fourth term as Chief Minister of the state.

40.s: Which one of the following statements about the Chief Minister of a State is not correct ?
o: The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor
The Chief Minister generally presides over the Cabinet
The Governor has to exercise all his functions on the
Ministers are appointed by the Governor on the advice

40.s: How long can a Minister continue without being elected to the State Assembly?

40.s:
Select the Constitutional Duties of the Chief Minister from the following by using the code given below:

40.x: According to Article 167, the duties of the Chief Minister of each State are to communicate to the Governor of the State all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the State and proposals for legislation; to furnish such information relating to the administration of the affairs of the State and proposals for legislation as the Governor may call for; and if the Governor so requires, to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers. 41.s: The membership of a State Legislative Council cannot exceed ____ of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly.
41.x: A Council cannot exceed one-third of the Assembly's strength nor be less than 40; Parliament fixes its actual strength.

Council is a **permanent body**.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the tenure of the State Legislative Council?
o: It is a permanent body, and one-sixth of its members retire every year.
It is a permanent body, and one-third of its members retire every second year.
It is dissolved every five years along with the Assembly.
It has a fixed tenure of six years as a whole House.
41.x: The Legislative Council is a permanent House. One-third of its members retire every second year, while each member has a six-year term.
41.tq: Separate the tenure of an individual member from the continuity of the House.
xs: The Council is a **permanent body**; **one-third** of members retire **every second year** — option **(2)**.
Each member serves **6 years**; the Council itself is **not dissolved**, unlike the Assembly's **5**-year term.
xa: Minimum age: **30** (**Art. 173**).
Size: min **40**, max **1/3** of the Assembly.

41.s: In a State Legislature, the certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill is issued by the
41.x: Under Article 199(3), the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
41.tq: Apply the 'who would do this job?' method to the certification power.
xs: The **Speaker of the Legislative Assembly** certifies a Money Bill — option **(1)**.
His decision is **final** (**Art. 199(3)**).
A Money Bill is **introduced only in the Assembly** on the **Governor's recommendation** — the Governor recommends, not certifies.
xa: Council must return a Money Bill within **14 days**; cannot reject or amend.
Speaker also decides **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.
Speaker has a **casting vote** on a tie (**Art. 189**).

41.s: The Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly can be removed by a resolution of a majority of all the then members after a notice of:
41.x: Under Article 179, removal requires a resolution by a majority of all the then members after fourteen days' notice.

Council: **Chairman** resigns to the **Deputy Chairman**.

41.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly?
o: The Speaker addresses the resignation to the Governor
The Speaker can be removed by a majority of all the then members after 14 days' notice
On dissolution, the Speaker continues until just before the new Assembly first meets
The Deputy Speaker acts with full powers when the Speaker's office is vacant
41.x: Under Article 179 the Speaker resigns by writing to the Deputy Speaker, not the Governor.
xa: **Deputy Speaker** post vacant in **8** states; **Jharkhand** had none for **21 years**.
Removal: **majority of all the then members**, **14 days' notice**.

41.s: In a bicameral State Legislature, the presiding officers are:
o: Speaker and Deputy Speaker – Assembly; Chairman and Deputy Chairman – Council
41.x: The Legislative Assembly has a Speaker and Deputy Speaker, while the Legislative Council has a Chairman and Deputy Chairman.
xa: Council: the **Chairman** resigns to the **Deputy Chairman**.
Assembly: the **Speaker** resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**.
**Telangana Council** Chairman = **Gutha Sukender Reddy**.

41.s: Under Article 190(3)(b), the resignation of a member of a State Legislative Assembly takes effect only when—
o: It is accepted by the Speaker
It is accepted by the Governor
It is published in the official gazette
It is accepted by the Election Commission
41.x: The resignation of an MLA takes effect only upon acceptance by the Speaker. For a member of the Legislative Council, acceptance is by the Chairman.
41.tq: Match the resignation with the presiding officer of the concerned House.
xs: An MLA's resignation takes effect only on **acceptance by the Speaker** — option **(1)**.
For a member of the Council, the **Chairman** accepts it (**Art. 190(3)(b)**).
xa: **Art. 190(4)**: seat vacated after **60 days'** absence without permission.
The **Speaker** himself resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**.
Disqualification under **Art. 191** is decided by the **Governor** on the **EC's opinion**.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Legislative Assembly from the Legislative Council in relation to a Money Bill?
o: A Money Bill may originate in either House, but the Council has the final decision.
The Council may reject a Money Bill if two-thirds of its members so decide.
A Money Bill can originate only in the Council on the Governor's recommendation.
A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Assembly, and the Council may make recommendations within 14 days.
41.x: A Money Bill is introduced only in the Legislative Assembly on the Governor's recommendation. The Council can only recommend changes and must return it within 14 days; it cannot reject or amend it.
41.tq: Identify who introduces, who recommends and who has the final word.
xs: A Money Bill is introduced **only in the Assembly**; the Council may only **recommend** within **14 days** — option **(4)**.
It is introduced by a minister on the **Governor's recommendation** (**Art. 207**).
The Council **cannot reject or amend** it (**Art. 198**); its recommendations may be rejected.
xa: The **Speaker** certifies a Money Bill (**Art. 199(3)**).
⚠ Council delay: **14 days** (Money Bill); **3 months** + **1 month** (ordinary Bill).
Demands for grants are **voted only in the Assembly**.

41.s: A Bill originating in the Legislative Council and rejected by the Legislative Assembly:
o: Is referred to a joint sitting
Returns to the Council for reconsideration
41.x: Such a Bill ends; the Council has no second chance and State Legislatures have no joint sitting.
xa: For Assembly Bills, the Council can delay **3 months** then **1 month**.
The Council has **no role in ratifying** constitutional amendments.

41.s: MLAs elect what fraction of the members of a State Legislative Council?
41.x: MLAs elect one-third of the Council's members; they also vote in Presidential and Rajya Sabha elections.

Council members are elected by **PR-STV**.

41.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Qualifications are **Art. 173**; Council composition **Art. 171**; Annual Financial Statement **Art. 202**.

**Arts 168-212** cover the State Legislature as a whole (APPSC-GS **2018**).

41.s:
Assertion (A): Article 169 deals with the creation or abolition of State Legislative Councils.
Reason (R): Article 202 deals with the Annual Financial Statement of a State.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

**Art. 211**: no discussion of a **HC judge's conduct**; **Art. 212**: courts not to inquire into proceedings.
**Art. 210**: language — Hindi/English or the state's official language.

41.s: The Governor's right to address and send messages to the House or Houses of the State Legislature is under Article:
41.x: Article 175 covers the address and messages; 174 deals with sessions and dissolution and 176 with the special address.
xa: Art. 174 rule: no more than **6 months** between sittings.
**Art. 172** = duration (**5 years**); **Art. 173** = qualifications (**25 / 30**).

41.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 210 — Language to be used in the Legislature
Article 187 — Secretariat of the State Legislature
Article 194 — Powers and privileges of State Legislatures
41.x: Article 212 concerns the exclusion of judicial inquiry into legislative proceedings. The Annual Financial Statement is dealt with under Article 202.

xs: **Article 212 — Annual Financial Statement** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**Art. 212** bars **courts from inquiring into proceedings**; the **Annual Financial Statement** is **Art. 202**.
The others are correct: **Art. 210** = language, **Art. 187** = secretariat, **Art. 194** = **privileges**.
xa: **Art. 211**: no discussion of a **HC judge's conduct**.
**Art. 208**: each House makes its **rules of procedure** (APPSC-GS **2018** key).
**Arts 202-207** = financial procedure; **Arts 198-199** = Money Bills.

41.s: Which Article bars discussion in the State Legislature of the conduct of a High Court judge in the discharge of duties?
41.x: Article 211 bars such discussion; Article 208 covers rules of procedure and Article 212 bars courts inquiring into proceedings.
xa: **Art. 194** = **privileges** of MLAs and committees.
**Art. 210** = language: **Hindi/English** or the state's official language.
**Art. 187** = **secretariat** of the state legislature.

41.s: Who is the Chairman of the Telangana Legislative Council?

Council: the **Chairman** resigns to the **Deputy Chairman**.

41.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about State Legislative Councils?
o: A Council gives a place to experts who cannot face elections
Its existence depends on the ruling party in the Assembly, as in Andhra Pradesh
A Council can permanently veto an ordinary Bill passed by the Assembly

Under **Art. 169** its existence depends on the **will of the Assembly**.
Money Bill: Council must return it within **14 days**.

41.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The State Legislative Council is a permanent body and cannot be dissolved.
The State Legislative Council cannot be abolished because it is a permanent body.
One-third of the Council members retire every two years.
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169.
41.x: Option B is incorrect. The Council is permanent, so it cannot be dissolved, but it can be abolished under Article 169. One-third of its members retire every two years.
41.tq: Discriminate between dissolving a House and abolishing it.
n: The State Legislative Council is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Council cannot be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Council can be abolished. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
One-third of the members of the State Legislative Council retire every 2 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Council of States is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Council of States cannot be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council cannot be dissolved on the recommendation of the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the Council cannot be abolished because it is a permanent body** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
The Council is **permanent** — it **cannot be dissolved** — but it **can be abolished** or created under **Article 169**.
**One-third** of members retire every **two years** — so (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: The **Assembly** is the opposite: **dissolvable** but cannot be **abolished**.
Council member's term is **six years**.
**AP** abolished its Council in **1985** and revived it in **2007**; **Tamil Nadu** abolished its Council in **1986**.

41.s: The Legislative Council must return a State Money Bill with its recommendations within:
41.x: The Council must return a Money Bill within 14 days, failing which it is deemed passed by both Houses.
n: The Legislative Council receives a Money Bill only for recommendations. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council must return a Money Bill within 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
A Money Bill is deemed to have been passed upon expiry of 14 days if the Legislative Council does not return it. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xa: The Council **cannot amend or reject** a Money Bill; the Assembly has **final authority** (**Art. 198**).
Money Bills are introduced **only in the Assembly**, on the **Governor's prior recommendation** (**Article 207**).
⚠ Council delay: **14 days** (Money Bill); **3 months** + **1 month** (ordinary bill).

41.s: On first passage, the Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill passed by the Assembly for a maximum of:
41.x: The Council can delay an ordinary Bill three months, then one month after it is repassed; it has no veto.
n: The Legislative Council has no veto power over ordinary bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council cannot permanently block legislation passed by the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for a maximum of 3 months after its first passage. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council can delay a re-passed ordinary bill for a maximum of 1 month. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Assembly can re-pass an ordinary bill after its first passage through the Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xa: The Assembly is the **originating and overriding** chamber (**Article 197**).
A bill **originating in the Council** and rejected by the Assembly **ends**.
There is **no joint sitting** in states, unlike Parliament (**Art. 108**).

41.s: Which of the following statements regarding State Legislature Bills is incorrect?
o: A State Money Bill originates in the Legislative Assembly.
The Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill for a maximum of 6 months.
The Governor’s recommendation is required for the introduction of a State Money Bill.
The Legislative Council gets 14 days to consider a State Money Bill.
41.x: Option B is incorrect: a Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for at most four months (three, then one), not six. A State Money Bill starts in the Assembly on the Governor's recommendation, and the Council has 14 days to consider it.
41.tq: Recall the Council's 3 + 1 month limit.
n: The Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill for three months the first time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill for one month the second time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Legislative Council’s maximum delaying power for an Ordinary Bill is four months. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A State Money Bill originates in the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A State Money Bill requires the Governor’s recommendation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Legislative Council gets 14 days to consider a State Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the Council **can delay an Ordinary Bill for a maximum of 6 months** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
The maximum delay is **four months** — **three months** first, then **one month** after re-passage.
A State Money Bill **originates in the Legislative Assembly** with the **Governor's recommendation**, and the Council gets **14 days** — so (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: The Council's power is **only delaying** — much weaker than the **Rajya Sabha's**.
**Speaker's certification** of a Money Bill is **sole and final** (**Art. 199(3)**).
The Council has **no role in ratifying** constitutional amendments.

41.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
41.x: Article 178 deals with the Speaker and Deputy Speaker. Article 170 covers Assembly composition, 173 the age qualification and 213 ordinances.
n: Article 170 concerns Assembly composition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Article 173 concerns the Assembly membership age of 25 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Articles 178 and 179 concern Speaker election and resignation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Article 213 concerns Ordinances. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xa: **Article 172**: duration (**5 years**); **Article 174**: sessions, prorogation, dissolution.
**Article 179**: Speaker's resignation and removal.
**Article 192**: disqualification decided by the **Governor**.

41.s: The minimum age for membership of a State Legislative Council is:
41.x: The minimum age is 30 for the Council (Article 171) and 25 for the Assembly (Article 170).
n: The Constitutional basis of the Legislative Assembly is Article 170. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Constitutional basis of the Legislative Council is Article 171. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The minimum age for membership of the Legislative Assembly is 25 years under Article 173. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The minimum age for membership of the Legislative Council is 30 years under Article 173. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xa: Assembly: maximum **500**, minimum **60**.

41.s: The term of a member of a State Legislative Council is:
41.x: Council members serve six years, with one-third retiring every two years; the Council is a permanent body.
n: The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Legislative Council is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
One-third of the Legislative Council members retire every two years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The term of a Legislative Council member is six years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xa: The Council **cannot be dissolved**, not even on the Governor's recommendation.
The **Rajya Sabha** follows the same pattern: **six** years, one-third retire every **two** years.
The Council is called the **Upper House** / **House of Elders**.

41.s: Which of the following statements regarding the two Houses is incorrect?
o: The Legislative Assembly is elected directly through the FPTP system.
The Legislative Assembly is a permanent body, with one-third of its members retiring every two years.

41.x: Option B is incorrect: the Legislative Council is the permanent House, with one-third retiring every two years. The Assembly has a five-year term and can be dissolved.
41.tq: Discriminate the dissolvable Assembly from the permanent Council.
n: The Legislative Assembly is elected directly through the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Council is elected indirectly through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and nomination. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Assembly has a five-year tenure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Assembly is subject to dissolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Council is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
One-third of the Legislative Council members retire every two years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
A Legislative Council member has a six-year term. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the Legislative Assembly is a permanent body, with one-third of its members retiring every two years** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
That describes the **Legislative Council**; the Assembly has a **five-year** term and is **dissolvable**.
The Assembly is **directly** elected by **FPTP**; the Council is **indirectly** elected by **PR-STV** plus **nomination**, with a **six-year** member term.
xa: Assembly = **Lower / Popular** House; Council = **Upper** House / **House of Elders**.
The Council **can be abolished** (**Article 169**); the Assembly cannot.
**Demands for grants** are voted **only** in the Assembly.

41.s: The Legislative Council's power to delay ordinary Bills is provided under Article:
41.x: Article 197 covers the Council's delay of ordinary Bills; 176 is the Governor's address and 207 the recommendation for Money Bills.
n: The Governor addresses the Legislative Assembly at the commencement of the first session after each general election under Article 176. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Governor addresses the Legislative Assembly at the first session of each year under Article 176. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Introduction of a Money Bill requires the Governor's prior recommendation under Article 207. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill for three months on the first occasion under Article 197. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]

xa: **Article 175** = optional address/messages; **176** = **mandatory** address at the first session of the year.
**Article 200** = Governor's assent / reservation.
**Articles 198-199** = State Money Bills.

41.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about a State Money Bill?
o: The Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is final
