41.s: In a bicameral State Legislature, a Money Bill can be introduced only in:
41.x: Money Bills start only in the Legislative Assembly; the Assembly is dissolvable with a five-year term, while the Council is permanent.
n: The Legislative Assembly is dissolvable and temporary. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Legislative Council is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
A State Money Bill can be introduced only in the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]

xa: First-time delay on an ordinary bill: **three months** — **four months** in all.

41.s:

41.s: The Legislative Assemblies of Goa and Mizoram have how many seats each?

Normal range under **Art. 170**: **60-500**.
**AP 175**; **Telangana 119**.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly presents the present strength of the Legislative Assemblies of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh respectively?
41.x: The Legislative Assemblies of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh have 175, 119 and 403 seats respectively.
41.tq: Read the three figures as a fixed sequence and reject near-value substitutions.
xs: Option (4) wrongly gives AP **176**; options (1) and (2) misstate Telangana and UP.
xa: AP's Council exists today; **six states** have Councils.

41.s: Which of the following is NOT a power or function of the Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly?
o: Approving the creation of a Legislative Council in the State
Giving the final decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill
Deciding disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, subject to judicial review
Adjourning or suspending the House in case of lack of quorum
41.x: The Speaker performs the first three functions. Creation or abolition of a Legislative Council involves an Assembly resolution followed by parliamentary law; it is not approved by the Speaker.
41.tq: Find the option assigning a constitutional function to the wrong authority.
xs: **Approving the creation of a Legislative Council** is not the Speaker's power — option **(1)**.
Creation needs an **Assembly special-majority resolution** and a **Parliament** law (**Art. 169**).
The Speaker does: decide **Money Bill** status, **Tenth Schedule** disqualification, and adjourn for **lack of quorum**.
xa: Tenth Schedule decisions are **subject to judicial review** (**Kihoto Hollohan 1992**).
Other powers: allows a **secret sitting**, appoints committee chairmen.
Chairs the **Business Advisory**, **Rules** and **General Purposes** Committees.

41.s: A person elected to both Houses of a State Legislature is required to vacate one of the memberships because—
o: The Constitution prohibits simultaneous membership of both Houses of the same State Legislature
An MLA cannot become an MLC under any circumstances
The Council is a nominated body and cannot have elected members
The Governor alone may permit only one membership
41.x: Article 190 prevents a person from being a member of both Houses of the Legislature of a State at the same time. It also bars simultaneous membership of legislatures of two States.
41.tq: Use the constitutional incompatibility rule to eliminate explanations based on the composition of the Council.
xs: **Art. 190** bars membership of **both Houses** of the same State Legislature — option **(1)**.
It also bars membership of **two states'** legislatures.
MLAs do elect **1/3** of MLCs, so the Council is not wholly nominated (option 3 wrong).
xa: **Art. 190(4)**: seat vacated after **60 days'** absence without permission.
**Art. 190(3)(b)**: resignation effective on **Speaker's/Chairman's acceptance**.

41.s: Which one of the following statements regarding demands for grants in a State Legislature is correct?
o: Demands for grants are voted by the Governor after discussion in the Council.
The Legislative Council votes on demands for grants, while the Assembly only discusses them.
Demands for grants are voted only in the Legislative Assembly, while the Council may discuss them.
Both Houses vote jointly on demands for grants.
41.x: The Legislative Assembly alone votes on demands for grants. The Legislative Council may discuss them but cannot vote on them.
41.tq: Separate the power to discuss from the power to vote.
xs: Demands for grants are **voted only in the Assembly**; the Council **discusses only** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) reverses the roles; there is no joint vote or Governor vote.
xa: Session order: **Governor's address** → **general discussion** → **voting on demands** (Assembly only).
Money Bill introduced **only in the Assembly** (**Art. 207**).
Financial procedure: **Arts. 202-207**; **Art. 202** = **Annual Financial Statement**.

41.s: Which State has the smallest Legislative Assembly?
41.x: Sikkim has the smallest State Assembly with 32 members; Puducherry has the smallest UT Assembly (33).
n: Sikkim has the smallest State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Sikkim Legislative Assembly has 32 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Puducherry has the smallest Union Territory Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Puducherry Legislative Assembly has 33 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Sikkim's 32-member Legislative Assembly is a special constitutional exception. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xa: Largest Assembly: **Uttar Pradesh** (**403**).
**Goa** and **Mizoram** have **40** seats each.
**AP** has **175** seats; **Telangana** **119**.
⚠ **Arunachal** has a minimum of **30** under **Art. 371H** but actually has **60**.

41.s: Which of the following has a Legislative Assembly of 40 seats or fewer but is NOT a State?
41.x: Puducherry (33 seats) is a Union Territory; Goa and Mizoram (40 each) and Sikkim (32) are States.
n: Sikkim has the smallest State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Sikkim Legislative Assembly has 32 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Goa Legislative Assembly has 40 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Mizoram Legislative Assembly has 40 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
Puducherry has the smallest Union Territory Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Puducherry Assembly has 33 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xa: Sikkim is a special exception (**Art. 371F**) below the standard minimum of **60**.
Puducherry = **30** elected + **3** nominated.
Largest Assembly: **Uttar Pradesh** (**403**).

41.s: The maximum strength of a State Legislative Assembly is:
41.x: An Assembly can have at most 500 and at least 60 members; Uttar Pradesh has the largest and Sikkim the smallest.
n: The maximum prescribed strength of a general State Legislative Assembly is 500 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The constitutional floor for the strength of a State Legislative Assembly is 60 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Uttar Pradesh has the largest State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Sikkim has the smallest State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The minimum prescribed strength of a State Legislative Assembly is 60 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xa: Sikkim's **32** is a special exception under **Art. 371F**.
Smallest UT Assembly: **Puducherry** (**33**).
**AP** has **175** seats; **Telangana** **119**.

41.s: Which of the following statements regarding State Legislative Councils is incorrect?
o: The largest Legislative Council is in Sikkim.
The minimum prescribed strength of a State Legislative Council is 40 members.
The provision relating to State Legislative Councils is contained in Article 171.
The maximum strength of a State Legislative Council is one-third of the strength of the State Assembly.
41.x: Option A is incorrect: Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council (100 members); Sikkim has no Council. A Council can be at most one-third of the Assembly and at least 40 (Article 171).
41.tq: Recall the largest Council.
n: The maximum prescribed strength of a State Legislative Council is one-third of the strength of the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The minimum prescribed strength of a State Legislative Council is 40 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The State Legislative Council is covered by Article 171. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the largest Legislative Council is in Sikkim** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
The **largest** Council is in **Uttar Pradesh** — **100** members.
The Council's provision is in **Article 171**: maximum **one-third** of the Assembly, minimum **40** — so (2), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: Sikkim is not among the **six** bicameral States: **AP, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, UP**.
Actual strength is fixed by **Parliament**.
⚠ Lists showing **J&K** are out of date — its Council was abolished in **2019**.

41.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the composition of a State Legislative Council?
o: One-sixth are elected by registered graduates
One-twelfth are elected by teachers of three years' standing
One-third are elected by local bodies
One-sixth are nominated by the Governor
41.x: Registered graduates elect one-twelfth; the one-sixth share is nominated by the Governor.
xa: ⚠ **1/3 – 1/12 – 1/12 – 1/3 – 1/6** = **local bodies – graduates – teachers – MLAs – Governor**.
**1/3** elected by **MLAs** from among non-members of the Assembly.
Mode of election: **PR-STV**.

41.s: The Governor nominates what fraction of the members of a State Legislative Council?
41.x: The Governor nominates one-sixth of the Council from literature, science, art, co-operative movement and social service, on Cabinet advice.
xa: Other shares: **1/3** local bodies, **1/12** graduates, **1/12** teachers, **1/3** MLAs.
Council size: max **1/3** of the Assembly, min **40** (**Art. 171**).
Significance: gives a place to **experts who cannot face elections**.

41.s: The minimum strength of a State Legislative Council is:
41.x: A Council must have at least 40 members; one-third are elected by MLAs, one-twelfth by graduates and one-sixth nominated.
n: One-third of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by MLAs. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
One-third of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by local authorities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
One-twelfth of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by graduates. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
One-twelfth of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by teachers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
One-sixth of the members of a State Legislative Council are nominated by the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xa: **Local bodies** elect **one-third**; **teachers** elect **one-twelfth**.
⚠ **1/3 – 1/12 – 1/12 – 1/3 – 1/6** = **local bodies – graduates – teachers – MLAs – Governor**.
Maximum size: **one-third** of the Assembly; **Uttar Pradesh** has the largest Council (**100**).
Graduates and teachers need at least **3 years** of standing.

41.s: Which of the following is NOT a field for nomination by the Governor to the State Legislative Council?
41.x: The valid fields are literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service; industrial activity is not one.
n: Literature is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Science is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Art is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The co-operative movement is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Social service is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Industrialists are not valid nomination categories for a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Governor’s five nomination fields for a State Legislative Council are literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, and social service. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xa: The Governor nominates **one-sixth** of the Council, on **Cabinet advice**.
⚠ The **co-operative movement** is a ground under **Article 171** but **not** for the Rajya Sabha (**Article 80**).
Other Council members are elected by **PR-STV**, by **secret ballot**.

41.s: A law of Parliament under Article 169 creating or abolishing a Legislative Council is passed by:
o: Two-thirds of members present and voting
A special majority with ratification by half the States
41.x: Parliament uses a simple majority, and such a law is not deemed an amendment under Article 368.
xa: Assembly resolution: **majority of total membership** + **2/3 of members present and voting**.
The **Governor has no role** in the resolution.
⚠ Assembly = **special majority**; Parliament = **simple majority**.

41.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the role of the Governor in the process under Article 169?
o: The Governor initiates the Assembly resolution for creation of the Council
The Governor alone can abolish the Legislative Council by notification
The Governor must approve the Assembly resolution before it is sent to Parliament
The Governor has no role in initiating or approving the resolution
41.x: The constitutional process is initiated by a special-majority resolution of the Legislative Assembly and completed through a law of Parliament; the Governor has no role in initiating or approving that resolution.
41.tq: Use the 'who would do this job?' test to reject powers wrongly assigned to the Governor.
xs: The **Governor has no role** in initiating or approving the resolution — option **(4)**.
The **Assembly** passes the resolution by **special majority**; **Parliament** then passes a law by **simple majority**.
xa: The law is **not deemed an amendment** under **Art. 368**.
The Council's existence depends on the **will of the Assembly**.
⚠ Assembly = special; Parliament = simple; Governor = **no role**.

41.s: Under Article 169, the resolution of a State Legislative Assembly for the creation or abolition of its Legislative Council must be passed by—
o: A simple majority of members present and voting
A majority of the total membership of the Assembly and at least two-thirds of the members present and voting
Two-thirds of the total membership of the Assembly
A majority of the total membership of both Houses sitting jointly
41.x: Article 169 needs a special majority: a majority of the total membership of the Assembly plus not less than two-thirds of members present and voting. A simple majority is what Parliament then uses for its law; two-thirds of total membership is not the test; States have no joint sitting.
41.tq: Assembly = special majority; Parliament = simple majority; not an Art 368 amendment.
xs: The resolution needs a **majority of total membership** and **at least two-thirds of members present and voting** — option **(2)**.
A **simple majority** is what **Parliament** uses for the follow-up law.
There is no joint sitting in State legislatures.
xa: The law is **not deemed an amendment** under **Art. 368**.
The **Governor has no role**.
APPSC-GS **2018** asked on **Art. 169**.

41.s: A State Assembly resolution for creation or abolition of a Legislative Council must be passed by:
o: A simple majority of members present
A majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting
Three-fourths of members present and voting
41.x: It needs a special majority (majority of total membership and two-thirds present and voting), but only requests and does not compel the Union.
n: The State Legislative Assembly resolution for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council requires a special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The special majority requires at least 50 percent of the total membership of the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The special majority requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting in the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly resolution for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council is recommendatory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly resolution does not legally compel the Union Government to introduce a bill in Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly initiates the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council by passing a resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xa: **Parliament** then acts by **simple majority**; the law is **not deemed an amendment** under **Art. 368**.
The **Governor has no role** in the resolution.
⚠ Assembly = **special majority**; Parliament = **simple majority**; Governor = **no role**.

41.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Jammu and Kashmir — Council continues after the 2019 Reorganisation Act
Andhra Pradesh — Council abolished in 1986 and revived in 2007
Andhra Pradesh — Council created for the first time in 2007
41.x: Tamil Nadu abolished its Legislative Council in 1986. Andhra Pradesh abolished its Council in 1985 and revived it in 2007, while the Jammu and Kashmir Council was abolished in 2019.
41.tq: Find the correctly matched historical pair among closely related Council changes.
xs: **Tamil Nadu** abolished its Council in **1986** — option **(3)**.
**AP** abolished its Council in **1985** (not **1986**) and revived it in **2007** — so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
**J&K's** Council was abolished by the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019**.
xa: Present list (**2026**): **AP, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, UP** — **six states**.
⚠ Lists showing **J&K** or only four states are out of date.
AP's Council again in flux in **2020-21**.

41.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of States having Legislative Councils at present?
o: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Kerala, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Goa
Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh
Telangana, Mizoram, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Sikkim
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh
41.x: The six States with Legislative Councils are Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh.
41.tq: Check every member of the six-State list; a single unicameral State makes the option wrong.
xs: The six states: **AP, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and UP** — option **(4)**.
**Goa**, **Kerala**, **Mizoram** and **Sikkim** have no Councils, so options (1), (2) and (3) fail.
xa: **J&K's** Council was abolished in **2019**.
**Tamil Nadu** abolished its Council in **1986**.
**Karnataka Council (2026)**: **Saleem Ahmed** elected Chairperson (**38-30**).
**Telangana Council** Chairman: **Gutha Sukender Reddy**.

41.s: In which of the following years or periods did Andhra Pradesh illustrate the politically fluctuating status of the Legislative Council?
41.x: Andhra Pradesh abolished its Legislative Council in 1985 (NTR government) and revived it in 2007; in January 2020 the Assembly resolved to abolish it again, but withdrew that resolution in November 2021. These swings show that the Council's fate depends on state politics.
41.tq: Recall the distinctive three-point chronology rather than selecting a sequence of unrelated years.
xs: AP's Council fate swung in **1985, 2007 and 2020-21** — option **(3)**.
AP **abolished** its Council in **1985** and **revived** it in **2007**.
xa: Criticism: a costly "**delaying chamber**" whose existence depends on the ruling party in the Assembly.
**Tamil Nadu** abolished its Council in **1986**.
Significance: checks **hasty legislation**.

41.s: The interval between the last sitting in one session of a State Legislature and the first sitting in the next session cannot exceed:
41.x: Article 174 requires that not more than six months intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next.
41.tq: Test the constitutional time limit directly and distinguish it from other legislative periods.
xs: The gap cannot exceed **six months** — option **(1)**.
This is the **Art. 174** rule: no more than **6 months** between the last sitting of one session and the first of the next.
xa: Many Assemblies met only to satisfy this **Art. 174** rule.
PRS **2025**: Assemblies sat an average of **24 days** (**Odisha 43**, **Nagaland 7**).
About **33%** of Bills passed in a single sitting.

41.s: Who among the following was the first woman legislator in India?
41.x: Muthulakshmi Reddy was India’s first woman legislator and served in the Madras Legislative Council.
41.tq: Use the first-in-history clue and distinguish legislative office from executive office.
xs: **Muthulakshmi Reddy** was India's **first woman legislator** — option **(2)**.
She sat in the **Madras Legislative Council**.
xa: The Council gives a place to **experts who cannot face elections**.
**Tamil Nadu** later abolished its Council in **1986**.
Governor nominates **1/6** of a Council from literature, science, art, cooperation and social service.

41.s: The minimum strength of a State Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, is:
41.x: The 91st Amendment (2003) caps a State ministry at 15% of the Assembly with a minimum of 12.
n: The Council of Ministers is capped at a maximum of 15 percent of the Assembly's strength under Article 164. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act of 2003 provides the 15-percent cap on the Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The minimum size of the Council of Ministers is 12 ministers, including the Chief Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xa: The cap is in **Article 164** (**164(1A)**).
A **non-member** minister may serve only **six consecutive months**.

41.s: In a Legislative Assembly consisting of 70 members, the quorum for a sitting would be—
41.x: Quorum is 10 members or one-tenth of the total membership, whichever is greater. For a 70-member House, 10 is greater than 7.
41.tq: Apply the ‘whichever is greater’ rule rather than simply calculating one-tenth.
xs: Quorum is **10 members**, which is greater than one-tenth of **70** (= **7**) — option **(2)**.
Rule (**Art. 189(3)**): **10 members or one-tenth** of the House, **whichever is greater**.
So option (1), **7**, is only the one-tenth figure; **35** and **70** are not the rule.
xa: The **Speaker** adjourns or suspends the House for **lack of quorum**.
**Art. 189** also: the Speaker has a **casting vote** on a tie.
Normal Assembly strength: **60-500** (**Art. 170**).

41.s: Which one of the following is NOT a ground of disqualification under Article 191 of the Constitution?
o: Being absent from the House for 60 days without permission
Being of unsound mind as declared by a competent court
41.x: Absence for 60 days without permission results in vacation of the seat under Article 190(4), not disqualification under Article 191.
41.tq: Distinguish disqualification under Article 191 from vacation of seat under Article 190.
xs: **Absence for 60 days without permission** is not an **Art. 191** ground — option **(3)**.
It vacates the seat under **Art. 190(4)**.
**Insolvency**, **office of profit** and **unsound mind** are Art. 191 grounds.
xa: Other Art. 191 grounds: **not a citizen**, Parliament's law (**RPA 1951**), **Tenth Schedule** defection.
**Art. 190**: no one can be a member of **both Houses** or of **two states'** legislatures.
**Art. 190(3)(b)**: MLA's resignation takes effect only on the **Speaker's acceptance**.

41.s: With reference to the Governor's address to the State Legislature, which one of the following is correct?
o: It is delivered before every sitting of the Legislative Assembly.
It is delivered on the first day of the first session of each year and is followed by discussion.
It is delivered on the last day of every annual session.
It is delivered only when the Legislative Council demands it.
41.x: The Governor addresses the Legislature on the first day of the first session of each year, and the address is followed by discussion in the House.
41.tq: Use the time phrase ‘first day of the first session’ as the key discriminator.
xs: The Governor's address is on the **first day of the first session of each year**, followed by **discussion** — option **(2)**.
It is not before every sitting or on the last day.
xa: **Art. 175** = Governor's address and messages; **Art. 176** = special address (mandatory at the first session).
Then **general discussion** → **voting on demands**.
**Art. 208**: each House makes its **rules of procedure**.

41.s: Which Constitutional Amendment ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Article 333?
41.x: The 104th Amendment Act, 2020 ended Anglo-Indian nomination; the 106th (2023) provides about one-third reservation for women.
n: Article 332 mandates reservation of Legislative Assembly seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe Legislative Assembly reservations are based on population ratios. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2020 ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Article 333. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2023 provides approximately one-third reservation for women in directly elected Assembly seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The women's reservation under the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act becomes effective after post-census delimitation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xa: Minimum age (**Article 173**): **Assembly 25**, **Council 30** years.
The Assembly is **directly elected** by **First-Past-the-Post**.
Maximum **500**, minimum **60** seats (**Article 170**).

41.s: The term of office of a Governor is:
41.x: The Governor's term is five years, subject to the President's pleasure, and continues until a successor takes over.
n: The Governor has a five-year term. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The Governor continues in office until the successor assumes office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xa: **Five years** is also the tenure of the **President**, **Lok Sabha**, a **State Legislative Assembly**, a **Panchayat** and a **Municipality**.
**Six years**: **Rajya Sabha** and **Legislative Council** members.
The Assembly can be extended **1 year at a time** during a National Emergency.

41.s: An extension of a State Assembly's term during a National Emergency cannot continue beyond ____ after the Emergency ceases.
41.x: Parliament may extend the term a year at a time during an Emergency, but not beyond six months after it ceases.
n: The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years under Article 172. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
During a National Emergency under Article 352, Parliament may extend the Legislative Assembly’s duration by law for one year at a time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Legislative Assembly’s duration may be extended only up to six months after the National Emergency ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xa: The Assembly may be **dissolved** earlier but cannot be **abolished**.
**Art. 174**: no more than **6 months** between sittings.

41.s: The members of a State Legislative Council are elected by which method?
o: Cumulative voting by the Legislative Assembly alone
First-past-the-post system by direct universal suffrage
Proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote
41.x: Members of a State Legislative Council are elected indirectly through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.
41.tq: Discriminate between the electoral system and the appointing authority.
xs: Council members are elected indirectly by **PR-STV** — **proportional representation by single transferable vote** — option **(4)**.
It is not direct election by universal suffrage; only **1/6** are **nominated** by the Governor.
xa: **Rajya Sabha** members are also elected by MLAs by **PR-STV**.
MLAs elect **1/3** of MLCs.
Members serve **6 years**; **1/3** retire every **second year**.

41.s: While a resolution for his removal is under consideration, the Speaker of a State Assembly:
o: Presides and has only a casting vote
Cannot speak but may vote in the second instance
Must leave the House and cannot take part
Does not preside, but may speak and vote in the first instance
41.x: Under Article 181 the Speaker does not preside but may speak and vote in the first instance.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "the Speaker will preside" is **not** a power (APPSC-G1 **2022** key).
Removal needs a **majority of all the then members** after **14 days' notice**.
Normally (**Art. 189**) he has no first-instance vote, only a **casting vote**.

41.s: Who presides over the State Legislative Council?
o: The Chairman elected by the Council from among its members
The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
41.x: Under Article 182, the Council elects its Chairman from among its own members. The Governor does not nominate the Chairman, and the Vice-President chairs only the Rajya Sabha.
41.tq: Discriminate the Council's Chairman from the Rajya Sabha's ex-officio Chairman.
n: The Chairman of the State Legislative Council is elected by the Council from among its members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Chairman of the Legislative Council is chosen by the Council members from among themselves under Article 182. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Governor does not nominate the Chairman of the Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: The Council is presided over by **the Chairman elected by the Council from among its members** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is under **Article 182**; the Chairman is **not nominated by the Governor**.
The **Speaker** presides over the **Legislative Assembly**, not the Council.

43.x: Article 137 provides review; Article 141 makes SC law binding and Article 142 allows orders for complete justice.
xa: Art. 142 uses: declared **10 TN bills assented** (Apr **2025**); **Right to Safe Travel** (**27 May 2026**).
HCs have **no equivalent power** (**Anil Kumar Jain v. Maya Jain**).
**Curative petition**: **Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002)**.

43.s: Which Article empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice?
43.x: Article 142 is a power specific to the Supreme Court; High Courts have no equivalent under it.
xa: **Art. 141**: SC's law binds all courts.
**Art. 143** advisory: the **16th Presidential Reference** (Nov **2025**) on bill timelines.
**Art. 129**: court of record with **contempt** power.

43.s: Which of the following statements about the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 is correct?
o: It defines only civil contempt and leaves criminal contempt undefined
It defines civil and criminal contempt, while the Constitution itself does not define contempt
It abolishes the Supreme Court’s constitutional contempt power
It applies only to proceedings before High Courts
43.x: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil and criminal contempt. The Constitution confers contempt powers on the Supreme Court and High Courts but does not itself define contempt.
43.tq: Separate the statutory definition from the constitutional conferment of contempt power.
xs: The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** **defines civil and criminal contempt**, while the **Constitution does not define** it — option **(2)** is correct.
It defines both types, not only civil; it does not abolish the SC's power under **Art. 129**.
It is not limited to HCs — contempt powers are in **Art. 129** (SC) and **Art. 215** (HC).
xa: The Act followed the **H.N. Sanyal Committee**.
**Art. 129** makes the SC a **court of record**.
Contempt power is listed among safeguards of **judicial independence**.

43.s: The e-SCR is associated with:
o: A registry for appointments through the collegium system
A free digital database of the Supreme Court’s reported judgments launched in 2023
An online system for filing presidential references under Article 143
An electronic voting system for Supreme Court proceedings
43.x: e-SCR means electronic Supreme Court Reports. It is a free digital database of the Court’s reported judgments, launched in 2023.
43.tq: Decode the official abbreviation and match it with its function and launch year.
xs: **e-SCR** is **a free digital database of the Supreme Court's reported judgments launched in 2023** — option **(2)** is correct.
It has nothing to do with collegium registries, **Art. 143** references or voting.
xa: **Curative petition**: created in **Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002)**.
**Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** defines civil and criminal contempt.
**Art. 141**: law declared by the SC binds all courts.

43.s: The expression “imperium in imperio” is used in the debate on the Collegium system to indicate criticism that it is
o: a forum exclusively for resolving Centre-State disputes
a self-contained authority operating within the State
a body subordinate to State legislatures
a constitutional body headed by the Union Law Minister
43.x: “Imperium in imperio” literally conveys the criticism that the Collegium functions like an authority within an authority, reflecting concerns about opacity and judges selecting judges.
43.tq: Translate the Latin expression into the institutional criticism it represents.
xs: "**Imperium in imperio**" criticises the Collegium as **a self-contained authority operating within the State** — option **(2)** is correct.
It goes with charges that the Collegium is **opaque** and amounts to "**judges selecting judges**".
The collegium is not a Centre-State forum, not under State legislatures, and not headed by the Law Minister.
xa: The collegium has **no mention in the Constitution**.
The other side of the debate: **executive delays** in notifying names.
Transparency debate revived by Justice **Ujjal Bhuyan** (**26 Aug 2026**).

43.s: Which one of the following proposals was associated with the private member's Bill concerning judicial appointments?
o: Abolition of Article 222 and direct election of High Court judges
A 90-day limit for the Centre to notify Collegium recommendations, along with social diversity and regional Supreme Court benches
Appointment of all Supreme Court judges by State legislatures
Replacement of the Collegium by the Finance Commission
43.x: The private member's Bill proposed social diversity in appointments, a 90-day period for the Centre to notify Collegium names and regional benches of the Supreme Court.
43.tq: Separate the specific contents of a proposal from unrelated constitutional mechanisms.
xs: The Bill proposed **a 90-day limit** for the Centre to notify Collegium names, **social diversity** and **regional SC benches** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was DMK MP **P. Wilson's** private member's Bill (**19 Feb 2026**).
Other options (direct election, State legislatures, Finance Commission) do not appear in it.
xa: **Art. 130** allows other seats by the **CJI's** decision with the Centre's approval.
There are **no regional benches yet**.
Standing Committee (**2023**) sought **women and marginalised** candidates via the MoP.

43.s: Which of the following is NOT correct when comparing the Supreme Court of India with the US Supreme Court?
o: India's Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143
India's appellate jurisdiction includes special leave under Article 136
The US Supreme Court lacks advisory jurisdiction
The US Supreme Court has a writ jurisdiction equivalent to Article 32
43.x: The key marks the claim of an Article 32-equivalent writ jurisdiction in the US Supreme Court as false.
xa: India: "**procedure established by law**" — narrower review; US: "**due process of law**".
The US Court has been called a "**third chamber**".
India blends **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.

43.s: India's constitutional system is described as synthesising
o: American parliamentary sovereignty with British judicial supremacy
American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty
French judicial supremacy with American parliamentary sovereignty
British federalism with American unitary government
43.x: The Indian system combines the American principle of judicial supremacy with the British principle of parliamentary sovereignty.
43.tq: Avoid reversing the two comparative constitutional influences.
xs: India synthesises **American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses the sources — the classic trap.
France and federal/unitary pairings are not part of the synthesis.
xa: US review = "**due process of law**"; Indian = "**procedure established by law**".
The US Supreme Court has been called a "**third chamber**".
India's SC has **advisory** (**Art. 143**) and **Art. 32** writ powers that the US Court lacks.

43.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 143:
1. Advice tendered by the Supreme Court is binding on the President in all cases.
2. On pre-Constitution disputes, the Supreme Court is bound to give its advice.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
43.x: Only 2 is correct: the Court must give its opinion on pre-Constitution treaty/agreement references under Article 143(2), but its advice does not bind the President.
n: Under Article 143, the Supreme Court is bound to give advice on pre-Constitution disputes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Advice tendered by the Supreme Court under Article 143 is not binding on the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xa: The **16th Presidential Reference** (**Nov 2025**) answered questions on bill timelines.

43.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 136 – Seat of the Supreme Court
Article 137 – Review of judgments or orders
43.x: Article 137 deals with review of judgments or orders. Article 130 concerns the seat of the Court, 131 original jurisdiction and 136 special leave petitions.
n: Article 130 provides for the seat of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 131 provides for the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 136 provides for Special Leave Petitions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 137 provides for the review of judgments and orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xa: Art. 131 is **exclusive**; Art. 32 writ jurisdiction is **not exclusive**.
**Article 143** = advisory jurisdiction.

43.s: The writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is provided under Article:
43.x: Writs are under Article 32; original jurisdiction 131, review 137 and advisory 143.
n: The Supreme Court has original and exclusive jurisdiction under Article 131. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has writ jurisdiction under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has review jurisdiction under Article 137. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: ⚠ **131** = original (exclusive); **32** = writ (not exclusive, HCs **Art. 226**); **136** = SLP; **143** = advisory (not binding).
Disputes on **President and Vice-President elections** (**71**): original, exclusive and final.
Appeals: **132 / 133 / 134** = constitutional / civil / criminal.

43.s: Civil appeals to the Supreme Court are governed by Article:
43.x: Civil appeals are under Article 133; constitutional appeals 132, criminal 134 and special leave 136.
n: The Supreme Court has constitutional appellate jurisdiction under Article 132. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has civil appellate jurisdiction under Article 133. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Arts 132 and 133 need an HC **certificate** under **Article 134A**.
Art. 134 appeals where an HC **reversed an acquittal into a death sentence** lie **as of right**.
Art. 136 is **not** available against **Military Tribunals**.

43.s: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court's power to grant Special Leave to Appeal is:
o: Discretionary and available against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal, subject to the stated exception
Mandatory and limited to High Court judgments
Advisory and limited to presidential references
Available only in civil proceedings involving a constitutional question
43.x: Under Article 136, the Court may, at its discretion, grant special leave to appeal against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal, except military tribunals (Article 136(2)).
43.tq: Recall Article 136 and its military exception.
n: The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136 permits special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The power under Article 136 is plenary and residual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136(2) does not apply to Military Tribunals or Armed Forces Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Special Leave Petitions do not lie against judgments or sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals under Article 136(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: Art. 136 power is **discretionary and available against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal**, subject to the exception — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is a **plenary and residual** power.
Exception: **Article 136(2)** — **not** against **courts-martial / Military Tribunals / Armed Forces Courts**.
xa: Advisory jurisdiction is a separate power — **Article 143**.
Constitutional / civil / criminal appeals: **132 / 133 / 134**.
India's appellate scope is **very wide** compared with the US Supreme Court.

43.s: The review jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 137 refers to its power to:
o: Review its own judgments or orders
Review High Court judgments on appeal
43.x: Article 137 concerns review of the Court's own judgments, which differs from judicial review of statutes.
n: The Supreme Court has review jurisdiction under Article 137. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments or orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Review jurisdiction under Article 137 is distinct from judicial review of statutes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Review is subject to **Parliamentary law** and **court rules**.
After a review petition is **dismissed**, a **curative petition** may follow (**Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002**).
**Article 141**: SC's law is **binding on all courts**.

43.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 143:
1. Under Article 143(1), the President may refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court.
2. Under Article 143(1), the Supreme Court may tender its opinion.
3. Under Article 143(2), the Supreme Court must tender its opinion on pre-constitutional matters.
Which of the above statements are correct?
43.x: All three are correct: the Court may give its opinion on references under Article 143(1) but must give one on pre-Constitution matters under 143(2).
n: The President can refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Under Article 143(1), the Supreme Court may tender its opinion on matters of public importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Under Article 143(2), the Supreme Court must tender its opinion on pre-constitutional matters. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Opinions are **not binding** on the President.
The **Third Judges Case (1998)** arose from a **Presidential Reference**.
The **16th Presidential Reference** came in **Nov 2025**.

43.s: An appeal under Article 134 where a High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences the accused to death:
o: Lies only to a larger High Court bench
Lies without a High Court certificate
43.x: Such an appeal lies as of right and needs no High Court certificate.
n: Article 132 covers appeals from High Court judgments involving a substantial question of law concerning the interpretation of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 133 covers appeals in civil proceedings involving a substantial question of law of general importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has reversed an acquittal into a death sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Capital-punishment reversals under Article 134 are appealable as of right without a High Court certificate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Art. 134 also covers cases where an HC **withdrew a trial** to itself.
HC certificates are issued under **Article 134A**.
**Article 136** SLP is **discretionary**.

43.s: The curative petition rests on the Supreme Court's inherent powers anchored in Article:
43.x: The curative petition, filed after dismissal of a review under Article 137, rests on inherent powers under Article 142.
n: The curative petition was evolved under the Supreme Court's inherent powers anchored in Article 142. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition prevents abuse of process. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition cures gross miscarriages of justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition is available after a review petition under Article 137 has been dismissed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: It was evolved in **Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)**.
**Article 142**: any decree or order for **complete justice**.
**e-SCR**: free digital database of reported judgments, launched **2023**.

43.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about appeals to the Supreme Court?
o: Civil appeals under Article 133 need a High Court certificate
Special leave under Article 136 needs a High Court certificate
Constitutional appeals under Article 132 need a High Court certificate
An appeal under Article 134(1)(a) after a death sentence on reversal of acquittal lies as of right
43.x: Special leave under Article 136 is granted at the Supreme Court's discretion and needs no High Court certificate.
n: An appeal under Article 132 requires a certificate from the High Court under Article 134A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The High Court must certify under Article 134A that the question in a civil appeal needs determination by the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has reversed an acquittal into a death sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has withdrawn a trial to itself. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Capital-punishment reversals under Article 134 are appealable as of right without a High Court certificate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136 permits special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Special Leave Petitions do not lie against judgments or sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals under Article 136(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Art. 136 covers **any judgment or order** of **any court or tribunal**, except military ones.
Art. 134 also covers cases where an HC **withdrew a trial** to itself.
SC's appellate scope is **very wide** — constitutional, civil, criminal, special leave.

43.s: Who was the longest-serving Chief Justice of India?
43.x: Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, the 16th CJI, was the longest-serving, from 22 February 1978 to 11 July 1985, over seven years.
43.tq: Recall the longest and shortest CJI tenures.
n: Justice Y.V. Chandrachud was the 16th Chief Justice of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Justice Y.V. Chandrachud was the longest-serving Chief Justice of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Justice Y.V. Chandrachud served from 22 February 1978 to 11 July 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Justice Y.V. Chandrachud served for over seven years as Chief Justice of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xs: The longest-serving CJI was **Justice Y.V. Chandrachud** — so option **(3)** is correct.
He was the **16th Chief Justice of India**, from **22 February 1978 to 11 July 1985** — over **seven years**.
**Kamal Narain Singh** was the **shortest-serving**; **M. Fathima Beevi** was the first woman SC judge, not a CJI.
xa: Kamal Narain Singh served **18 days** (**25 November 1991 to 12 December 1991**).
First CJI: **H.J. Kania**.
CJIs from AP: **K. Subba Rao** and **N.V. Ramana**.

43.s: The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court on a Presidential reference is under Article:
43.x: Article 143 provides advisory jurisdiction; Article 141 makes the Supreme Court's law binding.
n: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 143 concerns the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 143 concerns Presidential reference. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Articles 148 to 151 concern the Comptroller and Auditor-General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 214 provides for High Courts for States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Article 129**: SC a **Court of Record**; **215**: HCs Courts of Record.
**Article 216**: **constitution** of High Courts; **217**: appointment of HC judges.
CAG is removed in the **same manner** as an SC judge (**Art. 148**).

43.s: Which of the following statements regarding the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131 is incorrect?
o: It includes recovery of damages by a private party against the Union.
It excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262.
It covers disputes between one State and another State.
It covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right between the Centre and one or more States.
43.x: Option A is incorrect: Article 131 covers only disputes about legal rights between the Centre and States or between States. A private party suing the Union for damages goes to the ordinary courts.
43.tq: Recall that Article 131 applies only between governments.
n: The Supreme Court has original and exclusive jurisdiction under Article 131. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between one State and another State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover recovery of damages by a private party against the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between the Centre and one or more States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: The incorrect statement is that Article 131 **includes recovery of damages by a private party against the Union** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
Such recovery is **excluded** from original jurisdiction.

Art. 131 covers **federal disputes involving a legal right** — **Centre vs States** and **State vs State**; it **excludes inter-State water disputes** (**Article 262**) — so (2), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: Also excluded: **Finance Commission** matters (**Article 280**), **pre-Constitution treaties**, **political questions**.
Also excluded: adjustment of expenses (**Art. 290**) and **election disputes** of legislatures (go to HCs).
Art. 131 jurisdiction is **exclusive**.

43.s:
Which of the following are excluded from the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131?
1. Inter-State water disputes
2. Finance Commission matters
3. Disputes between States involving a legal right
43.x: Inter-State water disputes (Article 262) and Finance Commission matters (Article 280) are excluded; disputes between States about legal rights are the core of Article 131.
n: Article 131 covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between one State and another State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover Finance Commission matters under Article 280. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover recovery of damages by a private party against the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Also excluded: **political questions**, **pre-Constitution treaties**, **Art. 290** expense adjustments.
**Election disputes** of Parliament and state legislatures go to **High Courts**.
Art. 131 also covers **Centre and some states vs other states**.

43.s: The appointment of ad hoc judges in the Supreme Court is provided under Article:
43.x: Article 127 covers ad hoc judges; 126 the Acting CJI, 128 retired judges and 129 the Court of Record.
n: Article 126 provides for the appointment of an Acting Chief Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 127 provides for the appointment of ad hoc judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 128 concerns the attendance of retired judges at Supreme Court sittings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a Court of Record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
An ad hoc judge is appointed under Article 127 by the Chief Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xa: ⚠ **126** = acting CJI (President); **127** = ad hoc (CJI, HC judge); **128** = retired judges (both consents).
A retired judge under Art. 128 has full powers but is **not deemed a judge** of the court.
There are **no additional judges in the SC** — only in **High Courts** (**Art. 224**).

43.s: Which of the following is wrongly matched regarding the Supreme Court?
o: Ad hoc judge – Appointed by the CJI with the President's prior consent
Retired judge sitting – Requested by the CJI with the President's prior consent
Acting Chief Justice – Appointed by the President
Removal of a judge – Order by the CJI after an address by Parliament
43.x: Removal is by an order of the President after an address by Parliament, not by the CJI.
n: The Chief Justice appoints ad hoc judges with the prior consent of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Chief Justice requests retired judges to attend Supreme Court sittings with the prior consent of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xa: Art. 128 also needs the **judge's consent**.
Ad hoc judges are appointed to meet a lack of **quorum**.
An ad hoc appointee is an **HC judge** qualified for the SC.

43.s: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956 was enacted under which constitutional provision relating to the composition of the Supreme Court?
43.x: Article 124(1) provides the constitutional basis for determining the number of judges of the Supreme Court. Parliament may increase the number by law, and such an amendment requires only a simple majority.
43.tq: Match the statutory mechanism with the correct constitutional provision.
xs: The **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956** was enacted under **Article 124(1)** — option **(1)** is correct.
Under **Art. 124(1)**, **Parliament** increases the number of judges by law, by a **simple-majority** amendment of the 1956 Act.
**Art. 126** = acting CJI; **Art. 128** = retired judges sitting; **Art. 137** = review of its own judgments.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2025** key: the number of SC judges is increased by **Parliament**.
The **2026** increase came through the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026** (Art. **123**).

43.s: The process of appointing a High Court Chief Justice begins with a recommendation by:
o: The CJI and two senior-most Supreme Court judges
43.x: The CJI and two senior-most judges recommend first, followed by the Law Minister, the State, and appointment by the President.
xa: Candidates are chosen **from outside their parent High Court**.
**Punjab** Cabinet objected that the State was **bypassed** for the Punjab and Haryana HC Chief Justice (**9 Sep 2026**).

43.s: Which one of the following statements regarding additional judges is correct?
o: Additional judges are appointed under Article 128 for temporary vacancies in the Supreme Court.
Additional judges exist in High Courts under Article 224, but there are no additional judges in the Supreme Court.
Additional judges may be appointed in the Supreme Court under Article 224.
Additional judges are appointed only in the Supreme Court when its workload increases.
43.x: Article 224 deals with additional and acting judges of High Courts. The Supreme Court has no provision for additional judges of this kind.
43.tq: Distinguish the similar-sounding categories attached to the Supreme Court and High Courts.
xs: **Additional judges** exist only in **High Courts (Art. 224)**; there are **no additional judges in the SC** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 128** is about **retired judges** sitting, not additional judges.
Additional and **acting** judges are both HC features under Art. **224**.
xa: SC equivalents: **Art. 126** acting CJI; **Art. 127** ad hoc judges; **Art. 128** retired judges.
The SC's strength is raised by **Parliament** under **Art. 124(1)** — now **38**.

43.s: Which one of the following combinations correctly states the constitutional provisions relating to removal of judges?
o: Supreme Court judge—Article 124(4); High Court judge—Article 218
Supreme Court judge—Article 148; High Court judge—Article 324(5)
Supreme Court judge—Article 218; High Court judge—Article 124(4)
Supreme Court judge—Article 67(b); High Court judge—Article 61
43.x: Article 124(4) deals with removal of a Supreme Court judge, while Article 218 applies the relevant provisions to High Court judges.
43.tq: Use exact Article–office matching and reject swapped constitutional authorities.
xs: Removal: SC judge — **Article 124(4)**; HC judge — **Article 218** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 148** and **Art. 324(5)** are for the **CAG** and **CEC**, removed in the same manner as an SC judge.
**Art. 61** is **impeachment of the President**, not judges.
xa: Address by each House: **majority of total membership** + **two-thirds of present and voting**.
Grounds: only **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
⚠ The Constitution says "**removal**" for judges; "impeachment" only for the President.

43.s: The Comptroller and Auditor-General and the Chief Election Commissioner are removed from office in the same manner as:
43.x: Under Articles 148 and 324(5), the CAG and the CEC have removal protection comparable to that of a Supreme Court judge.
43.tq: Identify the constitutional office whose removal procedure is expressly borrowed rather than guessing from seniority.
xs: The **CAG** (**Art. 148**) and **CEC** (**Art. 324(5)**) are removed in the same manner as **a Supreme Court judge** — option **(1)** is correct.
An SC judge is removed by the President after an address by **both Houses** on **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
xa: Special majority: **majority of total membership** + **two-thirds of present and voting**.
HC judges are removed the same way under **Art. 218**.
⚠ "Impeachment" is used only for the **President** (Art. **61**).

43.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding removal of Judges of the Supreme Court in India?
o: No Judge of the Supreme Court has so far been removed through this constitutional process.
Justice Soumitra Sen was removed by the President after resigning.

43.s: The power of the Supreme Court of India to decide disputes between the Centre and the States falls under its
43.x: As a federal court, the Supreme Court decides the disputes between different units of the Indian Federation.
