44.s: A High Court consists of a Chief Justice and such other judges as may be deemed necessary by the:
44.x: Article 216 leaves the number to the President; it fixes no uniform strength.
xa: Sanctioned strength (**18 Sep 2025**): **1,122** for all HCs, of which **804** filled.
**30** HC judges appointed on **8 Aug 2026** (Madras **15**, Karnataka **6**).

44.s: In which country can courts not invalidate Acts of Parliament as in the US, because of parliamentary sovereignty?
44.x: Parliamentary sovereignty in the UK prevents US-style judicial review; Canada and Australia have judicial review.
xa: Origin: **USA**, **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.
India blends **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
Roots: **Sir Edward Coke** vs **King James I**.

44.s: The decisions taken by the President or Governor may be subjected to judicial review when they are challenged on grounds such as:
o: The personal popularity of the office-holder
Mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds
The absence of legislative approval for every executive act
44.x: Although constitutional protection applies to the office-holder in the manner specified by Article 361, the decisions themselves may be reviewed on grounds such as mala fides or irrelevant considerations. The review of President’s Rule in S.R. Bommai illustrates this principle.
44.tq: Distinguish reviewable grounds of invalidity from mere political disagreement.
xs: Decisions can be reviewed for **mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds** — option **(3)** is correct.
Example: President's Rule reviewed in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
Popularity or mere policy disagreement are not grounds.
xa: **Art. 361**: the **President/Governor** personally are **not answerable** to courts.
**Art. 74(2)** / **163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into**.
**44th Amendment (1978)** reversed the **38th**'s non-justiciability bar.

44.s: Which Article bars courts from inquiring into the advice of Ministers to the President?
44.x: Article 74(2) is the bar for advice to the President; Article 163(3) for advice to the Governor.
xa: **No mandamus** lies against the President/Governor (TH, **29 Jan 2026**).
Their decisions may still be reviewed for **mala fides** — **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT an evolution genuinely attributed to the Supreme Court?
o: Exemptions to Fundamental Rights expressly written in Articles 31A to 31C and Article 33
44.x: Exemptions and restrictions relating to Fundamental Rights in Articles 31A–31C and 33 are constitutional provisions, not judicial evolutions created by the Supreme Court.
44.tq: Distinguish a court-created doctrine from provisions expressly embedded in the Constitution.
xs: **Exemptions to Fundamental Rights** in **Arts. 31A-31C and 33** are written in the Constitution itself, not evolved by the Supreme Court — option **(3)**.
**Basic Structure** was evolved in **Kesavananda (1973)**; **continuing mandamus** and **expansion of Art. 21** are also genuine SC evolutions.
This exact point was asked in **APPSC 2017**.
xa: Other genuine SC evolutions: **PIL** and **removal of handcuffs** (prisoners' dignity).
**Continuing mandamus**: the case is kept open to **monitor compliance**.
Art. 21 expansion covered **livelihood (Olga Tellis)**, education, health and clean environment.

44.s: The Ninth Schedule was added to the Constitution of India by the—
44.x: The First Amendment (assent 18 June 1951) created the Ninth Schedule, following early land-reform rulings. The Fourth Amendment dealt with property compensation, the Seventh with reorganisation of States, and the 42nd was the 1976 omnibus amendment.
44.tq: 1st Amendment 1951 = Ninth Schedule.
xs: The **1st Amendment (1951)** created the **Ninth Schedule** (assent **18 June 1951**) — option **(1)**.
It followed early **land-reform** and reservation rulings (e.g. **Kameshwar Singh**).
xa: The 1st Amendment marked **75 years** in 2026.
**38th Amendment (1975)** made satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352** non-justiciable; **44th (1978)** reversed it.
⚠ **42nd (1976)** barred HCs from reviewing central laws → **43rd (1977)** restored the power.

44.s: The constitutional provisions relating to High Courts are contained in which Part, Chapter and range of Articles?
44.x: High Courts are in Part VI (the States), Chapter V, Articles 214–231. The Supreme Court is in Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124–147.
44.tq: Discriminate the Supreme Court's Articles (124–147) from the High Courts' (214–231).
n: The constitutional framework for High Courts is governed by Part VI, Chapter V of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Articles 214 to 231 deal with High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
High Courts are governed by Articles 214 to 231 in Part VI. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Supreme Court is governed by Articles 124 to 147 in Part V. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xs: High Courts are in **Part VI, Chapter V, Articles 214–231** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The Supreme Court is in **Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124 to 147** — option (2).
**Article 214** provides **a High Court for each State**.
xa: **Art. 231**: **common High Court** for two or more States/UTs, established by **Parliament**.
**Art. 230**: Parliament can extend an HC's jurisdiction to a **UT** (**7th Amendment Act, 1956**).
**Art. 241**: Parliament may constitute a High Court for a **UT**.

44.s:
Which of the following make a citizen eligible for appointment as a High Court judge?
1. Holding a judicial office in India for at least 10 years
2. Practising as an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years
3. Being a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President
44.x: Ten years in judicial office or as a High Court advocate qualifies a citizen; the distinguished-jurist route exists only for the Supreme Court.
n: A High Court judge must be a citizen of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]

A High Court judge must have held judicial office in India for at least 10 years or must have practised as an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
A High Court judge may qualify through at least 10 years of judicial office in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
A High Court judge may qualify through at least 10 years of practice as an advocate of a High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Constitution has no provision for appointing a distinguished jurist as a High Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 217 concerns the appointment and conditions of office of a High Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: HC judges retire at **62**.
They are appointed by the **President** by **warrant**; the **Governor has no power** to appoint.
Removal only for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.

44.s: The strength of the Supreme Court is determined by:
44.x: Under Article 124(1) Parliament fixes the Supreme Court's strength by law; under Article 216 the President fixes a High Court's.
n: The President of India decides and fixes the strength of judges for each High Court under Article 216. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Parliament decides the strength of the Supreme Court by law under Article 124(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 216 concerns the composition of High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: ⚠ HC strength is **not** fixed by **Parliament**, the **Governor** or the **Chief Minister**.
HC strength is **not uniform** — set per workload.
Sanctioned HC strength (**18 Sep 2025**): **1,122**, of which **804** filled.

44.s: The oath or affirmation by High Court judges is provided under Article:
44.x: Article 219 covers the oath; Article 220 restricts practice after retirement.
n: The oath of a High Court judge is administered by the Governor of the State under Article 219. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
A High Court judge addresses a resignation to the President of India under Article 217(1)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 220 restricts practice after a person has been a permanent High Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
A High Court judge may be removed only on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The removal mechanism for High Court judges is provided under Article 217(1)(b) read with Article 124(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 217 concerns the appointment and conditions of office of a High Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: A retired HC judge may plead only in the **Supreme Court** and **other High Courts**.
**Article 218** applies SC removal provisions to HCs.
Removal needs a **special majority** in **each House** — at least **50%** of total strength and **two-thirds** present and voting.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about a High Court Judge:
1. He addresses his written resignation to the Governor of the State.
2. He takes the oath before the Governor of the State.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
44.x: Only 1 is correct: the oath is taken before the Governor (Article 219), but the resignation is addressed to the President, who appoints the judge.
n: The Governor of the State administers the oath to High Court Judges under Article 219. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The oath of a High Court Judge is administered by the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
High Court Judges address their written resignations to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The resignation of a High Court Judge is addressed to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A High Court Judge addresses a resignation to the President of India under Article 217(1)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xa: Both SC and HC judges are appointed by the **President** by **warrant**.
HC judges are removed by the **President's** order after Parliament's **address**.

44.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Transfer of a High Court Judge – Article 215
Supreme Court as a Court of Record – Article 129
Oath of a High Court Judge – Article 222
High Court as a Court of Record – Article 219
44.x: Article 129 makes the Supreme Court a Court of Record. Transfer is under Article 222, the High Court oath under 219 and the High Court as Court of Record under 215.
n: Article 222 provides for the transfer of High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Governor of the State administers the oath to High Court Judges under Article 219. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The oath of a High Court Judge is administered by the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Supreme Court is a court of record under Article 129. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The High Court is a court of record under Article 215. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xa: Transfer is by the **President** on the advice of the **collegium** led by the **CJI**.
Transfer is **not** applicable to SC judges.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about Acting Judges of a High Court:
1. They are appointed when a permanent Judge is temporarily absent or is acting as Chief Justice.
2. An Acting Judge may continue in office beyond the age of 62 years.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
44.x: Only 1 is correct: acting judges fill in for absent permanent judges or those acting as Chief Justice, but their appointment ends at 62.
n: An Acting Judge is appointed when a permanent Judge is temporarily absent. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
An Acting Judge is appointed when a permanent Judge is acting as Chief Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
An Acting Judge’s appointment ceases at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xa: **Acting Chief Justice** is under **Article 223**.
**Retired judges** may sit under **224A**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about a High Court Judge:
1. The salary and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
2. The pension is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
3. The pension is charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
Which of the above statements are correct?
44.x: A High Court judge's salary is charged on the State's Consolidated Fund, but the pension on the Consolidated Fund of India; statement 3 is false.
n: The salary and allowances of High Court Judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Article 202(3) concerns the charging of High Court Judges’ salaries and allowances on the Consolidated Fund of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The pensions of High Court Judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Article 112(3)(d)(iii) concerns the charging of High Court Judges’ pensions on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The pension of a High Court Judge is not charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xa: SC salary and pension: both on the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
**Article 221**: HC **salaries, allowances and pensions**.
HC judges retire at **62**.

44.s:
Assertion (A): The retirement age of a High Court Judge is 62 years.
Reason (R): The retirement age of a High Court Judge was raised from 60 to 62 years by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
44.x: Both are true: the 15th Amendment (1963) raised the High Court retirement age from 60 to 62, which is why it is 62 now. R explains A.
44.tq: Recall the 15th Amendment's change.
n: The retirement age of a High Court Judge is 62 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The retirement age of High Court Judges was raised from 60 to 62 years by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
HC judges retire at **62**.
The age was **raised from 60** by the **15th Amendment Act, 1963** — which explains A.
xa: SC judges retire at **65**.
The 15th Amendment also inserted **224A** (retired HC judges).
Additional and acting judges also cannot serve beyond **62**.

44.s: Which of the following is a qualification specifically available for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge but not provided for appointment as a High Court Judge?
o: Taking an oath before a constitutional authority
Holding office until the prescribed retirement age
44.x: Under Article 124(3)(c), a distinguished jurist can be made a Supreme Court judge. No such route exists for High Courts.
44.tq: Recall the extra route to the Supreme Court.
n: A distinguished jurist is eligible for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge under Article 124(3)(c). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A distinguished jurist is not eligible for appointment as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Constitution has no provision for appointing a distinguished jurist as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India is the appointing authority for Supreme Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India is the appointing authority for High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **Being a distinguished jurist** is available only for the SC — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Article 124(3)(c)** makes a distinguished jurist eligible for the SC; there is **no such provision** for HCs.
Oath, retirement age and **appointment by the President** apply to both courts.
xa: HC qualification: **10 years** in **judicial office** or **10 years** as an **HC advocate**.
HC oath before the **Governor**; SC oath before the **President**.
Transfer (**Article 222**) applies only to HC judges.

44.s: What is the method of removal of a High Court Judge?
o: Removal by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha alone
Removal by the Governor at pleasure
An order of the President following an address by Parliament
44.x: Like a Supreme Court judge, a High Court judge is removed by the President's order after an address by Parliament (Article 217(1)). The Governor cannot remove judges.
44.tq: Recall that both courts' judges are removed the same way.
n: A High Court Judge is removed by an order of the President following an address by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of a High Court Judge is governed by Article 217(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: An HC judge is removed by **an order of the President following an address by Parliament** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **address** must pass **each House** by **special majority** — at least **50%** of the **total strength** and **two-thirds** present and voting.
Grounds: **proved misbehaviour** or **incapacity**; the **Governor** has no removal power, and **Article 61** impeachment is for the **President**.
xa: Removal under **Article 217(1)(b)** read with **Article 124(4)** and **Art. 218**.
Procedure: **Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968**.
Justice **Soumitra Sen** (Calcutta HC) resigned in **2011** after the Rajya Sabha voted for removal.

44.s: Who administers the oath of office to a Supreme Court Judge?
o: The Chief Justice of India or the senior-most Supreme Court Judge
The President of India or a person appointed by the President
44.x: A Supreme Court judge is sworn in by the President or someone the President appoints (Article 124(6)).
44.tq: Recall Article 124(6).
n: The oath of a Supreme Court Judge is administered by the President of India or a person appointed by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: The oath to an SC judge is administered by **the President of India or a person appointed by the President** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is under **Article 124(6)**.
The **Governor** administers the oath to **HC judges** (**Article 219**), not SC judges.
xa: SC judges' **resignation** is addressed to the **President** (**Article 124(2)(a)**).
SC judges retire at **65**.
SC judges are removed by the **President's** order after Parliament's address (**Article 124(4)**).

44.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Article 217 – Appointment of High Court judges by the President
Article 214 – A common High Court for two or more States
Article 230 – Extension or exclusion of HC jurisdiction over a Union Territory
Article 231 – A common High Court for two or more States
44.x: Article 214 provides a High Court for each State; a common High Court is under Article 231.
xa: **Art. 241**: Parliament may constitute a High Court for a **UT** or declare a UT court a High Court.
⚠ **214** = each State; **231** = common HC; **230** = UT jurisdiction; **241** = HC for a UT.
Art. 230 was asked in APPSC-GS **2023**.

44.s: The seat of the common High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh is at:
o: Leh in summer and Jammu in winter
Jammu in winter and Srinagar in summer
44.x: The common High Court sits at Jammu in winter and Srinagar in summer.
xa: **Puducherry** → Madras HC; **Lakshadweep** → Kerala HC.
**Delhi** is a UT with its **own HC**.
**Art. 241**: Parliament may constitute an HC for a **UT**.

44.s: Which of the following statements regarding the older High Courts in India is correct?
o: Calcutta High Court was established on 2 July 1862 and is the oldest High Court in India.
Madras High Court was established in 1862 and is the oldest High Court in India.
Allahabad High Court was established on 2 July 1862 and is the oldest High Court in India.
Bombay High Court was established in 1862 and is the only oldest High Court in India.
44.x: Calcutta High Court was established on 2 July 1862 and is the oldest High Court. Madras, Bombay and Allahabad are also among the four oldest High Courts; Madras was also established in 1862.
44.tq: Separate the oldest institution from the other High Courts established in the same year.
xs: **Calcutta HC** is the oldest, established on **2 July 1862** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Madras HC** was also set up in **1862**, but Calcutta is the oldest.
The **oldest four**: **Calcutta, Madras, Bombay, Allahabad**.
xa: Newest HC: **Andhra Pradesh** (**1 Jan 2019**).
Before **1954**, the **Madras HC (1862)** covered the Andhra districts.
India has **25 High Courts** (**29 Jun 2026**).

44.s: Under Article 241, a High Court for a Union Territory may be constituted by:
44.x: Article 241 authorises Parliament by law to constitute a High Court for a UT; the President alone has no such power.
xa: **Art. 230**: Parliament may **extend or exclude** an HC's jurisdiction over a UT (**7th Amendment, 1956**).
A new HC is created by a **Parliament law** and brought into being by **Presidential notification**.
**Delhi** has its own HC; **J&K and Ladakh** a common HC.

44.s: The Guwahati High Court has jurisdiction over Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and:
44.x: Guwahati covers Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh; Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura got their own HCs in 2013.
xa: Guwahati covered seven states until **23 March 2013**, when **Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura** got own HCs.
The Telangana HC stays at **Hyderabad**.
Bifurcation took India's HC count from **24 to 25**.

44.s: The appointment of an acting Chief Justice of a High Court is provided under Article:
44.x: Article 223 covers an acting Chief Justice; 224(1) additional judges, 224(2) acting judges and 224A retired judges.
xa: Additional judges are appointed for up to **2 years**, usually made permanent in about **two years**.
**Art. 224A** was inserted by the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
Retired judges sit with prior consent of the **President** and the judge.

44.s: Article 224A, on retired judges sitting in High Courts, was inserted by the:
44.x: Article 224A was inserted by the 15th Amendment, 1963; additional judges fall under Article 224(1).
xa: Additional judges are usually made permanent in about **two years** (TH, **9 Aug 2026**).

44.s: Under Article 217, a Judge of a High Court is appointed by the:
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
44.x: The President appoints after consulting the CJI, the Governor and, for a puisne judge, the HC Chief Justice.
xa: For a common HC, the **Governors of all states concerned** are consulted.
Proposal starts with the **HC collegium** (CJ + **2**) → SC collegium (CJI + **2**).
Qualifications: citizen + **10 years** judicial office or HC advocate.

44.s: The procedure for removal of a High Court judge is governed by the:
44.x: Article 218 and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 govern removal; a Governor cannot remove a judge by executive order.
xa: Grounds: **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
**Soumitra Sen** (Calcutta HC) resigned in **2011** after the RS voted for removal.
Motion against **G.R. Swaminathan** noticed by **107** MPs (Dec **2025**).

44.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about proceedings against High Court judges?
o: Justice Soumitra Sen was a judge of the Calcutta High Court
Soumitra Sen resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha voted for his removal
A motion against Justice G.R. Swaminathan was noticed by 107 MPs in December 2025
Yashwant Varma was formerly a judge of the Madras High Court
44.x: Yashwant Varma was formerly of the Allahabad High Court.
xa: Varma's inquiry report was to be tabled **despite his resignation** (LENSD **11 Jul 2026**).
Ethics codes: **1997 Restatement of Values** (**16** points) + **1999 in-house procedure**.
Removal procedure: **Art. 218** + **Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968**.

44.s: Which one of the following best describes the scope of writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226?
o: It extends only to disputes arising within the physical territory of the High Court
It is confined exclusively to enforcement of Fundamental Rights
It extends to Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, including where the cause of action arises within its territory
It can be exercised only on a reference from the Supreme Court
44.x: Article 226 enables High Courts to issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose. A High Court may act even when the respondent is outside its territory if the cause of action arises within it.
44.tq: Contrast the wider wording of Article 226 with the narrower purpose traditionally associated with Article 32.
xs: **Art. 226** covers **Fundamental Rights and other legal rights**, even beyond its territory **where the cause of action arises within** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is not confined to its physical territory or to FRs alone, and needs no SC reference.
Writs "**for any other purpose**" make it **wider than Art. 32**.
xa: **Art. 227**: superintendence over all courts and tribunals **except military tribunals**.
PIL may be filed under **Art. 32 (SC)** or **Art. 226 (HC)**.
HCs are primarily **courts of appeal**.

44.s: The High Court's superintendence under Article 227 covers:
44.x: Article 227 covers administrative and judicial superintendence and may be exercised suo motu.
xa: Art. 227 excludes **military tribunals**.
It is also **revisional** in nature.
**Art. 235** vests **control** over district and subordinate courts in the **HC**.

44.s: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was enacted pursuant to the recommendations of the:
44.x: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 followed the report of the H.N. Sanyal Committee.
44.tq: Associate the statute with the committee that directly preceded it.
xs: The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** followed the **H.N. Sanyal Committee** — option **(4)** is correct.
No link to the ARC or **Sarkaria** in the notes.
xa: **Civil contempt** = wilful disobedience; **criminal contempt** = scandalising or obstructing justice.
Exceptions: **fair criticism** + **accurate reporting**.
Contempt powers: **Art. 129** (SC) and **Art. 215** (HC).

44.s: Under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, wilful disobedience of a court's judgment or order is:
44.x: Civil contempt is wilful disobedience; criminal contempt covers scandalising or obstructing justice.
xa: The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** followed the **H.N. Sanyal Committee**.
Contempt power flows from **Court of Record** status — **Art. 129** (SC) and **Art. 215** (HC).
An HC punishes contempt of itself **and subordinate courts** (**Art. 215**).

44.s: Which State has the first fully paperless district court?
44.x: Kerala has the first fully paperless district court.
44.tq: Use the distinctive achievement-state association.
xs: **Kerala** has the first **fully paperless district court** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is part of the **digitisation** push with **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** and the **NJDG**.
xa: More than **4 crore cases** are pending in lower courts.
The **Department of Justice** web portal tracks district vacancies monthly.
Infrastructure scheme outlay: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**.

44.s: Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for court infrastructure, the normal Centre-State funding ratio is:
44.x: The normal ratio is 60:40, 90:10 for NE and Himalayan States, and 100% for UTs; it is monitored on the Nyaya Vikas Portal.
xa: It is a **Centrally Sponsored Scheme**.
Outlay: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**, incl. **₹50 crore** for **Gram Nyayalayas**.
Digitisation runs through **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)**.

44.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Article 143 – Advisory jurisdiction on a Presidential reference
Article 131 – High Court superintendence over subordinate courts
Article 227 – High Court superintendence over subordinate courts
44.x: Article 131 is the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in Centre-State disputes.
xa: **Art. 137** = SC **reviews its own judgments**.
**Art. 139A** (**44th Amendment 1978**) = SC may **transfer cases to itself**.
**Art. 141** = SC law binding on all courts.

44.s: Which Article makes legislative power subject to the provisions of the Constitution?
44.x: Article 245 makes legislative power subject to the Constitution; Articles 251 and 254 deal with repugnancy.

**Art. 13**: laws inconsistent with FRs are **void**.

44.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Article 13 – Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void
Article 32 – Supreme Court writs for Fundamental Rights
Article 137 – Supreme Court writs for Fundamental Rights
44.x: Article 137 permits the Supreme Court to review its own judgments; Supreme Court writs are under Article 32.
xa: This matches the **APPSC-G2 2023** PYQ.
⚠ **137** = review; **136** = Special Leave; **13** = void laws.
**Art. 226** covers FRs "**and any other purpose**".

44.s: Which 2024 case held that delimitation decisions can be reviewed if capricious?
44.x: Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod (2024) held delimitation review limited but possible if the decision is capricious.
