**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** and **Minerva Mills (1980)** also treat judicial review as an inviolable part of the Basic Structure.

45.s: Judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 cannot be abrogated by Parliament even through Article:
45.x: Being part of the basic structure, judicial review cannot be removed even by amendment under Article 368.
n: In Kesavananda Bharati in 1973, Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was declared an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Minerva Mills in 1980 reaffirmed that Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 is an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Parliament cannot abrogate Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 even through Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not vested in the Supreme Court alone. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xa: This was held in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)** and **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**.
Constitutional amendments themselves are subject to judicial review on the **Basic Structure** touchstone.

45.s:
Assertion (A): Constitutional amendments are subject to Judicial Review.
Reason (R): Such amendments can be tested on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
45.x: Both are true: constitutional amendments can be reviewed because courts test them against the basic structure. R explains A.
45.tq: Ask whether the basic-structure test explains why amendments can be reviewed.
n: Constitutional amendments are subject to Judicial Review on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Constitutional amendments** are subject to judicial review because they are tested on the **Basic Structure** touchstone.
xa: Judicial review under **Articles 32 and 226** is itself part of the Basic Structure (**Kesavananda Bharati 1973**, **Minerva Mills 1980**, **L. Chandra Kumar 1997**).
Parliament **cannot abrogate** it even through **Article 368**.
HCs review under **Articles 226 and 227**; the SC under **Article 32**.

45.s: After the abolition of the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the Airport Appellate Tribunal, their functions were primarily shifted to the:
45.x: The functions of the dissolved appellate tribunals were moved to the High Courts.
45.tq: Test the institutional destination of transferred functions.
xs: Functions of the abolished tribunals moved to the **High Courts** — option **(4)**.
Abolished: **Film Certification Appellate Tribunal**, **IPAB**, **Airport Appellate Tribunal** (**Tribunals Reforms Act 2021**).
xa: Also abolished: **Authority for Advance Rulings (Customs)** and **Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Tribunal**.
2021 Act: Chairperson up to **70**; members up to **67**.
**Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** struck down its re-enacted conditions.

45.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched with the National Tribunals Commission proposed under the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026?
o: Technical members — Two persons with at least 25 years’ experience
Chairperson — Former Supreme Court judge or former Chief Justice of a High Court
Tenure — Four years irrespective of age
45.x: The proposed tenure is five years or until the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier, not four years irrespective of age.
45.tq: Find the single altered numerical provision in an otherwise correctly matched list.
xs: **Tenure "four years irrespective of age"** is wrong — NTC tenure is **5 years or age 70**, whichever is earlier — option **(4)**.
Correct: HQ **New Delhi**; **2 technical** members with **25+ years'** experience; Chairperson **former SC judge or former HC Chief Justice**.
xa: NTC has **5** members: Chairperson + **2 judicial** + **2 technical**.
Judicial members are former HC CJs or judges, appointed in **consultation with the CJI**.
⚠ **2021 Act** = **4 years** (min. age 50) → struck down → **Bill 2026 NTC** = **5 years or age 70**.

45.s: The Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 was passed by the Lok Sabha on 10 August 2026 and by the Rajya Sabha on:
45.x: It passed the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2026; it repeals the 2021 Act and creates a National Tribunals Commission.
xa: Moved by Law Minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal**.
**Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** had ordered an NTC within **four months**.
NTC: HQ **New Delhi**, **5** members, tenure **5 years or age 70**.

45.s: In March 2026, the Election Commission set up 19 Appellate Tribunals headed by retired High Court judges to hear disputes relating to the electoral rolls of which State after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR)?
45.x: The Election Commission set up 19 Appellate Tribunals under retired High Court judges for West Bengal roll disputes after the SIR. Bihar, Assam and Kerala are not linked to these tribunals.
45.tq: 19 Appellate Tribunals → West Bengal rolls (SIR)
xs: The EC set up **19 Appellate Tribunals** under **retired HC judges** for **West Bengal** roll disputes after the **SIR** — option **(3)**.
Reported in TH, **22 Mar 2026**.
xa: **National Sports Tribunal**: **National Sports Governance Act, 2025**; appeals to the **SC**.
Proposal: universal **"Zero FIR"-style filing** for tribunals.
**Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026** creates the **NTC**.

45.s: Under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, which one of the following correctly describes the tenure and age framework?
o: Tenure of four years; minimum appointment age of 45 years; all members up to 70 years
Tenure of four years; minimum appointment age of 50 years; Chairperson up to 70 years and members up to 67 years
Tenure of five years; minimum appointment age of 45 years; Chairperson up to 67 years
Tenure of three years; minimum appointment age of 50 years; members up to 65 years
45.x: The 2021 framework prescribed a four-year tenure, a minimum appointment age of 50 years, a maximum age of 70 years for the Chairperson and 67 years for members.
45.tq: Split the option into tenure, minimum age and maximum-age components.
xs: 2021 Act: **4 years** tenure; minimum age **50**; Chairperson up to **70**, members up to **67** — option **(2)**.
⚠ Tenure was 4 years, not 5 or 3, and minimum age 50, not 45.
xa: **Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** struck down **minimum age 50** and **4-year tenure** (made **5 years**).
**Bill 2026 NTC** members: **5 years or age 70**.
Search-cum-Selection Committee now sends **one name** per vacancy.

45.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the National Tribunals Commission proposed in the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026?
o: Its headquarters is proposed at New Delhi
Its Chairperson must be a serving judge of the Supreme Court
Its functions include appointments, performance review and disciplinary inquiries
It is to have two judicial and two technical members besides the Chairperson
45.x: The Chairperson may be a former Supreme Court judge or a former High Court Chief Justice, not necessarily a serving SC judge.
xa: Technical members need **25+ years'** experience.
Tenure: **5 years or age 70**, whichever is earlier.
**Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended an NTC.

45.s: The Central Administrative Tribunal was established in:
45.x: The CAT was established in 1985.
xa: CAT (**1985**) was the **first** tribunal under Art. 323A.
**AP Administrative Tribunal**: **Art. 371D** (**32nd Amendment**).
CAT was set up under PM **Rajiv Gandhi**.

45.s: TDSAT judgments can be challenged in the:
45.x: In order to bring in functional clarity and strengthen the regulatory framework and the dispute settlement mechanism in the telecommunication sector, the TRAI Act of 1997 was amended in the year 2000 and TDSAT (Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal) was setup to adjudicate disputes and dispose of appeals. Regarding Telecom, Broadcasting and Airport tariff matters, the Tribunal's orders can be appealed to the Supreme Court but only on substantial questions of law, while in regard to cyber issues, the Tribunal's order can be appealed before High Court. Thus the correct answer is an option (c).

45.s: Within how many days, an appeal can be made by an aggrieved person by decision of the National Green Tribunal to the Supreme Court?
45.x: The National Green Tribunal was established on 18.10.2010 under the National Green Tribunal Act 2010 for effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to the environmental protection and conservation of forests and other natural resources including enforcement of any legal right relating to environment and giving relief and compensation for damages to persons and property and for matters connected therewith or incidental to it. It is a specialized body equipped with the necessary expertise to handle environmental disputes involving multi-disciplinary issues. The Tribunal shall not be bound by the procedure laid down under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but shall be guided by principles of natural justice. The Tribunal has the power to review its own decisions. If this fails, the decision can be challenged before the Supreme Court within ninety days.

46.s: The Union of India is?
o: Formed at the will of States
Dissolvable by Parliament with consent of majority State Assemblies
46.src: APPSC 2018 Special Qualifying Test for Appointment by Promot

46.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: United States of America — Federal country
46.x: Sri Lanka is identified as a unitary country, not a federal country. The United States, Switzerland and France are correctly classified as stated.
46.tq: Find the single country placed in the wrong constitutional category.
xs: **Sri Lanka** is a **unitary** country, not federal — so **Sri Lanka — Federal country** is the mismatch, option **(4)**.
**Switzerland** and the **USA** are federal; **France** is unitary — all correctly matched.
xa: Other federal countries: **Canada**, **Australia**, **Argentina**, Germany, Russia, Brazil.
Other unitary countries: **Britain / UK**, **Italy**, Japan, China.
**USA** was formed by agreement of states (**integration**).

46.s: Which one of the following is correct about the United Kingdom's constitutional system?
o: Parliament holds all law-making power, reflecting its unitary character.
It was formed by a compact among States.
Residual powers are divided between the centre and the provinces.
The judiciary distributes legislative subjects among the units.
46.x: The United Kingdom is a unitary country in which Parliament holds all law-making power.
xa: Unitary: one supreme central government; local units are its **creations** with **delegated powers**.
**Britain** has no judicial review over Acts of Parliament (parliamentary sovereignty).
India's parliamentary form follows the **British model**: nominal head = **President**.

46.s: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of a unitary form of government?
o: Local units being creations of the central government
Local units exercising powers delegated by the Centre
A constitutional division of powers between the Centre and the local units
46.x: A unitary government does not constitutionally divide sovereign powers between the Centre and local units. Local units derive their authority from the central government.
46.tq: Find the statement that belongs to federalism rather than unitary government.
xs: A **constitutional division of powers** is **not** a unitary feature — it marks a federation — option **(4)**.
Unitary: **one supreme central government**; local units are its **creations** with **delegated powers**.
xa: Federalism: **sharing of power** between Union and States, each supreme in its sphere, with an **independent umpire**.
**Confederation**: loose league of sovereign States that keep the **right to secede**.
India = "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

46.s: Which of the following is NOT a merit of a unitary government?
o: Maximum accommodation of regional diversity through autonomous governments
46.x: Uniform laws, quick decisions and a strong response to crises are merits of a unitary system. Accommodation of regional diversity through autonomous governments is more characteristic of federalism.
46.tq: Separate the advantages of centralisation from the advantages of regional autonomy.
xs: **Accommodating regional diversity** through autonomous governments is not a unitary merit — option **(3)**.
Unitary merits: **uniform laws and policy**, **quick decisions**, **strong crisis response**.
xa: Demerits: **over-centralisation**; local needs neglected; poorly suited to **large, diverse countries**.
**Holding-together** federations divide power to hold **diversity** together — e.g. **India**, Spain, Belgium.
India = "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

46.s: Federalism is a system in which:
o: all power is concentrated in one central authority
the Union and States share power, each supreme in its own sphere under a written Constitution
sovereign States form a loose league with a right to secede
local units exercise only powers delegated by the Centre
46.x: Federalism divides powers constitutionally between the Union and the States, each supreme in its own sphere, with an independent umpire to settle disputes.
xa: This was the answer in **APPSC-GS 2018**.
**Unitary**: units draw power from the Centre.
Essential federal feature: **independence of the judiciary** to settle Centre-State disputes (UPSC 2021).

46.s: The States and Union Territories of India are specified in which constitutional Schedule?
46.x: The First Schedule specifies the States and Union Territories of India. The Fourth Schedule deals with allocation of seats in the Council of States.
46.tq: Discriminate between the First Schedule’s territorial listing and nearby Schedule numbers with different subjects.
xs: States and UTs are specified in the **First Schedule** — option **(1)**.
The **Fourth Schedule** allots Rajya Sabha seats; the **Seventh** has the three Lists.
xa: **Art. 1(1)**: "**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States**".
Art. 3 laws amend the **First and Fourth Schedules** (**Art. 4**).
Rajya Sabha seats by population: **Uttar Pradesh 31**, small States **1**.

46.s: In the Indian constitutional scheme, the federal system can become unitary during an emergency
o: only with the consent of every State Legislature
only after a formal amendment of the Constitution
only after abolition of the Rajya Sabha
without a formal amendment of the Constitution
46.x: An emergency can substantially centralise the constitutional system and make it operate in a unitary manner without a formal constitutional amendment.
46.tq: Distinguish an operational change during emergency from a formal constitutional amendment.
xs: In an **Emergency** the federation becomes **unitary without a formal amendment** — option **(4)**.
This is a **unique feature** of **Part XVIII (Arts. 352-360)**.
xa: Ambedkar: "**federal in normal times and unitary in emergencies**".
National Emergency: Parliament may legislate on **State List** matters (**Art. 250**).
Financial Emergency (**Art. 360**): **never declared**.

46.s: Which of the following is a unitary feature of the Indian Constitution?
46.x: Single citizenship is a unitary feature; dual polity and bicameralism are federal features.
xa: Emergency (**Arts. 352-360**) turns the system unitary **without a formal amendment**.
USA has **dual** citizenship; India **single**.
**Rajya Sabha** = Upper House for States, but seats are **by population** (unequal representation).

46.s: An independent judiciary acting as umpire in Union-State disputes is regarded as:
o: a unitary feature of the Constitution
a Directive Principle of State Policy
46.x: An independent judiciary can act as an impartial umpire in Centre-State disputes, which is regarded as an essential feature of federalism.
xa: Federalism needs an **independent umpire** under a written constitution.
The **Supreme Court** acts as **guardian** of the Constitution.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: federalism is part of the **basic structure**.

46.s: K.C. Wheare gave which fuller description of the Indian constitutional system?
o: A unitary state with subsidiary federal features
A presidential state with subsidiary federal features
A confederation with subsidiary unitary features
A federal state with subsidiary unitary features
46.x: Wheare described India as a unitary state with subsidiary federal features rather than a federal state with subsidiary unitary features.
46.tq: Discriminate between the reversed federal–unitary formulations.
xs: **K.C. Wheare**: India is "**a unitary state with subsidiary federal features**" rather than a federal state with subsidiary unitary features — option **(1)**.
He is the standard answer for "**quasi-federal**".
xa: Wheare was a **British constitutional expert**.
Distractors in PYQs: **Ambedkar**, **Austin**, **Appleby**, **Morris-Jones**, **Sachchidananda Sinha**.
**Ivor Jennings**: "federation with a **strong centralising tendency**" (APPSC-G2 2025).

46.s: 'Federal in structure with unitary features' best describes the constitutional system of:
46.x: India is described as federal in structure with unitary features and as a Union of States.
xa: Debate labels: **"quasi-federal"** / federal system with **unitary bias**.
Media label: "**federal in structure, unitary in spirit**" (TH, 26 Mar 2026).
India is a **holding-together** federation (with Spain, Belgium); **USA**, Switzerland, Australia are **coming-together**.
Supreme Court: "**fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements**".

46.s: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the federal character of the Constitution was held to be:
o: one of the basic features of the Constitution
46.x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) listed the federal character among the basic features of the Constitution.
xa: **State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962)**: Constitution **not truly federal**.
**Bommai (1994)**: federalism part of the **basic structure**; **floor test**.
**Minerva Mills** reopened judicial review barred by the **38th Amendment**.

46.s: The Supreme Court has described the Indian Constitution as:
o: purely federal with no unitary features
fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements
purely unitary with a nominal federal distribution
46.x: The Constitution has been described as fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements, reflecting a federal distribution alongside strong centralising provisions.
xa: **State of West Bengal (1962)**: **not truly federal**; States **not sovereign**.
**Kesavananda (1973)** and **Bommai (1994)**: federal character is a **basic feature**.
Official label: **"federal in structure with unitary features"** (IYB 2026).

46.s: Which Article enables Parliament to legislate on a subject in the State List when the Rajya Sabha declares that it is necessary in the national interest?
46.x: Article 249 empowers Parliament to legislate on a State List subject following a Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest.
46.tq: Identify the Article from the specific constitutional trigger.
xs: **Article 249** lets Parliament legislate on a **State List** subject after a **Rajya Sabha** resolution in the national interest — option **(4)**.
The resolution needs **2/3 of members present and voting** and is valid **1 year**, renewable.
**Art. 250** = State List law during **National Emergency**; **Art. 356** = **President's Rule**.
xa: Laws under **Art. 250** lapse **6 months** after the emergency ends.
**Part XVIII (Arts. 352-360)** makes the federation **unitary without a formal amendment**.
Under Art. 356, Parliament/President exercise the **State's powers**.

46.s: Which of the following conditions is required for continuation of President’s Rule beyond one year?
o: A special majority in the Rajya Sabha alone
A National Emergency in operation and certification by the Election Commission
A resolution of the Inter-State Council
46.x: Continuation of President’s Rule beyond one year requires that a National Emergency is in operation and that the Election Commission certifies the difficulty of holding elections in the State.
46.tq: Identify the additional safeguards attached to extension beyond the normal period.
xs: President's Rule beyond **1 year** needs a **National Emergency** in operation plus **ECI certification** (**Art. 356(5)**) — option **(3)**.
Approval is within **2 months** by **simple majority**; maximum **3 years**.
xa: Ground: **failure of constitutional machinery** in a State; also **Art. 365**.
**One Nation, One Election** deferrals could clash with **Art. 356(5)** limits (TH 9 Mar 2026).
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** made Art. 356 proclamations **open to judicial review**.
AP under President's Rule in **1973** (Jai Andhra agitation).

46.s: The resolution authorising Parliament to legislate on a State List matter in the national interest is passed by:
o: the Rajya Sabha by two-thirds of members present and voting
the Rajya Sabha by a majority of the total membership
the Lok Sabha by a simple majority
both Houses by a special majority
46.x: Article 249 requires a resolution of the Rajya Sabha supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting. The Lok Sabha does not participate in passing this resolution.
46.tq: Separate the required House from the exact form of majority.
xs: The **Art. 249** resolution is passed by the **Rajya Sabha** by **2/3 of members present and voting** — option **(1)**.
It lets Parliament legislate on a **State List** subject in the **national interest**.
The resolution is valid **1 year**, renewable.
xa: **Art. 250**: Parliament legislates on State List during **National Emergency**; laws lapse **6 months** after it ends.
**Rajya Sabha** represents States — **bicameralism** is a federal feature.
These provisions turn the federation **unitary without a formal amendment**.

46.s: As part of asymmetric federalism, the administration of Scheduled Areas is provided for in which Schedule of the Constitution?
46.x: The Fifth Schedule deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas. The Fourth Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats, the Seventh Schedule holds the three legislative Lists, and the Tenth Schedule deals with anti-defection.
46.tq: Scheduled Areas → Fifth Schedule
xs: Administration of **Scheduled Areas** is in the **Fifth Schedule** — option **(2)**.
The **Fourth Schedule** allots **Rajya Sabha** seats; the **Seventh Schedule** has the three legislative lists.
xa: Other asymmetric provisions: **Art. 370** (J&K) and **Arts. 371 to 371J**.
**Art. 371D**: Andhra Pradesh.
**First Schedule** lists States and UTs (**Art. 1**).

46.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: India — dual citizenship and State constitutions
USA — three legislative lists and residuary powers with the Centre
India — single citizenship and a single integrated judiciary
USA — upper House seats allocated according to population of States
46.x: India has single citizenship and a single integrated judicial system. The other pairs reverse the constitutional features of India and the USA.
46.tq: Reject options that swap institutional features between the two federations.
xs: **India — single citizenship and a single integrated judiciary** — option **(3)**.
India has **no** dual citizenship or State constitutions (option 1 wrong).
**Three lists** with residuary power at the Centre is **India**, not USA; USA enumerates only federal powers and leaves the residue with the **States**.
US Senate seats are **equal (2 per State)**, not by population.
xa: India's federation: "**holding together**"; USA: "**coming together**".
India's **strong Centre** borrowed from **Canada**; **Concurrent List** from **Australia**.
Federal scheme, Governor, emergency provisions: **GoI Act 1935**.

46.s: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which was defeated in the Lok Sabha, proposed to increase the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to:
46.x: The Bill proposed increasing the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850.
46.tq: Test the exact numerical change rather than the related seat-freeze debate.
xs: The **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026** proposed raising the Lok Sabha maximum from **550 to 850** — option **(4)**.
The **Lok Sabha defeated** the Bill (LENSD 20 May 2026).
It proposed **+50% seats for every State**.
xa: The debate was framed around the **1971** seat freeze and **southern States**.
AP's seats would have risen **25 to 38**.

46.s: Under the proposed formula in the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, the number of Lok Sabha seats for Andhra Pradesh was to rise from 25 to:
46.x: The proposed 50 per cent increase would have raised Andhra Pradesh’s Lok Sabha seats from 25 to 38.
46.tq: Apply the stated percentage formula to the State-specific figures.
xs: AP's Lok Sabha seats were to rise from **25** to **thirty-eight** (**38**) under the **+50%** formula — option **(4)**.
Source: TH **17 Apr 2026**, on the **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026**.
xa: The Bill proposed Lok Sabha max **550 to 850**; it was **defeated** in the Lok Sabha.
Debate: the **1971** seat freeze and southern States.
**Art. 371D**: AP's special provisions.

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review is a unitary element of the Constitution.
2. Judicial review reinforces the federal principle.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
46.x: Judicial review supports federalism by upholding the division of powers; it is not a unitary feature like emergency provisions or All India Services.
n: Judicial Review reinforces the federal principle. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review preserves the constitutional distribution of powers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review enforces constitutional limits. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not a unitary element. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xa: ⚠ Unitary elements: **All India Services**, **Governor's appointment**, **Emergency provisions**.
**Essential federal feature:** **independence of the judiciary** — it settles Centre-State disputes (UPSC 2021).
"Not a federal feature" PYQ answers: **Office of the Governor** (APPSC-G1 2018) and **CAG** (APPSC-G2 2017).

46.s: Under which Part of the Constitution are the Emergency Provisions contained?
46.x: The emergency provisions are in Part XVIII, Articles 352–360. Part XX is amendment and Part XVI covers reservations for SCs, STs and others.
46.tq: Recall Part XVIII and its Articles 352 to 360.
n: Emergency provisions are governed under Part XVIII of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Emergency provisions are covered by Articles 352 to 360. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: Emergency provisions are in **Part XVIII** (**Articles 352 to 360**) — option **(4)** is correct.
Their unique feature: the federation becomes **unitary without a formal amendment**.
xa: Three types: **National Emergency (Art. 352)**, **President's Rule (Art. 356)**, **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**.
**K.M. Nambiar** called the President's emergency powers a "**fraud on the Constitution**".
⚠ "Art. 311 - Financial Emergency" is a mismatch; Financial Emergency is **Art. 360**.

46.s: The expression “Elephantine size” in relation to the Indian Constitution was used by
46.x: H.V. Kamath referred to the Indian Constitution as having an “Elephantine size.”
46.tq: Match the distinctive quotation with its author.
xs: **H.V. Kamath** used "**Elephantine size**" for the Constitution — option **(4)**.
This was asked in **APPSC GS 2018**.
xa: **Carl Friedrich**: India is "not a nation in the traditional western sense but a comprehensive culture of continental scope" (APPSC-G1 2022).
**K.C. Wheare**: "**quasi-federal**".
**Ambedkar**: "**not in a tight mould of federalism**".

46.s:
Assertion (A): Granville Austin described Indian federalism as cooperative federalism.
Reason (R): Ivor Jennings described India as a federation with a strong centralising tendency.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
46.x: Both descriptions are correctly attributed, but one scholar's view does not explain the other's.
xa: ⚠ **Wheare** = **quasi-federal** (the fifth member of this list).
**Granville Austin** praised the Constitution in "**The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation**".
**Harold Laski**: no India-specific characterisation in the notes → treat as distractor.

46.s: Who described the Indian Constitution as 'quasi-federal'?
46.x: K.C. Wheare called it quasi-federal; Morris Jones used 'bargaining federalism' and Austin 'cooperative federalism'.
xa: ⚠ **Wheare – Jennings – Austin – Morris-Jones – Appleby** = **quasi-federal – centralising tendency – cooperative – bargaining – extremely federal**.
**Paul Appleby** called India **"extremely federal"**.
**H.V. Kamath** spoke of the Constitution's **"elephantine size"** (APPSC GS 2018).
**Harold Laski** has no India-specific label in the notes — treat him as a distractor.

46.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a confederation from a federation?
o: A confederation is made of sovereign States that retain the right to secede.
A federation is a temporary league of sovereign States.
A confederation always has a stronger centre than a federation.
A federation needs no written division of powers.
46.x: A confederation is a loose league of sovereign States that generally keep the right to secede, while a federation creates a constitutional division of powers.
xa: **Ambedkar**: in India **no State has the right to secede** → Union is **indestructible**.
**Unitary**: units draw power from the Centre.
Coming-together federations: **USA**, Switzerland, Australia.

46.s: How does the origin of Indian federalism differ from that of the USA?
o: The USA was first unitary; India was formed by an agreement among States
The USA was formed by integration of States; India moved from a unitary colonial system to a federal one
Both arose from the break-up of unitary systems
Both were created by amendments made by their central governments
46.x: The US federation was formed by agreement and integration of States, while India converted a unitary colonial set-up into a federal one, giving it a centripetal bias.
xa: ⚠ **Integration** = USA (**coming together**); **disintegration** = India (**holding together**).
Framed after Partition + integration of **14 provinces and 500+ princely States**.
USA = "indestructible Union of **indestructible** states"; India = of **destructible** States.

46.s: Which historical circumstances particularly encouraged the framers of the Constitution to adopt a strong centralising design?
o: The prior existence of a fully developed confederation
The aftermath of Partition and the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States
The peaceful integration of only a few provinces before Independence
The absence of linguistic and cultural diversity
46.x: The Constitution was framed after Partition and during the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States. In that context, centralisation was viewed as indispensable for national integration.
46.tq: Link constitutional design to the historical context in which it was adopted.
xs: Framed after **Partition** and integration of **14 provinces and 500+ princely States**, centralisation looked **indispensable** — option **(2)**.
This is the **national-integration design** (TH 17 Feb 2026).
xa: India = **holding-together** federation with a **stronger Centre**.
**K. Santhanam**: Union's strength lies in refusing functions that do not belong to it.
Official label: "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

46.s: Which of the following countries represents a coming-together federation?
46.x: Switzerland is a coming-together federation in which independent States or units pool sovereignty while retaining equal power. India, Spain and Belgium are examples of holding-together federations.
46.tq: Separate examples of the two federation types rather than relying only on their definitions.
xs: **Switzerland** is a **coming-together** federation — option **(4)**.
**India**, **Spain** and **Belgium** are **holding-together** federations.
xa: Coming-together: independent States **pool sovereignty**, keep **equal power** — **USA**, Switzerland, Australia.
Holding-together: large country divides power to hold **diversity** together; **stronger Centre**.
⚠ USA = **integration**; India = **disintegration** (CDI view).

46.s: Which of the following subjects is dealt with by Article 2 of the Constitution?
o: Admission or establishment of new States not part of India
Formation of new States and alteration of existing State boundaries
Amendment of the Constitution through the special procedure
46.x: Article 2 concerns the admission or establishment of new States into the Union, particularly territories not already part of India.
46.tq: Separate Article 2, concerning admission or establishment, from Article 3, concerning existing States.
xs: **Art. 2** = **admission or establishment of new states** not part of India (e.g. **Sikkim**) — option **(1)**.
Forming new States / altering boundaries is **Art. 3**.
xa: **Art. 1**: "**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States**".
**Art. 4**: Art. 3 laws amend the **First and Fourth Schedules**; **not** Art. 368 amendments.
States and UTs are listed in the **First Schedule**.

46.s: A law made under Articles 3 and 4 that alters the First and Fourth Schedules is:
o: valid only if passed by a special majority
not deemed an amendment under Article 368
valid only after ratification by half the States
46.x: Article 4 permits consequential changes in the First and Fourth Schedules, and such a law is not deemed an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
xa: **First Schedule** = States and UTs; **Fourth Schedule** = Rajya Sabha seats **by population**.
Art. 3 Bill needs the **President's recommendation**; the state legislature's views are **not binding**.
No territorial guarantee → India = indestructible Union of **destructible** States.

46.s: India is characterised as:
o: A destructible Union of destructible States
An indestructible Union of destructible States
An indestructible Union of indestructible States
A destructible Union of indestructible States
46.x: India is an indestructible Union of destructible States; the US is an indestructible Union of indestructible States.
xa: Art. 3 laws pass by **simple majority**.
**Ambedkar**: Union is **indestructible**; no State has the **right to secede**.
The word "**Federation**" is **not used** anywhere in the Constitution.

46.s: The Constitution describes India as a:
46.x: India is a 'Union of States'; the Constitution does not use 'Federation of States'.
xa: Residuary powers: **Article 248** + **Entry 97, List I**.
USA: each State has its **own constitution**; in India the former **J&K** was the exception.
⚠ Residue: **Canada** = Centre (India's model); **USA and Australia** = states.

46.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about amendment of the Indian Constitution?
o: The Constitution is neither wholly rigid nor wholly flexible
Most provisions can be amended by Parliament without State ratification
Certain federal provisions need ratification by at least half the State Legislatures
46.x: The Constitution is neither wholly rigid nor wholly flexible.
xa: **Rigid** amendment for federal provisions is a **federal** feature.
**Flexibility** — power to amend vests in Parliament — is a **unitary** feature.
Emergency turns the system unitary **without a formal amendment**.

46.s: Officers of the All India Services are recruited through the:
46.x: AIS officers are recruited through the UPSC and serve both the Union and the States under central control.
xa: Provided under **Art. 312**: **IAS, IPS, IFoS**.
PYQ 2025: Governor, Central Services, **CAG** and Emergency powers all "**violate federal principles**".
Other integrated machinery: **CAG** and **Election Commission**.

46.s: Which single authority audits both Union and State accounts, regarded as a unitary feature?
46.x: A single CAG auditing Union and State accounts, central appointment of Governors, AIS control and emergency powers are unitary features.
xa: **Office of the Governor** was the "not a federal feature" answer (APPSC-G1 2018); **CAG** (APPSC-G2 2017).
CAG audits **both Union and State accounts**.
Emergency turns the system unitary **without a formal amendment**.

46.s: According to Dr B.R. Ambedkar, the use of the word 'Union' shows that:
o: the Union was formed by a compact of sovereign States
the Constitution is set in a tight mould of federalism
the States retain a right to secede
India is not the result of an agreement among States, and States cannot secede
46.x: Ambedkar stressed that India was not formed by an agreement among States, that States had no right to secede, and that the system could be unitary or federal as circumstances required.
xa: Ambedkar's two reasons for "Union": federation **not the result of an agreement** (unlike **USA**) and **no State can secede** → **centripetal bias**.
**K.C. Wheare** called India **"quasi-federal"**; **Ivor Jennings** — a federation with a **strong centralising tendency**.
Official label (IYB 2026): **"federal in structure with unitary features"**.

46.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Constitution is not truly federal and that the States are not sovereign?
o: State of West Bengal v Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
S. R. Bommai v Union of India
Minerva Mills v Union of India
46.x: In State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962), the Supreme Court held that the Constitution was not truly federal and that States were not sovereign. The case also concerned Parliament’s power to acquire State property.
46.tq: Match the case with its specific judicial characterisation of federalism.
xs: **State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962)** held the Constitution **not truly federal** and the States **not sovereign** — option **(1)**.
Parliament's law could **acquire State property** in that case.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** listed **federal character** among basic features; **S.R. Bommai (1994)** made federalism part of the **basic structure**.
**Minerva Mills** reopened judicial review of Emergency barred by the **38th Amendment**.
xa: SC in several rulings: "**fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements**".
**Bommai** limited misuse of **Art. 356** — proclamation open to **judicial review**; **floor test**.
**Mineral Area Development Authority v SAIL (July 2024, 9 judges, 8:1)**: royalty is **not a tax**; States can tax mineral rights.

46.s: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on:
46.x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act respectively.
46.tq: Recall the precise commencement date while distinguishing it from other major constitutional and legal dates.
xs: **BNS, BNSS and BSA** came into force on **1 July 2024** — option **(2)**.
They replaced the **IPC**, **CrPC** and **Evidence Act**.
Criminal law, procedure and evidence are **Concurrent** subjects (Entries 1, 2, 12).
xa: **Public order**, **police**, **prisons** are **State** subjects (Entries 1, 2, 4).
Concurrent **Entry 33**: trade and commerce in foodstuffs (used for Farm Laws).
In the Concurrent List, a **Union law prevails**.

46.s:
Assertion (A): The State of Jammu and Kashmir had a separate constitution and flag.
Reason (R): The former Article 370 provided special arrangements for the State.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
46.x: Article 370 provided the special arrangements, including a separate constitution and flag; they were made inoperative in August 2019.
xa: **Arts. 371 to 371J**: special provisions for Maharashtra, Gujarat, North-Eastern States, Sikkim, Goa, Karnataka and **Andhra Pradesh (371D)**.
The former **J&K** was the exception to "no State constitutions" in India.
**Fifth Schedule**: administration of **Scheduled Areas**.

46.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
46.x: Article 371D gives special provisions for Andhra Pradesh. Article 371 covers Maharashtra and Gujarat, 371A Nagaland, and 371J Karnataka (Sikkim is 371F).
xa: **Arts. 371 to 371J** cover **Maharashtra and Gujarat**, **North-Eastern States** (Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Mizoram), **Sikkim**, **Goa**, **Karnataka** and AP.
**Art. 370** (J&K) made **inoperative in August 2019**.
These provisions form India's **asymmetric federalism**.

46.s: Which one of the following is correct regarding State constitutions in India and the USA?
o: Every Indian State has its own constitution; no US State has one
Both Indian and US States have their own constitutions
Neither Indian nor US States have separate constitutions
Indian States generally have no separate constitutions; each US State has its own
46.x: Indian States generally do not have separate constitutions (the former Jammu and Kashmir was an exception), while each US State has its own.
xa: India: **single citizenship**; USA: **dual**.
Upper House: India by **population**; USA **2 seats** per State.
J&K's separate constitution ended when **Art. 370** was made inoperative in **August 2019**.

46.s: Which constitutional provision provides special treatment to Andhra Pradesh in respect of equal opportunities in public employment and education?
46.x: Article 371D provides special provisions for Andhra Pradesh concerning equal opportunities in public employment and education.
46.tq: Use the exact Article-number and subject pairing.
xs: **Article 371D** gives **Andhra Pradesh** special provisions for **equal opportunities in public employment and education** — option **(2)**.
AP is one of the States with special treatment under **Arts. 371 to 371J**.
xa: AP was under President's Rule in **1973** (Jai Andhra agitation).
Delimitation proposal: AP Lok Sabha seats **25 to 38** under the **+50%** formula (TH 17 Apr 2026).
Other 371-series States: **Maharashtra**, **Gujarat**, **Nagaland**, **Sikkim**, **Goa**, **Karnataka**.

46.s: Which of the following is part of judicial review?
o: Questioning the political wisdom of legislation
Examining the constitutionality of executive orders
46.x: Testing executive orders is part of judicial review; it does not question political wisdom, pre-screen Bills or act as an appeal.
n: Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of executive orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the political wisdom of legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not an ordinary appellate proceeding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the policy merits of legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xa: Judicial review reinforces the **federal principle** and preserves the **distribution of powers**.
It is **not** a **unitary** element; unitary elements include **All India Services**, the **Governor's appointment** and **Emergency provisions**.
It also does not question the **policy merits** or **advisability** of legislation.

46.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 3 — Power of Parliament to alter the area, boundaries or names of States
Articles 155–156 — Appointment and tenure of the Governor
Article 312 — Abolition of the Concurrent List
Article 1 — India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States
46.x: Article 312 concerns All-India Services. It does not provide for abolition of the Concurrent List; therefore, that match is incorrect.
46.tq: Check whether the Article is associated with the stated constitutional subject rather than accepting a familiar-looking number.
xs: **Art. 312** deals with **All India Services**, not abolition of the Concurrent List — option **(3)**.
**Art. 3** = alter state areas, boundaries, names; **Arts. 155-156** = Governor; **Art. 1** = "**Union of States**" — all correct.
xa: All India Services: **IAS, IPS, IFoS** — recruited by **UPSC**, serve States, **controlled by the Centre**.
⚠ Emergency provisions: **Arts. 352-360**.
**42nd CAA, 1976** moved **5 subjects** from State to **Concurrent** List.

46.s: Under the Seventh Schedule, the order of precedence in case of overlapping legislative fields is:
o: State List, Concurrent List, Union List
Concurrent List, State List, Union List
Union List, Concurrent List, State List
Union List, State List, Concurrent List
46.x: The order of precedence is Union List over Concurrent List over State List. In the Concurrent List, a valid Union law generally prevails over a State law in case of inconsistency.
46.tq: Remember the hierarchy as Union, Concurrent, State and reject the tempting placement of the State List above the Concurrent List.
xs: Precedence under the Seventh Schedule is **Union List > Concurrent List > State List** — option **(3)**.
In the **Concurrent List**, a **Union law prevails** over a State law.
The Seventh Schedule operates through **Article 246**.
xa: Entries: **Union 97 → 98**, **State 66 → 59**, **Concurrent 47 → 52** (original → now).
Union List = **national importance**, uniform law; State List = **local/regional importance**.
**Strong Centre** borrowed from **Canada**; **Concurrent List** from **Australia**.
Residuary powers: **Article 248** + **Entry 97, List I**.

46.s: Entry 92A in the Seventh Schedule was inserted by the:

Original counts: Union **97**, State **66**, Concurrent **47**.

46.s: The distribution of legislative subjects among the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Seventh Schedule operates through which Article?
46.x: Article 246 gives effect to the three Lists of the Seventh Schedule. Article 245 deals with the territorial extent of laws, Article 248 with residuary powers, and Article 254 with repugnancy.
46.tq: Seventh Schedule → Art 246
xs: The Seventh Schedule's three lists operate through **Article 246** — option **(2)**.
**Article 248** is the **residuary powers** Article (Part XI, Chapter I).
Precedence under it: **Union > Concurrent > State**.
xa: Three lists: **I - Union**, **II - State**, **III - Concurrent**.
**Art. 249**: Rajya Sabha resolution (**2/3 present and voting**) lets Parliament legislate on a State subject.
**Art. 250**: Parliament legislates on State List during **National Emergency**.
**101st CAA, 2016**: Art. 248 now "subject to **Article 246A**".

**Mineral Area Development Authority v SAIL (July 2024)**: royalty is **not a tax**; States can tax mineral rights.

**Opium** (export) — **Union** (Entry 59).

46.s: Which of the following can happen during a Financial Emergency?
o: Financial directions are given and salaries may be reduced
Parliament legislates on State List subjects
46.x: In a Financial Emergency, financial directions can be given and pay cut; State Budgets are passed by Parliament under President's Rule.
n: During a National Emergency, Parliament can make laws on subjects in the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]

During a Financial Emergency, the executive gives financial directions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]

46.s: If the Lok Sabha is dissolved before approving an Emergency proclamation already approved by the Rajya Sabha, it survives until ____ from the new Lok Sabha's first sitting.
46.x: The 30-day rule applies to National Emergency, President's Rule and Financial Emergency alike.

Financial Emergency survives for 30 days from the first sitting of a new Lok Sabha after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: Approval: **352** = **1 month** (**special** majority); **356** and **360** = **2 months** (**simple** majority).
**Special sitting:** notice by **1/10th of Lok Sabha** members → sitting within **14 days** to consider disapproval of a National Emergency.
Financial Emergency has **never** been declared.
