The terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies can be extended up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Laws made by Parliament on State List subjects during a National Emergency cease to operate 6 months after the Emergency is revoked. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: **Article 354:** the President may **modify** Centre-State **revenue** distribution, valid until the end of the **financial year** in which the proclamation ceases.
The Union's executive power extends to directing **any State** on how to use its executive power.
Proclamation is only on the **written advice** of the **Union Cabinet**.

46.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Proclamation of National Emergency – Requires written advice of the Union Cabinet
President's modification of revenue distribution – Ceases six months after the Emergency is revoked
Parliament's laws on State List subjects – Cease six months after the Emergency is revoked
46.x: Revenue modification lasts until the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases.
n: Laws made by Parliament on State List subjects during a National Emergency cease to operate 6 months after the Emergency is revoked. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Modification of revenue distribution under Article 354 remains valid up to the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The President can proclaim a National Emergency only upon the written advice of the Union Cabinet. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The National Emergency of 1975 was proclaimed on 25 June 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: The 1975 Emergency was on the ground of **Internal Disturbance** and withdrawn **21 March 1977**.
Parliament may extend the **Lok Sabha** term **1 year at a time** during an Emergency.
Parliamentary approval is needed within **1 month** (**special** majority).

46.s: The Concurrent List in the Indian Constitution was borrowed from:
46.x: The Concurrent List came from Australia; the strong Centre from Canada and the federal scheme from the 1935 Act.
xa: ⚠ **Strong Centre** = Canada; **Concurrent List** = Australia.
Residuary power: **Canada** model — with the Centre; **USA and Australia** — with the states.
Under the **GoI Act 1935** residuary power lay with the **Governor-General**.

46.s: Which one of the following about the use of Concurrent List entries is correct?
o: Entry 33 concerns only the organisation of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
The Union has used them for farm laws (Entry 33) and education measures such as the NEP and NMC Act.
Only State Legislatures can legislate on Concurrent subjects.
The Concurrent List bars Union laws on education.
46.x: Concurrent List entries permit Union legislation; cited examples include farm laws through Entry 33 and education measures such as the NEP and NMC Act.
xa: **Education** is Concurrent **Entry 25**, moved by the **42nd CAA, 1976**.
Suggested fix: a **narrower/tighter Concurrent List** and stronger **Inter-State Council** (TH, 2 Mar 2026).
**Constitution and organisation of High Courts** is Union **Entry 78**.

46.s: Institutions for scientific or technical education financed by the Government of India and declared by Parliament to be of national importance fall under:
46.x: Such institutions are under Union List Entry 64. Union Entry 66 covers coordination and standards in higher education, and Concurrent Entry 25 covers education generally. State Entry 32 is not the entry for these institutions.
46.tq: National-importance S&T institutions = Union 64; HE standards = Union 66
xs: **Institutions for scientific or technical education** financed by GoI and of **national importance** — **Union List, Entry 64** — option **(3)**.
**Union Entry 66** is **coordination and standards in higher education**.
**Concurrent Entry 25** is **education** in general.
xa: Education was moved to the Concurrent List by the **42nd CAA, 1976**.
Union List now has **98** entries.
⚠ **64** = institutions; **66** = standards.

46.s: Which Article of the Constitution confers on Parliament exclusive power to legislate on matters not enumerated in the State List or the Concurrent List?
46.x: Article 248 deals with residuary legislative powers and gives Parliament exclusive power over matters not included in the State or Concurrent Lists, including residuary taxes.
46.tq: Separate the specific residuary-power Article from the general distribution-of-powers Article.
xs: **Article 248** gives **Parliament alone** power over matters not in the State or Concurrent List — option **(1)**.
It works with **Entry 97, List I** and includes **residuary taxes** (gift tax, wealth tax, expenditure tax).
**Art. 249** = Rajya Sabha resolution; **Art. 250** = State subjects during National Emergency; **Art. 246** = the three lists.
xa: Art. 248 is in **Part XI, Chapter I**.
**101st CAA, 2016**: Art. 248 now "subject to **Article 246A**" (GST).
PYQ 2025: "Art. 248 = residuary" and "Parliament has exclusive power over items in no list" → **both correct**.
Residue with the Centre follows **Canada**; **USA and Australia** leave it with the states.

46.s: Article 248 was made subject to Article 246A by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
o: One hundred and third Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019
One hundred and first Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016
46.x: The One hundred and first Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, inserted the GST-related constitutional provisions, including the qualification of Article 248 by Article 246A.
46.tq: Distinguish the GST amendment from the major structural amendment dealing with transferred subjects.
xs: The **One hundred and first Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016** (**101st CAA**) made Art. 248 "**subject to Article 246A**" (GST) — option **(4)**.
The **42nd CAA, 1976** moved **5 subjects** to the Concurrent List.
xa: **Article 248** + **Entry 97, List I** = residuary power with **Parliament alone**.
**GST** arrived in **2017**, under the "cooperative-competitive" label.
Residuary taxes include **gift tax**, **wealth tax**, **expenditure tax**.

46.s: Which of the following correctly states where residuary powers lie?
o: India and Canada – States; USA – Centre
India, Canada, USA and Australia – all with the Centre
India and Canada – Centre; USA and Australia – States
46.x: Residuary powers lie with the Centre in India and Canada, and with the States in the USA and Australia; under the 1935 Act they were vested in the Governor-General.
xa: Residuary power: **Article 248** + **Entry 97, List I**.
**Strong Centre** borrowed from **Canada**; **Concurrent List** from **Australia**.
India vs USA: India has **three lists**; USA enumerates only **federal** powers.

46.s: Residuary legislative matters are associated with which entry of the Union List?
46.x: Union List Entry 97, read with Article 248, covers matters not enumerated in the State List or Concurrent List, including residuary taxation.
46.tq: Use the exact entry number to distinguish residuary power from neighbouring Union List entries.
xs: Residuary matters are **Entry 97** of the Union List — option **(1)**.
Read with **Article 248**, Parliament alone legislates on matters not in the State or Concurrent List.
xa: ⚠ **97** is also the **original** count of the Union List.
Residuary taxes: **gift tax**, **wealth tax**, **expenditure tax**.
**Entry 92A** (inter-state sales tax) added by the **6th CAA, 1956**.

46.s: Trade and commerce within a State is placed in which List, subject to the relevant Concurrent List entry?
46.x: Trade and commerce within a State is State List Entry 26, subject to Concurrent List Entry 33. Inter-State trade is Union Entry 42, and Entry 5 is local government.
46.tq: Separate intra-State (Entry 26) from inter-State (Entry 42) trade.
n: Trade and Commerce within a State belongs to the State List under Entry 26. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Trade and Commerce within a State is subject to List III, Entry 33. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: **Trade and commerce within a State** is **State List, Entry 26**, subject to Concurrent List **Entry 33** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Union List Entry 42** is **Inter-State** trade and commerce; **State Entry 5** is **local government**.
**Concurrent Entry 20** is **economic and social planning**.
xa: Concurrent **Entry 33** = trade and commerce in **foodstuffs**; the **Farm Laws** were made via Entry 33.
**Public order** = State **Entry 1**; **police** and **prisons** = State Entries 2 and 4.
**Population control and family planning** = Concurrent **Entry 20A**.

46.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Social security and social insurance — Concurrent List, Entry 23
Protection of wild animals and birds — Concurrent List, Entry 17
46.x: Protection of wild animals and birds is under Entry 17B of the Concurrent List, not Entry 17. Entry 17 concerns prevention of cruelty to animals.
46.tq: Find the single wrong entry in a cluster of closely related Concurrent List subjects.
xs: **Protection of wild animals and birds** is Concurrent **Entry 17B**, not Entry 17 — so option **(4)** is NOT correctly matched.
Concurrent **Entry 17** is **prevention of cruelty to animals**.
**Forests — 17A**, **Education — 25**, **Social security — 23** are correct.
xa: Forests, education and wild animals/birds were moved by the **42nd CAA, 1976**.
**Economic and social planning** — Concurrent **Entry 20**.
⚠ **Water** = State Entry 17; **cruelty to animals** = Concurrent Entry 17.

46.s: Elections to State Legislatures and elections conducted by the Election Commission fall respectively under:
46.x: Elections to the State Legislature are State List Entry 37 (subject to parliamentary law); elections conducted by the Election Commission are Union List Entry 72.
xa: The **Election Commission** runs elections to **Parliament** and **State legislatures** — an integrated (unitary) machinery.
**CAG** audits both Union and State accounts.
⚠ "Not a federal feature" answers: **Office of the Governor** (APPSC-G1 2018) and **CAG** (APPSC-G2 2017).

46.s:
Assertion (A): The 42nd Amendment moved the constitution and organisation of the Supreme Court and High Courts to the Concurrent List.
Reason (R): The 42nd Amendment moved five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
46.x: The administration of justice entry moved covers courts other than the Supreme Court and High Courts, so A is false; R is true.
xa: The other subjects moved: **education** and **forests**.
**Constitution and organisation of High Courts** is a **Union** subject (Entry 78).
⚠ **42nd** (1976) = State → Concurrent; **44th** (1978) = armed rebellion.

46.s: Population control and family planning was inserted in the Concurrent List as Entry:
46.x: Entry 20A was added by the 42nd Amendment, which also moved administration of justice to the Concurrent List.
n: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act transferred administration of justice from the State List to the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Administration of justice includes the constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Entry 20A was inserted into the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Entry 20A concerns population control and family planning. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Population control is a Concurrent List subject under Entry 20A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Family planning is a Concurrent List subject under Entry 20A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: Other transfers: **education**, **forests**, **weights and measures**, **protection of wild animals and birds**.
Constitution and organisation of **High Courts** = **Union** (Entry 78).
The Centre uses Concurrent entries for sweeping laws — e.g. **NEP** and **NMC Act** in education.

46.s: The expression 'Union of India' refers to:
46.x: The Union of India refers to the States; the Territory of India also includes UTs and acquired territories.
xa: ⚠ Territory is the **wider** term; Union = members of the federal system.
States and UTs are specified in the **First Schedule**.

46.s: A law under Article 3 to form a new State is passed by:
o: A special majority with State ratification
46.x: Article 3 laws need only a simple majority.
xa: The Bill needs the **President's recommendation** + reference to the state legislature (views **not binding**).
**Art. 4**: such laws are **not** Art. 368 amendments.
Result: "**an indestructible Union of destructible States**".

46.s: A Bill under Article 3 to alter the boundaries of a State can be introduced only on the recommendation of the:
46.x: An Article 3 Bill needs the President's recommendation and is referred to the State legislature, whose views do not bind Parliament.
xa: It passes by **simple majority**.
Such a law is **not** an **Art. 368** amendment (**Art. 4**).
Parliament altering state boundaries is counted a **unitary** feature.

46.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Indian federal structure?
o: The Constitution provides completely separate judicial and administrative machinery for every State
The Supreme Court is an independent adjudicator in Centre-State disputes
The Constitution provides for two sets of governments
The Constitution is written and supreme
46.x: India has an integrated judicial and administrative framework, not separate machinery for every State.
xa: Essential federal feature: **independence of the judiciary** (UPSC 2021).
The **Centre appoints High Court judges** — a unitary feature.
Other federal features: **Seventh Schedule** division, **rigid** amendment, **bicameral** legislature.

46.s: The Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister is collectively responsible to the:
46.x: Under Articles 74(1) and 75 the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; the President is the nominal head.
xa: Parliamentary form follows the **British model**.
The **real executive** = Council of Ministers under the **PM**.
India = "federal system with **unitary bias**".

46.s: Which case recognised federalism as part of the basic structure and opened Article 356 proclamations to judicial review?
46.x: S.R. Bommai (1994) recognised federalism as basic structure and limited misuse of Article 356.
xa: In the **coalition era (1989-2014)**, the **ISC** was set up (**1990**) and **Bommai (1994)** limited Art. 356.
**TH (23 Mar 2026)**: Bommai recalled against earlier misuse of Art. 356 amid a "hollowing federal spirit".
President's Rule: approval within **2 months**, **simple majority**, maximum **3 years**.
AP came under President's Rule in **1973** (**Jai Andhra** agitation).

46.s: Article 19 is suspended during a National Emergency only when the emergency is proclaimed on the ground of:
o: Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
External emergency involving war or external aggression
46.x: Article 19 is automatically suspended only when the National Emergency is based on war or external aggression. Article 20 and Article 21 cannot be suspended under Article 359 orders.
46.tq: Discriminate between the grounds of emergency for the limited suspension of Fundamental Rights.
xs: **Art. 19** is suspended only in an **external** emergency — **war or external aggression** — option **(2)** (**Art. 358**).
Other rights are suspended by order under **Art. 359**, **except Arts. 20 and 21**.
"**Internal disturbance**" is no longer a ground; it was replaced by **"armed rebellion"** by the **44th Amendment**.
Failure of constitutional machinery is the ground for **Art. 356**, not a National Emergency.
xa: National Emergency grounds: **war, external aggression, armed rebellion**.
National Emergencies: **1962, 1971, 1975**.
⚠ Trap: "internal disturbance" is no longer a ground (APPSC-GS 2018).

46.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Forty-fourth Amendment?
o: Emergency must be proclaimed on the Union Cabinet's written advice
It retained 'internal disturbance' as a ground for Emergency
It reduced the approval period for National Emergency to one month
One-tenth of Lok Sabha members can require a special sitting within 14 days to consider disapproval
46.x: The 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'.
xa: Parliament approval within **1 month**.
**Arts 20-21** made non-suspendable by the **44th Amendment (1978)**.
**38th Amendment** barred judicial review of Emergency; **Minerva Mills** reopened it.

46.s: A proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352 must be approved by Parliament within:
46.x: Article 352 needs approval within one month; Articles 356 and 360 within two months by simple majority.
xa: National Emergency is renewable every **6 months**.
President's Rule: maximum **3 years**; beyond **1 year** only with a National Emergency + **ECI certification**.

46.s: Financial Emergency is provided for under Article:
46.x: Financial Emergency is under Article 360, not Article 311.
xa: State Assembly terms can also be extended during a National Emergency.
**Art. 250** laws on State subjects lapse **6 months** after the emergency.
The **44th Amendment (1978)** replaced "internal disturbance" with **"armed rebellion"**.

46.s: The Inter-State Council was set up in:
46.x: The Inter-State Council was set up in 1990, during the 1989–2014 coalition era.
xa: **Morris Jones** called Indian federalism **"bargaining federalism"**.
Preceding phase **1977-89**: Janata interlude; **Sarkaria Commission (1983)**.
Next phase **2014 onward**: **NITI Aayog** (2015), **GST** (2017).

46.s: The allocation of Rajya Sabha seats to States is provided in the:
46.x: Seats are allotted broadly by population in the Fourth Schedule, unlike equal representation in the US Senate.
xa: **Unequal representation** in Rajya Sabha is counted as a **unitary feature**.
Rajya Sabha for States = **bicameral** legislature, a federal feature.
India vs USA: **single** vs **dual** citizenship; **single integrated** vs dual judiciary.

46.s: In Mineral Area Development Authority v. SAIL, the nine-judge Bench held by majority that royalty:
o: Is a fee under the Union List
Can be levied only by the Union
46.x: The 8:1 majority held royalty is not a tax and recognised that States can tax mineral rights.
xa: **Taxes on mineral rights** are in the **State List (Entry 50)**, subject to limits set by Parliament.
APPSC 2025 key: mineral-right taxes → **State**.

46.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 356 – Threat to the financial stability of India
Article 360 – Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
Article 352 – War, external aggression or armed rebellion
Article 352 – Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
46.x: Article 352 covers war, external aggression or armed rebellion; Article 356 covers failure of constitutional machinery in a State; Article 360 covers a threat to financial stability.
n: Article 352 provides for National Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
War is a ground for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
External aggression is a ground for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Armed rebellion is a ground for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Article 356 provides for President’s Rule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Failure of constitutional machinery in a State is the ground for imposing President’s Rule under Article 356. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Article 360 provides for Financial Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
A threat to the financial stability or credit of India is a ground for proclaiming Financial Emergency under Article 360. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
War, external aggression, or armed rebellion are the grounds for National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Failure of constitutional machinery is the ground for President’s Rule under Article 356. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: "**Internal disturbance**" was replaced by "**armed rebellion**" by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
Art. 356 also links to **Art. 365**.

46.s: How many times has a National Emergency been proclaimed in India?
46.x: National Emergencies were declared in 1962, 1971 and 1975; a Financial Emergency has never been declared.
n: National Emergency has been invoked 3 times in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
National Emergencies were invoked in 1962, 1971, and 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule has been invoked over 100 times across various States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency has never been invoked in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: The **1975** Emergency was proclaimed on **25 June 1975** on the ground of **Internal Disturbance**; withdrawn **21 March 1977**.
**AP** came under President's Rule in **1973** (Jai Andhra agitation).
**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas:** **25 June**.

46.s: Parliamentary approval of a National Emergency requires:
o: A special majority in both Houses
A special majority in the Lok Sabha only
A simple majority in both Houses
46.x: A National Emergency needs a special majority; President's Rule and Financial Emergency need simple majorities.
n: A National Emergency requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule requires a simple majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency requires a simple majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
A National Emergency has no maximum continuation limit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: Financial Emergency continues until **revoked** by the President.

46.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: National Emergency – six months at a time, up to three years
Financial Emergency – six months at a time, up to three years
President's Rule – six months at a time, up to three years
President's Rule – six months at a time, with no maximum limit
46.x: President's Rule continues six months at a time up to three years; a National Emergency has no maximum limit, and a Financial Emergency once approved continues until revoked.
n: A National Emergency continues for 6 months at a time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
A National Emergency has no maximum continuation limit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule continues for 6 months at a time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule can continue for a maximum of 3 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency continues until it is revoked by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: Approval: **352** within **1 month** (was **2 months** before the **44th Amendment**).

46.s: The last National Emergency was formally withdrawn on 21 March:
46.x: Emergencies were declared in 1962, 1971 and 1975; the last was lifted on 21 March 1977.
n: National Emergencies were invoked in 1962, 1971, and 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The National Emergency of 1975 was proclaimed on 25 June 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The 1975 National Emergency was formally withdrawn on 21 March 1977. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: The **1975** Emergency was on the ground of **Internal Disturbance**.
The **44th Amendment, 1978** replaced "internal disturbance" with "**armed rebellion**".
**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas** (**25 June**) recalls the **1975** Emergency.

46.s: The coalition era of Indian federalism, with more negotiated Centre-State relations, broadly spanned:
46.x: Congress dominance (1952–67), confrontation (1967–77), the Janata interlude (1977–89) and the coalition era (1989–2014).
xa: **Rajamannar Committee (1969)** — phase C; **Sarkaria Commission (1983)** — phase D.
**ISC (1990)** and **Bommai (1994)** — phase A.
Phase C ended with the **1975 Emergency**.

46.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
46.x: GST arrived in 2017, not 2015. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, while the other three pairs are correctly matched.
46.tq: Find the one shifted year among a set of correctly dated federal developments.
xs: **GST — 2015** is wrong: **GST** arrived in **2017** — option **(3)**.
**2015** is the year **NITI Aayog** replaced the Planning Commission.
**Sarkaria — 1983**, **ISC — 1990**, **Rajamannar — 1969** are correct.
xa: Rajamannar came in the **1967-77** phase of confrontation.
Sarkaria was appointed during **1977-89**.
**101st CAA, 2016** provided for GST (**Art. 246A**).

46.s: 'Samvidhan Hatya Diwas', which recalls the Emergency of 1975, is observed on:
46.x: Samvidhan Hatya Diwas is observed on 25 June, recalling the Emergency proclaimed in 1975. 26 January is Republic Day, 26 November is Constitution Day, and 15 August is Independence Day.
46.tq: 25 June = Samvidhan Hatya Diwas (1975 Emergency)
xs: **Samvidhan Hatya Diwas** is observed on **25 June**, recalling the **1975 Emergency** — option **(3)**.
Source: LENSD **26 Jun 2026**.
xa: National Emergencies: **1962, 1971, 1975**.
After 1975, the **44th Amendment (1978)** replaced "internal disturbance" with **"armed rebellion"**.
The **1967-77** phase ended in re-centralisation up to the **1975 Emergency**.

46.s: Which of the following is NOT a financial consequence of a National Emergency?
o: Transfers to States may be reduced or cancelled, subject to Parliament's approval
An obligatory increase in transfers of funds to States
The President may modify the distribution of revenues between the Union and States
The Union may issue directions affecting its financial relations with States
46.x: The President may modify revenue distribution and reduce or cancel transfers to States; an increase in transfers is not a specified consequence.
xa: Financial Emergency (**Art. 360**): **reduce salaries** of State employees and **SC/HC judges**; State **money bills reserved** for the President.
Financial Emergency has **never been declared**.
⚠ "**Art. 311** - Financial Emergency" is a mismatch; it is **Art. 360**.

46.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated federal consequence of a Financial Emergency under Article 360?
o: The Union may direct States regarding financial propriety.
The Union may direct reduction of salaries and allowances.
The Union automatically assumes all legislative powers of State Legislatures.
Money Bills of States may be required to be reserved for the President's consideration.
46.x: Article 360 can enable directions concerning State finances, salary reductions and reservation of State Money Bills. It does not automatically transfer all legislative powers of State Legislatures to the Union.
46.tq: Find the overbroad claim that exceeds the financial scope of Article 360.
xs: The Union does NOT **automatically assume all legislative powers** of State Legislatures under **Art. 360** — option **(3)**.

Under Financial Emergency the Centre can **direct financial propriety**, order **reduction of salaries and allowances** of State employees, and require State **money bills to be reserved** for the President.
It can also reduce salaries of Union employees and **SC/HC judges**.
xa: Ground of **Art. 360**: threat to the **financial stability or credit** of India.
Approval within **2 months**, **simple majority**.
Financial Emergency has **never been declared**.
⚠ "**Art. 311** - Financial Emergency" is a mismatch; it is **Art. 360**.

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. President's Rule does not directly suspend Fundamental Rights.
2. A Financial Emergency does not directly suspend Fundamental Rights.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
46.x: Only a National Emergency affects Fundamental Rights (Articles 358 and 359); President's Rule and a Financial Emergency do not suspend them directly.
n: President’s Rule does not directly suspend Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency does not directly suspend Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: **Art. 19** is suspended only in an **external** emergency (**Art. 358**).
Other rights are suspended by order under **Art. 359**, **except Arts. 20 and 21**.
The **44th Amendment, 1978** made **Articles 20 and 21** non-suspendable.

46.s: The 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' in Article 352 with:
46.x: It substituted 'armed rebellion', cut approval to one month, protected Articles 20–21 and required the Cabinet's written advice.
n: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 replaced “Internal Disturbance” with “Armed Rebellion” under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 reduced parliamentary approval time for a National Emergency from 2 months to 1 month. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 guaranteed that enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Article 359. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The President can proclaim a National Emergency only upon the written advice of the Union Cabinet. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
War, external aggression, or armed rebellion are the grounds for National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended during a National Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act established the non-suspendability of Articles 20 and 21 under Article 359. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: ⚠ Trap: "internal disturbance" is no longer a ground (APPSC-GS 2018).
**Special sitting:** notice by **1/10th of Lok Sabha** members → sitting within **14 days**.
The **38th Amendment** barred judicial review of Emergency; **Minerva Mills** reopened it.

46.s: During a National Emergency, the President may modify the distribution of revenues between the Union and States under Article:
46.x: Article 354 allows it; the change lasts until the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends.
n: Article 354 empowers the President to modify the constitutional distribution of revenues between the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Modification of revenue distribution under Article 354 remains valid up to the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]

46.x: Residuary subjects refer to matters that are not specifically mentioned in the Union List, State List, or Concurrent List under the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution. These subjects emerge due to changing circumstances, advancements in technology, or new policy needs. According to Article 248, the Parliament of India has exclusive power to legislate on these matters, meaning only the Union Legislature can make laws regarding them. Examples of residuary subjects include cyber laws, space research, atomic energy, artificial intelligence regulations, and foreign trade policies, as these areas were not foreseen when the Constitution was drafted. As new challenges arise, Parliament retains the authority to govern such subjects.

46.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of India?
o: It lists the distribution of powers between the Union
It contains the languages listed in the Constitution
It contains provisions for the administration of Tribal
It allocates seats in the Council of States
46.x: The Fourth Schedule allocates seats for each State of India in the Council of States. The 7th Schedule deals with the allocation of powers and functions between the Union and the States. Under the 8th Schedule, a list of 22 languages of India is recognized by the Constitution. The 5th and 6th Schedules give provisions for administration and control of the Scheduled Areas and Tribes.

46.s: Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of India deals with
o: Allocation of seats for the Council of States
46.x: The Fourth Schedule of the Constitution deals with the allocation of seats for the Council of States.

46.s: Land Reform comes under the subjects of –
46.x: Land Reforms are the subject of the State List. Land Reform Act has been added to Schedule IX of the Constitution and the IXth Schedule itself, by the 1st Amendment Act, 1951 to provide Constitutional protection to the states on matters of Land Reform Acts.

46.s: Andhra Pradesh was placed under President’s Rule in 1973 in the context of which movement?
46.x: Andhra Pradesh came under President’s Rule in 1973 during the Jai Andhra agitation.
46.tq: Link the year with the specific political event rather than a neighbouring movement.
xs: AP came under President's Rule in **1973** during the **Jai Andhra agitation** — option **(4)**.
APPSC option set: **1963/1983/1973/1985** — the answer year is **1973**.
xa: President's Rule (**Art. 356**): failure of constitutional machinery; approval within **2 months**.
Beyond **1 year** only with a National Emergency + **ECI certification**.
**Art. 371D**: AP's special provisions in employment and education.

47.s: The system of Panchayat Raj is mentioned in
The Panchayati Raj is included in the
Under Article 255, an Act passed without the required previous sanction but later assented to by the Governor or President is:
o: not invalid merely for want of that sanction
valid only if upheld by the Supreme Court
47.x: Article 255 treats the recommendation or previous sanction as procedural; subsequent assent prevents invalidity on that ground alone.
xa: **Art. 254**: **repugnancy** — Union law prevails; State law with **President's assent** prevails in that State.
State bills restricting **inter-state trade** need the **President's previous sanction** (Part XIII, **Arts. 301-305**).
**Art. 253**: laws to implement **international agreements**.

47.s: Repugnancy between Union and State laws is dealt with by Article:
47.x: Article 254 deals with repugnancy; Article 255 concerns recommendations and previous sanctions as procedural matters, and Article 248 with residuary powers.
xa: **246A** (**101st CAA**): both Parliament and States make **GST** laws; only Parliament for **IGST**.
**252** = law for **two or more States by consent**; **253** = **international agreements**.
**251** = inconsistency with laws under **249/250**.

47.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the territorial extent of laws?
o: Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India
A parliamentary law is not invalid merely because it has extra-territorial operation
A State Legislature may ordinarily legislate for another State's territory without any territorial connection
A State law needs a sufficient territorial nexus for extra-territorial reach
47.x: A State law requires a sufficient territorial nexus for any extra-territorial reach, so the last statement is false.
xa: ⚠ **Extra-territorial** laws = Parliament only; State needs **territorial nexus**.
**President's regulations** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** have the force of Parliament's Acts.
The **Governor** can bar or modify Parliament's Acts for **Scheduled Areas**.

47.s: A State law on a State List subject conflicts with a valid Parliamentary law under the Concurrent List. Which ordinarily prevails?
o: The later of the two laws
The law approved by the Governor
47.x: The Concurrent List has precedence over the State List, so a valid Parliamentary law on a Concurrent matter ordinarily prevails over an inconsistent State law.
xa: **Art. 251**: a law under **Art. 249/250** prevails over a conflicting State law.

47.s: Under Article 246(4), Parliament may legislate for areas not included in a State (Union Territories) on matters in:
o: The Union and Concurrent Lists only
47.x: Article 246(4) lets Parliament legislate for areas not included in a State on matters in all three Lists, not merely the Union List.
xa: **President's regulations** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** have the force of Parliament's Acts.

47.s: Article 246A was inserted by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
47.x: Article 246A was introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, which established the constitutional framework for GST.
47.tq: Match the distinctive constitutional article with the amendment that introduced it.
xs: **Art. 246A** was inserted by the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act** — option **(1)**.
Under it, **both** Parliament and States make **GST** laws; only Parliament for **inter-state supply (IGST)**.
xa: **Art. 246**: three lists in the **Seventh Schedule**.
**Art. 248** + **Entry 97** = residuary power, including **taxation**.

47.s: In India, the residuary power of legislation is vested in Parliament by which combination?
o: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List
Article 249 and Entry 97 of the State List
Article 250 and Entry 98 of the Concurrent List
Article 253 and Entry 97 of the Concurrent List
47.x: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List together confer residuary legislative power on Parliament.
47.tq: Link the constitutional article with the corresponding Seventh Schedule entry.
xs: Residuary power: **Article 248** and **Entry 97 of the Union List** — option **(1)**.
Parliament has **exclusive** power over any matter not in the State or Concurrent List.
**Art. 249** = Rajya Sabha resolution; **Art. 250** = Emergency; **Art. 253** = treaties.
xa: Covers residuary **taxation** as well.
⚠ **97** is also the **original** Union List count.
Borrowed from **Canada**.

47.s: A State Bill imposing reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest requires the previous sanction of the:
47.x: A State may impose reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest, but such a Bill needs the President's previous sanction.
xa: **Art. 255**: recommendations and previous sanctions are **matters of procedure only** — later **assent** cures the defect.
**Inter-state** trade = **Union**; trade **within** a State = **State**.

47.s: Articles 301 to 303 principally restrict Parliament from doing which of the following in relation to trade and commerce?
o: Making any law concerning inter-State trade
47.x: Articles 301 to 303 restrict discriminatory or preferential treatment between States in laws relating to trade and commerce.
47.tq: Distinguish a restriction against discrimination from a complete prohibition on regulation.
xs: **Arts. 301-303** stop Parliament from **preferring or discriminating between States** in trade laws — option **(1)**.
Discrimination is allowed only in **scarcity**.
xa: State restrictions on **inter-state trade**: reasonable, in **public interest**, with **President's previous sanction** (Part XIII, **Arts. 301-305**).
**Inter-state trade** is a **Union** subject; trade **within** a State is a State subject.

47.s: Under Article 251, if a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 conflicts with a State law:
o: both laws become void to the extent of conflict
47.x: Article 251 provides that a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 prevails over an inconsistent State law.
xa: The **State legislature's power is not suspended** under Art. 249 or 250.
**Art. 249** law ceases **6 months after the resolution lapses**; **Art. 250** law **6 months** after the emergency.

47.s: While an Article 249 resolution is in force, the State Legislature:
o: may legislate only with the Rajya Sabha's consent
loses its power, which passes to the Governor
may still legislate, but the Parliamentary law prevails in a conflict
stands dissolved for the duration of the resolution
47.x: An Article 249 resolution does not suspend the State Legislature's power, but the Parliamentary law prevails if the two conflict.
xa: **Art. 251**: the State law is **inoperative only while** the Union law lasts.
Same for **Art. 250** during an Emergency.
Art. 249 resolution: **2/3 present and voting**, **up to 1 year**.

47.s: Preventive detention for reasons connected with security of a State and public order falls under the:
47.x: Concurrent List Entry 3 covers preventive detention for State security and public order, while Union List Entry 9 covers it for defence, foreign affairs and security of India.
xa: The **Allahabad HC** criticised the **routine use** of preventive detention.

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Panchayati Raj and Municipalities are in the Union List.
2. Article 246A empowers both Parliament and State Legislatures to make GST laws.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
47.x: Article 246A gives both Parliament and State Legislatures power over GST; Panchayati Raj and Municipalities are State List subjects (Entry 5).
n: Article 246A gives Parliament simultaneous power to frame laws regarding Goods and Services Tax. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 246A gives State Legislatures simultaneous power to frame laws regarding Goods and Services Tax. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 246A breaks the strict exclusive-list dichotomy of Article 246. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Panchayati Raj is enumerated in the State List under Entry 5. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Municipalities are enumerated in the State List under Entry 5. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: Only **Parliament** legislates on **inter-state supply** (**IGST**).
Art. 246A breaks the strict exclusive-list dichotomy of **Article 246**.
⚠ Original list counts: **97/66/47**.

47.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 252?
o: Two or more State Legislatures must pass resolutions requesting parliamentary legislation
Any other State may adopt the law later by a resolution of its legislature
The requesting State Legislatures may independently repeal the law
Only Parliament can amend or repeal a law made under it
47.x: Only Parliament can amend or repeal a law enacted under Article 252; the requesting States cannot repeal it on their own.
xa: ⚠ **252** needs consent of **two or more states**; **253** needs **no state consent**.
Art. 252 Acts: **Prize Competition (1955)**, **Wild Life (1972)**, **Water (1974)**, **Urban Land Ceiling (1976)**, **Human Organs (1994)**.
"Art. 252 laws cannot be changed by states" is cited as a **centralising tool**.

47.s: A law made for a State during President’s Rule continues after the Proclamation ends until:
o: the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts it
the Supreme Court declares it permanent
the Governor issues an ordinance replacing it
47.x: Such a law does not automatically lapse when President’s Rule ends. It continues until the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts it.
47.tq: Test the post-emergency effect instead of confusing continuation with automatic repeal.
xs: A President's Rule law continues until the **State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts** it — option **(1)**.
It does not lapse automatically when the Proclamation ends.
xa: Such laws are made by **Parliament** or the **President by delegation** (**Art. 356**).
Contrast: **Art. 250** laws lapse **6 months** after the emergency; **Art. 249** laws **6 months** after the resolution lapses.

47.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched regarding Parliament's power to legislate on State List matters?
o: Article 252 – Request by a single State Legislature
Article 356 – President's Rule in a State
47.x: Article 252 needs resolutions from the legislatures of two or more States, not one State alone. The other pairs are correct.
xa: The fifth route: **Art. 253** — **international agreements**.
After an Art. 252 law, **only Parliament** can amend/repeal it.
Other States may **adopt** the law by resolution.

47.s: A Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 remains in force for a period not exceeding:
47.x: An Article 249 resolution lasts up to one year and may be renewed any number of times, one year at a time.
xa: Majority: **2/3 of members present and voting** (APPSC-GS 2025).
Laws **cease 6 months after** the resolution lapses.
State power is **not suspended** but the Union law prevails (**Art. 251**).

47.s: Parliament can legislate on a State List subject to implement an international convention under:
47.x: Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws implementing treaties, agreements and conventions, even on State List subjects.
xa: Applies to the **whole or any part of India**; includes decisions of **international bodies** (APPSC-GS 2018).
⚠ **252** = consent of **two or more states**; **253** = **no state consent**.

47.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Trade and commerce within a State — Union List
47.x: Agriculture is a State List subject, so B is correct. Trade and commerce within a State is a State List subject (not Union), while currency and foreign loans are Union List subjects (not State or Concurrent).
47.tq: Use the list allocation of familiar subjects to eliminate swapped entries.
xs: **Agriculture — State List** — option **(2)**.
Trade and commerce **within** a State is a **State** subject, not Union (option 1).
**Currency** and **foreign loans** are **Union** subjects (options 3 and 4 wrong).
xa: ⚠ **Inter-state** trade = Union; trade **within** a State = State.
Farm Laws used Concurrent **Entry 33** although agriculture is **State List Entry 14**.
Other State subjects: **public health and sanitation**, **markets**, **fisheries**.

47.s: The Supreme Court's advisory opinion of November 2025 was reported in connection with which issue?
o: Deemed assent and timelines for Governors and the President
Allocation of residuary powers to States
Transfer of forests to the Union List
47.x: The advisory opinion rejected deemed assent and fixed timelines concerning Governors and the President.
47.tq: Identify the constitutional controversy from the paired concepts rather than from a general federalism label.
xs: The SC advisory opinion (**Nov 2025**) rejected **deemed assent** and **fixed timelines** for **Governors/President** — option **(1)**.
It concerns assent to State bills, linked to **Art. 254(2)** reservation by the Governor.
xa: Under **254(2)**, the Governor may reserve a bill as an exception to **aid-and-advice**.
A State law with **President's assent** prevails **in that State**.
Parliament can later **override** it with a fresh law.

47.s: Parliament exercises the legislative powers of a State Legislature during President's Rule under Article:
47.x: Under Article 356 Parliament exercises the State Legislature's powers; Article 250 applies during a National Emergency and Article 252 on request of two or more States.
n: Article 250 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects during the operation of a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 252 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects following requests by at least two State Legislatures through resolutions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 356 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects following a proclamation of President’s Rule in a State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Under Article 356, Parliament exercises the legislative powers of the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: The five special circumstances: **Art. 249, 250, 252, 253** and **356**.
**President's Rule laws** stay in force after PR ends until the state legislature repeals, alters or re-enacts them.
⚠ A request by **one** state is **not** valid under Art. 252.

47.s: A law made by Parliament under Article 249 remains in force for what period after the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses?
47.x: A law under Article 249 ceases six months after the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses (each resolution lasts one year and can be renewed).
47.tq: Separate the one-year resolution from the six-month grace period.
n: A law enacted under Article 249 remains in force for one year. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
A law enacted under Article 249 ceases six months after the related Rajya Sabha resolution lapses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: A law made under **Article 249** ceases **six months** after the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses — option **(4)**.
The resolution needs **two-thirds of members present and voting** and is in force **not exceeding 1 year**.
xa: The resolution is **renewable** any number of times, **1 year at a time**.
The State's power to legislate on the same matter is **not suspended**.
**Art. 251:** on conflict with a law under **249/250**, the **Union** law prevails.

47.s: A law made by Parliament on a State List subject under Article 250 ceases to have effect ____ after the National Emergency ends.
47.x: Laws made under Article 250 lapse six months after the Emergency ends.
n: Article 250 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects during the operation of a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 250 legislation ceases six months after the National Emergency ends. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: The law can extend to the **whole or any part of India**.
During an Emergency, State List laws are made by **Parliament**, not any minister (APPSC-GS 2023).
**Art. 251:** the State law is inoperative only while the Union law lasts.

47.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Article 249 – Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest
Article 356 – Proclamation of President's Rule in a State
Article 252 – Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest
47.x: Article 252 is triggered by a request of two or more State Legislatures; the Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest is Article 249.
n: Article 249 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects through a Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 250 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects during the operation of a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 252 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects following requests by at least two State Legislatures through resolutions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 356 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects following a proclamation of President’s Rule in a State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: The fifth gateway: **Art. 253** — implementing **international agreements**; **no state consent** needed.
⚠ **252** = consent of **two or more states**; **253** = **no state consent**.
Acts under Art. 252: **Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972**, **Water Act 1974**, **Urban Land Ceiling Act 1976**.

47.s: Under Article 249, a Rajya Sabha resolution authorising Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest must be passed by:
o: The unanimous vote of all Rajya Sabha members
A majority of members present and voting
At least two-thirds of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha
At least two-thirds of members present and voting
47.x: Under Article 249 the Rajya Sabha resolution needs two-thirds of the members present and voting — not two-thirds of total membership.
n: Article 249 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects through a Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
An Article 249 resolution requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting in the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: The **Article 249** resolution needs **two-thirds of members present and voting** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is **not** two-thirds of total membership, a simple majority, or unanimity.
xa: The resolution is valid **up to 1 year**, renewable.
Laws made under it **cease 6 months** after the resolution lapses.
It allows Parliament to legislate on a **State List** subject in the **national interest**.

47.s: Regulations having the force of Acts of Parliament for Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep are made by the:
o: Chief Secretary of the Union Territory
47.x: Regulations made by the President for Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep have the force and effect of an Act of Parliament.
xa: The **Governor** can bar/modify Parliament's Acts for **Scheduled Areas**.
The **Governor of Assam** has a similar role for Assam tribal areas.

47.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 254(2)?
o: A repugnant State law on a Concurrent List subject prevails in that State if it receives the President's assent
The State law must be reserved for the consideration of the President
Parliament can later amend or repeal such a State law by a fresh law
Such a State law, once assented to, prevails throughout India
47.x: A State law assented to under Article 254(2) prevails only in that State, not throughout India.
xa: Repugnancy applies to the **Concurrent List** field.

47.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about preservation of livestock (cow slaughter)?
o: Parliament can legislate on it through Articles 249, 250 or 252
Preservation of livestock is a State List subject
Article 48 is relevant to constitutional policy on preservation of livestock
Parliament may legislate on it only through the ordinary Union List power
47.x: Being a State subject, Parliament can legislate on it through routes such as Articles 249, 250 or 252, not through the ordinary Union List power.
xa: **Prevention of cruelty to animals** is a separate **Concurrent** subject (**Entry 17**).
Parliament can reach State subjects only via **Arts. 249, 250, 252, 253, 356**.

47.s: Which of the following is INCORRECT about repugnancy on Concurrent List subjects?
o: Repugnancy is dealt with under Article 250.
In a conflict, the Central law generally prevails.
The Central-law rule has an exception relating to Presidential assent.
A reserved State law that gets Presidential assent may prevail under Article 254(2).
47.x: Repugnancy on Concurrent subjects is dealt with by Article 254, not Article 250 (Emergency legislation).
n: Article 254 governs repugnancy between Central and State legislation on a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Central legislation prevails when it conflicts with State legislation on a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

A State law can prevail over conflicting Central legislation when the State law was reserved for the President’s assent and received that assent under Article 254(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 250 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects during the operation of a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: **Proviso:** Parliament can later **override** such a State law with a **fresh law**.
**Article 250** = Parliament on the State List during an **Emergency**.

47.s: Article 248 is located in which Part of the Constitution?
47.x: Article 248 is located in Part XI, which deals with relations between the Union and the States and extends from Articles 245 to 263.
47.tq: Match the article with its constitutional Part, not merely with its subject.
xs: **Article 248** (residuary powers) lies in **Part XI** — option **(3)**.
Part XI covers **Relations between the Union and the States**, **Art. 245-263** (APPSC-GS 2023).
Its Chapter I (**Arts. 245-255**) deals with legislative relations.
xa: **245** = territorial extent; **246** = subject-matter (three lists); **247** = additional courts.
**248** + **Entry 97 of the Union List** = Parliament's exclusive residuary power, including **taxation**.
**249 / 250** = State List — national interest / Emergency; **254** = repugnancy.

47.s: Which case upheld a State prohibition law under the doctrine of pith and substance?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce
State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa
47.x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the prohibition law was upheld under pith and substance; its incidental encroachment did not change its true character.
xa: ⚠ **Balsara (1951)** = pith and substance; **Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953)** = colourable legislation.
**Harmonious construction**: entries read together so both operate.
**Repugnancy (Art. 254)**: Union law prevails in the **Concurrent** field.

47.s: Which doctrine requires legislative entries to be read together so that each can operate harmoniously?
47.x: Harmonious construction requires apparently overlapping entries to be interpreted together so that both retain operative effect.
47.tq: Discriminate among neighbouring doctrines by their operative principle.
xs: **Harmonious construction** reads entries together so that **both operate** — option **(2)**.
**Pith and substance** looks at a law's **true nature**; **repugnancy** (**Art. 254**) makes Union law prevail; **colourable legislation** bars doing indirectly what cannot be done directly.
xa: Pith and substance case: **State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara (1951)**.
Colourable legislation case: **K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v State of Orissa (1953)**.
Under **254(2)**, a State law with **President's assent** prevails in that State.

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Articles 256 to 263 deal with administrative relations.
2. Article 263 deals with the Inter-State Council.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
47.x: Articles 256-263 cover administrative relations, ending with Article 263 on the Inter-State Council.
n: Articles 256 to 263 concern administrative relations. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 263 concerns the Inter-State Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Articles 245 to 255** = **Legislative relations**; both sets sit in **Part XI**.
**Articles 268 to 281** = **Distribution of revenues**; **Article 280** = **Finance Commission**.
**Articles 301 to 307** = **Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse**.

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Articles 268 to 281 deal with the distribution of revenues.
2. Article 281 deals with the recommendations of the Finance Commission.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
47.x: Articles 268-281 deal with distribution of revenues, ending with Article 281 on the Finance Commission's recommendations (the Commission itself is Article 280).
n: Articles 268 to 281 concern the distribution of revenues. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 281 concerns the recommendations of the Finance Commission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Articles 256 to 263** = **Administrative relations**; **Article 263** = **Inter-State Council**.
**Article 253** = laws to implement **international agreements**.
**Article 248** = **Residuary powers** in Parliament.

47.s: What is the effect of the Doctrine of Severability?
o: The whole statute is declared void
Only the unconstitutional part is declared void, if separable
A law is tested only by its title
Parliament must re-enact the entire law
47.x: Under severability, only the unconstitutional part of a law is struck down if it can be separated; the rest survives.
n: Only the offending or unconstitutional portion of a statute is declared void under the Doctrine of Severability. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The valid portion of a statute remains intact under the Doctrine of Severability if it can be separated from the offending portion. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xa: Cases: **A.K. Gopalan (1950)** and **State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)**.
⚠ **Eclipse** concerns **pre-constitutional** laws, which stay **dormant**, not permanently void.
Most doctrines are **judicially evolved**, not written in the Constitution.

47.s: A pre-Constitution law that conflicts with a Fundamental Right stays dormant and revives if that right is amended. This is the Doctrine of:
47.x: Under the doctrine of eclipse such a law is not dead ab initio but only overshadowed, and it revives when the right is amended.
n: Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are not dead ab initio under the Doctrine of Eclipse. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights remain overshadowed or dormant under the Doctrine of Eclipse. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
A pre-constitutional law eclipsed by Fundamental Rights becomes active if the relevant Fundamental Right is amended. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xa: **Severability:** only the **offending portion** is void.
**Basic Structure:** **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, **Article 368**.

47.s:
Assertion (A): The Doctrine of Pith and Substance helps resolve overlaps between legislative fields.
Reason (R): It examines the true nature and essence of a law rather than its incidental encroachment on another List.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
47.x: Both are true: the doctrine of pith and substance settles overlaps between the Lists by looking at a law's true nature, ignoring incidental effects on another List. R explains A.
n: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance resolves overlaps between legislative fields. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The Doctrine of Pith and Substance examines the true nature and essence of a law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Incidental encroachment by a law on another legislative List does not determine its validity under the Doctrine of Pith and Substance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Pith and Substance** resolves **overlaps** between legislative fields by the law's **true nature and essence**; **incidental encroachment** does not decide validity.
xa: Basis: **Article 246** and the **Seventh Schedule**.
