63.s: From 1 July 2024, electoral offences such as bribery, undue influence and personation are contained in:
63.x: From 1 July 2024 these offences are in Chapter IX of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Sections 169–177); earlier they were in IPC Chapter IXA.
xa: **Corrupt practice** is a **Section 100** ground for voiding an election.
**Art. 329(b)** is the constitutional base of the election-petition bar.

63.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: NOTA first used in a Lok Sabha general election – 2013
63.x: VVPAT was first used at Noksen in 2013; EVMs were first used at Parur in 1982 and NOTA in a Lok Sabha general election in 2014.
xa: NOTA was introduced in **2013** (PUCL).
An **SC hearing** on EVM totalisers was held on **2 Sep 2026**.

63.s: A candidate can win a State Assembly election without obtaining more than 50 per cent of the votes because Assembly elections follow the:
o: Proportional representation by single transferable vote
63.x: Under first-past-the-post, the candidate with the most valid votes wins even without 50 per cent.
n: The Legislative Assembly election uses the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
A candidate does not need an absolute majority of more than 50 percent to win under the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The candidate securing the highest number of valid votes wins under the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xa: FPTP is used for the **Lok Sabha** and **Assemblies**.
**PR-STV** is used for **Rajya Sabha**, **Legislative Councils**, **President** and **Vice-President**.
PR was rejected for the Lok Sabha due to **fragmentation and unstable** governments.

63.s: The right to register a secret negative vote (NOTA) was linked by the Supreme Court to Article:
63.x: The Court linked a secret negative vote to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).
n: The Supreme Court linked the right to register a negative vote in secrecy with the Freedom of Speech and Expression. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
The right to register a negative vote in secrecy is linked with Article 19(1)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
xa: The judgment directed the **mandatory introduction** of the **NOTA button** on EVMs.
NOTA symbol designed by **NID, Ahmedabad**.
NOTA first used in the Lok Sabha in **2014** → **1.1%** of votes.

63.s: Which of the following statements regarding NOTA is incorrect?
o: A fresh poll is not automatically held merely because NOTA receives the maximum votes.
The contesting candidate with the highest valid votes is declared elected even when NOTA has the maximum votes.
NOTA is a symbolic expression only.
NOTA automatically invalidates the election whenever it receives more votes than every candidate.
63.x: Option D is incorrect: NOTA is only symbolic. Even if it tops the count, the candidate with the most votes wins and no fresh poll is held.
63.tq: Remember that NOTA is a symbolic rejection.
n: NOTA is a symbolic expression only. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
Under NOTA, the candidate with the highest valid votes among the contestants is declared elected. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
The claim that an election is cancelled and a fresh poll is held if NOTA receives the majority or highest votes is false. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
Under the First-Past-the-Post system, the election is not cancelled merely because NOTA receives the maximum votes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
Under the First-Past-the-Post system, the contesting candidate securing the highest number of valid votes among the candidates is declared elected. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **NOTA automatically invalidates** the election when it tops the count — option **(4)**.
NOTA is a **symbolic expression only**; the candidate with the **highest valid votes** is **declared elected** and no fresh poll is held.
xa: Under **First-Past-the-Post** the election is **not cancelled** merely because NOTA gets the **maximum votes**.
NOTA is **not abstention** — it is active use of the **statutory right to vote**.
NOTA was struck down for Rajya Sabha and Council polls in **2018**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about NOTA:
1. Exercising NOTA is active participation in the electoral process.
2. NOTA is equivalent to abstention.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
63.x: Using NOTA is voting, by registering a negative choice; it is not the same as abstaining.
n: Exercising NOTA is not non-voting or abstaining. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
Exercising NOTA is the active exercise of the statutory right to vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
Exercising NOTA registers a neutral or negative choice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
A NOTA voter attends the polling booth. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
xa: ⚠ The old **Rule 49-O** was the abstention procedure, recorded in **Form 17-A**.

63.s: An Electronic Voting Machine is best described as:
o: A judicial mechanism for resolving election disputes
An electoral system based on proportional representation
An electronic vote recording and counting apparatus

n: An EVM is an electronic vote-recording apparatus. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
An EVM is an electronic vote-counting apparatus. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
An EVM is not an electoral system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
xs: An **EVM** is an **electronic vote-recording and vote-counting apparatus** — option **(4)**.

xa: EVMs are used for **Lok Sabha** and **State Assembly** elections.
Deployed under the **superintendence, direction and control** of the **ECI**.

63.s:

63.s: Which of the following is NOT a category of observer appointed by the Election Commission under Section 20B?

63.s: Recognition of political parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 is distinct from registration under which provision?

Paragraph 16A of the Election Symbols Order, 1968

63.s: The six-month requirement for holding a by-election does NOT apply when:
o: The vacancy arises in a reserved constituency
The vacancy arises from the resignation of the member
The vacancy arises during a session of the House

63.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Voter Helpline app — Search name in electoral roll
ECINET — Exclusive platform for election petitions
63.x: ECINET is a unified platform merging more than 40 Election Commission applications and websites; it is not an exclusive platform for election petitions.

63.x: Delimitation means the process of fixing the number of seats and boundaries of territorial constituencies in each State/UT for the Lok Sabha and Legislative assemblies. It also includes determining the seats to be reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) in these Houses. The 'delimitation process' in India is performed by the 'Delimitation Commission' that is set up under an Act of Parliament. In India, such Delimitation Commissions have been constituted 4 timesin 1952 under the Delimitation Commission Act, 1952, in 1963 under the Delimitation Commission Act, 1962, in 1973 under the Delimitation Act, 1972 and in 2002 under the Delimitation Act, 2002. The delimitation of four north-eastern States by the Delimitation Commission of 2002 (Chairman-Justice Kuldip Singh) was deferred due to security risks, by four separate presidential orders, all issued on 8 February 2008, for Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Manipur. The orders regarding these States were rescinded on 28 February 2020. Subsequently, the Government of India has again constituted the Delimitation Commission under the Section 3 of the Delimitation Act, 2002 for these four States as well as the UT of Jammu and Kashmir on 6 March 2020, under the chairpersonship of Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai. In March 2021, the four north-eastern States were removed from the purview of the reconstituted Commission. The Indrajit Gupta Committee concerned state funding of elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
Federal dialogue and coordination mechanisms were the exam focus for the Punchhi Commission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
The Rajamannar Committee represented a state-level initiative for federal autonomy. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
Punchhi Commission is categorized under federalism, Centre–State Relations, and coordination and dialogue mechanisms. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
The Indrajit Gupta Committee is a classic elimination option under Centre–State questions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
The recommendation for a permanent Inter-State Council or Inter-Governmental Council belongs to the Sarkaria Commission, not the Punchhi Commission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
xa: ⚠ The permanent ISC recommendation is **Sarkaria's**, **not** Punchhi's.
Years: Rajamannar **1969-71**; Sarkaria **1983-88** (**247** recommendations); Punchhi **2007-10**; Indrajit Gupta **1998**.
"Which is NOT on Centre-State relations?" → **Indrajit Gupta Committee** (APPSC-G2 2025).

64.s: A candidate forfeits the security deposit when the candidate fails to secure more than which proportion of the total valid votes polled?
64.x: A candidate loses the security deposit if they win no more than one-sixth of the valid votes.
64.tq: Recall the one-sixth rule.
n: A candidate forfeits the security deposit if the candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the total valid votes polled. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
xs: The deposit is forfeited if the candidate fails to get more than **one-sixth** of the **total valid votes** — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 34** deposits: **₹25,000** (Lok Sabha), **₹10,000** (Assembly), half for SC/ST.
xa: The **1996** RP (Amendment) Act brought **higher security deposits**.
It also required more proposers for independents/unrecognised parties.
Election petition: within **45 days** (**Sec. 81**).

64.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the death of a contesting candidate?
o: The election is automatically cancelled in every case of the death of a candidate.
The death of a candidate no longer automatically countermands the election.
The change was made through the 1996 Amendment.
Recognized political parties may nominate a replacement within a set timeframe.
64.x: Option A is incorrect: since the 1996 amendment, a candidate's death no longer cancels the election automatically. A recognised party can name a replacement within a set time.
64.tq: Recall the 1996 change on a candidate's death.
n: The Representation of the People Act, 1951 was amended in 1996 to cap the number of constituencies a candidate could contest at two. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
Before the 1996 amendment, elections were automatically countermanded upon the death of a contesting candidate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
After the 1996 amendment, elections are no longer automatically countermanded upon the death of a contesting candidate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
Recognized political parties may nominate a replacement for a deceased contesting candidate within a set timeframe. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the election is **automatically cancelled** on every candidate's death — option **(1)**.
After the **1996 amendment**, death **no longer** automatically countermands the election.
A **recognised political party** may **nominate a replacement** within a set timeframe.
xa: **Countermanding** now happens only on the death of a **recognised-party** candidate.
The **1996** Act also made poll day a **paid holiday** (**Sec. 135B**) and banned liquor **48 hours** before poll (**Sec. 135C**).
Bypolls within **6 months** (**Sec. 151A**).

64.s:
Which of the following were recommended by the Dinesh Goswami Committee?
1. State funding of elections
2. Use of Electronic Voting Machines
3. Allocation of State Legislative Council seats
Select the correct answer:
64.x: The Goswami Committee recommended State funding of elections and EVMs, leading to the 1996 RPA amendment; Council seat allocation was not its subject.
n: The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended state funding of elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended the use of electronic voting machines. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended measures subsequently enacted in the 1996 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1951. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xa: Goswami was the **broadest review**: time limits for bye-elections, strengthening the EC, anti-defection; flagged **musclemen**.
**Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998)** = **State funding of elections**, partial funding **in kind**.
⚠ **Vohra (1993)** = **crime–politics nexus**.

64.s: Which of the following pairs relating to the RPA, 1951 is correctly matched?
64.x: Section 33A concerns disclosure of criminal antecedents; Section 8 is disqualification on conviction, 29A registration of parties and 123 corrupt practices.
xa: **Sec. 34** = security deposit; **Sec. 81** = petition within **45 days**.

64.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the corrupt practices covered by Section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951?
o: Failure to file an election expenditure account within 30 days
Appeal on the grounds of religion or caste
64.x: Section 123 covers corrupt practices such as bribery, undue influence and appeals based on religion or caste. Filing the expenditure account within 30 days is governed by Section 78.
64.tq: Find the provision belonging to a neighbouring compliance area rather than the corrupt-practices list.
xs: **Failure to file an expense account within 30 days** is not a Sec. 123 corrupt practice — option **(1)**; it falls under **Sec. 78**.
**Sec. 123** covers **bribery, undue influence, appeal on religion/caste**.
xa: Failure to file accounts can lead the **ECI** to **disqualify** the candidate.
Bribery and undue influence are now offences in **BNS** too.

64.s: The reform principle 'one candidate, one seat' addresses:
o: Candidates contesting from more than one constituency
64.x: The Law Commission proposed 'one candidate, one seat' for candidates contesting from more than one constituency; the ECI proposed the vacating candidate bear by-election costs.
xa: Winner of both must vacate one within **14 days**.

64.s: Which one of the following was a major provision of the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996?
o: Removal of the limit on constituencies from which a candidate may contest
Reduction of security deposits and proposers for independent candidates
Abolition of by-elections within six months
Capping a candidate’s contest to two constituencies and increasing security deposits
64.x: The 1996 amendment capped contests at two constituencies, increased security deposits, and required more proposers for independents and unrecognised parties.
64.tq: Identify the option that combines the principal nomination-related changes without reversing them.
xs: The **RP (Amendment) Act, 1996** capped contests at **two constituencies** and raised **security deposits** — option **(4)**.
It increased (not reduced) deposits and proposers, and it kept bypolls within **6 months** (**Sec. 151A**).
xa: It limited **countermanding** to the death of a **recognised-party** candidate.
It added a **paid holiday** (**Sec. 135B**) and **liquor ban** (**Sec. 135C**).
Offences under the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** became a disqualification.

64.s: A person elected from two constituencies must vacate one of them within:
64.x: Under Section 70 one seat must be vacated within 14 days; the two-constituency cap in Section 33(7) came with the 1996 amendment.
xa: **30 days** is the deadline for filing expense accounts (**Sec. 78**).

64.s: Under Section 8 of the RPA 1951, conviction resulting in imprisonment of ____ or more attracts disqualification.
64.x: Section 8 disqualifies on conviction with two years' imprisonment or more; Lily Thomas removed protection during pendency of an appeal.
xa: Period: **term plus 6 years** after release.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about election expense accounts:
1. Section 77 of the RPA 1951 requires a candidate to keep an account of election expenses.
2. Section 78 requires the account to be filed with the Returning Officer within 30 days.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: Sec. 77 requires the candidate to keep expense accounts. Statement 2 is wrong: under Sec. 78 the account is filed with the District Election Officer, not the Returning Officer, within 30 days. So A; B and C accept the wrong statement 2, D rejects the correct statement 1.
64.tq: 77 = keep accounts, 78 = file with DEO in 30 days.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
**Sec. 77** requires keeping **expense accounts**.
Statement 2 is wrong: under **Sec. 78** the account goes to the **District Election Officer** within **30 days**, not the Returning Officer.
xa: Failure → the **ECI** can **disqualify** the candidate.
Limits rest on **Rule 90** of the **1961** Rules.

64.s: Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, is criticised in the context of party expenditure because it:
o: Prohibits all expenditure on election campaigns
Places a ceiling only on the expenditure of candidates, not on the election expenditure incurred directly by political parties
Places a ceiling only on political parties, not on candidates
Requires all campaign expenditure to be incurred in cash
64.x: The perceived loophole is that Section 77 caps candidate expenditure while not imposing a comparable ceiling on the parties’ own election spending.
64.tq: Ask who bears the statutory ceiling to expose the candidate-party distinction.
xs: **Sec. 77** caps only **candidate** spending, not **parties'** own election spending — option **(2)**.
It does not ban campaign spending or require cash; it does not cap parties.
xa: Travel of **20 star campaigners** is excluded from the candidate's limit.
Unfinished agenda: a **party spending cap**.

64.s: A candidate contesting an election to the Lok Sabha or a State Assembly can contest from a maximum of how many constituencies under Section 33 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951?
64.x: Under Section 33(7) of the RPA, 1951, a candidate can contest from at most two constituencies, a limit added in 1996.
64.tq: Recall the two-constituency limit.
n: Section 33 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, limits a candidate to contesting from a maximum of two constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
A candidate can contest from a maximum of two Lok Sabha constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
A candidate can contest from a maximum of two State Assembly constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
xs: A candidate can contest from at most **two** constituencies — option **(4)** — under **Section 33(7), RPA 1951**.
The cap was added by the **1996** amendment after **Devi Lal** contested **three Lok Sabha seats** in **1991**.
xa: A winner of both seats must vacate one within **14 days** (**Sec. 70**).
Reform proposal: **one candidate, one seat** (**Law Commission 255th report**).
ECI proposal: the vacating candidate pays for the bypoll.

64.s:
Assertion (A): The ceiling on the number of constituencies from which a candidate may contest was introduced through an amendment to the RPA, 1951 in 1996.
Reason (R): The amendment followed the 1991 election in which Devi Lal contested from three Lok Sabha seats.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
64.x: Both are true: the 1996 amendment capped contests at two constituencies after Devi Lal stood from three Lok Sabha seats in 1991. R explains A.
64.tq: Recall the Devi Lal case behind the 1996 cap.
n: Devi Lal contested from three Lok Sabha seats in the 1991 elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Representation of the People Act, 1951 was amended in 1996 to cap the number of constituencies a candidate could contest at two. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
The **1996** amendment capped contests at **two** constituencies because **Devi Lal** had contested **three Lok Sabha seats** in **1991**.
xa: Before **1996** there was **no cap** (UPSC 2021 key).
Provision: **Section 33(7), RPA 1951**.
Winner of both must vacate one within **14 days** (**Sec. 70**).

64.s: The judgment in Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) is associated with which of the following conclusions?
o: Disqualification of legislators was transferred from Parliament to the Election Commission.
Only a sitting legislator can be disqualified after a three-month period.
A convicted legislator remains protected until the disposal of the appeal.
A convicted legislator is disqualified immediately, without protection during the pendency of an appeal.
64.x: The Lily Thomas judgment held that conviction leads to immediate disqualification and that an appeal does not provide protection against that disqualification.
64.tq: Test the holding of a landmark judgment against closely related but reversed legal effects.
xs: **Lily Thomas (July 2013)**: a convicted legislator is **disqualified immediately**, with **no protection while appeal pending** — option **(4)**.
It struck down **Sec. 8(4)**, the **3-month appeal buffer** for sitting members.
xa: Disqualification follows conviction with **2+ years** (**Sec. 8**).
**Ramesh Dalal (2005)**: sitting MP/MLA convicted with 2+ years barred from contesting.

64.s: Mandatory disclosure by candidates of criminal cases, assets, liabilities and education was laid down in:
o: Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India
Lily Thomas v. Union of India
Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India
64.x: ADR (2002) made such disclosure mandatory; PUCL placed the voter's right to know in Article 19(1)(a).
xa: **PUCL (2013)** ordered the **NOTA** option.

64.s: In ADR v Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme mainly because it violated:
o: The right to equality under Article 14
The voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a)
The right to life under Article 21
The freedom of association under Article 19(1)(c)
64.x: The five-judge bench unanimously held that donor anonymity violated voters' right to information, part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). Articles 14, 21 and 19(1)(c) were not the ground stated for striking the scheme down.
64.tq: Bonds struck down = Art 19(1)(a) right to information (15 Feb 2024).
xs: The scheme violated voters' **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)** — option **(2)**.
Articles **14**, **21** and **19(1)(c)** were not the stated ground.
xa: **PUCL (2003)**: voter's **right to know** is part of Art. 19(1)(a).
**PUCL (2013)**: right to reject (NOTA) also flows from Art. 19(1)(a).

64.s: ECIL, one of the two public sector undertakings that manufacture EVMs, is headquartered in:
64.x: BEL is based in Bengaluru and ECIL in Hyderabad.
xa: BEL and ECIL also make **VVPATs**.
AP angle: **ECIL** is the EVM maker based in **Hyderabad**.

64.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Supreme Court's position on EVMs is NOT correct?
o: In ADR v ECI (2024), the Court refused to order a return to paper ballots.
The Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld the use of EVMs.
In ADR v ECI (2024), the Court ordered a return to paper ballots.
The Court has considered safeguards relating to VVPAT verification.
64.x: The Supreme Court refused to order a return to paper ballots in ADR v ECI (2024). The other statements correctly reflect the Court's approach to EVMs and verification safeguards.
64.tq: Identify the reversed judicial conclusion in the NOT question.
xs: The NOT-correct statement: "ADR v ECI **ordered a return to paper ballots**" — option **(3)**.
In fact **ADR v ECI (2024)** **refused** a return to paper ballots; the SC has **repeatedly upheld EVMs**.
xa: It also rejected **100% slip counting**.
ECI admitted EVMs "are still a subject of frequent public questioning" (**2 Sep 2026**).

64.s: Under ADR v. ECI (2024), symbol-loading units are to be sealed and preserved for:
64.x: The Court rejected ballot papers and 100% VVPAT counting, but ordered SLUs preserved for 45 days and allowed runners-up to seek checking of 5% of EVMs.
xa: The check is of the EVMs' **burnt memory**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu (2019)** raised the VVPAT tally to **5** polling stations per segment.

64.s: Which case held that VVPAT is necessary for free and fair elections and directed its introduction in phases?
o: State of Karnataka v Prathik Parasrampuria
64.x: In Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013), the Supreme Court held that VVPAT was needed for free and fair polls and required phased introduction.
64.tq: Match the judicial case with its distinctive electoral reform.
xs: **Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013)** held VVPAT needed for free and fair polls, to be brought **in phases** — option **(1)**.
**ADR v ECI** = 2024 EVM/VVPAT safeguards; **PUCL** = NOTA; **Prathik Parasrampuria** = black money.
xa: VVPAT debuted at **Noksen**, **2013**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu (2019)**: tally from **1 to 5** polling stations per segment.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about NOTA:
1. In PUCL v Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court traced the right to reject to Article 19(1)(a).
2. NOTA was first used in a Lok Sabha election in 2013.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: PUCL (2013) linked the right to reject to Article 19(1)(a). Statement 2 is wrong: NOTA was first used in the 2013 Assembly elections; its first Lok Sabha use was in 2014. So A; B and C accept the wrong statement 2, D rejects the correct statement 1.
64.tq: NOTA: 2013 Assembly polls first, 2014 first Lok Sabha.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
**PUCL (2013)** traced the right to reject to **Art. 19(1)(a)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: NOTA's first Lok Sabha use was **2014**; **2013** was the Assembly elections.
xa: In **2014** NOTA got **1.1%** (over **60 lakh** votes).
NOTA button added on **27 Sept 2013**.

64.s: Which of the following correctly describes the phased rollout recommended by the Ram Nath Kovind High-Level Committee?
o: Local-body elections first, followed by Lok Sabha elections after five years
All elections to be held on the same day without any transitional phase
Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council elections together first, followed by Assembly elections
Lok Sabha and Assembly elections together first, followed by local-body elections within 100 days
64.x: The committee recommended holding Lok Sabha and Assembly polls together initially, followed by local-body elections within 100 days.
64.tq: Track the sequence and the specific 100-day interval in the proposed phased model.
xs: The **Kovind Committee** recommended a **phased rollout**: **Lok Sabha and Assembly** polls together first, then **local-body elections within 100 days** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It did not propose a same-day poll without transition, nor local bodies first.
xa: Committee chair: ex-President **Ram Nath Kovind** (**2023-24**); members included **Amit Shah** and **Ghulam Nabi Azad**.
The **129th Amendment Bill, 2024** inserts **Art. 82A** and amends **Arts. 83, 172 and 327**.
Lok Sabha + Assembly polls were held together **1951-52 to 1967**.
JPC still examining the Bill (**Feb 2026**).

64.s: Under Section 34 of the RPA 1951, the security deposit for a general-category Lok Sabha candidate is:
64.x: It is ₹25,000 for the Lok Sabha and ₹10,000 for an Assembly; SC/ST candidates pay half.
xa: Deposit is forfeited below **one-sixth** of valid votes.
The **1996** amendment raised security deposits.

64.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about judgments on criminalisation of politics?
o: In Public Interest Foundation (2018), the Court itself imposed disqualification on framing of charges
Public Interest Foundation (2018) ordered publicity of candidates' criminal records
Public Interest Foundation (2018) left disqualification on framing of charges to Parliament
Lily Thomas removed protection from disqualification during pendency of an appeal
64.x: The Court did not itself impose disqualification on framing of charges; it left the issue to Parliament.
xa: ECI (**Sep 2025**) also requires **reasons for selecting** such candidates.
Law Commission **244th Report (2014)** urged barring candidates once charges are framed.

64.s: Under the ECI's requirement, political parties fielding candidates with criminal records must publish the details of those records and:
o: An undertaking to resign if convicted
The reasons for selecting such candidates
64.x: Parties must publish the criminal-record details and the reasons for selecting such candidates; withdrawal is not required.
xa: Affidavits on criminal cases, assets, liabilities, education date from **2002**.
ADR data: **31%** of MPs and **29%** of MLAs face serious charges.

64.s: Barring candidates upon framing of charges in serious offences was recommended by which Law Commission report?
64.x: The recommendation was made in the Law Commission's 244th Report of 2014.
xa: ⚠ LENS cites it as "Law Commission, **2015**".
**Public Interest Foundation (2018)** left this question to **Parliament**.

64.s:
On criminalisation of politics, consider the following statements:
1. A PIL seeking a lifetime ban on convicted legislators is pending.
2. 12 special courts have been set up for cases involving MPs and MLAs.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
64.x: A PIL seeking a lifetime ban on convicted legislators is pending, and 12 special courts have been established for cases involving MPs and MLAs.
xa: ADR: **31%** MPs, **29%** MLAs with serious charges.
Unfinished agenda: disqualification on **framing of charges**.

64.s: The current election expenditure limit for a Lok Sabha candidate in a larger State is:
64.x: The limit is ₹95 lakh (earlier ₹70 lakh), raised by the Conduct of Elections (Amendment) Rules, 2022; ₹40 lakh is the Assembly limit.
xa: Smaller States: **Rs 75 lakh** (LS), **Rs 28 lakh** (Assembly).
Earlier: Rs **70** lakh (LS) and Rs **28** lakh (Assembly) for larger States.

64.s: For a political party to retain tax exemption under the stated provisions, which combination is relevant?
o: No donation above ₹2,000 in any form and no record of larger donations
No cash donation above ₹20,000 and records only of donations above ₹2,000
No cash donation above ₹2,000 and proper records of donations above ₹20,000
Acceptance of unlimited cash donations provided they are reported after the election
64.x: The stated conditions include no cash donation above ₹2,000 and maintenance of records for donations above ₹20,000. These are referred to under Section 12 of the Income Tax Act, 2025, replacing the earlier reference to Section 13A of the 1961 Act.
64.tq: Keep the two monetary thresholds separate instead of reversing their functions.
xs: **No cash donation above Rs 2,000** and **records of donations above Rs 20,000** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) swaps the two thresholds.
xa: ⚠ **Rs 2,000** = cash cap; **Rs 20,000** = record threshold.
Now under **Sec. 12, Income Tax Act 2025**; earlier **Sec. 13A**, IT Act **1961**.

64.s: The Supreme Court's decision in Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India also invalidated which change associated with electoral political funding?
o: Abolition of political party registration under the RPA
Removal of the corporate donation cap under the Companies Act
Compulsory disclosure of all cash donations by parties
Restriction on donations by individual citizens
64.x: The Court struck down the removal of the corporate donation cap from the Companies Act.
64.tq: Identify the allied legal provision affected by the judgment, not merely the main scheme.
xs: It also struck down the **removal of the corporate donation cap** from the **Companies Act** — option **(2)**.
The notes record no ruling on party registration, cash disclosure or individual donations.
xa: Ground: violation of voters' **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)**.
ADR: **60% (₹19,083 cr)** of party funds in **2004-23** came from undisclosed sources.

64.s: The decision in N. Chandrababu Naidu v Union of India (2019) changed the random VVPAT-EVM tally from:
o: Two to five polling stations per district
One to five polling stations per Assembly segment
One to ten polling stations per parliamentary constituency
Five to ten polling stations per Assembly segment
64.x: The 2019 decision raised the random VVPAT-EVM tally from one to five polling stations per Assembly segment.
64.tq: Remember both sides of the judicially ordered numerical increase.
xs: **N. Chandrababu Naidu v UoI (2019)** raised the random VVPAT–EVM tally from **one to five polling stations** per **Assembly segment** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The tally unit is the **Assembly segment**, not a district or parliamentary constituency.
xa: **ADR v ECI (Apr 2024)** rejected **100% slip counting** and a **return to paper ballots**.
In that case, symbol-loading units are sealed for **45 days**; runners-up can seek a check of **5% of EVMs**.
**Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013)**: VVPAT is needed for free and fair polls; introduce it **in phases**.

64.s: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended:
o: Full state funding and a lifetime ban on convicted legislators
Simultaneous elections and a constructive no-confidence motion
Partial state funding and barring persons charged with serious offences
64.x: The Second ARC recommended partial state funding and barring persons charged with serious offences.
xa: Its report was titled "**Ethics in Governance**" (chair **Veerappa Moily**).
**Indrajit Gupta (1998)** and **Goswami (1990)** also backed public funding.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about electoral bonds:
1. They were sold only by the State Bank of India.
2. They were issued in denominations from ₹1,000 to ₹10 crore.
3. They were bearer bonds valid for 15 days.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: SBI was the only seller. Statement 2 is wrong: the range was ₹1,000 to ₹1 crore. Statement 3 is correct: they were bearer bonds valid for 15 days. So C; A, B and D all include the wrong statement 2.
64.tq: Bonds: SBI only, ₹1,000-₹1 crore, 15 days, encashable by parties with 1% votes.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Electoral bonds were sold **only by SBI**, as **bearer bonds** valid **15 days**.
Statement 2 is wrong: denominations ran from **₹1,000 to ₹1 crore**, not ₹10 crore.
xa: The scheme was notified in **2018** (via Finance Act **2017** amendments).
Only parties with at least **1%** of the vote in the last election could encash them.
Struck down in **ADR v UoI** on **15 Feb 2024**.

64.s: A political party could encash electoral bonds only if it had secured at least what percentage of votes in the last election?
64.x: Only a registered political party that had secured at least 1% of the votes in the last election could encash electoral bonds.
64.tq: Recall the statutory eligibility threshold rather than the general registration requirement.
xs: A party could encash electoral bonds only with at least **1 per cent** (**1% of the vote**) in the last election — so option **(2)** is correct.
Only **registered parties** meeting this **1%** threshold could encash; the bonds were sold only by **SBI** as **bearer bonds**.
xa: Denominations: **₹1,000 to ₹1 crore**; each bond was valid for **15 days**.
The scheme was notified in **2018** via **Finance Act 2017** amendments.
Struck down as **unconstitutional** by a unanimous **five-judge Constitution Bench** in **ADR v UoI** (**15 Feb 2024**) — it violated the **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)**.
⚠ Donor anonymity was hailed in older notes as a "**transparency**" gain.

64.s: In the 2024 electoral bond judgment, the Supreme Court directed ____ to provide donor data to the Election Commission.
64.x: A five-judge Constitution Bench unanimously struck down the scheme and directed SBI to provide donor data to the ECI.
xa: Case: **ADR v Union of India, 15 Feb 2024**.
⚠ **ADR v UoI** 2002 = disclosure; **ADR v ECI** 2024 = EVM/VVPAT.

64.s: A State funding model in which the State bears all legitimate costs and private donations are banned is:
64.x: Bearing all legitimate costs while banning private donations describes full funding; funding may be full or partial, in cash or in kind.
xa: Countries with public funding: **Germany, Sweden, Japan** (+ **Canada**).
Against: **heavy fiscal burden**; does not stop **off-book cash**.

64.s: VVPAT slips must be counted in which of the following circumstances?
o: Whenever EVM data and Form 17C do not match
Whenever postal ballots exceed the number of EVM votes
Only in constituencies using postal ballots
Only when the winning candidate requests it after the declaration of results
64.x: VVPAT slips are required to be counted wherever the EVM data and Form 17C do not match.
64.tq: Apply the verification rule to a specific discrepancy rather than to a general recount demand.
xs: **VVPAT slips must be counted wherever EVM data do not match Form 17C** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is one of the **new ECI rules** on counting; postal ballots relate to a different rule (below).
xa: The **penultimate EVM/VVPAT round** is counted only after **postal ballots** are finished.
**ADR v ECI (April 2024)**: candidates placed **2nd and 3rd** can seek a check of **5% of EVMs' burnt memory** within **7 days**.
ECI objects that **totalisers** would make **EVM, VVPAT and Form 17C** checks harder.

64.s: A proposed safeguard for maintaining governmental accountability under simultaneous elections is based on which model?
o: The Westminster model of an unelected executive
The American model of judicial review
The German model of a constructive vote of no-confidence

66.s: Which one of the following statements regarding political parties and the Constitution of India, as originally adopted, is correct?

It neither recognised only national parties nor prescribed a two-party or coalition system.
xa: Parties first entered the Constitution via the **anti-defection law** (**Tenth Schedule**, **52nd Amendment, 1985**).
India has a **multi-party system**, unlike the two-party **UK** and **USA**.
Parties are classed by ECI status as **national**, **state** and **registered-unrecognised**.

66.s:

xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
Coalitions bring **consensus building** but **slow decisions**, **policy reversals/delays**.
**Compromises dilute strong measures**.
xa: Checks and balances: **no single party holds absolute power**; **regional representation** in national policy.
**Federalism** became more **bargained** after **1989**.
Major consequence (APPSC key): **increased role of regional and small parties**.

66.s:
Assertion (A): The “Congress System” referred to a one-party dominant system in India.
Reason (R): It characterized a democratic, multi-party electoral landscape dominated by the Congress party after independence.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
66.x: Both are true: the 'Congress system' meant one party dominating a competitive, multi-party democracy. R gives that meaning, so R explains A.
66.tq: Recall Kothari's idea of the Congress system.
n: Rajni Kothari coined the term “Congress System.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
The Congress System characterized India’s democratic, multi-party electoral landscape after independence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
The Congress party dominated India’s democratic, multi-party electoral landscape after independence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
The "**Congress System**" meant a **one-party dominant** system: Congress **dominated** a **democratic, multi-party** electoral landscape after **independence**.
xa: Coined by **Rajni Kothari**.
It ended with the **1989** general election.
⚠ **Kothari** = "Congress system"; **Morris-Jones** = "one-party dominance"; **Weiner** = party building.

66.s: Which of the following pairs (Term/work – Scholar) is correctly matched?

xa: ⚠ Other notes credit "**one-party dominance**" to **W.H. Morris-Jones**, Kothari only with "Congress system".
**Myron Weiner** = Congress as a party-building organisation.

66.s: Which general election marked the end of the 'Congress System'?
66.x: The 1989 general election ended the Congress system and began the era of minority and coalition governments.
n: The 1989 General Election marked the end of the Congress System. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]

69.x: Sir Ross Barker was the first Chairman of the Public Service Commission set up on 1 October 1926 on the Lee Commission's advice. Satyendranath Tagore was the first Indian to clear the ICS (1864). Lord Lee headed the 1924 Commission that recommended the PSC but did not chair it. Sir Samuel Hoare was not its chairman.
69.tq: 1926 PSC: Lee recommended, Ross Barker chaired.
xs: **Sir Ross Barker** was the first chairman of the PSC set up on **1 Oct 1926** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Satyendranath Tagore** was the first Indian to clear the ICS (**1864**).
The **Lee Commission** (**1924**) only recommended the PSC.
xa: **GoI Act 1919** first provided for a PSC.
**GoI Act 1935**: **Federal PSC** + provincial PSCs.

69.s: The report of a Joint State Public Service Commission is laid before each concerned State Legislature by the:

69.s: Which one of the following functions is performed by the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission in addition to recruitment to State services?
o: Conducting examinations for the lower judicial service
Auditing the accounts of the State Government
Appointing judges of the High Court
69.x: The APPSC conducts recruitment examinations for State services and examinations for the lower judicial service under Article 234.
69.tq: Distinguish a recruitment function from constitutional appointments and auditing.
xs: APPSC also conducts **lower judicial service examinations** (**Art. 234**) — option **(1)**.
Audit, appointing High Court judges and local-body elections are not PSC functions.
xa: Main function: **State service recruitment**.
APPSC is an **SPSC** under **Art. 315**.
SPSC = "**watchdog of the merit system**".

69.s: The Lokpal Selection Committee is chaired by the:

The Governor of the State appoints the State Public Service Commission Chairperson. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 137-141]
The President of India appoints the Finance Commission Chairperson under Article 280. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 137-141]
The Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the Lokpal Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 137-141]
xa: ⚠ SPSC chairman: **Governor appoints, President removes**.

69.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 318 – Expenses of the Commissions charged on the Consolidated Fund
Article 319 – Bar on holding office after ceasing to be a member
Article 322 – Bar on holding office after ceasing to be a member
Article 319 – Regulations on conditions of service

xa: **Art. 316**: appointment and term; **Art. 317**: removal and suspension.
**Art. 320**: functions; **Art. 321**: extension of functions.
**Art. 323**: reports — UPSC to **President**, SPSC to **Governor**.

69.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 316 — Appointment and term of members
Article 317 — Functions of Public Service Commissions
Article 323 — Reports of Public Service Commissions
Article 315 — Public Service Commissions for the Union and States
69.x: Article 317 deals with removal and suspension of members. Functions of Public Service Commissions are dealt with in Article 320.

xs: **Article 317 — Functions** is wrongly matched — so option **(2)** is the answer.
**Art. 317** deals with **removal and suspension**; **functions** are in **Art. 320**.
The other pairs are right: **316** appointment and term, **323** reports, **315** PSCs for the Union and States.
xa: Art. 317 grounds: **insolvency**, **paid outside employment**, **infirmity**, **misbehaviour** (after **Supreme Court** reference).
**Art. 321**: extension of functions by an **Act**.
**Art. 322**: expenses charged on the **Consolidated Fund**.

69.s: Under Article 320, the Union Public Service Commission conducts examinations primarily for appointment to
o: only Group B and Group C posts

xs: UPSC conducts exams for **All-India, Central and Group-A services** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Group B/C posts** and the **highest diplomatic posts** are outside UPSC's purview; State services are for the **SPSC**.
xa: Consulted on **methods of recruitment**, **promotion and transfer**, **suitability of candidates**.
Consulted on **disciplinary matters** and temporary appointments of **more than one year**.
Functions are in **Art. 320**.

69.s: The strength of the UPSC and of a State PSC is determined, respectively, by the:
69.x: The Constitution does not fix the strength; the President decides it for the UPSC and the Governor for an SPSC.

69.s: The Chairman of a State Public Service Commission is appointed by ______ and can be removed by ______.
69.x: The Chairman of an SPSC is appointed by the Governor but can be removed only by the President, a favourite exam trap (APPSC 2019).
xs: SPSC Chairman: appointed by **the Governor**, removed by **the President** — option **(4)**.

69.s: A constitutional requirement relating to the background of members of a Public Service Commission is that

at least one-fourth of the members must have served in Parliament
at least half the members must have held government office for at least ten years
all members must have served in the judiciary for ten years

No rule requires all members to be Union officers, MPs or judges.
xa: Strength is **not fixed by the Constitution**; UPSC usually **9-11** members.
**Acting Chairman** is appointed by the **President**.
**No second term** in the same office.

69.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about removal of members of Public Service Commissions?

Insolvency is a ground for removal
Paid employment outside the duties of office is a ground for removal
Infirmity of mind or body is a ground for removal

69.s: Which of the following is included within the meaning of misbehaviour for the purpose of Article 317?
o: Failure to secure unanimous decisions in the Commission
Refusal to accept a temporary appointment
Disagreement with a recommendation of the Commission
Being interested in a government contract or sharing in its profit
69.x: Misbehaviour includes being interested in a government contract or sharing in its profit under Article 317(4).

xs: Misbehaviour includes **being interested in a government contract or sharing in its profit** — option **(4)**, under **Art. 317(4)**.
Misbehaviour is proved only after reference to the **Supreme Court**.
xa: Other grounds: **insolvency**, **paid outside employment**, **infirmity of mind or body**.
The SC's advice is **binding**.
The member may be **suspended** during the SC inquiry.

69.s: In the case of alleged misbehaviour by a member of a Public Service Commission, which procedure is constitutionally required?
o: The Governor conducts the inquiry and gives the final decision in every case
The Union Cabinet conducts the inquiry and recommends removal to the concerned Commission
The President refers the matter to the Supreme Court, and removal follows only if the Court upholds the charge
Parliament must pass an impeachment resolution by special majority
69.x: For misbehaviour, the President refers the matter to the Supreme Court. The member may be removed only when the Supreme Court upholds the cause, and its advice is binding.
69.tq: Follow the constitutional sequence: reference, judicial examination and binding outcome.
xs: The **President refers** the matter to the **Supreme Court**, and removal follows **only if the Court upholds** it — option **(3)**.
The SC's advice is **binding**; there is no **impeachment** or Cabinet/Governor inquiry.
xa: President (Governor for SPSC) may **suspend** the member during the inquiry.
Misbehaviour includes interest in a **government contract** (**Art. 317(4)**).
Even SPSC members are **removed by the President**, not the Governor.

69.s:

69.s:
Consider the following statements about the Finance Commission:

69.s:

Reason (R): A member of a State Public Service Commission holds office for six years or until the age of 62, whichever is earlier.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

69.s: Which one of the following is NOT permissible for a member of a State Public Service Commission after ceasing to hold office?
o: Becoming Chairman of the same or another State Public Service Commission
Accepting any other employment under the Government of India
Becoming a member of the UPSC
69.x: A former SPSC member may become UPSC Chairman or member, or Chairman of the same or another SPSC, but cannot accept any other government employment.

He may become **chairman/member of UPSC** or **chairman of that/another SPSC** (**Art. 319**).
xa: **UPSC Chairman**: no further employment under GOI or any State.
**UPSC member**: may become **UPSC Chairman** or **SPSC Chairman**, nothing else.

69.s: Which of the following is ordinarily subject to consultation with the UPSC?
o: Temporary appointments for more than one year
Temporary appointments for less than one year
Group B and Group C posts
Claims of SCs and STs to services and posts

**Recruitment**, **suitability** of candidates and **promotion and transfer** principles are core consultation matters.
xa: Excluded: **reservations**, temporary appointments of **less than a year**.

69.s: Under Article 321, the functions of the UPSC can be extended by:
o: An executive order of the President
A resolution of the Rajya Sabha
69.x: Functions are extended only by an Act of Parliament (State Legislature for an SPSC), which may cover local bodies, corporate bodies and public institutions.

**Art. 322**: expenses on the **Consolidated Fund**.

69.x: The President (Governor for an SPSC) may exclude posts by regulations, which are laid for 14 days, not 30.

PSCs are not concerned with **classification, pay or training**.

69.s: The State Public Service Commission is commonly described as the watchdog of the
69.x: The SPSC is described as the watchdog of the merit system in public services.

69.s: Which authority must approve every case in which the advice of the UPSC is not accepted?
o: The Appointments Committee of the Cabinet
The Union Public Service Commission itself

71.x: The Public Accounts Committee is one of the most important Committees of the Parliament. This committee is an important tool of Parliament to establish a financial check on the executive. This committee was set up first in 1921 under the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1919; and it has been in existence since then. At present, it consists of 22 members (15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha). Since 1967, the Chairman of the committee has been selected from the opposition. The function of the committee is to examine the annual audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) of India. The reports are laid before the Parliament by the President.

o: To examine the financial account of the government

71.x: The Public Accounts Committee is a Parliamentary committee that controls public expenditure. The function of this committee is to examine the report of accounts of the Union Government submitted by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and to lay this report before each House of the Parliament. Its aim is to highlight the misuse and misappropriation of public expenditure before each House of the Parliament. It also recommends action against those public authorities who are found responsible for the misuse of the expenses. It also counterchecks the public expenditure on the basis of the report of the Comptroller and Auditor-General. The member of opposition of the Lok Sabha is appointed as the Chairman of this Committee (since 1967-68). The report of the Public Accounts Committee is submitted to the Lok Sabha.

71.x: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) is appointed by the President under Article 148 of the Constitution. Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not a correct
71.x: The Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) is a constitutional functionary, independent of Parliament/ legislature and the executive. The CAG is responsible for- • Audit of Ministries and departments of the Government of India and the State Governments. • Audit of the Central and State Government, Public Sector Undertakings and other autonomous bodies and authorities, which are financed from Government funds. • Audit of receipts of the Union or States. • Audit of accounts, stores, and stock. • Audit of companies and corporations. The broad objectives of an audit are to ensure legality, regularity, economy, efficiency and effectiveness of financial management and public administration, mainly through assessment as to: • whether the financial statements are properly prepared, are complete in all respects and are presented with adequate disclosures (financial audit); • whether the provisions of the Constitution, the applicable laws, rules and regulations made thereunder and various orders and instructions issued by competent authority are being complied with (compliance audit); and • The extent to which an activity, programme or organisation operates economically, efficiently and effectively (performance audit). Hence, option (b) is correct.
