106.tq: Distinguish residence-based classifications by identifying the location created after marriage.
xs: A couple setting up a **new home** away from both sets of parents is **neo-local** residence — option **(1)** is correct.
**Patrilocal**, **matrilocal** and **bilocal** all involve living with a natal family.
xa: ⚠ **Duo-local** = spouses stay with their **own natal families**; **neo-local** = new home.
Other bases of family type: **descent** (patrilineal/matrilineal) and **authority** (patriarchal/matriarchal).
**Lakshadweep Muslims** are **duolocal** ("Taravad").

106.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Duo-local — spouses reside with their own natal families
Bilocal — descent traced exclusively through the mother
Matrilocal — spouses establish an entirely independent residence
Patrilocal — spouses reside with the wife’s natal family
106.x: In a duo-local arrangement, spouses stay with their respective natal families. The other options confuse residence and descent categories.
106.tq: Separate residence classifications from descent classifications.
xs: **Duo-local** = spouses stay with their **own natal families** — option **(1)** is correct.
Bilocal is a **residence** type, not descent; independent residence is **neo-local**, not matrilocal.
xa: ⚠ **Neo-local** = new home.
**Lakshadweep Muslims**: duolocal, "Taravad".
Descent types: **patrilineal**, **matrilineal**.

106.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Joint or extended family – Two or more generations
Patriarchal family – Authority of the father or senior male
Matrilineal family – Descent through the father
106.x: Matrilineal descent is traced through the mother's line.
xa: Mates: **monogamous**; **polygamous** (polygyny/polyandry).
⚠ **Matriliny ≠ matriarchy**; power usually stays with men.

106.s: A person’s family consisting of the family into which he or she is born is called the:
106.x: The family of orientation is the family into which a person is born, whereas the family of procreation is established after marriage.
106.tq: Discriminate between two closely related sociological terms by their time of formation.
xs: The family one is **born into** is the **family of orientation** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **family of procreation** is the one **set up after marriage** — option (4) is the trap.
xa: **Murdock**: family = **common residence, economic co-operation, reproduction**.
**MacIver**: group defined by sex relationships precise + enduring enough for **procreation and upbringing**.

106.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a factor contributing to the rise of single-parent and female-headed households?
106.x: Widowhood, marital instability and male migration are identified as causes of rising single-parent and female-headed households. Expansion of joint-family residence is not listed as a cause.
106.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated causes rather than merely naming a related family feature.
xs: **Expansion of joint-family residence** is not a cause — option **(2)** is correct.
Single-parent / **female-headed households** rise due to **widowhood, marital instability, male migration** — options (1), (3), (4).
xa: **Dual-income** urban households: pressure on **child care + caregiving** (UPSC).
**Women's employment** also raises female-headed households.

106.s: Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has recently advocated:
o: Replacing joint families with nuclear households
A return to the joint family and incentives for families with two or more children
A two-child limit with penalties for larger families
106.x: In the context of declining fertility, Naidu urged a return to the joint family and incentives for having two or more children.
xa: **NFHS-6** TFR **2.0**; NFHS-5 urban TFR **1.6**.
AP's **1985** succession amendment preceded the central **2005** amendment by **20 years**.

106.s: Which of the following is described as a basic and primary social institution?
106.x: The family is the basic, primary social institution, the first place where a person is socialised.
106.tq: Recall the family as the primary institution.
n: Family is a basic and primary social institution. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-36]
xs: The **family** is a **basic** and **primary social institution** — option **(3)**.
Its functions: **reproduction**, **socialization**, **emotional support**, **economic security**, **cultural transmission**.
xa: Scholars of family: **George Peter Murdock**, **Talcott Parsons**, **Irawati Karve**.
⚠ Family of **orientation** = born into; family of **procreation** = set up after marriage.
Census 2011: over half of all households were **nuclear**.

106.s: Which of the following is described as the first school of the child?
106.x: The family is the child's first school, teaching language, customs, values, traditions and norms before any formal schooling.
106.tq: Recall why the family is the first school.
n: Family is the first school of the child. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xs: The **family** is the **first school** of the child — option **(2)**.
It teaches **language**, **customs**, **values**, **traditions** and **norms**, and basic education **before school**.
xa: It **develops discipline** and **moral values** and encourages learning habits.
A child learns **manners** and **respect for elders** in the family.
Murdock's **educational** function = **socialization of children**.

106.s: According to Talcott Parsons, the two irreducible functions of the family are:
o: Primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of adult personality
106.x: Parsons identified primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of the adult personality as the family's two irreducible functions.
xa: **Murdock**: 4 universal functions; **Ogburn**: 7 functions.
General functions: **biological, economic, socialisation, psychological**.

106.s: Persistent failure of family functions, for example through abuse or alcoholism, is termed:
106.x: Dysfunction is the persistent failure of the family's biological, economic, socialisation or psychological functions, e.g. through abuse or alcoholism.
xa: **Ogburn**: "**loss of functions**" — only affection stays.
**High-risk families**: single-parent / **female-headed**, **dual-income** urban, elderly-care strain.

106.s:
Consider the following statements about the family:
1. It discourages acceptable behaviour.
2. It introduces religious beliefs and rituals.
3. It protects members from social and economic risks.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
106.x: The family passes on religious beliefs and rituals and protects members from social and economic risks; statement 1 is false because the family encourages acceptable behaviour.
n: Family encourages acceptable behaviour. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family discourages deviant behaviour. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family introduces religious beliefs. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family introduces religious rituals. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family preserves religious traditions. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family protects members from social risks. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family protects members from economic risks. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xa: It celebrates festivals such as **Diwali**, **Eid**, **Christmas**, **Gurpurab**.
It supports **children**, **women**, **elderly persons** and **disabled persons**.
The family is the **first school** of the child.

106.s: Which of the following pairs of Murdock's family functions is correctly matched?
106.x: In Murdock's scheme the reproductive function is the birth of children; economic means cooperation, educational means socialisation, and sexual regulation means regulating sexual relations.
n: According to George Peter Murdock, sexual regulation means regulation of sexual relations. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
According to George Peter Murdock, the reproductive function means the birth of children. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
According to George Peter Murdock, the economic function means economic cooperation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
According to George Peter Murdock, the educational function means socialization of children. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xa: These are **George Peter Murdock**'s **four universal functions** (study of **250** societies).
**Ogburn** listed **7** functions; **Talcott Parsons** **2** irreducible ones.
⚠ **4 – 7 – 2** = **Murdock – Ogburn – Parsons**.

106.s: Who identified the four universal functions of the family?
106.x: George Peter Murdock named four universal functions of the family: sexual regulation, reproduction, economic cooperation and education.
106.tq: Recall Murdock's four universal functions.
n: George Peter Murdock identified four universal functions of the family. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xs: **George Peter Murdock** identified the **four universal functions** of the family — option **(2)**.
They are **sexual regulation**, **reproductive**, **economic** and **educational**.
xa: **Ogburn**: **7** functions, all except affection passing to outside agencies ("**loss of functions**").
**Talcott Parsons**: **2** — primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personality.
Murdock's definition: **common residence, economic co-operation, reproduction**.

106.s: High-risk families are best described as families facing:
o: Only economic difficulties such as poverty and unemployment
Only health-related challenges and chronic illness
Only the problems of single-parent households
Severe social, economic, health, psychological or environmental challenges harming members' well-being
106.x: High-risk families face serious social, economic, health, psychological or environmental problems that harm their members; they are not limited to one kind of problem.
n: High-risk families are families facing severe social, economic, health, psychological, or environmental challenges. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
xa: Characteristics: **poverty**, **unemployment**, **domestic violence**, **substance abuse**, **single-parent households**.
Also: **chronic illness** or **disability**, **child neglect and abuse**, **family conflicts**.
Types in India: **female-headed** households, **dual-income urban** households, families needing **elderly care**.

106.s:
Consider the following causes of high-risk families:
1. Poverty, debt burden and job insecurity are economic factors.
2. Family breakdown, migration and social exclusion are social factors.
3. Mental stress, depression and addiction are psychological factors.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
106.x: All three are correct: poverty, debt and job insecurity are economic causes; breakdown, migration and exclusion social causes; stress, depression and addiction psychological causes.
n: Poverty is an economic factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
Debt burden is an economic factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
Job insecurity is an economic factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
Family breakdown is a social factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
Migration is a social factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
Social exclusion is a social factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
Mental stress is a psychological factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
Depression is a psychological factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
Addiction is a psychological factor causing high-risk families. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
xa: Characteristics include **domestic violence**, **substance abuse** and **child neglect and abuse**.
Single-parent / **female-headed** households are rising due to widowhood, marital instability and **male migration**.
**Elderly care** depends on filial piety, strained by nuclearisation and migration.

106.s: Which statement correctly describes Karve’s understanding of jointness in a family?
o: Jointness exists only when all members are related through the mother.
Jointness is based on functional unity and obligations, and may also involve common property.
Jointness is defined only by the number of married couples.
106.x: Karve emphasised functional unity and obligations more than co-residence; she also described the joint family as a residential unit holding common property.
106.tq: Avoid the extreme interpretation that reduces jointness to residence alone.
xs: **Karve**: jointness = **functional unity and obligations** more than co-residence, also a unit holding **common property** — option **(3)** is correct.
Option (2) is wrong because she stressed functions over **co-residence**.
xa: ⚠ **Mahuva** study = **I.P. Desai**; **developmental cycle** = **A.M. Shah**.
**A.M. Shah**: **family ≠ household**.

106.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the tharawad among Tiyans, some Moplas and Bants?
o: A patrilocal household in which the eldest son inherits
A duolocal household of Lakshadweep Muslims called Taravad
A household headed by the heiress’s husband called nokma
A household consisting of a woman, her siblings and her sisters’ children, without the husband in the unit
106.x: Among Tiyans, some Moplas and Bants, the tharawad consists of a woman, her siblings and her sisters’ children; the husband is not part of the unit.
106.tq: Use the membership details to distinguish similar matrilineal systems.
xs: Among **Tiyans, some Moplas, Bants**, the **tharawad** = **a woman, her siblings and her sisters' children**, **no husband in the unit** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (2) is the **Lakshadweep** Taravad; option (3) is the **Garo nokma** household.
xa: These communities are in **Malabar / Kanara**.
**Nair tharavad** (Kerala): **Marumakkathayam**, abolished in **1975**.

106.s: Which category of urban family is associated with a joint family form and strong elder-male authority?
106.x: The proprietary class is described as having joint families and strong elder-male authority.
106.tq: Match the urban income category with its authority structure.
xs: The **proprietary class** has **joint** families and **strong elder-male authority** — option **(3)** is correct.
The other urban categories by income are **entrepreneurial-cum-professional** and **service**.
xa: **T.K. Oommen** reads urban families by **livelihood, income, authority structure, social milieu, value pattern**.
**UPPSC 2014** asked how Oommen distinguished urban families.

106.s: In the Khasi matrilineal system, the youngest daughter inherits. This practice is known as:
106.x: Inheritance by the youngest daughter is called ultimogeniture and is associated with the Khasi of Meghalaya.
106.tq: Distinguish inheritance by the youngest child from inheritance by the eldest child.
xs: Inheritance by the **youngest daughter** among the **Khasi** is **ultimogeniture** — option **(1)** is correct.
Khasi families are also **matrilocal** (Meghalaya).
xa: ⚠ **Khasi** = youngest daughter; **Garo** = **Machong**.
**Garo**: the heiress's husband (**nokma**) heads the household.

106.s: In the Garo matrilineal system, ‘Machong’ refers to the matrilineage, while the household is headed by the:
106.x: Among the Garo, Machong is the matrilineage and the heiress’s husband, called nokma, heads the household.
106.tq: Separate the name of the lineage from the title of the household head.
xs: Among the **Garo**, the heiress's husband, the **nokma**, heads the household — option **(4)** is correct.
**Machong** is the Garo **matrilineage**; **tharavad** is the Nair unit; **coparcener** is a Mitakshara term.
xa: **Khasi**: **ultimogeniture** (youngest daughter inherits).
Matriliny ≠ matriarchy; **power usually stays with men**.

106.s: The Marumakkathayam system of the Nair tharavad in Kerala was abolished by which of the following?
106.x: The Nair tharavad followed Marumakkathayam (matrilineal inheritance), which was abolished by the Joint Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975. The Hindu Succession Act 1956 is the central succession law, the Special Marriage Act 1954 governs civil marriage, and the Family Courts Act 1984 set up family courts; none of them abolished Marumakkathayam.
106.tq: Marumakkathayam (Nair, Kerala) ended by the 1975 Abolition Act.
xs: **Marumakkathayam** of the **Nair tharavad** was abolished by the **Joint Family System (Abolition) Act 1975** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Hindu Succession Act 1956** is part of the **Hindu Code**; the **Family Courts Act 1984** set up family courts.
xa: **Tiyans, some Moplas, Bants** (Malabar/Kanara) also have a **tharawad** without the husband.
AP's **1985** succession amendment came 20 years before the central **2005** amendment.

106.s: The Mitakshara school of Hindu law is based on Vijnaneshwara’s commentary on the:
106.x: Mitakshara is Vijnaneshwara’s commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, composed in the Kalyani Chalukya court.
106.tq: Match the legal school with its foundational text and commentator.
xs: **Mitakshara** is **Vijnaneshwara**'s commentary on the **Yajnavalkya Smriti**, at the **Kalyani Chalukya** court — option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ Do not confuse with **Dayabhaga**, which is **Jimutavahana**'s work.
xa: Mitakshara prevailed in **most of India**: **coparcenary right by birth**, **survivorship**.
**Dayabhaga** (**Jimutavahana**): **Bengal and Assam**; right only on the **father's death**.

106.s: The 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act made daughters:
o: Eligible heirs only if the father died after 2005
Members of the Dayabhaga school by law
Guardians of all family property irrespective of descent
106.x: The 2005 amendment to Section 6 made daughters coparceners by birth.
106.tq: Recall the exact legal status and statutory provision introduced by the amendment.
xs: The **2005** HSA amendment made daughters **coparceners by birth** under **Sec. 6** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) is wrong: **Vineeta Sharma** (**2020**) held it applies **whether or not the father was alive in 2005**.
xa: AP's **1985** succession amendment came **20 years** earlier.
HSA **1956** was part of the **Hindu Code** (Ambedkar).

106.s: In Vineeta Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that daughters' coparcenary rights by birth apply:
o: Only if the father was alive on 9 September 2005
Whether or not the father was alive in 2005
Only if the daughter was unmarried
106.x: Vineeta Sharma (2020) held that daughters' coparcenary rights by birth apply irrespective of whether the father was alive in 2005.
xa: The **2005** amendment made daughters **coparceners by birth** (**Sec. 6**).
Mitakshara: **coparcenary right by birth**.

106.s: Who was the main advocate of the Hindu Code, of which the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 formed a part?
106.x: B.R. Ambedkar was the main advocate of the Hindu Code, which included the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara and Jimutavahana the Dayabhaga, the two classical schools of inheritance; Irawati Karve was a sociologist of the joint family and kinship.
106.tq: Hindu Code (HSA 1956) = Ambedkar.
xs: **B.R. Ambedkar** was the main advocate of the **Hindu Code**, including the **Hindu Succession Act 1956** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Vijnaneshwara** wrote the **Mitakshara**; **Jimutavahana** the **Dayabhaga**; **Karve** studied jointness.
xa: **2005** amendment: daughters = **coparceners by birth**.
**Vineeta Sharma** (**2020**) widened its application.

106.s: The Family Courts Act, 1984, followed the recommendations of which report?
106.x: The Family Courts Act, 1984 followed the 59th Law Commission Report of 1974.
106.tq: Link the statute to its specific recommending report and year.
xs: The **Family Courts Act 1984** followed the **59th Law Commission Report (1974)** — option **(1)** is correct.
The other report numbers and years in the options are not the ones the Act followed.
xa: **953** family courts in **29 States/UTs** as of **31 Jul 2025** (**IYB 2026**).
**BNSS 2023**: maintenance for wives, children, indigent parents, divorced wives.

106.s: Which statement about Andhra Pradesh's succession law amendment is correct?
o: It was enacted in 2005, along with the central amendment
It was enacted after the central amendment of 2005
It was enacted in 1995, 10 years before the central amendment
It was enacted in 1985, 20 years before the central amendment of 2005
106.x: Andhra Pradesh made its succession amendment in 1985, 20 years before the central amendment of 2005.
xa: The central **2005** amendment made daughters **coparceners by birth** (**Sec. 6**).
**Vineeta Sharma** (**2020**): the 2005 amendment applies whether or not the father was alive in **2005**.
The **Hindu Succession Act 1956** was part of the **Hindu Code**, with **Ambedkar** its main advocate.

106.s:
Assertion (A): The family provides socially approved sexual relations.
Reason (R): Regulation of sexual behaviour by the family prevents social disorder.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
106.x: Both are true: the family provides socially approved sexual relations, and regulating sex in this way prevents social disorder. R explains A.
106.tq: Ask whether preventing disorder explains regulation.
n: Family provides socially approved sexual relations. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family prevents social disorder by regulating sexual behaviour. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xs: Both are true and R is the correct **explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
The family provides **socially approved sexual relations**, and by **regulating sexual behaviour** it **prevents social disorder**.
xa: It ensures the **continuity** of society through **reproduction**.
It **protects** infants, children, the elderly and sick members.
**Sexual regulation** is one of **Murdock**'s four universal functions.

106.s: Guardianship among Hindus is governed by the:
106.x: The Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act covers guardianship; adoption falls under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act.
xa: HAMA and the Guardianship Act are both of **1956**; the **Family Courts Act** is of **1984**.
Family courts followed the **59th Law Commission Report (1974)**; **953** courts as of **31 Jul 2025**.
**Hindu Succession Act** (**1956**), amended **September 9, 2005**: **daughters** got **equal coparcenary rights** by birth.
⚠ **Mitakshara** = right by birth; **Dayabhaga** = right only on the father's death.

106.s: Murdock defined the family by common residence, economic co-operation and:
106.x: Murdock's three features of the family are common residence, economic co-operation and reproduction.
xa: ⚠ **Orientation** = born into; **procreation** = set up after marriage.
Murdock studied **250 societies** and found **4 universal functions**.

106.s:
Consider the following statements about Ogburn on family functions:
1. Ogburn listed seven functions of the family, including status-giving and affectional functions.
2. Ogburn held that the affectional function was passing to outside agencies.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
106.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: Ogburn held that all functions except affection were passing to outside agencies ('loss of functions'). So '1 only'.
106.tq: Affection is the one function the family keeps.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — **1 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
**1**: **Ogburn** listed **7** functions, including **status-giving** and **affectional**.
**2** is wrong: all functions **except affection** pass to outside agencies — **"loss of functions"**.
xa: Ogburn's 7: economic, protective, religious, recreational, educational, status-giving, affectional.
⚠ **4 – 7 – 2** = **Murdock – Ogburn – Parsons**.

106.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about studies on the persistence of the joint family?
o: Milton Singer and Orenstein held that industrial urbanisation has not dissolved the joint family
Ramkrishna Mukherjee found joint families over-represented in agriculture and casual labour
Ramkrishna Mukherjee found joint families over-represented in trade and higher occupations
M.S. Gore found that nuclear households rise but emotional bonds persist
106.x: Mukherjee found joint families over-represented in trade and higher occupations, not agriculture and casual labour.
xa: Joint family persists: **Singer, Orenstein, Mukherjee, Gore**.
Continuity side of the debate: **Srinivas, Shah, Gore**.

106.s: I.P. Desai's study of degrees of jointness in households was conducted in:
106.x: I.P. Desai studied jointness in Mahuva and identified five degrees of jointness.
xa: Marxist **I.P. Desai** links nuclear households to **capitalism**.
⚠ **Developmental cycle** = **A.M. Shah**, not Desai.

106.s: 'The Household Dimension of Family in India' (1973) was written by:
106.x: A.M. Shah wrote it, distinguished family from household, and gave the developmental cycle of households.
xa: Shah: joint family **changes in structure but continues in function**.
⚠ **Mahuva** = **I.P. Desai**.

106.s: Which scholar argued that the family reproduces patriarchy?
106.x: Leela Dube argued the family reproduces patriarchy; Kapadia pioneered family studies and Shah gave the developmental cycle.
xa: **M.S. Gore**: nuclear households rise but emotional bonds persist.
**Mukherjee**: joint families over-represented in **trade + higher occupations**.

106.s: The matrilineal Khasi and Garo communities are associated with which State?
106.x: The Khasi and Garo are associated with Meghalaya.
xa: ⚠ **Khasi** = youngest daughter inherits; **Garo** = **Machong**.
⚠ **Matriliny ≠ matriarchy**.

106.s: In matrilineal systems, power usually remains with:
106.x: Matriliny traces descent through women, but power usually stays with men; matriliny is not matriarchy.
xa: Example: among the **Garo**, the heiress's husband (**nokma**) heads the household.
Authority types: **patriarchal**, **matriarchal**.

106.s: The Dayabhaga school of Hindu law, prevalent in Bengal and Assam, is associated with:
106.x: Dayabhaga is Jimutavahana's school; under it a son's right arises only on the father's death, unlike Mitakshara.
xa: Mitakshara: **Vijnaneshwara** on the **Yajnavalkya Smriti**.
**HSA 2005**: daughters became **coparceners by birth** (**Sec. 6**).

106.s: Which one of the following changes is associated with industrialisation and its impact on the family?
o: The family changes from a production unit into a consumption unit
The family becomes independent of economic factors
The family changes from a consumption unit into a production unit
106.x: Industrialisation changes the family from a production unit into a consumption unit and contributes to the economic independence of youth.
106.tq: Test the cause-effect relationship rather than selecting an extreme generalisation.
xs: **Industrialisation** turns the family from a **production unit** into a **consumption unit** — option **(1)** is correct.
It also makes **youth economically independent**; option (3) reverses the change.
xa: **Urbanisation/migration**: limited housing; **rural-urban migration** breaks up joint families.
**Women's employment**: more **female-headed households**.

106.s: Which one of the following is a major family-related consequence of urbanisation and migration?
o: Break-up of joint families due to rural-urban migration
Strengthening of joint ownership of agricultural land
106.x: Limited urban housing and rural-urban migration contribute to the break-up of joint families.
106.tq: Link the stated social factor with its specific structural consequence.
xs: **Rural-urban migration** breaks up **joint families** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Limited housing** in cities adds to this.
xa: Census **2001 → 2011**: rural joint households fell **20.1% → 16.8%**; urban **16.5% → 14.6%**.
⚠ **Singer, Orenstein**: industrial urbanisation has **not dissolved** the joint family.

106.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about changes in family structure in India?
o: Legislation and marital dissolution may bring more separation, single parenting and divorce
Urbanisation invariably eliminates all emotional bonds among members of joint families
Women's employment may lead to more female-headed households
M.S. Gore found that nuclear households rise but emotional bonds persist
106.x: Urbanisation does not invariably end emotional bonds; M.S. Gore found that bonds persist even as nuclear households rise.
xa: **Industrialisation**: production unit → **consumption unit**.
Single-parent households rise from **widowhood, marital instability, male migration**.

106.s:
Assertion (A): Urban families may be studied through livelihood, authority structure, social milieu and value pattern.
Reason (R): Urban families are classified only by the number of persons residing in the household.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
106.x: A is true. R is false: urban families are not classified only by household size.
xa: This is **T.K. Oommen**'s urban typology (**UPPSC 2014**: answer "**all of**" these).
Income categories: **proprietary**, **entrepreneurial-cum-professional**, **service**.

106.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about household types between Census 2001 and 2011?
o: The share of nuclear households rose in rural India (50.7% to 52.1%)
The share of joint households fell in urban India (16.5% to 14.6%)
The share of joint households fell in rural India (20.1% to 16.8%)
The share of nuclear households rose in urban India
106.x: Urban nuclear households fell from 54.3% to 52.3% between 2001 and 2011.
xa: **Census 2011**: over half of all households were **nuclear**.
**I.P. Desai** (Mahuva): **61%** nuclear, **39%** joint.

106.s: NFHS-6 (2023–24) was released by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with which institution as the nodal agency?
o: International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai
106.x: NFHS-6 was released by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, with the International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai, as the nodal agency.
106.tq: Apply the institutional-role trap by distinguishing the releasing ministry from the nodal agency.
xs: **NFHS-6** (**2023-24**) was released by **MoHFW** with **IIPS Mumbai** as nodal agency — option **(1)** is correct.
IIPS stands for the **International Institute for Population Sciences**, Mumbai.
xa: NFHS-6 covered **6.79 lakh households**, **715 districts**.
NFHS-6 **TFR 2.0**; NFHS-5 urban TFR **1.6**, rural **2.1**.

106.s: In NFHS-5, the urban total fertility rate was:
106.x: NFHS-5 reported urban and rural TFRs of 1.6 and 2.1; NFHS-6 reported an overall TFR of 2.0.
xa: NFHS-6 nodal agency: **IIPS Mumbai** (released by **MoHFW**).
CM **Chandrababu Naidu** urged incentives for **2+ children** as fertility falls (**Jun 2026**).

106.s: Elderly care in Indian families has traditionally rested on:
106.x: Elderly care rests on filial piety, which nuclearisation and migration now strain, creating a need for alternative care.
xa: Both points are **UPSC** themes on high-risk families.
Single-parent households rise from **widowhood, marital instability, male migration**.

106.s: Under which 2023 law do maintenance provisions cover wives, children, indigent parents and divorced wives?
106.x: The BNSS, 2023 contains the maintenance provisions for wives, children, indigent parents and divorced wives.
xa: **Family Courts Act 1984** followed the **59th Law Commission Report (1974)**.
**953** family courts as of **31 Jul 2025**.

106.s: Which of the following statements about the functions of family is incorrect?
o: Emotional security provides love, affection and care.
Inheritance of property refers to the collective consumption of goods and services.
106.x: Option B is incorrect: inheritance of property means passing on wealth and property. Consuming goods together is a separate economic function. Emotional care, reproduction and social control are correctly described.
106.tq: Match each family function to its meaning.
n: Family ensures the continuity of society through reproduction. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family encourages acceptable behaviour. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family transfers wealth and property through inheritance. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family consumes goods and services collectively. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family provides love. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family provides affection. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family provides care. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xs: The **incorrect** statement is option **(2)**: **inheritance** transfers **wealth and property**; it is not **collective consumption**.
**Consuming goods and services collectively** is a separate **economic** function.
**Emotional security**, **reproduction** and **social control** are correctly described.
xa: Economic functions also include providing **food**, **shelter** and **clothing**.
Emotional functions: **love, affection and care**, **confidence** and **self-esteem**.
Biological function: reproduction ensures the **continuity** of society.

106.s: Which of the following is a social cause rather than a characteristic of high-risk families?
106.x: Substance abuse, single-parent households and family conflict characterise high-risk families; social exclusion is a social cause.
xa: Other characteristics: **domestic violence**, **chronic illness**, **child neglect and abuse**.
Economic factors: **poverty**, **debt burden**, **job insecurity**.
Psychological factors: **mental stress**, **depression**, **addiction**.

106.s: The family gives each person several identities. Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
106.x: The family gives a person caste, religious, language and national identities; nationality corresponds to national identity, not language identity.
n: Family provides caste identity. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family provides religious identity. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family provides language identity. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family provides national identity. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
Family provides social status. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xa: It **transfers traditions** from one generation to another.
It **transfers wealth and property** through **inheritance**.
It introduces **religious beliefs and rituals**.

107.s: Sambandham was traditionally associated with:
o: A marriage acquired by service at the bride's home
A widow's marriage with her husband's brother among Gonds
A formal monogamous marriage under the Special Marriage Act
A consensual informal union among Namboothiris and Nairs under Kerala's matrilineal system
107.x: Sambandham was a consensual and informal union associated with Namboothiris and Nairs under Kerala's matrilineal system.
107.tq: Identify the regional community and social setting linked to the customary union.
xs: **Sambandham** was a **consensual, informal union** among **Namboothiris and Nairs** under **Kerala's matrilineal** law — so option **(4)** is correct.
Marriage by **service** at the bride's home is the **Gond** way of acquiring a mate, not Sambandham.
A widow marrying her husband's brother is **Levirate** (Gond, Munda); the **Special Marriage Act** marriage is a formal civil marriage.
xa: Sambandham was asked in the **APPSC 2025 PYQ**, alongside **Niyoga**.
**Niyoga**: a wife cohabits with a designated man to beget a child when the husband is **impotent or dead**.
⚠ **Anuloma** = **hypergamy** (man higher); **Pratiloma** = **hypogamy** (woman higher, condemned).

107.s: Niyoga traditionally involved:
o: A bride being obtained through exchange between two families
A wife cohabiting with a designated man to beget a child when her husband was impotent or dead
A husband marrying his wife's sister after her death
A lower-caste man marrying a higher-caste woman
107.x: Niyoga permitted a wife to cohabit with a designated man for begetting a child when her husband was impotent or dead.
107.tq: Apply the definition to the family situation described in the question.
xs: **Niyoga** was a **wife cohabiting with a designated man to beget a child** when her husband was **impotent or dead** — so option **(2)** is correct.
A husband marrying his deceased wife's sister is **Sororate**, not Niyoga.
A lower-caste man marrying a higher-caste woman is **Pratiloma** (hypogamy), which was condemned.
Bride **exchange** is a tribal way of acquiring a mate (e.g. **Atta Satta** in Rajasthan).
xa: Niyoga figured in the **APPSC 2025 PYQ**, together with **Sambandham** (Namboothiris and Nairs, Kerala).
⚠ **Levirate** = widow marries her husband's brother (**Gond, Munda**); **Sororate** = widower marries his wife's sister.
**Later Vedic** changes: child marriage emerges, **Swayamvara** declines, widow remarriage discouraged, same-gotra marriage barred.

107.s: Which one of the following trends is associated with the Later Vedic period?
o: Swayamvara became increasingly dominant and widow remarriage was encouraged.
Child marriage emerged, Swayamvara declined and widow remarriage was discouraged.
Marriage within the same gotra became compulsory.
All restrictions on marriage within the same gotra were removed.
107.x: The Later Vedic period saw the emergence of child marriage, decline of Swayamvara, discouragement of widow remarriage and prohibition of marriage within the same gotra.
107.tq: Recognise the cluster of social changes rather than an isolated reversal.
xs: In the **Later Vedic** period, **child marriage emerged**, **Swayamvara declined** and **widow remarriage was discouraged** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses the trend: Swayamvara declined and widow remarriage was discouraged, not encouraged.
Options (3) and (4) are wrong: **same-gotra marriage was barred**, neither compulsory nor freed of restrictions.
xa: **Gotra exogamy** — barring marriage within one's own gotra — remains a core rule of Hindu mate selection.
**Niyoga** and **Sambandham** are other customary forms asked in the **APPSC 2025 PYQ**.
⚠ **Anuloma** (hypergamy) was tolerated; **Pratiloma** (hypogamy) was condemned.

107.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Anuloma from Pratiloma marriage?
o: Anuloma involved a lower-varna man and Pratiloma a higher-varna man.
Anuloma was condemned, whereas Pratiloma was generally tolerated.
Anuloma involved a higher-varna man and a lower-varna woman, whereas Pratiloma involved the reverse.
Both terms denoted marriage between members of the same varna.
107.x: Anuloma referred to a higher-varna man marrying a lower-varna woman and was tolerated. Pratiloma referred to a lower-varna man marrying a higher-varna woman and was condemned.
107.tq: Compare the direction of varna status and then apply the approval distinction.
xs: **Anuloma** = a **higher-varna man** marrying a **lower-varna woman**; **Pratiloma** = the reverse — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses the definitions, and option (2) reverses the judgement: it was **Pratiloma** that was **condemned**.
Neither term means same-varna marriage; that is **endogamy**.
xa: Anuloma is also called **hypergamy**; Pratiloma is **hypogamy**.
**Endogamy** operates at the **varna, caste, sub-caste** level; **Ghurye** saw it as the defining feature of caste.
⚠ **Levirate** = husband's brother; **Sororate** = wife's sister.

107.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Polygyny means one man having many wives.
2. Fraternal polyandry means marriage to sisters.
3. Levirate means a widow marries her husband's brother.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
107.x: Polygyny is one man with several wives and the levirate is a widow marrying her husband's brother; statement 2 is false because fraternal polyandry is marriage to brothers.
n: Polygyny means one man and many wives. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Fraternal polyandry is marriage to brothers. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Levirate is a marriage in which a widow marries her husband's brother. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Sororate is a marriage in which a widower marries his wife's sister. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
xa: **Polyandry** = one woman, many husbands; **monogamy** = one husband, one wife.
Levirate is found among the **Gond** and **Munda**.
⚠ **Anuloma** = **hypergamy**; **Pratiloma** = **hypogamy** (condemned).

107.s: Marriage into a higher caste (anuloma) is called:
107.x: Hypergamy (anuloma) is marriage into a higher caste; hypogamy (pratiloma) into a lower caste.
n: Endogamy refers to marriage within one's own social group. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 51-52]
Exogamy refers to marriage outside one's own social group. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 51-52]
Hypergamy is also known as Anuloma. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 51-52]
Hypergamy refers to marriage into a higher caste. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 51-52]
Hypogamy is also known as Pratiloma. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 51-52]
Hypogamy refers to marriage into a lower caste. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 51-52]
xa: Anuloma: **high-caste male** with **low-caste female**; Pratiloma: **low-caste male** with **high-caste female**.
**Sapinda** (HMA Sec. 3(f)): **3** generations on the mother's side, **5** on the father's.
⚠ The Delhi HC upheld **HMA Sec. 5(v)** — the sapinda bar (APPSC 2025 PYQ).

107.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Satyashodhak marriage tradition?
o: It required a Brahmin priest and dowry payment.
It was a form of marriage exclusively involving several men and several women.
It used no dowry and no Brahmin priest.
It could be solemnised only by a Marriage Officer under the SMA.
107.x: Satyashodhak marriage, started by Savitribai Phule, used no dowry and no Brahmin priest.
107.tq: Reject the options that import features of other marriage forms or solemnisation systems.
xs: **Satyashodhak marriage** used **no dowry and no Brahmin priest** — option **(3)**.
Option (1) is the reverse; a **Marriage Officer** solemnises marriages under the **Special Marriage Act**, not Satyashodhak marriages.
xa: It was started by **Savitribai Phule**.
**Periyar** institutionalised **self-respect marriages**, validated by HMA **Sec. 7-A** (TN, **1967**).
**Uberoi**: companionate marriage, rising age at marriage, **serial monogamy**, more divorce.

107.s: According to Manu Smriti, which type of marriage is considered the highest form and involves giving the daughter to a qualified, educated and virtuous groom?
107.x: In Manu Smriti, Brahma marriage, where the father gives his daughter to a learned, virtuous groom without dowry or bride price, is the highest form.
107.tq: Recall the eight forms in order, highest to lowest.
n: Brahma Marriage involves the father voluntarily giving his daughter to a qualified groom. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Brahma Marriage involves giving the daughter to an educated groom. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Brahma Marriage involves giving the daughter to a virtuous groom. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Brahma Marriage is considered the highest form of marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Brahma Marriage involves giving a daughter to a learned and worthy groom. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
xs: **Brahma Marriage** is the **highest form** in **Manu Smriti** — option **(4)**.
The father gives his daughter to a **qualified, educated, virtuous** groom learned in the **Vedas**, with **no dowry** and **no bride price**.
**Daiva** → priest at a sacrifice; **Arsha** → symbolic gift; **Prajapatya** → duty and family life.
xa: Manu recognizes **eight** types of Hindu marriage.
Approved (**Prashasta**): Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Prajapatya.
Modern equivalent of Brahma: an **arranged marriage** based on qualifications.

107.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Brahma Marriage is regarded as the highest form of marriage.
Arsha Marriage involves a symbolic gift such as a cow and a bull from the groom.
Prajapatya Marriage involves the purchase of the bride by giving wealth to her family.
Daiva Marriage involves giving the daughter to a priest who officiates a sacrifice.
107.x: Option C is incorrect: buying the bride with wealth is Asura marriage. Prajapatya marriage stresses duty, family welfare and children.
107.tq: Discriminate Asura (bride price) from Prajapatya (duty).
n: Daiva Marriage involves giving a daughter to a priest performing a sacrifice. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Prajapatya Marriage is based on duty and family life. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Brahma Marriage is considered the highest form of marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Daiva Marriage involves giving the daughter to a Ritvik priest. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
The Ritvik priest in Daiva Marriage officiates a sacrifice. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Daiva Marriage is linked with religious rituals. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
The groom in Daiva Marriage is a priest. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Arsha Marriage is performed after receiving a symbolic gift such as a cow and a bull from the groom. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Prajapatya Marriage emphasizes family welfare. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Prajapatya Marriage emphasizes procreation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Asura Marriage involves the groom giving wealth to the bride's family. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Asura Marriage involves purchasing the bride. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Asura Marriage involves a bride price. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Arsha Marriage involves receiving symbolic gifts from the groom. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Asura Marriage involves purchasing the bride by giving wealth to her family. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Arsha Marriage involves only a symbolic exchange. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Prajapatya Marriage is performed with blessings emphasizing duty. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
xs: The **incorrect** statement is option **(3)**: purchasing the bride with wealth is **Asura** marriage, not **Prajapatya**.
**Prajapatya** emphasizes **duty**, **family welfare** and **procreation**.
**Brahma** is the highest form; **Arsha** involves a **cow and a bull**; **Daiva** gives the daughter to a **Ritvik priest**.
xa: **Asura** is **disapproved**: a **bride price**, with wealth as the primary consideration.
**Arsha** was common among **sages** and **hermits**.
In Prajapatya, **husband and wife share responsibilities**.

107.s:
Assertion (A): Paisacha Marriage is the most condemned form of marriage according to Manu Smriti.
Reason (R): It involves deceit, intoxication, coercion or exploitation of a woman without her consent.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
107.x: Both are true: Paisacha marriage, taking a woman by deceit, intoxication or force without consent, is the most condemned form because of that lack of consent. R explains A.
107.tq: Ask whether lack of consent explains the condemnation.
n: Paisacha Marriage is the most condemned form in Manusmriti. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Paisacha Marriage involves deceit. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Paisacha Marriage involves intoxication. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Paisacha Marriage involves coercion. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Paisacha Marriage involves exploitation of a woman without her consent. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Paisacha Marriage involves taking a woman through deceit or exploitation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Paisacha Marriage is the most condemned form of marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Paisacha Marriage is considered immoral and sinful. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
xs: Both are true and R is the correct **explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
**Paisacha** involves **deceit**, **intoxication**, **coercion** or exploitation **without her consent** — hence the **most condemned form**.
xa: It is considered **immoral and sinful**.
**Rakshasa** = **forceful abduction** after battle, also disapproved.
**Asura** = purchasing the bride; also disapproved.

107.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Daiva marriage – Marriage through forceful abduction
Gandharva marriage – Marriage by mutual love and consent
Asura marriage – Bride purchased by giving wealth to her family
Rakshasa marriage – Marriage through forceful abduction
107.x: In Daiva marriage the daughter is given to a priest officiating at a sacrifice; abduction is Rakshasa.
n: Daiva Marriage involves giving a daughter to a priest performing a sacrifice. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Daiva Marriage involves giving the daughter to a Ritvik priest. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
The Ritvik priest in Daiva Marriage officiates a sacrifice. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
The groom in Daiva Marriage is a priest. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Gandharva Marriage is based on the mutual love of the couple. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Gandharva Marriage is based on the consent of the couple. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Asura Marriage involves the groom giving wealth to the bride's family. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Asura Marriage involves purchasing the bride. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Asura Marriage involves a bride price. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Rakshasa Marriage involves the forceful abduction of a woman. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Gandharva Marriage is based on mutual love and consent. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Asura Marriage involves purchasing the bride by giving wealth to her family. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Rakshasa Marriage involves forceful abduction after battle. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Gandharva Marriage is a love marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
xa: Gandharva example: **Shakuntala and Dushyanta**.
Rakshasa is associated with **Kshatriyas**.
⚠ Gandharva is **conditionally accepted** yet listed among the **Aprashasta** marriages.

107.s:
Consider the following statements about forms of marriage:
1. Prajapatya marriage emphasises duty, family welfare and procreation.
2. Rakshasa marriage involves forceful abduction of a woman.
3. Gandharva marriage requires parental approval.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
107.x: Prajapatya stresses duty and children and Rakshasa is abduction; statement 3 is false because Gandharva marriage needs no parental approval.
n: Arsha Marriage is performed after receiving a symbolic gift such as a cow and a bull from the groom. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Prajapatya Marriage emphasizes family welfare. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Prajapatya Marriage emphasizes procreation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Gandharva Marriage does not require parental approval. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Rakshasa Marriage involves the forceful abduction of a woman. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Arsha Marriage involves receiving symbolic gifts from the groom. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Gandharva Marriage is based on mutual love and consent. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Rakshasa Marriage involves forceful abduction after battle. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Arsha Marriage involves only a symbolic exchange. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Prajapatya Marriage is performed with blessings emphasizing duty. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
Gandharva Marriage is a love marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-76]
xa: **Brahma**: no dowry, no bride price — the highest form.
**Daiva**: groom is a **priest** at a sacrifice.
**Paisacha**: the most condemned form.

107.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Daiva marriage – Daughter given to a priest performing a sacrifice
Rakshasa marriage – Marriage after receiving symbolic gifts
Arsha marriage – Marriage after receiving symbolic gifts
Prajapatya marriage – Marriage based on duty and family life
107.x: Rakshasa marriage is by forceful abduction; marriage after symbolic gifts is Arsha.
xa: Approved: **Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Prajapatya**.
Disapproved: **Gandharva, Asura, Rakshasa, Paisacha**.
Manu Smriti lists **eight** forms.

107.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Rakshasa Marriage is associated with Kshatriyas.
II. Abduction-type marriages are mentioned in epics as examples of Rakshasa Marriage.
III. Gandharva Marriage is based on the purchase of the bride by the groom.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
107.x: I and II are correct: Rakshasa marriage is linked with Kshatriyas, and abduction marriages appear in the epics. III is false because buying the bride is Asura marriage, not Gandharva.
107.tq: Discriminate Gandharva (love) from Asura (purchase).
xs: Statements I and II are correct — option **(2)**, **I and II only**.
**Rakshasa** marriage is associated with **Kshatriyas**; **abduction-type marriages** are mentioned in **epics**.
III is false: purchasing the bride is **Asura**; **Gandharva** is based on **mutual love and consent**.
xa: Rakshasa occurs **after warfare** or conflict.
Gandharva example: **Shakuntala and Dushyanta**.

107.s: Manu Smriti recognises how many types of Hindu marriage?

107.x: A Muslim wife may seek khula by mutual consent and may invoke the Dissolution of Muslim Marriage Act, 1939. Grounds include lack of maintenance for two years, imprisonment of seven or more years and cruelty.
107.tq: Match the legal routes with the community-specific law and avoid importing provisions from another statute.
xs: A Muslim wife may seek **Khula by mutual consent** or use the **Dissolution of Muslim Marriage Act 1939** — option **(2)**.
Section **13B** belongs to the **Hindu Marriage Act**, and the Family Court is not limited to SMA cases.
xa: DMMA grounds include **no maintenance for 2 years**, **7+ years' imprisonment**, cruelty.
**Muslim Women Act 2019**: instant triple talaq **void + illegal**; up to **3 years' jail**.
**Nikah** is conducted by a **Kazi** (**Kazis Act 1880**).

107.s: Which was the first South Asian nation to register a same-sex marriage?
107.x: Nepal was the first South Asian nation to register a same-sex marriage (APPSC 2025 PYQ). In India, the Supreme Court in Supriyo (2023) refused to read same-sex marriage into the Special Marriage Act; Sri Lanka and Bangladesh are not cited as having done so.
107.tq: First in South Asia: Nepal.
xs: **Nepal** was the **first South Asian nation** to register a **same-sex marriage** — option **(2)**.
In **India**, **Supriyo (Oct 2023)** refused to read same-sex marriage into the SMA.
xa: This was an **APPSC 2025 PYQ**.
In Supriyo, **CJI Chandrachud** was in the minority.
Changing trends (Uberoi): companionate marriage, rising age at marriage, **serial monogamy**, more divorce.

107.s: Which of the following was the custom practised during the ancient period that allows married women to cohabit with a designated male for the sole purpose of procreating a child if her husband was impotent or had died?
A consensual and informal relationship practised in accordance to matrilineal laws of Kerala that prevailed among Namboothiris and Nairs is known as:
Marriage by purchase of bride was known as
107.x: In ancient Hindu marriage classifications, the Asura form involved the groom's family paying a bride-price (money or goods) to the bride's family in exchange for marriage. This was considered one of the lower, materialistic forms of marriage compared to the more approved Brahma or Daiva forms. It reflects marriage practices recorded in Dharmashastra texts.

107.s: ' Diku Andi ' means:
o: Marriage by exchange in Koya and Savara tribes
Marriage by capture in Naga tribes
Marriage by probation in Kuki tribe
Marriage by negotiation in Ho tribes

107.x: Goa was the only state in India to have the Common Civil Code. At present, Uttarakhand has enforced the uniform civil code on 27 January, 2025.
