⚠ **Wirth** = urbanism; **Redfield** = folk-urban continuum; **Metcalfe** = little republics.
**Industrialisation** drives urbanisation by creating jobs.

115.s: The term ‘footloose labour’, as used by Jan Breman, refers to:
o: Circular migrant workers moving among seasonal, casual and informal jobs
Highly skilled workers employed permanently by multinational firms
Permanent agricultural labourers tied to one village
115.x: Jan Breman’s Footloose Labour (1996) describes circular migrant workers who move between seasonal, casual and informal employment.
115.tq: Match the author and title with the exact labour-mobility concept.
xs: **Jan Breman**'s "**footloose labour**" means **circular migrants** moving among **seasonal, casual and informal jobs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is not permanent or skilled employment.
xa: Breman's book **Footloose Labour** appeared in **1996**.
Main migrant **source States: UP and Bihar**.
**Milton Singer** — When a Great Tradition Modernizes (urban **Madras**).

115.s: Which of the following pairs (scholar – concept) is correctly matched?
o: N. K. Bose – Hindu method of tribal absorption
N. K. Bose – Tribe-caste continuum and secondary state formation
T. K. Oommen – Hindu method of tribal absorption
115.x: N. K. Bose is linked with the Hindu method of tribal absorption; Surajit Sinha with the tribe-caste continuum and secondary state formation; T. K. Oommen with tribal autonomy movements.
xa: **Jan Breman** — "footloose labour"; **Milton Singer** — urban Madras.
**Marriott** — universalisation and parochialisation.
AP has **34 ST communities**; India has **705** ST groups.

115.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
115.x: Rampura in Mysore was studied by M.N. Srinivas. Shamirpet was associated with S.C. Dube, Sripuram with Andre Beteille, and Kishan Garhi with McKim Marriott.
115.tq: Start with the sure village–scholar pair and eliminate swapped associations.
xs: **Rampura** (Mysore, Karnataka) was studied by **M.N. Srinivas** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Shamirpet** was studied by **S.C. Dube**, not Beteille.
**Sripuram** (Thanjavur) was studied by **Andre Beteille**, not Marriott; **Kishan Garhi** by **McKim Marriott**, not Dube.
xa: Srinivas wrote **The Remembered Village** and gave the concept of **dominant caste**.
**Senapur** (Jaunpur, UP) = **Morris Opler and R.D. Singh**; also **Bernard Cohn**.
Beteille's Sripuram study = **Caste, Class and Power**; Marriott's = **Village India**.
S.C. Dube's Shamirpet study = **Indian Village (1955)**.

115.s: Who among the following was also associated with the study of Senapur in Jaunpur district?
115.x: Senapur in Jaunpur was associated with Morris Opler, R.D. Singh and Bernard Cohn.
115.tq: Test the additional scholar attached to a familiar village-study location.
xs: **Senapur** (Jaunpur, UP) was studied by **Morris Opler and R.D. Singh**, and also by **Bernard Cohn** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Louis Wirth** wrote on urbanism, **Robert Redfield** on the folk-urban continuum (Mexico) and **Milton Singer** studied urban **Madras** — none studied Senapur.
xa: **Rampura** = **M.N. Srinivas**; **Shamirpet** = **S.C. Dube**.
**Kishan Garhi** = **McKim Marriott** (Village India); **Sripuram** = **Andre Beteille**.
⚠ Shamirpet (near Hyderabad) is the Telugu-region village study — by **Dube**.

115.s: The criteria for identifying Census towns have remained unchanged since:
115.x: Census towns are administratively villages meeting population, male non-farm workforce and density tests; the criteria are unchanged since 1981.
xa: Census town tests: population **≥5,000**, **≥75% of male workers** in non-farm work, density **≥400/sq km**.
The **RGI** is keeping the criteria for **Census 2027**.
**MoHUA** told a parliamentary panel (headed by **Magunta Sreenivasulu Reddy**) the definition is outdated.

115.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the criteria for a census town?
o: At least 75% of male workers engaged in non-agricultural activities
Population density of at least 400 persons per square kilometre
At least 60% of male workers engaged in non-agricultural activities
115.x: A census town must have at least 75%, not 60%, of its male workers engaged in non-agricultural activities, in addition to the population and density criteria.
115.tq: Target the close numerical trap in a three-condition definition.
xs: **60% of male workers** is NOT a census-town criterion — the test is **≥75%** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The three tests are population **≥5,000**, **≥75%** male workers in non-farm work and density **≥400/sq km**.
xa: Criteria unchanged since **1981**; retained for **Census 2027**.
**Statutory towns** are notified by States and run by **ULBs**.

115.s: The urban share of India’s population increased in which of the following sequences?
115.x: India’s urban population share rose from 11% in 1901 to 27.81% in 2001 and 31.16% in 2011.
115.tq: Read the figures in chronological order and reject reversed percentage trends.
xs: India's urban share rose **11% in 1901, 27.81% in 2001 and 31.16% in 2011** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Urban centres rose from **1,827 (1901)** to **7,935 (2011)**.
xa: "Hidden urbanisation": satellite data (DEGURBA) put India about **63%** urban in **2015** (EAC-PM).
**16th Finance Commission** projects urbanisation of **41% by 2031**.
**AP** was **29.47%** urban in 2011 — below India's **31.16%**.

115.s: The concept of ‘hidden urbanisation’ refers to the finding that satellite and built-up data placed India’s urban population at approximately what level in 2015?
115.x: Satellite and built-up data using DEGURBA placed India’s urbanisation at about 63% in 2015, more than double the Census figure of 31%.
115.tq: Compare alternative measurement methods rather than confusing the Census and satellite estimates.
xs: Satellite/built-up data (**DEGURBA**) put India at about **63%** urban in **2015** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is more than double the Census figure of **31%** (**EAC-PM**).
**41%** is the 16th FC's projection for **2031**; **68.8%** is the Census 2011 rural share.
xa: Census 2011 urban share: **31.16%**; urban centres **7,935**.
Criticism: the rural-urban binary leaves fast-urbanising areas under **panchayats** with little fiscal power.
MoHUA called the **Census Town** definition outdated; **RGI** keeps it for **Census 2027**.

115.s: What is the Registrar General of India's position on the Census Town definition?
o: Replacing it with a satellite-based definition for Census 2027
Dropping the Census Town category for Census 2027
Applying it only to Scheduled Areas
115.x: Although criticised as outdated, the Census Town definition is being retained by the Registrar General for Census 2027.
xa: Census towns are **administratively villages** meeting all three tests.
⚠ Census town = **5,000 – 75% – 400**; unchanged since **1981**.
"Hidden urbanisation": satellite data put India about **63%** urban (2015), vs Census **31%**.

115.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Primary urbanisation – Orthogenetic
2. Secondary urbanisation – Heterogenetic
3. Cities of moral order – Technical and commercial centres
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
115.x: Primary urbanisation is orthogenetic and secondary urbanisation heterogenetic; cities of moral order are cultural or temple centres, not technical and commercial centres.
xa: ⚠ Orthogenetic = primary = **moral order**; heterogenetic = secondary = **technical order**.
Technical-order cities: **commercial, administrative, colonial port cities**.
Typology by **Redfield and Singer**; UPPSC 2013 asked primary urbanisation = **Great tradition**.

115.s: Which of the following is a problem associated with urbanisation?
o: End of segregation between rich and poor
115.x: Urban problems include crime with high density, maladjustment, rich-poor segregation and alienation.
xa: Other problems: **lack of social control** and **environmental degradation**.
Caste persists in cities via **slum concentration**, residential segregation and caste job networks.
ES 2025-26: informality is a **structural outcome** of rapid urbanisation.

115.s: The Economic Survey 2025-26 treats urban informality such as slums and informal labour as:
o: A temporary aberration to be eradicated
A structural outcome of urbanisation to be integrated
A result of excess fiscal autonomy of cities
115.x: The Survey sees informality as a structural outcome of rapid urbanisation to be integrated; cities lack fiscal autonomy due to institutional fragmentation.
xa: Informality = **slums, informal labour, unregistered firms**.
**16th FC** raised the ULB share of local-body grants from **36% to 45%**.
ES 2025-26: urban wages **1.7-2 times** rural.

115.s:
Consider the following statements about rural-to-urban migration:
1. Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are the main source States.
2. Monsoon failure and rural unemployment act as push factors.
3. Urban wages are about 3 to 4 times rural wages.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
115.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: urban wages are about 1.7-2 times rural wages. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **UP and Bihar** are the main source States.
Statement 2 correct: **monsoon failure** and **rural unemployment** are push factors.
Statement 3 wrong: ES 2025-26 puts urban wages at **1.7-2 times** rural wages.
xa: Policies against distress migration: **SPMRM (Rurban Mission, 2016)** and **PMEGP** through **KVIC**.
Migration leaves **ageing parents** behind.
About **35%** of rural households lack quality healthcare within **5 km** (ES 2025-26).

115.s: The motto "rural soul, urban amenities", aimed at checking distress migration, is associated with which initiative?
115.x: The Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission (SPMRM, 2016) follows the idea of 'rural soul, urban amenities'. PMEGP is a KVIC-run employment programme. The Smart Cities Mission is an urban scheme. A Census Town is a Census category, not a policy.
xs: "**Rural soul, urban amenities**" is the motto of the **Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission (SPMRM, 2016)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**PMEGP** is an employment programme run through **KVIC**; a **Census Town** is a Census category, not a policy.
xa: Both SPMRM and PMEGP target **distress migration**.
AP: **359 panchayats** classified under the **Rurban** cluster scheme.
Push factors of migration: **monsoon failure**, **rural unemployment**.

115.s: Which of the following is a noted institutional feature of tribal society?
115.x: Tribal society may have a common name and dialect, animism or totemism, youth dormitories and a simple economy.
xa: Other features: territorial community, **claim of common ancestor**, hereditary chieftainship, **clan system**.
**Imperial Gazetteer**: common name, dialect and territory; originally **endogamous**.
Tribe vs peasant: tribe = **subsistence economy**, common control of land and forest.

115.s: As per 2011 data, Andhra Pradesh's urban population share was:
115.x: Andhra Pradesh's urban share was 29.47% in 2011, up from 24.13% in 2001, leaving about 70.5% rural.
xa: AP urban population: **173.5 lakh**, projected **190.9 lakh by 2029**.
**AP has 123 ULBs**.
Urbanisation concentrated in **Visakhapatnam** and **Krishna**.
⚠ **40.81%** is Krishna district's urban share, not the State's.

115.s: Which district was the most urbanised in Andhra Pradesh as per the 2011 figures?
115.x: Visakhapatnam (47.45%) was the most urbanised district, followed by Krishna (40.81%); Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and West Godavari were below India's 1991 level.
xa: Least urbanised: **Srikakulam 16.16%**, **Prakasam 19.56%** (APSES 2024-25 p.182).
28 districts: highest **Visakhapatnam 89.69%**, lowest **Polavaram 2.84%**.
CDI suggests Tier-2 cities (**Kurnool, Ongole, Rajahmundry**) to absorb migration.

115.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Scheduled Tribes in Andhra Pradesh (2011 data)?
o: They formed 5.53% of the State's population
The entire Scheduled Tribe population lived within Scheduled Areas
115.x: Only about 12.9 lakh of the 27.39 lakh tribals lived in the Scheduled Areas.
xa: Scheduled Areas: **16,267.63 sq km (~10.15%)** with **3,512 villages**.
Districts: **Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Anakapalli, Eluru**.
India's ST sex ratio is **990** against the all-India **940**.

115.s: Which of the following districts of Andhra Pradesh has Scheduled Areas?
115.x: Scheduled Areas in Andhra Pradesh lie in Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Anakapalli and Eluru districts.
xa: Scheduled Areas: **16,267.63 sq km (~10.15%)** with **3,512 villages**.
About **12.9 lakh** tribals live in them (APSES 2024-25 p.251).
AP STs: **27.39 lakh = 5.53%**; **34 ST communities**.

115.s:
Which of the following districts were less urbanised in 2011 than India was in 1991?
1. Visakhapatnam
2. Srikakulam
3. West Godavari
Select the correct answer:
115.x: Srikakulam and West Godavari (with Vizianagaram) were below India's 1991 urbanisation level of 22.87%; Visakhapatnam was not.
xa: ⚠ By APSES figures, **Prakasam** (19.56%) was also below it.
Least urbanised: **Srikakulam 16.16%**.
Largest rural population in absolute numbers: **East Godavari** (APPSC-G2 2017).

115.s: Which district had the largest rural population in absolute numbers in Andhra Pradesh?
115.x: East Godavari had the largest rural population in absolute numbers.
115.tq: Separate absolute population from percentage share.
xs: **East Godavari** had the largest rural population in absolute numbers — so option **(4)** is correct (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).
**Srikakulam** is the least urbanised by share, while **Visakhapatnam** and **Krishna** are the most urbanised.
xa: AP is about **70.5% rural** (2011).
AP urban share **29.47%** (2011) vs India's **31.16%**.
Below India's 1991 level (**22.87%**): **Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, West Godavari**.

115.s: Which one of the following criteria for deciding an urban area, according to Census of India, is not correct? All places with:
o: Either a Municipality or Corporation or Cantonment
At least 60% of the male population engaged in non-
A density of population of at least 400 persons per
115.x: All the areas, which include Municipality, Municipal Corporation, Cantonment Board or Notified Town Area Committee come under the urban areas if the following three conditions are satisfied- (1) There must be a minimum population of 5000. (2) A Minimum 75% of working men are engaged in non-agricultural activities, and (3) ‘Population density’ must be at least 400 people per square kilometre.

116.s: Casteism is best described as:
o: A form of occupational specialisation without social hierarchy
A system of universal brotherhood cutting across caste groups
A hereditary social group with a traditional occupation
Discrimination and prejudice against people because of their caste
116.x: Casteism is the evil form of the caste system involving discrimination and prejudice based on caste, along with concentration of power, money and prestige in a few castes.
116.tq: Distinguish the attitude and practice of casteism from the institution of caste.
xs: **Casteism** is **discrimination and prejudice against people because of their caste** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is the **evil form** of the caste system: power, money and prestige **concentrate in a few castes**.
A **hereditary group with a traditional occupation** (option 3) describes **caste** the institution, not casteism.
xa: ⚠ Caste = institution (may exist **without hostility**); casteism = **partisan attitude and practice**.
**Kaka Kalelkar**: casteism = "an overriding, blind and supreme group loyalty".
Casteism produces **discrimination, conflict and vote-bank politics**.

116.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes caste from casteism?
o: Caste is a social structure, whereas casteism is partisan loyalty to one's own caste against others
Caste and casteism are identical terms for hereditary endogamy
Caste rests on political mobilisation, whereas casteism rests on hereditary occupation
Casteism is a social structure, whereas caste is partisan loyalty to one's own caste
116.x: Caste is a social structure of hereditary, endogamous identity; casteism is the attitude of partisan loyalty and using caste for gain.
xa: **Kaka Kalelkar**: casteism = "blind and supreme group loyalty".
Casteism hinders **national integration** and excludes castes from the economy.
**Rajni Kothari** (Caste in Indian Politics, **1970**): politics **politicises** caste.

116.s:
Consider the following statements about endogamy and casteism:
1. Endogamy keeps caste boundaries and the idea of caste 'purity' intact.
2. About a quarter of Indian marriages are now inter-caste.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
116.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: only about 5% of Indian marriages are inter-caste. Hence '1 only'; 'Both' and '2 only' fail on statement 2, 'Neither' fails on statement 1.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **endogamy** keeps caste boundaries and "**purity**" intact.
Statement 2 wrong: only about **5%** of Indian marriages are inter-caste (Aug 2025), not a quarter.
xa: **Dr. Ambedkar Scheme** for inter-caste marriages gives **₹2.5 lakh** per couple to weaken endogamy.
Honour-killing paradox: **TN, Telangana, Maharashtra, Kerala** show more inter-caste unions and more honour killings.
**Lata Singh (2006)**: no bar on inter-caste marriage.

116.s: Which of the following has contributed to the persistence of casteism in electoral politics?
o: Prohibition of caste associations from acting as pressure groups
Complete separation of elections from social identities
Decline of caste-based vote banks and caste associations
Political mobilisation through caste-based vote banks and caste politics
116.x: Caste-based vote banks and caste politics have increased, and caste associations may act as pressure groups in electoral politics.
116.tq: Identify the causal factor rather than an absolute reversal of the trend.
xs: **Political mobilisation through caste-based vote banks and caste politics** keeps casteism alive — so option **(4)** is correct.
Caste-based vote banks have **increased**, and caste associations act as **pressure groups**.
xa: Origin of caste in electoral politics: **Minto-Morley Reforms, 1909** (separate electorates).
**Samajwadi Party** and **RJD** grew out of backward-caste mobilisation.
**Rajni Kothari**: politics **politicises** caste.
TN: **Gounders, Mukkulathors and Vanniyars** used caste solidarity to enter the legislature.

116.s: Which one of the following is NOT a manifestation of caste prejudice in urban areas?
o: Caste associations continuing to operate in cities
Complete disappearance of caste identity among migrants
Caste networks deciding access to informal jobs
116.x: Migrants may carry caste prejudice into cities. Caste networks, caste associations and caste stickers on vehicles may persist, so caste identity does not completely disappear.
116.tq: Find the option using an absolute claim that contradicts the limits of urban anonymity.
xs: **Complete disappearance of caste identity among migrants** is NOT a manifestation — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Migrants carry caste prejudice into cities**; caste networks decide **informal jobs**.
Caste associations and **caste stickers on vehicles** persist (UPSC).
xa: Housing: upper-caste **landlords refuse tenants**; workplace discrimination.
**Caste-based matrimonial sites** are another manifestation.
**UP** banned caste rallies and caste signboards after an **Allahabad HC** directive.

116.s: Kaka Kalelkar defined casteism as:
o: A division of labour based on hereditary occupation
A system of political representation for disadvantaged groups
A voluntary association based on economic interests
An overriding, blind and supreme group loyalty
116.x: Kaka Kalelkar described casteism as “an overriding, blind and supreme group loyalty” that ignores justice, fair play and universal brotherhood.
116.tq: Use the exact wording of a thinker’s definition to avoid look-alike interpretations.
xs: **Kaka Kalelkar** defined casteism as "**an overriding, blind and supreme group loyalty**" — so option **(4)** is correct.
Such loyalty ignores **justice, fair play and universal brotherhood**.
xa: **Ambedkar**: caste is "not just a division of labour, but also a **division of labourers**".
**Rajni Kothari**: politics does not just use caste, it **politicises** it.
Casteism = **partisan loyalty** to one's own caste against others.

116.s: According to B.R. Ambedkar, caste is not merely a division of labour but also a:
116.x: Ambedkar stated that caste is “not just a division of labour, but also a division of labourers.” He argued that it splits the working class and blocks collective bargaining.
116.tq: Test the precise completion of a well-known quotation.
xs: **Ambedkar**: caste is "not just a division of labour, but also a **division of labourers**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
It **splits the working class** and **blocks collective bargaining**.
xa: Ambedkar wrote **Annihilation of Caste (1936)**, Who Were the Shudras? and **Mooknayak**.
He founded the **Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924)**.
He embraced **Buddhism** on **14 Oct 1956** at **Nagpur**.

116.s: Rajni Kothari’s central observation in Caste in Indian Politics (1970) was that:
o: Politics does not just use caste; it politicises caste
Politics merely reflects caste without changing it
Caste has no role in electoral mobilisation
116.x: Rajni Kothari argued that politics does not merely use caste but also politicises it, thereby transforming caste into a political resource.
116.tq: Test the precise distinction between using a social identity and politicising it.
xs: **Rajni Kothari** held that politics **does not just use caste; it politicises caste** — so option **(1)** is correct.
His book **Caste in Indian Politics** appeared in **1970**.
xa: **Kaka Kalelkar**: casteism = "blind and supreme group loyalty".
Political manifestation: **caste-based voting** + caste associations as **pressure groups**.
Parties court caste leaders at every level (**caste arithmetic**).

116.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with B.R. Ambedkar?
116.x: Annihilation of Caste was associated with B.R. Ambedkar and was published in 1936. The other works or organisations belong to Phule, Jashuva and Periyar respectively.
116.tq: Separate the works and dates of four anti-caste thinkers instead of relying on the common theme.
xs: **Annihilation of Caste — 1936** is Ambedkar's — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Satyashodhak Samaj** is Phule's (**1873**); **Gabbilam (1941)** is Jashuva's; **Self-Respect Movement (1925)** is Periyar's.
xa: Ambedkar also wrote **Who Were the Shudras?** and **Mooknayak**.
He founded the **Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924)**.
Embraced **Buddhism**, **14 Oct 1956**, **Nagpur**.

116.s: Periyar E.V. Ramasamy was jailed in 1924 in connection with the:
116.x: Periyar was jailed during the Vaikom Satyagraha (1924) and led the Self-Respect Movement from 1925.
xa: ⚠ **Vaikom (1924)** = Periyar jailed; **Self-Respect Movement** = **1925**.
**Jyotiba Phule**'s **Satyashodhak Samaj** dates to **1873**.
**Sree Narayana Guru**: "**One Caste, One Religion, One God for Man**".

116.s:
Consider the following statements about Sree Narayana Guru:
1. He launched the Self-Respect Movement in 1925.
2. He performed the Aruvippuram Shiva consecration in 1888.
3. He gave the message 'One Caste, One Religion, One God for Man'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
116.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the Self-Respect Movement (1925) was Periyar's. Statements 2 and 3 are correct; he is also linked with the SNDP Yogam. Hence '2 and 3 only'.
116.tq: Self-Respect Movement = Periyar, not Narayana Guru.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 wrong: the **Self-Respect Movement (1925)** was **Periyar**'s.
Statement 2 correct: **Aruvippuram Shiva consecration** in **1888**.
Statement 3 correct: "**One Caste, One Religion, One God for Man**".
xa: He is linked with the **SNDP Yogam**.
⚠ **1888** is also Phule's '**Mahatma**' title.
**Periyar** was jailed in the **Vaikom Satyagraha (1924)**.

116.s: The casteist element in electoral politics in India is traced back to the:
116.x: The casteist element in electoral politics is traced to the Minto-Morley Reforms of 1909, particularly their provision for separate electorates.
116.tq: Distinguish between closely associated constitutional and electoral milestones by year.
xs: The casteist element in electoral politics goes back to the **Minto-Morley Reforms, 1909** — so option **(1)** is correct.
They introduced **separate electorates**.
xa: ⚠ **Communal G.O.** = **1921** (Justice Party), not 1909.
Caste enumeration returns in **Census 2027**; **Bihar caste survey** (2022-23) cited as model.
**Samajwadi Party** and **RJD** grew out of backward-caste mobilisation.

116.s: Which pair of political parties grew out of backward-caste mobilisation?
o: Samajwadi Party and Rashtriya Janata Dal
Bahujan Samaj Party and Telugu Desam Party
Justice Party and Communist Party of India
Indian National Congress and Bharatiya Janata Party
116.x: The Samajwadi Party and the Rashtriya Janata Dal grew out of backward-caste mobilisation.
116.tq: Match the political parties with the social mobilisation from which they emerged.
xs: The **Samajwadi Party** and **RJD (Rashtriya Janata Dal)** grew out of backward-caste mobilisation — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Justice Party** mobilised Reddys, Kammas, Kapus and Velamas against Brahmin dominance in Andhra.
xa: TN: **Gounders, Mukkulathors and Vanniyars** used caste solidarity to enter the legislature.
Origin of caste in elections: **Minto-Morley, 1909**.
Post-**Karamchedu**, Dalits formed independent **Dalit Mahasabhas**.

116.s:
Consider the following statements about the Justice Party era in Andhra:
1. It mobilised Reddys, Kammas, Kapus and Velamas against Brahmin dominance.
2. It won the Communal G.O. in 1909.
3. It laid the ground for these castes' dominance in post-independence Andhra politics.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
116.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Communal G.O. was won in 1921 (1909 is the Minto-Morley Reforms). Hence '1 and 3 only'.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: the **Justice Party** mobilised **Reddys, Kammas, Kapus and Velamas** against Brahmin dominance.
Statement 2 wrong: the **Communal G.O.** was won in **1921**; **1909** is Minto-Morley.
Statement 3 correct: it laid the ground for their dominance in **post-independence Andhra politics**.
xa: AP angle: intermediate-caste (**Reddy/Kamma/Kapu**) political dominance.
**Karamchedu** massacre led Dalits to form independent **Dalit Mahasabhas**.
⚠ **Minto-Morley 1909** = separate electorates; **Communal G.O. 1921** = Justice Party.

116.s: Which of the following pairs about the Dalit response in Andhra Pradesh after the Karamchedu massacre is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Post-Karamchedu Dalit mobilisation – Break from the Congress and the Communists
Post-Karamchedu Dalit mobilisation – Katti Padma Rao and Manda Krishna Madiga
Post-Karamchedu Dalit mobilisation – Independent Dalit Mahasabhas
Post-Karamchedu Dalit mobilisation – Led by the Justice Party against Brahmin dominance
116.x: The post-Karamchedu mobilisation was through independent Dalit Mahasabhas, not the Justice Party's anti-Brahmin movement.
xa: Justice Party won the **Communal G.O. (1921)**.
AP angle: **Reddy/Kamma/Kapu** dominance; Dalit assertion after Karamchedu.
**Gurram Jashuva** (Vinukonda, Guntur) — pioneer of **Telugu Dalit literature**.

116.s: The debate over counting caste in the Census centres on whether it would:
o: Ossify caste identities or expose existing inequity
End reservations or extend them to all castes
Weaken caste associations or ban them
Replace the Census or merge it with the SECC
116.x: The debate is whether caste enumeration would ossify caste identities or instead expose existing inequities for corrective policy.
xa: The **2022-23 Bihar caste survey** is cited as a model.
**Rajni Kothari**: politics **politicises** caste.
Article **17** abolished untouchability.

116.s: In Ghurye's features of caste, the exception to endogamy is:
116.x: Caste involves restricted occupational choice and endogamy, with hypergamy (anuloma) as the exception.
xa: The exception to endogamy is **hypergamy (anuloma)**.
Only about **5%** of Indian marriages are inter-caste (Aug 2025).
⚠ Caste may exist without hostility; **casteism** is the partisan practice.

116.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the UGC Promotion of Equity in Higher Educational Institutions Regulations, 2026?
o: The Supreme Court upheld the Regulations without any stay
They defined caste-based discrimination as discrimination against SC, ST and OBC members
The case arose in the context of student suicides
The case is titled Abeda Salim Tadvi v. Union of India
116.x: The Supreme Court stayed the Regulations in the interim.
xa: Criticism: the SC/ST/OBC-only definition **excluded general-category students**.
National Helpline **14566** for FIRs under the Atrocities Act.

116.s: In Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court directed safe houses for couples to be set up in:
116.x: The Court held khap interference illegal, laid down preventive, remedial and punitive measures, and directed safe houses in every district.
xa: **Tamil Nadu** announced a safe house in each district "in line with" Shakti Vahini.
⚠ **Lata Singh** = **2006**; **Shakti Vahini** = **2018**.
Spouse choice is protected by **Art. 21**.

116.s:
Assertion (A): In Lata Singh v. State of UP (2006), the Supreme Court held there is no bar on inter-caste marriage and directed police to protect such couples.
Reason (R): The case authorised caste panchayats to settle disputes involving consenting adults.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
116.x: A is true. R is false: caste panchayats were not authorised to interfere in marriages of consenting adults.
xa: Shakti Vahini directed **safe houses** in every district.
Choosing a spouse is protected by **Art. 21**.
Inter-caste marriage incentive: **₹2.5 lakh** per couple.

116.s: Which Article of the Constitution abolishes untouchability?
116.x: Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 14 gives equality before law and Article 15 bars caste discrimination.
xa: **PCR Act 1955** and **SC/ST (PoA) Act 1989** penalise untouchability and atrocities.
Spouse choice across caste is protected by **Art. 21**.
Haldwani "**purification**" ritual after Kharge's rally was attacked as **untouchability**.

116.s: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 primarily provide for:
o: Promotion of inter-caste marriages through financial incentives
116.x: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 provide penal safeguards against untouchability and atrocities.
116.tq: Link each statute to its central legal purpose rather than its year alone.
xs: The **PCR Act 1955** and **SC/ST (PoA) Act 1989** **penalise untouchability and atrocities** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Inter-caste marriage incentives come from the **Dr. Ambedkar Scheme** (**₹2.5 lakh**), not these Acts.
xa: National Helpline **14566** handles FIRs under the **Atrocities Act**.
**Art. 17** abolished untouchability.
UP's caste-rally ban **exempted PoA cases**.

116.s: Under the Dr. Ambedkar Scheme for Social Integration through Inter-Caste Marriages, the incentive provided per couple is:
116.x: The scheme provides an incentive of ₹2.5 lakh per couple. It seeks to weaken the practice of endogamy through inter-caste marriages.
116.tq: Use direct numerical recall and distinguish closely spaced monetary figures.
xs: The **Dr. Ambedkar Scheme for Social Integration through Inter-Caste Marriages** gives **₹2.5 lakh** per couple — so option **(3)** is correct.
Its aim is to **weaken endogamy**.
xa: Only about **5%** of Indian marriages are inter-caste.
**PM-DAKSH** = skilling; **Venture Capital Fund for SCs** (2 Sep 2026).
National Helpline **14566** — FIRs under the Atrocities Act.

116.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with a support measure for Scheduled Castes?
o: National Helpline 14566 — Assistance relating to FIRs under the Atrocities Act
Venture Capital Fund for SCs — Safe houses in every district
Ambedkar Overseas Vidya Nidhi — Police protection for khap victims
116.x: National Helpline 14566 relates to FIRs under the Atrocities Act. PM-DAKSH is associated with skilling, the Venture Capital Fund supports SC entrepreneurs, and Ambedkar Overseas Vidya Nidhi supports SC students studying abroad.
116.tq: Start with the sure scheme-function pair and eliminate swapped institutional roles.
xs: **National Helpline 14566** — FIRs under the **Atrocities Act** — is correctly matched — so option **(1)** is correct.
**PM-DAKSH** is for **skilling**; **Ambedkar Overseas Vidya Nidhi** is for SC students abroad.
**Safe houses** come from **Shakti Vahini (2018)**, not the Venture Capital Fund.
xa: **Venture Capital Fund for SCs** (2 Sep 2026).
AP's Vidya Nidhi: **₹36 crore** (2024-25).
Inter-caste marriage incentive: **₹2.5 lakh** per couple.

116.s: The Supreme Court has held that choosing a spouse, including across caste lines, is protected under:
116.x: The choice of a spouse, including the choice to marry across caste, is protected as part of personal liberty under Article 21.
116.tq: Match the constitutional protection with the precise Article rather than a neighbouring fundamental right.
xs: The Supreme Court held that **choosing a spouse**, including across caste, is protected by **Article 21** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Lata Singh v. State of UP (2006)**: no bar on inter-caste marriage; police must protect such couples.
xa: **Shakti Vahini (2018)**: khap interference in marriage of consenting adults is **illegal**.
**Art. 17** abolishes untouchability; **Art. 15(2)** bars denial of access to shops and public places.
⚠ **Lata Singh** = **2006**; **Shakti Vahini** = **2018**.

116.s: Saha Pankti Bhojanam, meaning inter-caste dining, was organised in Andhra Pradesh by:
116.x: AP reformer Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu organised Saha Pankti Bhojanam as an initiative promoting inter-caste dining.
116.tq: Identify the regional reformer by the specific social reform activity.
xs: **Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu** organised **Saha Pankti Bhojanam** (inter-caste dining) in AP — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Sree Narayana Guru** worked in Kerala (**Aruvippuram**); **Periyar** led the **Self-Respect Movement**; **Gurram Jashuva** was a poet (**Gabbilam**).
xa: Jashuva is a pioneer of **Telugu Dalit literature**.
Justice Party won the **Communal G.O. (1921)**.
AP: **Ambedkar Overseas Vidya Nidhi** (**₹36 crore**, 2024-25).

117.s: Which one of the following best distinguishes religious fundamentalism from communalism?
o: Fundamentalism is mainly doctrinal and seeks a return to literal scripture, whereas communalism politically mobilises religious identity against other communities.
Fundamentalism is always directed against another community, whereas communalism reforms one's own community.
Communalism is concerned only with religious doctrine and is unrelated to power or resources.
Fundamentalism and communalism both necessarily involve inter-group conflict.
117.x: Religious fundamentalism is mainly doctrinal, emphasising a return to fundamentals and literal scripture. Communalism is political mobilisation of religious identity against other communities to seek power and resources.
117.tq: Discriminate between look-alike concepts by comparing their direction, objective and method.
xs: **Fundamentalism** is mainly **doctrinal** (return to literal scripture); **communalism** is **political mobilisation of religious identity against other communities** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Fundamentalism is aimed at **reforming one's own community**; communalism at **other communities**, seeking power and resources.
Fundamentalism **can exist without inter-group conflict**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Communalism is **always relational** — "us vs them".
Fundamentalism is often **anti-modern**.
**Political** communalism uses religion for **votes**.

117.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about religious fundamentalism and communalism?
o: Religious fundamentalism is often directed at reforming one's own community.
Communalism constructs an 'us versus them' relationship.
Religious fundamentalism cannot exist without inter-group conflict.
117.x: Fundamentalism can exist without inter-group conflict, so this statement is false; the others are correct.
xa: Fundamentalism = return to "**fundamentals**" and literal scripture.
Communalism seeks **power and resources**.
**Ram Ahuja**: "communal persons" practise politics through religion.

117.s: Which of the following statements about religious fundamentalism is incorrect?
o: It is marked by group inclusiveness.
It involves literal interpretation of scriptures.
It is associated with religious conservatism.
117.x: Option A is incorrect: fundamentalism is marked by group exclusiveness, not inclusiveness. It also involves literal reading of scripture, conservatism and resistance to change.
n: Religious fundamentalism involves group exclusiveness. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Religious fundamentalism involves the literal interpretation of scriptures. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Religious fundamentalism involves religious conservatism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Religious fundamentalism involves resistance to change. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
xs: The incorrect statement is that fundamentalism is marked by **group inclusiveness** — option **(1)**; the notes list **group exclusiveness**.
**Literal interpretation of scriptures**, **religious conservatism** and **resistance to change** are listed features.
xa: Religious fundamentalism = **strict adherence** to religious beliefs; often **rejects modern interpretations**.
Causes: **identity crisis**, **globalization**, **social insecurity**, **political mobilization**, **economic inequalities**.
⚠ Fundamentalism reforms one's **own community** and can exist without inter-group conflict; **communalism** is always "**us vs them**".

117.s:
Which of the following are causes of religious fundamentalism?
1. Identity crisis
2. Group exclusiveness
3. Social insecurity
Select the correct answer:
117.x: Identity crisis and social insecurity (with globalisation) are causes; group exclusiveness is a feature of fundamentalism, not a cause.
n: Identity crisis is a cause of religious fundamentalism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Religious fundamentalism involves group exclusiveness. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]
Globalization is a cause of religious fundamentalism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 64-65]

o: It mandated a State Security Commission.
It directed district nodal officers to prevent mob violence.
It mandated a Police Complaints Authority.
It directed separation of investigation from law-and-order duties.
118.x: District nodal officers against mob violence came from Tehseen Poonawalla (2018), not Prakash Singh.
xa: **Ramji Lal Modi** upheld **Sec. 295A**.
**Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan (2014)**: SC asked the **Law Commission** to define hate speech.
Police inaction and **biased intelligence** are causes of riots.

118.s: Which of the following pairs (case – subject) is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Prakash Singh v. Union of India – Police reforms
Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. Union of India – Police reforms
Ramji Lal Modi v. State of UP – Validity of Section 295A
Tehseen Poonawalla – Nodal officers for mob violence
118.x: Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan concerned the request to define hate speech; police reforms came from Prakash Singh.
xa: Prakash Singh = **2006**; Tehseen Poonawalla = **2018**.
**Law Commission 267th Report** (2017) recommended **harm-based** definitions.

118.s: The Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025 provides for imprisonment ranging from:
118.x: The Bill, described as the first State-level law to define hate speech, provides for two to ten years' imprisonment and covers organisational liability.
xa: Hate speech is **not specifically defined** in central law.
**Law Commission 267th Report** (**2017**) on hate speech.
The **2011** Communal Violence Bill was **never passed**.

118.s: Which statement about Partition is correct?
o: About 40 million people crossed the borders; deaths are estimated at 2 lakh to 20 lakh
About 14–18 million people crossed the borders; death estimates range from 2 lakh to 20 lakh
About 14–18 million people crossed the borders; deaths were uniformly estimated at 2 lakh
Population movement was limited to Punjab and did not affect Bengal
118.x: An estimated 14–18 million people crossed the borders; death estimates range from 2 lakh to 20 lakh, with many historians near 10 lakh.
xa: Partition = **largest forced migration in history** (UPSC).
Police during Partition were **complicit or helpless**.
**Veena Das** (Critical Events) analysed Partition's impact on **women**.

118.s: How many people, mostly kar sevaks, were burnt on the Sabarmati Express near Godhra on 27 February 2002?
118.x: The Godhra train burning killed 59 people, mostly kar sevaks; it was investigated by a Supreme Court-appointed SIT.
xa: **1,169** were killed in the riots that followed.
The **Nanavati-Mehta Commission** (2002) was set up by the **Gujarat govt**.
⚠ **Nanavati** = 1984 anti-Sikh riots; **Nanavati-Mehta** = Gujarat 2002.

118.s: Ghettoisation following communal riots refers to the
o: temporary migration of workers to industrial areas
legal segregation of citizens by the State
movement of communities into religiously segregated neighbourhoods
division of a district into administrative wards
118.x: Ghettoisation is the movement of communities into religiously segregated neighbourhoods after communal violence.
118.tq: Distinguish a social consequence from formal legal or administrative segregation.
xs: **Ghettoisation** = **communities move into religiously segregated neighbourhoods** after riots — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is a social consequence of riots, not legal or administrative division.
xa: **Displacement**: Partition = **largest forced migration in history**.
**Polarisation**: weaker **social capital**, threat to unity in diversity.
**Loss of trust**: guilty of **1984** and **2002** not brought to book.

118.s: Which one of the following is NOT a consequence of communal violence?
o: Loss of faith in the police and courts
Harm to India's global image and diaspora
118.x: Communal violence causes polarisation and weakens social capital; it does not strengthen it.
xa: **Ghettoisation** follows riots.
**Veena Das** analysed gendered violence in **Critical Events**.
Low conviction and case withdrawals **weaken deterrence**.

118.s: Who analysed the impact of Partition and communal riots on women in Critical Events?
118.x: Veena Das analysed the impact of Partition and communal riots on women in her work Critical Events.
xa: Partition = **largest forced migration in history**.
Consequences include **ghettoisation**, **displacement**, **polarisation**.
**National Foundation for Communal Harmony** supports **child victims** of violence.

118.s: The Prevention of Communal and Targeted Violence Bill, 2011 was drafted by the:
118.x: The National Advisory Council drafted the Bill, which was never passed.
xa: **Congress** promised a similar law in **Assam** (2 Apr 2026).
The draft was attacked as **one-sided**.
**Karnataka's 2025 Bill** is the first State-level law to **define** hate speech.

118.s:
Assertion (A): The National Integration Council includes Union ministers, Chief Ministers and eminent persons.
Reason (R): The National Integration Council is chaired by the Union Home Minister.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
118.x: A is correct about the NIC's membership, but R is false: the NIC is chaired by the Prime Minister.
xa: The NIC is criticised as **inactive** (UPSC Polity).
**MHA Guidelines** cover **prevention, containment and response**.
**Home Guards** first raised in **Dec 1946**.

118.s: Home Guards were first raised in December 1946 primarily to
o: help the police control civil disturbance and communal riots
replace the regular police in all districts
118.x: Home Guards were first raised in December 1946 to assist the police in controlling civil disturbance and communal riots.
118.tq: Match the organisation’s origin date with its original operational purpose.
xs: **Home Guards** were first raised in **Dec 1946** to **help the police control civil disturbance and communal riots** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They assist, not replace, the regular police.
xa: **1946** was also the year of **Direct Action Day** and **Noakhali** (Bengal).
**National Integration Council**: chaired by the **PM**.
**NFCH** supports **child victims** and **inter-faith dialogue**.

118.s: Which of the following statements about hate speech in India is correct?
o: It is not specifically defined in Indian law
It is defined exclusively by the Supreme Court
It is specifically and comprehensively defined in the Constitution
It is defined only in the Indian Penal Code and nowhere else
118.x: Hate speech is not specifically defined in Indian law.
118.tq: Distinguish the absence of a specific statutory definition from the existence of provisions that regulate related conduct.
xs: Hate speech is **not specifically defined in Indian law** — so option **(1)** is correct (Mar 2026).
**Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan (2014)**: SC asked the **Law Commission** to define it.
xa: **Law Commission 267th Report (2017)**: harm-based definitions (**incitement + targeting**).
**Karnataka Bill 2025**: first State-level law to **define** hate speech.
Only **20.2%** conviction under **Sec. 153A** (NCRB).

118.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the history of communal incidents in Hyderabad's old city?
o: 1978 — disturbances after the Rameeza Bee case
2007 — beginning of construction of Mecca Masjid
118.x: Hyderabad's old city witnessed notable riots in 1978 after the Rameeza Bee case. Telangana was formed in 2014, Mecca Masjid was completed in 1693, and its blast occurred in 2007.
118.tq: Check the event-year pairing and reject options that attach unrelated historical events to the date.
xs: **1978 — disturbances after the Rameeza Bee case** is correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
**1990** was another riot year, not the mosque's completion (**1693**); Hyderabad has been in **Telangana since 2014**; **2007** is the **blast**, not the start of construction (**1614**).
xa: **Mecca Masjid** was begun by **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah** in **1614**, completed by **Aurangzeb** in **1693**.
**Mecca Masjid blast**: **18 May 2007**; followed by tension and police firing.
Present AP: **riots fell 53.88%** in 2025.

118.s: Who began the construction of Mecca Masjid in Hyderabad in 1614?
118.x: Construction of Mecca Masjid was begun by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah in 1614; it was completed in 1693.
xa: **Mecca Masjid blast**: **18 May 2007** — tension and police firing.
Hyderabad old city riots: **1978** (Rameeza Bee case) and **1990**.
**Sanjeev Balyan** figures in the **Muzaffarnagar** riot case, not Hyderabad.

118.s: According to the AP Home Department's annual note (January 2026), riots in Andhra Pradesh in 2025:
118.x: The AP Home Department's annual note (1 Jan 2026) reported that riots in AP fell by 53.88% in 2025. 20.2% is the NCRB conviction rate under Sec. 153A, and 500% is the reported rise in hate-speech cases between 2014 and 2020. 'Rose by 53.88%' reverses the direction.
xs: AP's **riots fell by 53.88%** in 2025 (AP Home Department note, **1 Jan 2026**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**20.2%** is the NCRB conviction rate under **Sec. 153A**; **500%** is the hate-speech case rise (**2014-2020**).
xa: AP angle: **Hyderabad old-city** history and a **sharp fall** in riots in 2025.
Hyderabad old city riots: **1978** and **1990**.
**Mecca Masjid blast**: **18 May 2007**.

118.s: Which of the following is not true about Justice G. T. Nanavati, who was appointed to enquire into the Godhra train carnage and the Gujarat communal riots?
o: He served as Chief Justice of Karnataka
He served as Chief Justice of Orissa High Court
He served as a member of the Enquiry Commission on the anti-Sikh riots of 1984
He served as Chief Justice of Madras High Court
118.x: Justice G. T. Nanavati is best known for heading the commission that investigated the 2002 Godhra train burning and the subsequent Gujarat riots. He was, however, not a member of the earlier enquiry commission set up to investigate the 1984 anti- Sikh riots, making that statement the incorrect one.

118.s: The Indian National Congress agreed in 1947 to the partition of the country mainly because
o: the principle of Two-Nation theory was then acceptable to them
it was imposed by the British Government and the Congress was helpless in this regard
they wanted to avoid large-scale communal riots
India would have otherwise lost the opportunity to attain freedom
118.x: By 1946–47, communal violence had intensified after Direct Action Day and subsequent riots. Congress leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel accepted Partition as a practical solution to prevent prolonged civil war and bloodshed.

118.s:
With reference to Home Guards, consider the following statements:
1. Home Guards are raised under the Home Guards Act and Rules of the Central Government.
2. The role of the Home Guards is to serve as an auxiliary force to the police in maintenance internal security.
3. To prevent infiltration on the international border/ coastal areas, the Border Wing Home Guards Battalions have been raised in some States.
How many of the above statements are correct?
118.x: Home Guards are a voluntary force to assist the police in controlling civil disturbance and communal riots. They are raised by the State governments under State Acts. Thus the Central Government does not directly raise Home Guards. Hence, Statement 1 is incorrect. In addition to assisting the police in maintaining internal security, home guards can also assist the community in times of emergency such as air raids, fires, cyclones, earthquakes, and epidemics. Various Border Wing Home Guards (BWHG) Battalions have been raised in the border States viz. Punjab, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Meghalaya, Tripura and West Bengal to serve as an auxiliary to the Border Security Force for preventing infiltration on the international border/coastal areas. Hence statements 2 and 3 are correct.

119.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the consequences of regionalism?
o: Balanced development is a negative consequence.
Giving backward regions a voice through regional parties is a positive consequence.
The Tripura TTAADC is cited as an example of intergroup solidarity.
Openings for extremists is a negative consequence.
119.x: Balanced development is listed as a positive consequence of regionalism, not a negative one.
xa: Other positives: cultural pride, **local innovation, accountability**.
Other negatives: **law-and-order breakdowns**, political exploitation, **inter-state disputes**, new linguistic minorities.
Hostility to migrants: **Shiv Sena, MNS**.

119.s:
Assertion (A): Regional sentiment can become a negative feature of regional-party politics.
Reason (R): Regional sentiment may be exploited for electoral votes.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
119.x: Both statements are true, and the exploitation of regional sentiment for votes explains why it can become a negative feature of regional-party politics.
119.tq: Test whether the stated political motive directly explains the identified negative consequence.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A true: regional sentiment can be a **negative** of regional-party politics.
R true and the reason: it may be **exploited for votes**.
xa: Positive side: **backward regions get represented**.
Negatives of regionalism: **parochialism**, **political exploitation**, openings for **extremists**.
Hostility to migrants: **Shiv Sena, MNS**.

119.s: Which one of the following correctly states the linguistic diversity figures associated with demands for linguistic States?
o: 14 official languages and about 1,635 mother tongues
28 official languages and about 2,635 mother tongues
22 official languages and about 1,635 mother tongues
22 official languages and about 635 mother tongues
119.x: The linguistic diversity figures cited are 22 official languages and approximately 1,635 mother tongues. Emotional attachment to language contributed to demands for linguistic States.
119.tq: Check both figures together; changing either the language count or the mother-tongue count makes the option incorrect.
xs: India has **22 official languages and about 1,635 mother tongues** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This **linguistic identity** fed demands for linguistic states.
xa: First linguistic state: **Andhra State**, **1 October 1953**, capital **Kurnool**.
**SR Act 1956**: **14 states + 6 UTs**.
⚠ **14** is the number of states under the 1956 Act, not of official languages.

119.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the causes of regionalism?
o: The sons-of-the-soil feeling is strongest where migrants compete with local agricultural labourers for farm work.
Neglect of sub-regions led to demands for Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Telangana.
Regional kingdoms and British divide-and-rule fed historical memory.
The sons-of-the-soil feeling is strongest where migrants and local educated youth compete for middle-class jobs.
119.x: The sons-of-the-soil feeling is strongest where migrants and local educated youth compete for middle-class jobs, not farm work.
xa: The sons-of-the-soil doctrine grew out of the **job shortage of the 1960s-70s**.
Uneven industrialisation: **Bombay and West Bengal** held **59%** of capital (1948).
UPPSC 2008: all such causes — "**all the above**".

119.s: The Dravida Nadu demand is an example of which form of regionalism?
119.x: Dravida Nadu represents secessionism; Telangana represents a demand for a separate State within the Union.
xa: River disputes: **Cauvery** (TN, KA, KL), **Krishna, Narmada, Ravi**.
⚠ **Secessionism** = out of India; **separatism** = new state inside the Union.
Earlier full-statehood cases: **Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim**.

119.s: Which of the following represents a demand for a new State within the Indian Union rather than secession?
119.x: Uttarakhand sought a new State within the Union; Dravida Nadu, Khalistan and Greater Nagaland were secessionist demands.
xa: Dates: **Dravida Nadu (1960s)**, **Khalistan (1980s)**, **Greater Nagaland (NSCN, 1980)**.
Other separatist cases: **Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Telangana**.
**Autonomy** demands: Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal (since the **1960s**).

119.s:
Consider the following pairs (type of regionalism – meaning):
1. Supra-state – Several States sharing interests
2. Inter-state – Conflict between States
3. Intra-state – A region within a State seeking recognition
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
119.x: All three are correct: supra-state regionalism is States sharing interests, inter-state is conflict between States, and intra-state is a region within a State seeking recognition.
xa: Inter-state boundary disputes: **Maharashtra-Karnataka (Belagavi)**, Assam-Mizoram, Assam-Nagaland.
Intra-state demands led to **Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Telangana**.
Capital dispute: **Chandigarh** (Punjab vs Haryana).

119.s: In 1948, Bombay and West Bengal together held about what share of India's industrial capital?
119.x: Bombay and West Bengal held 59% of capital in 1948, an example of the uneven industrialisation that feeds regionalism.
xa: Exam angle (**UPPSC 2008**): uneven development, fear of losing cultural identity and political prominence are **all** causes.
Neglected sub-regions demanded new states: **Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Telangana**.
Industrialised states now resent acting as **net fiscal donors**.

119.s: The Dar Commission was appointed in:
119.x: The Dar Commission came in 1948, followed by the Visalandhra Mahasabha (1949), Swami Sitaram's fast (1951) and the SRC (1953).
xa: The Dhar Commission (**S.K. Dhar**) **rejected language** as the basis.
**Andhra State** formed **1 October 1953**; this "**Andhra exception**" forced the SRC.
SRC report **1955**: **16 states + 3 territories**.

119.s: Which one of the following correctly states the recommendation of the Dhar Commission?
o: It rejected language as the basis and preferred administrative convenience.
It recommended the immediate creation of states strictly on a linguistic basis.
It recommended the merger of Andhra State with Telangana.
It recommended the creation of 16 states and 3 territories.
119.x: The Dhar Commission rejected language as the basis for reorganising provinces and preferred administrative convenience.
119.tq: Discriminate between the recommendations of the Dhar Commission, SRC and the States Reorganisation Act.
xs: The **Dhar Commission** **rejected language as the basis** and preferred **administrative convenience** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**16 states + 3 territories** was the **SRC** (1955); the merger of Andhra State with Telangana came from the **SR Act 1956**.
xa: Dhar Commission: **1948**, headed by **S.K. Dhar**.
The SRC also **rejected "one language, one state"**.
⚠ SRC report = **16 + 3**; SR Act 1956 = **14 states + 6 UTs**.

119.s: Who was the Chairman of the States Reorganisation Commission appointed in December 1953?
119.x: Fazl Ali chaired the SRC; K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru were its members.
xa: SRC report: **16 states + 3 territories**; rejected "one language, one state".
SR Act 1956: **14 states + 6 UTs**.
The **Andhra exception** (Andhra State, 1953) forced the SRC.

119.s: The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created:
119.x: The 1956 Act created 14 states and 6 UTs; the SRC (1955) had recommended 16 states and 3 territories.
xa: The Act **merged Andhra State with Telangana** → Andhra Pradesh.
SRC: **Fazl Ali**, **K.M. Panikkar**, **H.N. Kunzru**.

119.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 on Andhra Pradesh?
o: It created Telangana as a separate state along with Andhra State.
It divided Andhra State into Andhra and Telangana.
It merged Andhra State with Telangana to form Andhra Pradesh.
It merged Andhra State with Tamil Nadu to form Andhra Pradesh.
119.x: The Act merged Andhra State with Telangana to form Andhra Pradesh.
119.tq: Use the merger relationship and reject the split or wrong-state alternatives.
xs: The **SR Act 1956** **merged Andhra State with Telangana to form Andhra Pradesh** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It did not divide the State; Telangana became separate only in **2014**.
xa: SR Act 1956: **14 states + 6 UTs**.
Andhra State (**1953**) had its capital at **Kurnool**.
**Telangana movements**: **1969** agitation and the **2009-14** phase.

119.s: Andhra State, formed on 1 October 1953 as India's first linguistic State, had its capital at:
119.x: Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953 with Kurnool as its capital. Hyderabad became the capital only after the 1956 merger with Telangana formed Andhra Pradesh; Guntur and Visakhapatnam were never its capital.
xs: **Andhra State** (formed **1 October 1953**) had its capital at **Kurnool** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Hyderabad** became the capital only after the **1956** merger with Telangana.
xa: It was India's **first linguistic state**.
The **SR Act 1956** merged it with Telangana → **Andhra Pradesh**.
**Swami Sitaram's fast** (**1951**) preceded it.

119.s:
Consider the following statements about regional parties in India:
1. They rose prominently in the late 20th century.
2. They commonly demand more powers and funds for states.
3. They reduce the political diversity of Indian federalism.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
119.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: regional parties rose in the late 20th century and demand more powers and funds for states. Statement 3 is wrong: they represent state interests and add political diversity to Indian federalism. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses 2 and options with 3 are wrong.
119.tq: Regional parties add diversity; they do not reduce it.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: regional parties rose in the **late 20th century**.
Statement 2 correct: they demand **more powers and funds** for states.
Statement 3 wrong: they **add political diversity** to Indian federalism.
xa: Leaders: **M.G. Ramachandran** (TN), **N.T. Rama Rao** (AP), **Jyoti Basu** (WB).
Positive: **backward regions get represented**; negative: regional sentiment **exploited for votes**.
Steps to contain regionalism include the **National Integration Council**.

119.s: Which of the following is NOT listed among government steps to contain regionalism?
119.x: The Eleventh Schedule (panchayats) is not among the listed measures; the NIC, Articles 44 and 51A, and the Fifth, Sixth and Eighth Schedules are.
xa: Regionalism's negatives include **inter-state disputes** and **new linguistic minorities**.
India has **22** official languages.
SR Act 1956: **14 states + 6 UTs**.

119.s: In the North-South debate after the defeat of the 131st Amendment Bill, 2026, southern states feared lifting the seat freeze based on the Census of:
119.x: Southern states feared lifting the seat freeze based on the 1971 Census; industrialised states also resented being net fiscal donors.
xa: The debate followed the **131st Amendment Bill, 2026**'s defeat in the **Lok Sabha**.
**Autonomy** demands from TN, Punjab, AP, WB date from the **1960s**.
Regional parties add **political diversity** to federalism.

119.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: First linguistic reorganisation commission – Andhra Movement
First new state of the 2000 reorganisation – Chhattisgarh
First major ethnic movement leading to state formation – 7th Constitutional Amendment, 1956
First amendment addressing regional imbalance indirectly – States Reorganisation Commission, 1953
119.x: Chhattisgarh was the first new state of 2000; the SRC (1953) was the first linguistic reorganisation commission, the Andhra Movement the first ethnic movement to win a state and the 7th Amendment (1956) indirectly addressed regional imbalance.
n: The States Reorganisation Commission was the first Linguistic Reorganisation Commission in 1953. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
The State Reorganisation Commission was first established in 1953. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
The Andhra Movement was the first major ethnic movement leading to state formation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
The Andhra Movement was the first movement leading to linguistic state formation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
Chhattisgarh was the first new State after the 2000 reorganisation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
The 7th Constitutional Amendment of 1956 was the first Constitutional Amendment addressing regional imbalance indirectly. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
xa: **Andhra State** — the **first linguistic state** — formed **1 October 1953**, capital **Kurnool**.
**Potti Sriramulu** was the first to **fast unto death** for a linguistic state.
SRC chair **Fazl Ali**, with **K.M. Panikkar** and **H.N. Kunzru**; report: **16 states + 3 territories**.
⚠ SR Act **1956** created **14 states + 6 UTs** (not 16 + 3).

119.s: The sons-of-the-soil doctrine holds that a State belongs to:
o: All its residents, irrespective of language
Only those born in the State before 1950
Its main linguistic group, with others treated as outsiders however long they have lived there
The Union, which alone decides its cultural identity
119.x: The doctrine treats the main linguistic group as locals and others as outsiders; it grew with the job shortages of the 1960s and 1970s.
xa: **Shiv Sena** (1960s) targeted **South Indians**; **MNS** targeted **North Indians** (**2008**).
**Assam Movement** (**1979-85**) against **illegal immigrants**.
Feeling is strongest where migrants and **local educated youth** compete for **middle-class jobs**.

119.s: In the 1960s, the Shiv Sena's sons-of-the-soil campaign in Maharashtra initially targeted:
119.x: The Shiv Sena of the 1960s targeted South Indians; the MNS targeted North Indians in 2008.
xa: ⚠ **Shiv Sena** = South Indians (1960s); **MNS** = North Indians (2008).
**Mulki rules** — local-residence preference in **Hyderabad/Telangana** jobs.
Anti-Hindi agitations → **two-language formula**.

119.s: The Mulki rules were primarily associated with:
o: Reservation of jobs for Scheduled Tribes in Agency areas
Use of Telugu as the official language
Preference for local residents in jobs in Hyderabad/Telangana
Restriction of land transfers in Scheduled Areas
119.x: The Mulki rules gave local residents preference in jobs in Hyderabad/Telangana and fed the agitations of 1969 and 1972–73.
xa: **Telangana movements**: **1969** agitation and **2009-14** phase → statehood in **2014**.
Sons-of-the-soil doctrine: state belongs to its **main linguistic group**.

119.s: The Anti-Hindi agitations in Tamil Nadu are associated with which outcome?
119.x: The Anti-Hindi agitations of 1937, 1965 and 1986 in Tamil Nadu led to the two-language formula.
119.tq: Distinguish the policy outcome of the language movement from outcomes of other regional movements.
xs: TN's **anti-Hindi agitations** led to the **two-language formula** — so option **(2)** is correct.
They took place in **1937, 1965, 1986**.
The **Mulki rules** are Hyderabad's; **Chandigarh** is a capital dispute; **Greater Nagaland** is secessionist.
xa: **Dravida Nadu** (**1960s**) was a secessionist demand from the same region.
**Autonomy** demands came from TN, Punjab, AP, WB (since the 1960s).
**M.G. Ramachandran** — regional party leader of TN.

119.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about State laws reserving private jobs for locals?
o: AP's 2019 Act reserved 75% of private industrial jobs for locals.
Haryana's 2020 Act was struck down by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in November 2023.
Jharkhand's 2021 Act reserved 75% of lower-salary private jobs.
Haryana's 2020 Act was the first such law in India.
119.x: Andhra Pradesh's 2019 Act was the first such law; Haryana's came in 2020.
xa: Haryana's Act was **struck down by the Punjab & Haryana High Court (Nov 2023)**.
AP's Act was **challenged in the AP High Court**.
⚠ First 75% law = **AP (2019)**; struck down = **Haryana**.

119.s: The Haryana State Employment of Local Candidates Act, 2020 was struck down in November 2023 by which court?
119.x: The Punjab and Haryana High Court struck down the Haryana law in November 2023 as unconstitutional.
119.tq: Discriminate between the State concerned and the court that delivered the ruling.
xs: The **Punjab and Haryana High Court** struck down Haryana's **2020** Act in **Nov 2023** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It held the law **unconstitutional**.
xa: **APPSC-G2 2025** asked which state's 75% quota was struck down — **Haryana**.
Objection: it contradicts **Articles 14, 15, 16 and 19**.

119.s: Under Article 16(3) of the Constitution, a residence requirement for employment under a State may be prescribed only by:
119.x: Article 16(3) allows only Parliament to prescribe a residence requirement (it did so through the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957). The State Legislature, Governor and State PSC have no such power; Article 16(2) otherwise bars discrimination by place of birth or residence.
xs: Under **Art. 16(3)**, only **Parliament** can prescribe a residence requirement — so option **(3)** is correct.
Parliament did so via the **Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957**.
xa: **Art. 16(2)** bars discrimination in public employment on **place of birth and residence**.
States' 75% laws: **AP 2019**, **Haryana 2020**, **Jharkhand 2021**.

Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru)to re-examine the whole demand. It submitted its report in September 1955 and broadly accepted language as the basis of the reorganisation of states but rejected the theory of 'one language-one state' and suggested the abolition of the four-fold classification of states and territories. The Government of India, while accepting these recommendations with certain modifications, enacted the States Reorganisation Act (1956) and the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act (1956). The Act abolished the distinctions among Part A, Part B and Part C states provided by the original Constitution. As a result, 14 states and 6 union territories were created on November 1, 1956.

123.s: Which of the following was a significant departure introduced by the Tendulkar Committee methodology?

It excluded non-food expenditure from the poverty line.
It restored the calorie anchor as the sole basis of poverty estimation.
It dropped the calorie anchor and included health and education expenditure.

123.x: The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 was passed by the Parliament in August, 2005 and came into force on 2 February, 2006. Its name changed to MNREGA on 2nd October 2009. 124.x: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a milestone document in the history of human rights. The UDHR, established on 10 December, 1948 is not a legally binding treaty. It sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected. It contains 30 Articles covering important human rights. Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person (Article 3). Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being (Article 25). 125.s:

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

A is false, but R is true

2. The right to vote in India is a Fundamental Right under Part III of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.

Statement 2 wrong: the **right to vote** is only a **statutory right**, not a Fundamental Right.
xa: The **UDHR** was proclaimed on **10 December 1948** (**Human Rights Day**); it has **30 articles**.

Consider the following statements:
I. The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act became effective in 1990.
II. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was enacted in 2005.
III. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act became effective in 2006.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
125.x: All three are correct: the SC/ST Atrocities Act came into force in 1990, and the Domestic Violence Act was enacted in 2005 and came into force in 2006.
125.tq: Keep each Act's enactment and commencement years apart.
n: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act became effective in 1990. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was enacted in 2005. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act became effective in 2006. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(2)**.
I: the **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act** (**1989**) became **effective** in **1990** (**30 January 1990**) — correct.
II and III: the **Domestic Violence Act** was enacted in **2005** and enforced **26 October 2006** — correct.
xa: The Atrocities Act has **23 sections**.
**Protection of Civil Rights Act**: **1955**; **PESA**: **1996**.
**Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act**: **1986**.

125.s: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA) was enacted in:
125.x: MISA, an internal security statute, was enacted in 1971.
n: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act was enacted in 1971. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The Maintenance of Internal Security Act was an internal security statute. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
xa: **Protection of Civil Rights Act**: **1955**.

125.s: Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits
o: Traffic in human beings and forced labour
125.x: Traffic in human beings and forced labour. Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar). This provision addresses exploitative practices such as human trafficking and bonded labour. It is part of the Right against Exploitation guaranteed under the Fundamental Rights.

125.s:
Which of the following are envisaged by the Right against Exploitation in the Constitution of India?
1. Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
2. Abolition of untouchability
3. Protection of the interests of minorities
4. Prohibition of employment of children in factories and mines
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
125.x: Statements 1 and 4 are correct: Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar (forced labour) and other similar forms of forced labour. Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years in any factory, Indian Polity: Constitutional Framework PMF IAS IP – 16 mine or other hazardous activities like construction work or railway work. But it does not prohibit their employment in any harmless or innocent work. Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect: While these rights are important, they do not form part of the Right against Exploitation. The abolition of untouchability under Article 17 falls within the Right to Equality and prohibits the practice of untouchability in any form. Similarly, the protection of minority interests is provided for in Articles 25 to 30 and mainly concerns the Right to Freedom of Religion and Cultural and Educational Rights.

125.s: Which one of the following is a human right as well as a fundamental right under the Constitution of India?
Which Article under the fundamental rights is directly related to the exploitation of children?

Other than the Fundamental Rights, which of the following parts of the Constitution of India reflect/reflects the principles and provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)?
1. Preamble
2. Directive Principles of State Policy
3. Fundamental duties
Select the correct answer using the given code below:
125.x: Preamble is correct: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution embodies key values such as justice, equality, and liberty, which are also fundamental principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR). It pledges to secure for all citizens justice—social, economic, and political; equality of status and opportunity; and fraternity that upholds individual dignity and national unity. These principles resonate with Articles 1 and 2 of the UDHR, which affirm the inherent dignity and equal rights of all human beings. The Directive Principles of State Policy are correct: Although not legally enforceable, the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) guide the Indian state in establishing a welfare system that fosters social and economic justice. Articles 36 to 51 of the Constitution outline principles such as fair wages, the right to work, education, public health, and protections for children and women. These principles align with several articles of the UDHR, including the rights to work, fair wages, social security, education, and an adequate standard of living.
