This aligns with Article 29 of the UDHR, which asserts that everyone has duties to the community and that the exercise of rights and f

125.s: Which statement is true in relation to the Protection of Human Rights Act?
o: The Act came into force on 23rd September, 1993
The Act came into force on 28th September, 1993
The Act came into force on 23rd September, 1995
The Act came into force on 28th September, 1995
125.x: The Protection of Human Rights Act came into force on the 28th Day of September 1993. It extends to the whole of India.

125.s: When did the Protection of Human Rights Act come into force in India?
125.x: On 28 September, 1993, the Human Rights Protection Act came into force in India. It protects and promotes Human Rights.

125.s: In the definition of armed forces under the Protection of Human Rights Act, which of the following is not included?
125.x: Under the Act, 'armed forces' means the naval, military and air force and includes other armed forces of the Union. Hence Armed Forces of the State are not included in the Act.

125.s: Which of the following rights is not under the purview of the National Human Rights Commission ?
125.x: Section 2(M) of the Human Rights Protection Act, 1993 defines ‘Public Servant’. It shall have the same meaning assigned to the term under Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.

125.s: Every member of the Commission, Sate Commission and every officer appointed or authorized by the Commission or State Commission to exercise functions under the Protection of Human Rights Act is to be deemed
125.x: Every member of the Commission, State Commission and every officer appointed or authorised by the Commission or State Commission to exercise functions under the Protection of Human Rights Act is to be deemed a Public Servant. It is as per the legal definition of Public Servant (Section 21 of IPC)

125.s: An advocate may be specified by the State Government for the purpose of conducting of cases in Human Rights courts as Special Public Prosecutor who has been in practice for not less than :
125.x: Under section 31 in the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, a Special Public Prosecutor for every Human Rights court, the State government shall, by notification, specify a public prosecutor or appoint an advocate who has been in practice as an advocate for not less than 7 years, as a Special Public Prosecutor for the purpose of conducting cases in that court.

125.s: Which of the following is not a Social Act?
125.x: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA) was enacted in 1971 and was repealed in 1977. This Act was enacted for the maintenance of internal security. Thus, it is not a Social Act, while the other three mentioned Acts were enacted for prevention of social evils.

125.s: Bonded Labour was abolished in India, by an Act of Parliament enacted in the year –
125.x: Article 23(1) of the Constitution prohibits the traffic in human beings and forced labour. Any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Ordinance, 1975 was promulgated by the President on 25 October, 1975. To replace the said Ordinance, the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Bill, 1976 was introduced in the Parliament. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Bill, 1976 was passed by both the Houses of Parliament, and it became an Act in 1976.

126.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the legal status of the National Human Rights Commission?
o: A statutory body created under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
A constitutional body established directly under Part III of the Constitution
A judicial body created by the Supreme Court in 1993
An executive body created by a resolution of the Union Cabinet in 1994
126.x: The NHRC is a statutory body created under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; it is not a constitutional body.
126.tq: Distinguish statutory status from constitutional status and identify the enabling legislation.
xs: The **NHRC** is a **statutory body** created under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993** — option **(1)**.
It is **not a constitutional body**, nor a judicial or Cabinet-created body; "constitutional body" and "established 1994" are both wrong (**APPSC 2023**).
xa: It conforms to the **Paris Principles**.
⚠ NHRC (statutory) vs **UPSC/CAG** (constitutional) — the most repeated classification question.
The **NCM** is also statutory (**NCM Act 1992**).

126.s: The establishment of the NHRC conforms to the
126.x: The NHRC was established in conformity with the Paris Principles relating to national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights.
126.tq: Match the institution with the exact international principles associated with its status and functioning.
xs: The NHRC conforms to the **Paris Principles** — option **(2)**.
They are UNGA (**1993**) standards of **independence, pluralism and broad mandate** for national human-rights institutions.
xa: The **PHRA, 1993** was framed in their light.
**GANHRI** accredits NHRIs as **"A"** (fully compliant) or **"B"** based on conformity with them.
NHRC constituted **12 October 1993**.

126.s: Which one of the following statements about constituting a State Human Rights Commission is correct?
o: An SHRC can be constituted only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment.
A State Government may constitute an SHRC under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
Every State Government is constitutionally required to constitute an SHRC.
Only the NHRC can constitute an SHRC.
126.x: Constitution of an SHRC is optional; the State Government may constitute one under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
126.tq: Test the significance of the word ‘may’ by contrasting an optional power with a mandatory duty.
xs: A **State Government "may" constitute an SHRC** under the **PHRA, 1993** — option **(2)**.
Constituting an SHRC is **optional** — not a constitutional duty, and neither Parliament nor the NHRC creates it.
xa: SHRC chair: former **HC Chief Justice or Judge**; **three** members.
SHRC members are **appointed by the Governor** but **removable only by the President**.
Criticism: **optional creation**, advisory powers and **vacancies** weaken SHRCs.

126.s: Who was the first Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission?
126.x: Justice Ranganath Misra was the first Chairperson of the NHRC, constituted on 12 October 1993.
xa: Ordinance: **28 Sept 1993**.
Present Chairperson: **Justice V. Ramasubramanian**.
⚠ "NHRC is a **constitutional body**" is also false (**APPSC-GS 2023**).

126.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Paris Principles?
o: They prescribe the procedure for prosecuting custodial deaths before Human Rights Courts.
They prescribe standards of independence, pluralism and a broad mandate for national human-rights institutions.
They establish the jurisdiction of State Human Rights Commissions over Union Territories.
They classify national human-rights institutions as A or B categories.
126.x: The Paris Principles, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1993, set standards of independence, pluralism and a broad mandate for national human-rights institutions.
126.tq: Match the international principles with their institutional purpose, not with accreditation labels or domestic jurisdiction.
xs: The **Paris Principles** prescribe standards of **independence, pluralism and a broad mandate** for **national human-rights institutions** — option **(2)**.
They were adopted by the **UN General Assembly** in **1993**; the **A/B** grading is done by **GANHRI**, not the Principles.
xa: The **PHRA, 1993** was framed in their light.
**GANHRI** accredits NHRIs as **"A"** (fully compliant) or **"B"**.
UT functions of SHRCs are conferred by the **Central Government** (**2019**) — unrelated to the Principles.

126.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the constitutional status of the institutions listed below?
o: NHRC is statutory, whereas UPSC and CAG are constitutional bodies.
NHRC and UPSC are constitutional, whereas CAG is statutory.
NHRC, UPSC and CAG are all statutory bodies.
NHRC is constitutional, whereas UPSC and CAG are statutory.
126.x: The NHRC is a statutory body, while the Union Public Service Commission and the Comptroller and Auditor General are constitutional bodies.
126.tq: Split the options by classification and watch for the statutory–constitutional reversal.
xs: The **NHRC is statutory**, whereas **UPSC and CAG** are **constitutional** — option **(1)**.
This is the **most repeated classification question**.
xa: The NHRC was created by the **PHRA, 1993**.
"NHRC is a constitutional body" was keyed **false** in **APPSC-GS 2023**.
The **NCM** is also statutory (**NCM Act 1992**).

126.s:
Assertion (A): After the 2019 amendment, the NHRC has seven deemed members.
Reason (R): The 2019 amendment added the Chairpersons of the NCBC and NCPCR and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities to the four existing deemed members.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
126.x: Adding these three heads to the four earlier deemed members made seven, so R explains A.
xa: Deemed members before 2019: chairpersons of **NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCW**.
**NCSC and NCST** chairpersons were themselves added by the **2006** amendment.

126.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the composition of the NHRC?
o: It includes one former or serving Judge of the Supreme Court.
At least one woman must be among its human-rights experts.
It includes one former or serving Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court.
It includes two persons having knowledge of human rights.
126.x: The NHRC includes three persons with knowledge of human rights, at least one of whom must be a woman.
xa: Chairperson: former **CJI or SC Judge**.
Deemed members: chairpersons of **NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCW** + (2019) **NCBC, NCPCR, CCPD**.
Appointment by the **President** on a **PM-led six-member committee's** recommendation.

126.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about deemed members of the NHRC?
o: The NCSC and NCST Chairpersons became deemed members through the 2006 amendment.
Only the Chairpersons of the commissions concerned are deemed members.
A deemed member is identical in status to an ordinary NHRC member.
The NCBC Chairperson was added as a deemed member in 2019.
126.x: The deemed-member provision does not convert the Chairpersons into ordinary NHRC members.
xa: Before 2019: **4** deemed members; after 2019: **7**.
2019 additions: **NCBC**, **NCPCR**, **Chief Commissioner for PwDs**.
The 2006 amendment also cut SHRC size from **five to three**.

126.s: Which one of the following statements about the pre-2019 and post-2019 composition of the NHRC is correct?
o: The number of human-rights experts fell from three to two after 2019.
Before 2019, only a former CJI was eligible as Chairperson; after 2019, a Supreme Court Judge was also included.
Before 2019, the Chairperson could be any Supreme Court Judge, but after 2019 only the former CJI was eligible.
The number of deemed members fell from seven to four after 2019.
126.x: Before 2019, the Chairperson had to be a former Chief Justice of India. After 2019, a Judge of the Supreme Court was also eligible; the number of human-rights experts and deemed members increased.
126.tq: Compare the direction of each amendment and reject options that reverse the change.
xs: Before **2019** only a former **CJI** could chair; after 2019 a **Judge of the Supreme Court** is also eligible — option **(2)**.
Option (3) reverses this; human-rights experts **rose** from two to three and deemed members **rose** from **4** to **7**.
xa: The term changed from **5 years or 70** to **3 years or 70**.
SHRC chair widened from HC **Chief Justice** only to **CJ or Judge** of a High Court.
The **5-year reappointment limit** was removed.

126.s: A sitting Judge of the Supreme Court or a sitting Chief Justice of a High Court can be appointed to the NHRC only after consultation with the
126.x: Appointment of a sitting Supreme Court Judge or a sitting High Court Chief Justice requires consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
126.tq: Test the mandatory consultation requirement by asking which authority is specifically associated with judicial appointments.
xs: A sitting **SC judge** or **HC Chief Justice** is appointed only **after consulting the Chief Justice of India** — option **(1)**.
The CJI is consulted but is **not** on the selection committee.
xa: For an SHRC, a sitting HC judge or district judge needs consultation with the **Chief Justice of the High Court**.
Selection committee: **PM** (chair), **Speaker**, **Deputy Chairman of RS**, **LoPs** of both Houses, **Home Minister**.
Appointment is by the **President** (APPSC **2025**).

126.s: A member of the NHRC submits a written resignation during the tenure of office. To whom should it be addressed?
126.x: A Chairperson or member of the NHRC resigns by writing addressed to the President of India.
126.tq: In an authority-based scenario, ask who receives the formal resignation rather than who recommends the appointment.
xs: An NHRC member resigns in writing **to the President of India** — option **(1)**.
SHRC members resign **to the Governor** (both under the **2006 amendment**).
xa: The **President** also appoints and removes NHRC members.
Term: **3 years or age 70**, whichever earlier.
After office: **ineligible for further employment** under Centre or States.

126.s: For removal of the NHRC Chairperson on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, the President refers the matter to the:
126.x: The President refers such cases to the Supreme Court for inquiry; grounds like insolvency allow direct removal by the President.
xa: SHRC members too are **removable only by the President** on the same grounds.
Resignation: NHRC → **President**; SHRC → **Governor**.
Appointment: **President** on a **PM-led** committee's recommendation.

126.s: After demitting office, the Chairperson or a member of the NHRC is
o: eligible for employment under either the Central or State Government without restriction
ineligible for further employment under the Central or any State Government
eligible for any post under the Central Government but not under a State Government
eligible only for judicial employment under the Central Government
126.x: The Chairperson and members are not eligible for further employment under the Central Government or any State Government after leaving office.
126.tq: Watch for the reversed distinction between post-tenure ineligibility and eligibility for government employment.
xs: After office the Chairperson or member is **ineligible for further employment** under the **Central or any State Government** — option **(2)**.
However, they are **eligible for reappointment** to the Commission.
xa: Term: **3 years or age 70** (since **2019**).
⚠ "Member is not eligible for re-appointment" is the **wrong** statement (MPPSC).
The **5-year reappointment limit** was removed in 2019.

126.s: The Chairperson and members of the NHRC are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Prime Minister. Which one of the following is NOT a member of that committee?
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
126.x: The six-member committee is the Prime Minister (chair), Speaker of the Lok Sabha, Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, Leaders of Opposition in both Houses and the Union Home Minister. The Chief Justice of India is not a member; he is only consulted before a sitting SC Judge or HC Chief Justice is appointed.
126.tq: Appointed by President; PM-led 6-member committee; CJI only consulted.
xs: The **Chief Justice of India** is not a member of the committee — option **(4)**.
The committee: **PM** (chair), **Speaker of Lok Sabha**, **Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha**, **Leaders of Opposition** in both Houses, **Union Home Minister**.
The CJI is only **consulted** before a sitting SC judge or HC Chief Justice is appointed.
xa: SHRC committee: **CM** (chair), Assembly **Speaker**, **State Home Minister**, **LoP**; plus Council Chairman and LoP in bicameral States.
A **vacancy** in the committee does not invalidate its decisions.
Members are **removed by the President**.

126.s: The Chairperson of a State Human Rights Commission can be removed only by the:
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
126.x: The Governor appoints the SHRC Chairperson, but only the President can remove them.
xa: Resignation is addressed **to the Governor** (**2006**).
Selection committee is headed by the **Chief Minister**.
⚠ Both NHRC and SHRC chairs are **removed by the President**.

126.s: The selection committee for a State Human Rights Commission is headed by the:
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
126.x: The Chief Minister chairs it, with the Speaker, State Home Minister and Leader of Opposition; the High Court Chief Justice is only consulted.
xa: SHRC members are **appointed by the Governor**.
On a vacancy, the **Governor** may authorise a member to act as Chairperson.
A **vacancy** in a committee does not invalidate its decisions.

126.s: After the 2006 amendment, a State Human Rights Commission consists of how many members, including the Chairperson?
126.x: The 2006 amendment reduced it from five to three: the Chairperson, a judicial member and a person with human-rights knowledge or experience.
xa: SHRC chair: former **HC Chief Justice or Judge** (since **2019**).
The 2006 amendment also enabled the NHRC to **transfer complaints** to SHRCs.
SHRCs in rich States get only **80 paisa per capita**; several have **over 40% vacancies**.

126.s: Which of the following pairs relating to State Human Rights Commissions is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Inquiry powers – Same civil-court powers as the NHRC
126.x: An SHRC has no power to punish violators or enforce its recommendations as decrees; they are advisory.
xa: SHRC jurisdiction: subjects in the **State List** and **Concurrent List**.
The SHRC sends its **annual report** to the **State Government**; laid before the **State Legislature**.
"**Toothless tiger**" criticism: non-binding advice, one-year bar, armed-forces limit.

126.s: A State Human Rights Commission inquires into violations relating to subjects in the:
126.x: An SHRC covers the State and Concurrent Lists; the NHRC covers all subjects.
xa: **UTs (2019)**: the **Central Government may confer** a UT's functions on an SHRC; **Delhi** is handled by the NHRC.
An SHRC will **not inquire** into a case already before the NHRC or another statutory commission.
The **2006 amendment** lets the NHRC **transfer complaints** to SHRCs.

126.s: Which of the following is correct about overlapping complaints before the NHRC and an SHRC?
o: An SHRC may inquire into a case already pending before the NHRC.
The NHRC may take up a matter pending before an SHRC.
The NHRC and an SHRC may inquire simultaneously into the same matter.
An SHRC will not inquire into a case already being inquired into by another statutory commission.
126.x: The arrangement bars simultaneous inquiry by the SHRC, NHRC or another statutory commission into the same pending matter.
xa: The **2006 amendment** enabled the NHRC to **transfer complaints** to the concerned SHRC.
Matters **sub judice** are not taken up.
The NHRC's purview is limited to violations by **public servants**.

126.s: The NHRC cannot inquire into a matter after how long from the date of the alleged act?
126.x: The NHRC is barred after one year from the alleged act; a review committee wanted this relaxed where sufficient cause exists.
xa: The **SHRC** is subject to the same **one-year bar**.
⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces).
The time bar is part of the "**toothless tiger**" criticism.

126.s: GANHRI accredits:
126.x: GANHRI accredits national human-rights institutions ('A' for fully compliant, 'B' for others), based on independence and effectiveness.
xa: Paris Principles: UNGA, **1993**.
The **NHRC** was set up in conformity with the Paris Principles.
The NHRC is a **statutory body** under the **PHRA, 1993**.

126.s: In the Gade Sai Krishna custodial-death case, the NHRC directed which combination of authorities to submit a report?
o: The Union Home Ministry, DGP and District Collector
The State Election Commission, DGP and Chief Justice of the High Court
The Governor, Speaker and Advocate-General of Andhra Pradesh
The Andhra Pradesh SHRC, DGP and Chief Secretary
126.x: In the Gade Sai Krishna case, the NHRC directed the Andhra Pradesh SHRC, the Director General of Police and the Chief Secretary to report.
126.tq: Use the authority-and-function trap by distinguishing reporting authorities from constitutional offices.
xs: The NHRC directed the **AP SHRC**, **DGP** and **Chief Secretary** to report — option **(4)**.
It took cognisance of the alleged **custodial death** of **Gade Sai Krishna** (**28 Jun 2026**).
xa: Reports were sought **within a week**.
Custodial deaths must be reported to the NHRC within **24 hours**.
Other safeguards: **post-mortem videography**, **independent investigation**.

126.s: Which of the following statements regarding the NHRC's High-Level Selection Committee is incorrect?
o: The committee consists of six members, including the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the Selection Committee
The President of India appoints the NHRC based on the committee's recommendations
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is a member of the Selection Committee
126.x: Option D is incorrect: the Rajya Sabha's Deputy Chairman, not its Chairman, sits on the NHRC selection committee. The Prime Minister chairs the six-member committee, and the President appoints on its advice.
126.tq: Recall the NHRC selection committee's members.
n: The President of India appoints the NHRC Chairperson and members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The President of India makes appointments to the NHRC based on the recommendations of a six-member High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Deputy Chairman represents the Rajya Sabha on the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** is a committee member — option **(4)**.
The **Deputy Chairman** of the Rajya Sabha represents the House on the **six-member** committee.
The **Prime Minister** chairs it, the **Speaker** of the Lok Sabha sits on it, and the **President** appoints on its recommendation.
xa: Other members: **Union Home Minister**, **Leaders of the Opposition** in both Houses.
A **vacancy** in the committee does not invalidate its decisions.
SHRC committee is headed by the **Chief Minister**; SHRC members are **removable only by the President**.
First NHRC Chairperson: **Justice Ranganath Misra**.

126.s: Under the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019, reappointment of NHRC members:
o: is limited to the Chairperson for one further term
is barred after the first term
is permitted, the earlier five-year limit having been removed
needs a compulsory gap of five years
126.x: The 2019 amendment removed the earlier five-year limit, so members remain eligible for reappointment, subject to the 3-year/70 term.
xa: Term after 2019: **3 years or 70**.
⚠ "Member is not eligible for re-appointment" is the wrong statement (MPPSC).
After office: **ineligible for further government employment**.

126.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019?
o: It reduced the term of NHRC members to three years or the age of 70.
It allowed a former High Court Judge to be SHRC Chairperson.
It raised the deemed members of the NHRC from four to seven.
It made members ineligible for reappointment.
126.x: The 2019 amendment removed the five-year limit on reappointment, so members remain eligible for reappointment.
xa: The **2019** amendment also raised human-rights members to **three**, at least **one woman**.
NHRC chair: former **CJI or SC Judge** (earlier only former CJI).
The **2006** amendment cut SHRC size from **five to three**.

126.s: The NHRC can intervene in court proceedings involving human-rights allegations with the approval of the:
126.x: It needs the approval of the court concerned, not the Central Government.
xa: Since 2006 it may also recommend **interim relief even during inquiry**.
2006 also enabled the NHRC to **transfer complaints** to the concerned SHRC.
Custodial deaths must be reported within **24 hours**.

126.s: With reference to the Chairperson of a State Human Rights Commission, which one of the following is correct?
o: He resigns by writing addressed to the Governor and holds office for 3 years or till 70, whichever is earlier.
He resigns by writing addressed to the President and holds office for 5 years or till 65.
He resigns by writing addressed to the Chief Minister and holds office for 3 years or till 70.
He resigns by writing addressed to the Chief Justice of the High Court and holds office for 5 years or till 70.
126.x: Since 2006 the SHRC Chairperson resigns in writing to the Governor, and since 2019 the term is 3 years or 70, whichever is earlier. The President only removes (and receives NHRC resignations); the Chief Minister heads the selection committee; the High Court Chief Justice is only consulted on sitting judges.
126.tq: SHRC: appointed by Governor, resigns to Governor, removed by President.
xs: The SHRC chair resigns **in writing to the Governor** and holds office for **3 years or till 70**, whichever earlier — option **(1)**.
The **President** receives **NHRC** resignations; **5 years** was the pre-**2019** term.
xa: Resignation rule from the **2006 amendment**; term rule from **2019**.
Removal of the SHRC chair is **only by the President**.
The **CM** heads the selection committee; the HC Chief Justice is only consulted.

126.s: The 2006 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act enabled the NHRC to:
o: Convert every district court into a Human Rights Court
Transfer all NHRC members to State service
Transfer complaints to the concerned SHRC
126.x: The 2006 amendment enabled the NHRC to transfer complaints to the concerned State Human Rights Commission.
126.tq: Identify the precise transfer power and reject broader institutional powers not stated in the law.
xs: The **2006 amendment** enabled the NHRC to **transfer complaints** to the concerned **SHRC** — option **(4)**.
It gave no power to dissolve SHRCs or move members; **Human Rights Courts** are notified by the State Govt under the PHRA.
xa: Other 2006 changes: **NCSC and NCST** chairs as deemed members; jail visits **without intimating the State Govt**.
Also: **interim relief** even **during inquiry**; SHRC cut from **five to three**.
Resignation: NHRC → **President**, SHRC → **Governor**.

126.s: Which of the following is a power of the NHRC?
o: Visiting jails to study inmates' living conditions
Unrestricted investigation of the armed forces
126.x: The NHRC may visit jails and has civil-court powers, but its recommendations are advisory and it cannot directly investigate the armed forces.
n: The NHRC has all the powers of a civil court while inquiring into complaints. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC visits jails and detention centres to study the living conditions of inmates. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The recommendations of the NHRC are advisory in nature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The recommendations of the NHRC are recommendatory in nature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC does not directly execute criminal sentencing. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC does not have direct or unrestricted investigative powers over the armed forces. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC suggests reforms based on its study of jail and detention-centre conditions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The NHRC does not act as a regular court of law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
xa: **Time bar**: no inquiry **after one year** from the alleged act.
⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces).
Since **2006**, NHRC may visit jails **even without intimating the State Govt**.

126.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about how the NHRC may take up an inquiry?
o: It may take suo motu cognisance.
It may inquire into a complaint solely against a private individual with no public servant involved.
It may act on a petition presented to it.
It may act on a direction of a court.
126.x: The NHRC's jurisdiction concerns violations or negligence by public servants, so a purely private complaint is outside it.
xa: It may **intervene** in court proceedings with the **court's approval**.
Time bar: no inquiry **after one year** from the alleged act.
Sub judice matters are not taken up.

126.s: While inquiring into complaints, the NHRC has the powers of a:
126.x: The NHRC has civil-court powers such as summoning persons, examining them on oath, requiring documents and requisitioning public records.
xa: It can also **receive evidence on affidavit**.
The **SHRC** has the same inquiry powers.
Yet it has **no power to punish** violators.

126.s: With respect to relief, the National Human Rights Commission may:
o: Grant relief only after a criminal court records conviction
Recommend compensation and interim relief, including during the inquiry
Punish the public servant and recover the amount directly
Award final compensation in every case without recommendation
126.x: The NHRC may recommend compensation, prosecution and interim relief. Since the 2006 amendment, it may recommend interim relief even during the inquiry.
126.tq: Apply the distinction between recommending relief and directly awarding or enforcing it.
xs: The NHRC may **recommend compensation and interim relief**, including **during the inquiry** — option **(2)** (since **2006**).
It cannot itself **punish** or award final compensation; it only recommends.
xa: It may also recommend **prosecution**.
Government must inform it of **action taken within one month**.
Armed forces: Centre informs it of action within **three months**.

126.s: The Supreme Court entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the implementation of which law in 1997?
o: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
126.x: In 1997, the Supreme Court entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
126.tq: Pair the judicial direction with the exact statute rather than a neighbouring social-justice law.
xs: In **1997** the SC entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the **Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976** — option **(3)**.
It is one of the NHRC's **specialised mandates**, alongside custodial and encounter deaths.
xa: **Custodial deaths**: report within **24 hours**; post-mortem videography.
**Encounter deaths**: reporting + magisterial inquiry per **PUCL v Maharashtra (2014)**.
**Transgender welfare**: **Advisory 2.0** (May **2026**).

126.s: In cases of custodial death, information is required to be reported to the NHRC within what period?
126.x: Custodial deaths are to be reported to the NHRC within 24 hours; post-mortem videography and independent investigation are also associated safeguards.
126.tq: Test the exact reporting deadline using nearby but distinct time intervals as distractors.
xs: Custodial deaths must be reported to the NHRC within **24 hours** — option **(3)**.
Other safeguards: **post-mortem videography** and **independent investigation**.
xa: **Gade Sai Krishna** case: NHRC directed the **AP SHRC**, DGP and Chief Secretary to report within a week (**28 Jun 2026**).
**Encounter deaths**: magisterial inquiry (**PUCL v Maharashtra, 2014**).
SC (**1997**): NHRC monitors the **Bonded Labour** Act, **1976**.

126.s: After the NHRC sends its inquiry report with recommendations, the Government concerned must inform the Commission of the action taken within:
126.x: The Government must inform the Commission of the action taken on its report within one month. Three months is the period for the Central Government to report action in armed-forces cases; six months and one year are not the prescribed periods (one year is the time bar for inquiry).
126.tq: Action taken: 1 month (general), 3 months (armed forces).
xs: The Government must inform the NHRC of **action taken within one month** — option **(1)**.
**Three months** applies to the Centre in **armed-forces** cases; **one year** is the **time bar** for inquiries.
xa: ⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces); time bar **one year**.
Recommendations are **advisory**.
NHRC annual report is laid before **each House of Parliament** with a memorandum of action taken.

126.s: Which of the following correctly describes the position regarding Union Territories after the 2019 change?
o: Every Union Territory must constitute an independent SHRC, including Delhi.
The Central Government may confer the human-rights functions of a Union Territory on an SHRC, while Delhi’s functions are handled by the NHRC.
Only the concerned State Government may confer Union Territory functions on an SHRC.
The NHRC has no role in the human-rights functions of Union Territories.
126.x: The Central Government may confer the human-rights functions of a Union Territory on an SHRC. Delhi’s human-rights functions are handled by the NHRC itself.
126.tq: Ask who holds the power and then distinguish Delhi’s special position from the general rule.
xs: The **Central Government may confer** a **UT's** human-rights functions on an **SHRC**; **Delhi's** functions are handled by the **NHRC** — option **(2)** (**2019**).
So UTs need not set up their own SHRC, and the NHRC does have a role.
xa: SHRC jurisdiction: **State List** and **Concurrent List** subjects.
SHRCs are **optional** — a State Government "may" constitute one.
No overlap: SHRC and NHRC do not inquire into the same pending matter.

126.s: While dealing with complaints of human-rights violations by members of the armed forces, the NHRC may:
o: Order the State Government to prosecute the personnel compulsorily
Directly punish the personnel concerned after a summary trial
Transfer the matter to any private tribunal for final adjudication
Seek a report from the Central Government and make recommendations
126.x: In armed-forces cases, the NHRC may seek a report from the Central Government and make recommendations. Its powers are more restricted than in ordinary public-servant cases.
126.tq: Ask which authority supplies the report and avoid attributing direct punitive power to the Commission.
xs: In **armed-forces** cases, the NHRC may only **seek a report from the Central Government** and **make recommendations** — option **(4)**.
It cannot punish, order prosecution or send matters to a private tribunal.
The **Centre** informs it of action within **three months**.
xa: "Armed forces" = **naval, military and air forces**, incl. other armed forces of the Union (**Sec. 2**).
The armed-forces limit is part of the "**toothless tiger**" criticism.
In ordinary cases, the action-taken report is due within **one month**.

126.s: In cases concerning the armed forces, the Central Government is required to inform the NHRC of the action taken within:
126.x: In armed-forces cases, the Central Government must inform the NHRC of the action taken within three months.
126.tq: Distinguish the armed-forces response period from the general one-month reporting period.
xs: In **armed-forces** cases the Centre must inform the NHRC of action taken within **three months** — option **(2)**.
**One month** is the general action-taken period; **one year** is the time bar for inquiries.
xa: ⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces); time bar **one year**.
In armed-forces cases the NHRC may only **seek a report from the Central Government** and recommend.
"Armed forces" = **naval, military and air forces**, incl. other armed forces of the Union (**Sec. 2**).

126.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the legal effect of recommendations made by the NHRC?
o: They can be ignored without any communication to the Commission.
They are advisory, although the Government must respond to the Commission.
They are binding decrees enforceable as judgments of a civil court.
They automatically impose criminal liability on the public servant.
126.x: NHRC recommendations are advisory and cannot be compelled as binding orders. The Government is required to inform the Commission of the action taken.
126.tq: Distinguish an advisory recommendation from an enforceable judicial order.
xs: NHRC recommendations are **advisory**, though the **Government must respond** — option **(2)**.
They are **not binding** decrees and impose no criminal liability; the Government **cannot be compelled**.
xa: Government must inform the Commission of **action taken within one month**.
The NHRC has **no power to punish** violators — it only **recommends** compensation or prosecution.
Non-binding advice is part of the "**toothless tiger**" criticism.

126.s: The annual report of a State Human Rights Commission is submitted to the State Government and thereafter laid before the:
o: Parliament with a memorandum of action taken
State Legislature with a memorandum of action taken
126.x: The SHRC submits its annual report to the State Government, which lays it before the State Legislature along with a memorandum of action taken.
126.tq: Track the reporting chain and distinguish the State Legislature from Parliament.
xs: The SHRC's **annual report** goes to the **State Government** and is laid before the **State Legislature** with a **memorandum of action taken** — option **(3)**.
**Parliament** receives the **NHRC** report, not the SHRC's.
xa: NHRC report goes to the **Central Govt** (and State Govt concerned) and is laid before **each House of Parliament**.
Older notes say the NHRC report goes "to the **President**".
SHRC powers mirror the NHRC's — **civil court** powers, **one-year** bar, **advisory** nature.

126.s: The Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission is constituted by:
o: Parliament under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014
The Andhra Pradesh Government under the PHRA, 1993
126.x: The AP SHRC is constituted by the Andhra Pradesh Government under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
xa: Constituting an SHRC is **optional** — a State Government "**may**" constitute one.
SHRC chair: former **HC Chief Justice or Judge**; appointed by the **Governor**.
SHRC jurisdiction: **State List** and **Concurrent List** subjects.

126.s: The NHRC is criticised as a 'toothless tiger' mainly because:
o: It lacks civil-court powers during inquiries
It is not a statutory body
126.x: The criticism rests on its non-binding advice, along with the one-year bar and limits on armed-forces complaints.
xa: The NHRC has **no power to punish** violators.
**Allahabad HC** said the NHRC exceeded its mandate by directing an EOW probe into **558** aided madrasas (**30 Apr 2026**).
SHRCs are weakened by **optional creation**, **advisory powers** and **vacancies**.

126.s: When was the Human Rights Commission of India constituted?
126.x: The National Human Rights Commission was constituted in 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, establishing India's primary statutory body dedicated to investigating human rights violations.

126.s: According to the National Human Rights Commission Act, 1993, who amongst the following can be its chairman?
o: Any serving Judge of the Supreme Court
Any serving Judge of the High Court
Only a retired Chief Justice of India
Only a retired Chief Justice of High Court
126.x: Originally, the NHRC Chairperson had to be a retired Chief Justice of India. After the 2019 amendment, eligibility expanded to include any former Supreme Court Judge. Thus, appointment of serving judges or retired High Court Chief Justices is not allowed, and option 3 reflects the earlier rule but is no longer exclusively correct.

126.s:
Consider the following organisations/bodies in India:
1. The National Commission for Backward Classes
2. The National Human Rights Commission
3. The National Law Commission
4. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
How many of the above are constitutional bodies?
126.x: The National Commission for Backward Classes is a constitutional body: It was set up in 1993 by an act of Parliament. The 102 nd Amendment Act of 2018 gave constitutional status to the. NCBC. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is not a constitutional body: It is a statutory body constituted under the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993, which was later amended by the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA) 2006. The National Law Commission is not a constitutional body: The Law Commission of India (executive body) is a non-statutory body and is constituted by a notification of the Government of India, Ministry of Law and Justice, Department of Legal Affairs, with a definite set of terms of reference to carry out research in the field of law. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission is not a constitutional body: It is a statutory body established in 1988 under the Consumer Protection Act (CPA) 1986. It is headed by a sitting or a retired Judge of the SC or a sitting or a retired CJHC. Jurisdiction: To entertain a complaint valued at more than two crores and Appellate and Revisional jurisdiction from the orders of the State Commissions or the District Commissions.

126.s: According to the National Human Rights Commission Act, 1993 who amongst the following can be its Chairman?
o: Any Serving Judge of the Supreme Court
Any Serving Judge of the High Court
Only a retired Chief Justice of India
Only a retired Chief Justice of a High Court
126.x: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India was established on 12 October, 1993. Justice Ranganath Misra was the first president of NHRC and his tenure in office was from 12 October, 1993 to 24 November, 1996.

126.s: Who presides over the committee constituted for the appointment of members of the State Human Rights Commission?
126.x: According to Section 22 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, the Chairperson and Members shall be appointed by the Governor after obtaining the recommendation of a Committee consisting of (a) the Chief Minister-chairperson; (b) Speaker of the Legislative Assembly-member, (c) Minister in-charge of the Department of Home in that Statemember; (d) Leader of the Opposition in the Legislative Assembly-member: and where there is a Legislative Council in a State, the Chairman of that Council and the Leader of the Opposition in that Council shall also be members of the Committee.

126.s: Who is not a member of the committee for the appointment of Chairperson and members of the National Human Rights Commission?
o: Speaker of the House of People
Chairman of the Council of States
Leader of opposition in the House of People
Leader of opposition in the Council of States
126.x: Section 4 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 lays down that the Chairperson and the members of the Commission are appointed by the President of India, on the recommendations of a Committee consisting of: The Prime Minister, the Speaker of the House of the People, Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Home Affairs in the Government of India, leader of the Opposition in the House of the People, leader of the Opposition in the Council of States and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States. The chairman of the Council of States is not a member of the National Human Rights Commission.

126.s: Who is not a member of the committee constituted for recommendations of appointment of chairperson and other members of National Human Rights Commission?
o: Speaker of the House of the People
Leader of the Opposition in the House of the People
Chairman of the Council of States

126.s: The term of office of members of the National Human Rights Commission from the date on which he/she enters upon his/her office is
o: five years or till the age of 65 years
five years or till the age of 70 years
six years or till the age of 65 years
six years or till the age of 70 years
126.x: According to 'The Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019 the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is to be headed by a former Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court. The Chairman of NHRC holds the office for 3 years or till he attains the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier. Thus Both (A) and (R) are wrong.

126.s: A Sitting Judge of the High Court or a Sitting District Judge can be appointed as a member of the State Human Rights Commission after consultation with?
o: the Chief Justice of the High Court of the concerned
the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of India
126.x: The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 provides for the creation of the State Human Rights Commission at the State level. Currently, 25 states have constituted the State Human Rights Commissions through official Gazette notifications. The Chairperson and members are appointed by the Governor on the recommendations of a committee consisting of the Chief Minister as its head, the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, the State's Home Minister and the leader of opposition. In case of a state having a Legislative Council the Chairman of the council and the leader of the opposition in the council would also be members of the committee. A Sitting Judge of a High Court or a sitting District Judge can be appointed only after consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court of the concerned state.

126.s: Chairperson and Members of the State Human Rights Commission are appointed by.
o: Chief Justice of the High Court of the concerned State

126.s: Chairperson and members of State Human Rights Commission are appointed by –
126.x: The State Human Rights Commission’s Chairman is appointed by the Governor. The Governor makes these appointments on the recommendation of a Committee comprising the Chief Minister (Chairman), Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, State Home Minister and the opposition leader of the Legislative Assembly (Members). In the case of a state having a Legislative Council, the chairman of the Council and the leader of the opposition in the council would also be members of the committee.

126.s: In the event of occurrence of any vacancy in the Office of the Chairperson of the State Commission, who can authorize one of the members to act as Chairperson?
o: The Chief Justice of the High Court
The Chairperson of the National Human Rights
126.x: The Governor can appoint one of the members of the State Commission as an acting chairman in the following two cases- (a) When the office of the Chairman falls vacant; (b) When the chairman is unable to perform his functions due to absence or some other reason.

126.s: Which one of the following is not the function of the State Human Rights Commission?
o: Enquire suo-moto the violation of Human Rights
Review the protection of Human Rights
To punish for the violation of Human Rights
126.x: All the above options are the functions of the Human Rights Commission except to punish for the violation of Human Rights.

126.s:
Analyze the statements with reference to National Human Rights Commission :
(i) The Human Rights Commission, encourages organizations working in the field of Human Rights.
(ii) The work of the Commission is also to conduct research in the field of Human Rights. Answer from the following.
o: Statement (i) is the correct explanation of Statement
126.x: The functions of the National Human Rights Commission have been given in section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The functions of the Commission include undertaking and promoting research in the field of human rights. The Commission also encourages the efforts of nongovernmental organisations and institutions working in the field of human rights. Hence both the statements are correct but statement II does not explain the statement I.

126.s: While dealing with complaints of violation of Human Rights by the members of the armed forces, the Commission either on its own motion or on receipt of a petition will?
o: give directions to the concerned police officers to
seek a report from the Central Government
126.x: The commission has limited role, powers and jurisdiction with respect to violation of Human rights by the members of the armed forces. In this sphere, the commission may seek a report from the central Government and make its recommendations.

126.s: The State Commission submits its annual report to the?
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
126.x: The State Human Rights Commission submits its annual report to the State Government. The reports are laid before the State Legislature, along with a memorandum of action taken on the recommendations of the Commission and the reason for non-acceptance of any of such recommendations.

127.s: Which of the following case–principle pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Nilabati Behera – Compensation for custodial death
Joginder Kumar – Arrest must be justified; a relative may be informed
Arnesh Kumar – No automatic arrest for offences up to seven years
D.K. Basu – No automatic arrest for offences up to seven years
127.x: D.K. Basu laid down arrest safeguards like the arrest memo and medical examination; the seven-year rule is from Arnesh Kumar.
xa: ⚠ **1993 – 1994 – 1997 – 2014** = **Nilabati – Joginder – D.K. Basu – Arnesh**.
Arnesh Kumar's checklist: **CrPC s.41**, now **BNSS s.35**.
Nilabati compensation is under **Arts 32/226**.

127.s: Which of the following is NOT a mandatory safeguard associated with D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal?
o: Automatic arrest in every offence punishable up to seven years
127.x: D.K. Basu required safeguards such as an arrest memo, identification of officers, informing kin and medical examination. Automatic arrest for offences up to seven years is contrary to the safeguard approach associated with Arnesh Kumar.
127.tq: Find the one proposition that reverses the arrest-safeguard principle.
xs: **Automatic arrest in every offence up to seven years** is not a D.K. Basu safeguard — option **(3)**.
**D.K. Basu (1997)** mandated an **arrest memo**, **ID of officers**, **informing kin** and a **medical check**.
In fact **Arnesh Kumar (2014)** barred **automatic arrest** for offences up to **7 years**.
xa: **Joginder Kumar (1994)**: arrest must be justified, not routine.
**Nilabati Behera (1993)**: compensation for custodial death.
**PUCL v Maharashtra (2014)**: **16-point** encounter guidelines.

127.s: How many directives on police reform did the Supreme Court issue in Prakash Singh v Union of India (2006)?
127.x: Prakash Singh (2006) issued seven directives: State Security Commission, DGP from a UPSC panel with a 2-year tenure, 2-year tenure for field officers, separation of investigation from law and order, Police Establishment Board, National Security Commission and Police Complaints Authorities. Five, six and ten are wrong counts.
xs: **Prakash Singh v UOI (2006)** issued **seven** directives — option **(3)**.

They are: **State Security Commission**; **DGP from UPSC panel** (**2-year** tenure); **2-year** tenure for field officers; separate investigation; **Police Establishment Board**; **National Security Commission**; **PCAs**.
xa: ⚠ **PUCL (2014)** has **16** points; Prakash Singh has **7** directives.
**Arnesh Kumar (2014)**: no automatic arrest up to **7 years**.
PCAs exist at **State and district levels**.

127.s: The guidelines in PUCL v State of Maharashtra (2014) concerning encounter deaths consisted of how many points?
127.x: PUCL v State of Maharashtra (2014) laid down 16-point guidelines for encounter deaths.
127.tq: Recall the exact count attached to the leading encounter-death guidelines case.
xs: **PUCL v Maharashtra (2014)** laid down guidelines of **16 points** on **encounter deaths** — option **(2)**.
⚠ Do not confuse with the **7 directives** of **Prakash Singh (2006)** on police reform.
xa: Key points: record the **tip-off**, register an **FIR**, independent probe by **CID or another police station**, **magisterial inquiry**.
Also: inform **NHRC/SHRC**, medical aid, inform kin, **forensic check of weapons**.
**No out-of-turn promotion or gallantry award** until cleared.

127.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the directives in Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006)?
o: A State Security Commission was envisaged.
Field officers were to get a two-year tenure.
The DGP was to get a five-year tenure.
127.x: The DGP was to be selected from a UPSC panel and given a two-year tenure, not five years.
xa: Also: **separate investigation from law and order**, **National Security Commission**, **PCAs**.
Total: **7 directives**.
The colonial **Police Act 1861** still remains in force.

127.s: Under the Prakash Singh framework, the State Police Complaints Authority is headed by a:
127.x: The State PCA is headed by a retired judge and handles serious misconduct such as custodial death; PCAs exist at State and district levels.
xa: There is a call for **PCAs with statutory backing**.
Prakash Singh (**2006**) issued **7 directives**.
⚠ PCAs are a Prakash Singh directive, not a creation of the **Police Act 1861**.

127.s: Under the PUCL guidelines on encounter deaths, which of the following is barred until the officers involved are cleared?
127.x: The guidelines require recording the tip-off, an FIR and an independent probe, and prohibit out-of-turn promotion or gallantry awards until clearance.
xa: A **magisterial inquiry** is also required.
Inform **NHRC/SHRC**; **forensic check** of weapons.
PUCL (**2014**) has **16** points.

127.s: Which of the following correctly states the position of the NHRC regarding encounter deaths?
o: They are treated as serious violations requiring mandatory reporting, post-mortem videography and independent investigation.
They can be investigated only by the armed forces.
They require only an internal police report and no post-mortem.
They are treated as routine police actions requiring no special reporting.
127.x: The NHRC treats encounter deaths as serious violations and requires mandatory reporting, post-mortem videography and independent investigation.
127.tq: Match the rights-protection body with its prescribed procedural safeguards.
xs: The **NHRC** treats encounter deaths as **serious violations** needing **mandatory reporting, post-mortem videography and independent investigation** — option **(1)**.
They are not routine police actions and are not left to internal reports or the armed forces.
xa: **PUCL (2014)**: **16-point** guidelines, including a **magisterial inquiry**.
Way forward: **body-worn cameras** (Delhi Police) and better **forensic capacity**.
Only **3 convictions** for **2,253** custody deaths.

127.s: Which of the following pairs (case — holding) is correctly matched?
o: Bachan Singh (1980) — Categories of rarest cases
Machhi Singh (1983) — Death penalty held constitutional
Bachan Singh (1980) — 'Rarest of rare': life the rule, death the exception
127.x: Bachan Singh (1980) laid down 'rarest of rare'; Jagmohan Singh (1973) upheld the death penalty and Machhi Singh (1983) set categories of rarest cases.
xa: **Epuru Sudhakar (2006)**: pardon/remission open to limited **judicial review**.
**Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)**: inordinate delay → **commute to life**.
**Law Commission 262nd (2015)**: abolish except **terrorism and waging war**.

127.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014)?
o: Solitary confinement before rejection of a mercy petition is illegal.
Delay in deciding a mercy petition can never justify commutation.
At least 14 days should ordinarily separate rejection of mercy and execution.
Unexplained delay may justify commuting death to life imprisonment.
127.x: The Court held that inordinate, unexplained delay may justify commutation of a death sentence.
xa: **Art. 72** (President) and **Art. 161** (Governor) are the mercy powers.
**Epuru Sudhakar (2006)**: limited **judicial review** of pardon.
**Bachan Singh (1980)**: **life is the rule**, death the exception.

127.s: The decision in Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh (2006) is associated with which proposition?
o: Mercy powers are completely immune from judicial scrutiny.
Pardon and remission are open to limited judicial review.
Only the Supreme Court may decide mercy petitions.
A Governor may pardon every death sentence.
127.x: Epuru Sudhakar (2006) established that the exercise of pardon or remission powers is subject to limited judicial review.
127.tq: Identify the precise extent of judicial review without confusing limited review with complete judicial control.
xs: **Epuru Sudhakar v Govt of AP (2006)**: **pardon and remission** are open to **limited judicial review** — option **(2)**.
So mercy powers are not immune; the **Governor** still cannot pardon a death sentence (**Art. 161**).
xa: **Art. 72**: the **President** can pardon a death sentence.
**Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)**: unexplained delay → **commute to life**.
**Machhi Singh (1983)**: categories of rarest cases.

127.s: A death sentence passed by a Sessions Court must be confirmed by the:
127.x: A death sentence passed by a Sessions Court requires confirmation by the High Court.
xa: Appeal to SC under **Arts 132, 134, 136**.
**Art. 72**: the **President** can pardon a death sentence.
**Art. 161**: the **Governor** cannot pardon a death sentence but can commute/remit/suspend.

127.s: An appeal against a death sentence may reach the Supreme Court under which combination of constitutional provisions?
127.x: Appeals in such matters may lie to the Supreme Court under Articles 132, 134 and 136.
127.tq: Recall the exact constitutional Article cluster instead of nearby judicial provisions.
xs: Appeals reach the Supreme Court under **Articles 132, 134 and 136** — option **(1)**.
First the Sessions Court sentence needs **High Court confirmation**.
xa: **Nilabati Behera** compensation is under **Arts 32/226** — writ jurisdiction, not appeals.
**Art. 72** (President) can pardon death sentences and **court-martial** cases.
Capital offences now in the **BNS** (murder **s.103**).

127.s:
Assertion (A): The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence under Article 161.

2. Statement-II: In India, prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 which expressly kept the subject of prisons in the control of Provincial Governments. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is the correct
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
127.x: Answer is (a): 'Prisons' is a State subject under the State List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. The management and administration of Prisons fall exclusively within the domain of the State Governments and are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894, and the Prison Manuals of the respective State Governments. Thus, States have the primary role, responsibility, and authority to change current prison laws, rules, and regulations. Therefore, the Prisons Act of 1894 placed responsibility for prisons under the jurisdiction of Provincial governments (State governments), which explains why State governments have the authority to establish their own rules and regulations for prison management.

127.x: As per the provisions of the Constitution of India, ‘prisons’/ ‘persons detained therein’ is a ‘State’ subject under entry 4 of the State List. In India, prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 which vested the Provincial Governments (now States) with the power to make rules on prisons so the responsibility of prisons management and prisoners’administration solely vests with State Governments who alone are competent to make appropriate legislative provisions in this regard. However, given the critical role that efficient prison management plays in the criminal justice system, recently, the Ministry of Home Affairs has finalised a comprehensive ‘Model Prisons Act, 2023’, which may serve as a guiding document for the States, and for adoption in their jurisdiction. Hence statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 2 is the correct explanation of statement 1.
